Start here

This guide explains all the content in your GRA 4164 course folder in plain language. Each topic starts with a picture in words, then gives the exact definition the examiner wants, then a tiny worked example with every number shown. It was built from a complete reading of every lecture deck, notebook and data file in ~/Downloads/Text_as_Data (see _exam_prep_work/coverage_log.md), and checked against the 2025 exam and its official evaluation guidelines.

You don’t need to have read the lectures. Every chapter is a complete lesson on its own. Nothing appears before it is explained: no word, no symbol, no number. If you ever find something that isn’t explained, that’s a fault in this guide, not in you.

How each chapter is laid out:

  1. Why this exists: the real-life problem the method solves.
  2. The idea in everyday words: how it works, step by step, with an analogy. Technical names are introduced only after the idea they name.
  3. Walk-through example: a tiny example, slowly. Every table says what its rows, columns and cells are, and every number says where it comes from. When the computer calculates something you’d never do by hand, the guide says so and shows you how to read the result.
  4. The formula, explained (where there is one): each symbol in plain words, then the whole formula read aloud.
  5. What the exam asks, and how to answer: exam questions with model answers, plus what each answer is saying in plain words.
  6. Exam tips: what a top-grade answer must include, common mistakes, and key terms with their plain meanings.
  7. Quick self-test: each question with what it’s asking in plain words, the answer, and why.
  8. Words used in this chapter: a lookup list of every term.

Labels you will see:

  • Exam priority: ★★★ appeared on the 2025 paper or is central, ★★ likely as true/false or a short question, ★ background.

The course in one story

Computers can’t read. They can only work with numbers. So the whole course is about one question: how do you turn text into numbers, so that a computer can find patterns in lots of text, far more than a human could read?

The course tells this story in three steps. Each step is smarter than the one before.

  1. Step 1 — Count words (Bag-of-words). Throw all the words of a document into a bag and count them. Word order is lost: “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” look the same. It’s crude, but it works surprisingly well. Methods built on counting:
    • word lists (“dictionaries”): you choose the words to look for, for example “uncertain”, “risk”, “crisis”;
    • sorting documents into groups (e.g. spam or not spam);
    • finding hidden themes in a pile of documents (topic models).
  2. Step 2 — Give each word a meaning-location (Word embeddings). Instead of only counting, give each word a set of coordinates, like a spot on a map, so that words with similar meanings sit close together: “king” sits near “queen”, and “apple” near “banana”. The computer learns these spots by noticing which words appear near each other in lots of text.
  3. Step 3 — Read words in context (Large Language Models, like ChatGPT). In step 2, a word has one fixed spot. But “bank” means different things in “river bank” and “bank loan”. LLMs read the whole sentence and adjust each word’s meaning to its neighbours. They learn this by reading huge amounts of text and practising guessing the next word, billions of times.

The exam asks about all three steps, then gives you a business problem and asks which tools you would use.

Mini-dictionary: words that come up again and again

You don’t need maths for any of these. Each one is just an idea.

  • Document: one piece of text you analyse. One email, one speech, one survey answer, one news article.
  • Corpus: your whole collection of documents. For example, 1,000 survey answers.
  • Variable: anything you measure that can change from case to case. Examples: price, age, or “is this email spam?”.
    • Continuous variable: a number on a smooth scale that can take any value. Height, price, temperature.
    • Categorical variable: a label from a fixed set. Spam / not spam; party A / party B; happy / angry / neutral.
  • Model: a recipe the computer follows to turn inputs into an answer. “Look at the words → guess if it’s spam.”
  • Estimate / train a model: let the computer tune the recipe’s settings by looking at examples, until it gets the examples mostly right. Like adjusting the oven temperature until the cake comes out right.
  • Parameters / weights: those settings, the numbers inside the recipe that get tuned. A big LLM has billions of them.
  • Regression: predicting a number from other information by finding the best-fitting line. Example: predicting a house’s price from its size. In a “text regression”, the information is word counts.
  • Classification / classifier: predicting a category instead of a number. Spam or not spam? Positive or negative review? Naive Bayes is one classifier taught in the course, a spam-filter-style method (explained in question 1(g)).
  • Supervised learning: you give the computer examples with the right answers attached, for example 500 emails a human has already marked “spam” or “not spam”, and it learns from those. Like a student learning from a workbook with an answer key.
  • Unsupervised learning: you give the computer data with no answers, and it finds structure on its own, for example sorting comments into themes nobody named in advance. Like sorting a pile of photos into groups without being told what the groups are.
  • Self-supervised learning: the answers come free from the data itself. Hide the next word of a real sentence and ask the computer to guess it; the real text is the answer key. This is how LLMs learn.
  • Matrix: a table of numbers, like a spreadsheet, with rows and columns. Nothing more.
  • Vector: a list of numbers, like one row of that spreadsheet, e.g. (3, 0, 1). You can draw a short list as an arrow on a graph: (3, 1) means “3 steps right, 1 step up”.
  • Dimension: one position in that list, or one column of the spreadsheet. “300 dimensions” means a list of 300 numbers.
  • Token: the pieces an LLM actually reads. Often a whole word, sometimes a piece of a word (“un” + “believ” + “able”).
  • Layer: one processing step inside a model. Models pass the text through many layers in a row, like a factory line where each station adds something.

In plain words. If a word on this guide ever stops you, look for it here or in the “What the words mean” box in that chapter. If it isn’t in either place, that’s a gap in this guide, not in you.

Part I — Turning text into numbers

1. What “text as data” is, the workflow, and the four challenges (Lecture 1)

Exam priority: ★ Low — background, but it feeds the ethics/ESG question and the business-case reflection

Why this exists

Picture a phone company that gets 10,000 online reviews every month. The boss asks two questions. Are customers happier this month than last month? What do they complain about most?

Nobody has time to read 10,000 reviews. A computer could get through them in seconds. But a computer cannot read. It can only work with numbers: add them, compare them, sort them.

So someone has to turn the reviews into numbers first. After that, the computer can count, compare and spot patterns. That whole job, from raw text to an answer, is what this course calls text as data.

The course gives four real examples of why people do this:

  • Predicting stock prices from news articles.
  • Measuring the mood of customer reviews: are they positive or negative? Measuring the mood of a text has a name: sentiment analysis.
  • Reading political speeches to understand what a politician stands for.
  • Detecting fake news from the way it is written.

The idea in everyday words

The big picture. Think of a huge pile of letters written in a language the computer cannot read. You sort the letters, clean them up, and turn each one into a row in a spreadsheet. After that, the computer can do maths on the spreadsheet, even though it never “understands” the letters. That is the whole idea.

The course defines it like this:

  • “Text data refers to information captured in written form (e.g., documents, emails, social media, etc.)”
  • “Using computational techniques to analyze and extract meaningful patterns from text”
  • “Popular in various domains like finance, political science, marketing, and more”

In plain words: text data is anything written down. “Computational techniques” means methods a computer runs. The goal is to find useful patterns in the text.

Two words you need first. One piece of text you study, such as one review, one email or one speech, is called a document. The whole collection of documents is called the corpus. All 10,000 reviews together are the corpus. Each single review is a document.

The five steps. Every text-as-data project follows the same five steps, in the same order, like a recipe. A fixed order of steps like this is called a workflow.

Step 1: get the text. First you need the text on your computer. This step is called text collection. The course names three ways to do it:

  • A small program visits web pages and copies the text off them, like a very fast copy-paste. This is called scraping.
  • Some websites offer a “service door” where a program can ask for data and get it back in a neat form. That door is called an API.
  • The text may already sit in an organised digital filing cabinet. That is a database.

The course says a good way to store collected text is JSON: a simple text format that keeps data in labelled boxes, such as “review: …, date: …”.

Step 2: tidy the text. Raw text is messy. “Great” and “great” should be the same word, and “!!!” or “:(” usually carry no use for counting. Tidying the text before you count is called preprocessing (or cleaning). Two tidying jobs have their own names:

  • Cutting the text into small pieces, usually single words, is called tokenization. Each piece is a token. “Bad phone” has 2 tokens.
  • Turning each word into its dictionary form, so “studies” becomes “study” and “ran” becomes “run”, is called lemmatization.

Step 3: turn the words into numbers. Now each document has to become a row of numbers. One number that describes a document, such as “how many times the word ‘battery’ appears”, is called a feature. So this step is called feature extraction: pulling numbers out of the text. The course names three tools for it:

  • Count how often each word appears and ignore the order of the words. This is called bag-of-words. The table of those counts, with one row per document and one column per word, is called the document-term matrix.
  • Adjust the counts so that rare, telling words count more and everyday words count less. This is called TF-IDF.
  • Give every word a list of numbers, chosen so that words with similar meanings get similar numbers. These are called word embeddings.

Step 4: let a method find the pattern. Now a method takes the numbers and produces an answer. Such a method is called a model, and this step is called modeling. A model often learns from examples that a human has already marked, such as 1,000 reviews already labelled “happy” or “unhappy”. Those examples are the training data. A model is built from an algorithm: a fixed list of instructions the computer follows. The course names four kinds of modeling:

  • Putting each document into one box from a fixed list, such as “spam” or “not spam”, or “positive” or “negative”. This is text classification, and the method that does it is a classifier.
  • Letting the computer put similar documents into groups, without telling it the groups in advance. This is clustering.
  • Finding the main themes that run through many documents. This is topic modeling.
  • Using a very large program trained on huge amounts of text, which can read and write language, such as ChatGPT. This is an LLM (large language model).

Step 5: check the answer. Finally, you ask: does the result make sense, and is it correct? You read a few documents yourself and compare. If the computer got them wrong, you find out which step went wrong. This step is called interpretation and evaluation.

Here are the five steps exactly as the course lists them, with the example tools in brackets. Every tool was explained above.

  1. Text Collection (Scraping, APIs, Databases)
  2. Preprocessing (Cleaning, Tokenization, Lemmatization)
  3. Feature Extraction (Bag-of-Words, TF-IDF, Word Embeddings)
  4. Modeling (Text Classification, Clustering, Topic Modeling, LLMs)
  5. Interpretation and Evaluation

In short: get the text, tidy it, turn it into numbers, run a method on the numbers, then check the answer.

The four challenges. The course names four things that make text hard for computers.

Challenge 1: there is too much text. Think of billions of tweets, or whole internet archives. The sheer amount is called the volume. You need smart ways to store it. And one normal computer is too slow to process it, so the job is split over many computers working at the same time, like many cashiers instead of one. Splitting a job this way is called parallel and distributed computing. Data this large is called big data.

Challenge 2: the text is messy. Real text, such as social media posts and comments, is full of typos, slang and abbreviations like “gr8”. It follows no clear rules for punctuation or grammar. Text like this is called noisy, unstructured text. It needs cleaning, tokenization and normalization: making different spellings count as the same thing, such as turning an emoji into a word or fixing “gud” to “good”.

Challenge 3: words can mean more than one thing. “Bank” can be a place for money or the side of a river. When a word or sentence can mean several things, that is called ambiguity. Each separate meaning of a word is a word sense. You can only tell which sense is meant from the words and situation around it. Those surroundings are called the context. Mood, tone and what the writer intends also depend on context. The course warns that sentiment analysis “may misinterpret sarcasm or humor”. Sarcasm is saying the opposite of what you mean, like “Great, it broke again.”

Challenge 4: right and wrong. Questions of right and wrong are called ethics. The course names three problems:

  • Bias (an unfair tilt): “Algorithms may pick up biases present in the training data”. If a model learns from unfair old decisions, it repeats the unfairness. The course example: “Predictive models for hiring based on biased language data in resumes”.
  • Privacy: text often holds personal details, and they may be used without consent (the person saying “yes, you may use it”).
  • Transparency: a model is transparent if you can see why it decided something. A model that gives answers without showing its reasons is a black box. The course talks about “black-box models”.

The table below sums up the four challenges. Each row is one challenge. The middle column says what it means. The right column gives the course’s own example.

Challenge What it means Course example
1. Handling large datasets (Big Data) Volume (huge amounts of text), storage (needs efficient data management), processing (needs parallel and distributed computing) “analysing billions of tweets or entire internet archives”
2. Noisy, unstructured text Typos, slang, abbreviations; no clear rules for punctuation or grammar; needs cleaning, tokenization, normalization (emojis, misspellings) informal social media posts or comments
3. Language ambiguity and context A word can mean different things in different contexts; sentiment, tone and intent need context “bank” = financial institution or riverbank; sentiment analysis “may misinterpret sarcasm or humor”
4. Ethical concerns Bias in data (“Algorithms may pick up biases present in the training data”); privacy (personal data without consent); transparency (“black-box models”) “Predictive models for hiring based on biased language data in resumes”

Walk-through example

Let’s follow two short reviews through all five steps.

  • Review 1: “Great phone!!! but the battery is NOT good :(”
  • Review 2: “Bad phone.”

Both sentences are our own illustration, not from the course.

Step 1, collection. We scrape both reviews from the shop’s website, or ask for them through its API. We store them, for example as JSON.

Step 2, preprocessing. We make every letter small, remove “!!!”, “:(” and the full stop, and cut each review into words.

  • Review 1 becomes 8 tokens: great, phone, but, the, battery, is, not, good.
  • Review 2 becomes 2 tokens: bad, phone.

Step 3, feature extraction. We make a small table of counts. Here is how to read it before you look:

  • Each row is one review.
  • Each column is one word we care about: “great”, “good” and “bad”.
  • Each cell says how many times that word appears in that review.
Review ↓ / Word → great good bad
Review 1 1 1 0
Review 2 0 0 1

Let’s work out one cell out loud. Take row “Review 1”, column “great”. The word “great” appears once in review 1, so the cell is 1. Now take row “Review 1”, column “bad”. “Bad” does not appear in review 1, so the cell is 0.

This little table is a tiny document-term matrix. A real project might then adjust the counts with TF-IDF.

Step 4, modeling. We need a method that turns the counts into a label. Here is a very rough rule, made up for this example: count the happy words (“great” and “good”), then subtract the unhappy words (“bad”). A score above 0 means “happy”. A score below 0 means “unhappy”.

  • Review 1: 1 + 1 − 0 = 2, so “happy”.
  • Review 2: 0 + 0 − 1 = −1, so “unhappy”.

A real project would use a classifier that learned from training data. The idea is the same: numbers in, label out.

Step 5, interpretation and evaluation. We read the reviews ourselves. Review 2 is labelled correctly. Review 1 is wrong. A human sees the customer is unhappy with the battery. The word “not” flipped the meaning of “good”, and our counting missed it. That is challenge 3 (context) biting. And it is exactly why the checking step exists.

What this approach is good at, and where it breaks.

  • Good at: reading huge amounts of text fast, and in the same way every time.
  • Good at: spotting trends over time, such as “complaints about the battery doubled this month”.
  • Breaks when: the meaning hides in context, like “not good”, sarcasm, or a word with two meanings.
  • Breaks when: the text it learns from is unfair or private. Then the results can be unfair or break privacy rules.

Reading the course code

This chapter has no code. The course names its tools: Python, a programming language, and Jupyter, a notebook where you mix code and notes. It also names three libraries, which are ready-made toolboxes of code: NLTK and spaCy (for text) and Pandas (for tables). The exam has not asked students to write code.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

This topic will probably not get its own 5-point question. It comes in through three side doors.

Door 1: the ethics question about LLMs. In 2025 this was Q4(a), on ethics and ESG. ESG stands for Environmental, Social and Governance: a way of judging a company’s effect on the planet, on people, and on how it is run. The official marking guide wanted two answers:

  • These models use a lot of energy, so they have a big carbon footprint (the amount of greenhouse gas an activity releases).
  • They learn from huge piles of text “often used without permission/copy right issues”. Copyright is an author’s legal right to control copies of their work.

The guide also says “Other answers might also be ok, but need to be well grounded”. So bias, privacy and transparency from this chapter can earn extra marks, as long as you explain them well.

Door 2: the business-case reflection question (2025 Block 5). Here you think through a real company problem. Walk through the workflow steps in order: collect the text → clean it → turn it into numbers (features) → fit a model → check the results (collect → clean → features → model → evaluate).

Door 3: True/False items. For example: “TF-IDF is a modeling step”. That is FALSE. The course puts TF-IDF under feature extraction, the “turn text into numbers” step.

A likely short question: “Explain in 2–5 sentences: Why is ethics a challenge in automated text processing?” (“Automated text processing” means letting a computer read and judge text for us.)

Model answer Models learn from training text, so they can pick up the biases in it. For example, a hiring model trained on biased language in resumes can treat candidates unfairly (Lecture 1, slide 17). Text often contains personal data, which raises privacy issues if it is collected without consent. Many models are black boxes, so it is hard to explain why they made a decision.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: A computer learns from old text and copies its unfairness, the way a child picks up a parent’s prejudices. If past hiring favoured one group, the model will too. Text often holds personal details, so collecting it without asking is a privacy problem. And many models cannot tell you why they decided something.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • The five workflow steps in the right order, with one example tool for each step (for instance scraping, tokenization, TF-IDF, a classifier, checking by hand).
  • For each challenge (something that makes text hard for computers): name it, say why it happens, and give the course’s example. The examples are “bank” (river bank or money bank?), sarcasm (saying the opposite of what you mean), and biased resumes (a hiring model copying unfair patterns).
  • In the reflection question, say at which step of the workflow each pitfall (hidden trap) bites. For example, ambiguity (a word or sentence with more than one meaning) hurts at the modeling step. Bias hurts at the interpretation step, when you read the results.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Putting TF-IDF or bag-of-words (two ways of turning text into word counts) under “modeling”. They belong to feature extraction, the “turn text into numbers” step.
  • Putting lemmatization (turning a word into its dictionary form, e.g. “ran” → “run”) under feature extraction. It belongs to preprocessing, the cleaning step.
  • Writing “ethics” without saying which kind (bias, privacy or transparency) and why it happens.

Key terms to use

  • text as data: treating written words as numbers to analyse
  • corpus: the whole collection of texts you study
  • workflow: the fixed order of project steps
  • collection: gathering the texts onto your computer
  • preprocessing: cleaning the text before counting
  • feature extraction: turning cleaned text into numbers
  • modeling: running a method on those numbers
  • interpretation and evaluation: reading results and checking they hold
  • noisy/unstructured text: messy text with typos, slang, no format
  • ambiguity: one word, several possible meanings
  • context: surrounding words that fix the meaning
  • word sense, e.g. “bank”: which meaning of a word is meant
  • bias: unfair patterns copied from training text
  • privacy: personal details in texts need protecting
  • transparency: being able to explain a model’s decisions
  • black box: a model whose reasoning you cannot see

Quick self-test

  1. True or false: “Lemmatization is part of the preprocessing step.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Lemmatization turns each word into its dictionary form (“ran” → “run”, “mice” → “mouse”). Preprocessing is the cleaning stage, before any counting happens. Does the first belong inside the second?

    True. Why: Lemmatization tidies words up before you count them, like sorting laundry before you wash it. The course lists it under Preprocessing, next to cleaning and tokenization (splitting text into single words).

  2. True or false: “TF-IDF is a modeling technique in the text-as-data workflow.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: TF-IDF is a way to score words: a word that shows up a lot in one text but rarely in others gets a high score. A “modeling technique” is a method from the later stage, where you use the numbers to predict or find patterns. Does TF-IDF belong to that later stage?

    False. Why: TF-IDF only turns text into numbers. It is like weighing the ingredients, not cooking them. The workflow calls that step feature extraction, and modeling comes after it.

  3. True or false: “Sarcasm is an example of the ‘noisy text’ challenge.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Sarcasm is saying the opposite of what you mean (“Great, my train is late again”). “Noisy text” is the course’s label for messy writing. Is sarcasm filed under that label?

    False. Why: Noisy text means messy spelling and wording: typos, slang and abbreviations like “gr8”. A sarcastic sentence can be spelled perfectly. Its problem is the meaning, so the course files it under language ambiguity and context (words whose meaning depends on the situation).

  4. Explain in 2–5 sentences: “Why is ethics a challenge in automated text processing?”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: If we let a computer read and judge text for us, why can that be unfair or harmful?

    Answer: use the model answer in “What the exam asks, and how to answer” above. Why: It names three separate problems, each with its cause: bias (the model copies unfairness from its training text, as in the hiring example), privacy (personal data used without consent) and transparency (black-box models cannot explain their decisions).

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • text as data: treating written text as something you can count and measure. Example: counting how many reviews mention “battery”.
  • data: any collected facts or records. Example: a list of all reviews with their dates.
  • document: one piece of text you study. Example: one review, one email or one speech.
  • corpus: the whole collection of documents. Example: all 10,000 reviews together.
  • workflow: the fixed order of steps you follow, like a recipe. Example: collect → clean → numbers → model → check.
  • sentiment / sentiment analysis: sentiment is the positive or negative mood of a text; sentiment analysis measures it. Example: “I love it” is positive.
  • text collection: getting the text onto your computer. Example: downloading all reviews from a website.
  • scraping: a program that visits web pages and copies the text off them. Example: copying every review page of a shop.
  • API: a “service door” a website offers so programs can ask it for data directly. Example: a news site that hands your program articles in a neat file.
  • database: an organised digital filing cabinet for data. Example: a company’s store of all customer emails.
  • JSON: a simple text format that stores data in labelled boxes. Example: “review: Bad phone, date: 3 May”.
  • preprocessing / cleaning: tidying the text before counting. Example: making “Great” and “great” the same.
  • tokenization: cutting text into small pieces, usually single words. Example: “bad phone” → “bad”, “phone”.
  • token: one of those pieces. Example: “Bad phone” has 2 tokens.
  • lemmatization: turning each word into its dictionary form. Example: “studies” becomes “study”.
  • normalization: making different spellings count as the same thing. Example: fixing “gud” to “good”.
  • feature: one number that describes a document. Example: “how many times ‘battery’ appears”.
  • feature extraction: turning cleaned text into numbers the computer can use. Example: counting every word in each review.
  • bag-of-words: counting words and ignoring their order. Example: “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” give the same counts.
  • document-term matrix: the table of word counts, one row per document, one column per word. Example: the small review table above.
  • TF-IDF: re-weighting word counts so that rare, telling words count more. Example: “battery” scores higher than “the”.
  • word embeddings: a list of numbers for each word, so similar words get similar numbers. Example: “good” and “great” end up close together.
  • model / modeling: a method that takes the numbers and produces an answer. Example: a rule that says “happy” or “unhappy”.
  • training data: the examples a model learns from. Example: 1,000 reviews a human has already marked happy or unhappy.
  • algorithm: a fixed list of instructions a computer follows. Example: “add the happy words, subtract the unhappy ones”.
  • text classification / classifier: putting each document into one box from a fixed list; the classifier is the method that does it. Example: “spam” or “not spam”.
  • clustering: letting the computer group similar documents without being told the groups. Example: reviews falling into a “delivery” group and a “battery” group.
  • topic modeling: finding the main themes running through many documents. Example: discovering that news is about “sport”, “politics” and “weather”.
  • LLM (large language model): a very large program trained on huge amounts of text that can read and write language. Example: ChatGPT.
  • interpretation and evaluation: asking “does this result make sense, and is it correct?” Example: reading 20 reviews to check the labels.
  • big data: so much data that one normal computer struggles to store or process it. Example: billions of tweets.
  • parallel / distributed computing: splitting a big job over many computers at the same time. Example: many cashiers instead of one.
  • noisy / unstructured text: text with no fixed form and lots of mess. Example: “gr8 fone lol”.
  • ambiguity: when a word or sentence can mean more than one thing. Example: “bank”.
  • context: the words and situation around a word that tell you what it means. Example: “bank” next to “river” or next to “loan”.
  • word sense: one of the meanings a word can have. Example: “bank” has a money sense and a river sense.
  • sarcasm: saying the opposite of what you mean. Example: “Great, it broke again.”
  • ethics: questions of right and wrong. Example: is it fair to judge job seekers by a computer that learned from unfair old decisions?
  • pitfall: a hidden trap that makes your result wrong if you don’t watch for it. Example: “not” being missed by word counting.
  • bias: an unfair tilt that a model copies from its examples. Example: a hiring model that prefers one group because past hiring did.
  • privacy / consent: privacy is keeping personal information safe; consent is the person saying “yes, you may use it”. Example: using customer emails without asking breaks both.
  • transparency / black box: a transparent model shows why it decided something; a black box gives answers without reasons. Example: a model that rejects a loan and cannot say why is a black box.
  • ESG: Environmental, Social and Governance, a way of judging a company’s effect on the planet, people and how it is run. Example: an investor checking a firm’s pollution and working conditions.
  • carbon footprint: how much greenhouse gas an activity releases. Example: training a big LLM uses a lot of electricity.
  • copyright: the legal right of an author to control copies of their work. Example: a newspaper’s articles used for training without permission.
  • Python / Jupyter / library: Python is a programming language; Jupyter is a notebook mixing code and notes; a library is a ready-made toolbox of code. Example: NLTK, spaCy and Pandas are libraries.
  • True/False item: an exam question where you say whether a statement is true or false. Example: “TF-IDF is a modeling step” (False).

Sources: Intro_to_text_as_data.pdf (Lecture 1), slides 7 and 10–17; Lecture 2a, slide 4 (JSON as a storage format); Lecture 2b, “Why Python?” slide; 2025 exam Q4(a) and Block 5 with the official marking guide

2. Preprocessing: cleaning, tokenization, stop words, stemming vs lemmatization, n-grams, and search as a measurement choice

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — likely as True/False items (“not” as a stop word, stemming vs lemmatisation, n-grams) and as pitfalls in the reflection question

Why this exists

Every year, the president of the United States gives a speech to Congress about how the country is doing. It is called the State of the Union speech. The course uses a collection of these speeches as its example texts.

Picture a history researcher with all of them. She wants to know: did presidents talk about war more in some decades than in others? She asks the computer to count the word “war”. Several things go wrong at once:

  • The computer sees “War”, “war” and “WAR” as three different things.
  • It finds the letters “war” hidden inside “toward” and “warm”, and counts those too.
  • It counts little words like “the” and “of” thousands of times, which tells her nothing.
  • Some speeches are much longer than others, so they mention everything more often.

Before any counting makes sense, the text has to be tidied, and the search has to be done with care. This chapter is about that tidying, and about the traps hidden inside it.

The idea in everyday words

The big picture. Tidying is like peeling vegetables before cooking. Peeling a potato is sensible. But if you “clean” a strawberry the same way, you lose the fruit. Every cleaning step throws something away. Sometimes what you throw away is exactly what mattered. The course’s rule is: “clean with purpose, not on autopilot”.

Tidying raw text before you count anything is called preprocessing.

Why text needs tidying. To a computer, a piece of text is a row of characters. Programmers call such a piece of text a string. “The”, “the” and “THE” are three different strings, even though to you they are one word. Preprocessing makes the same word look the same every time.

The steps, one by one. The course does the steps in a fixed order. A fixed chain of steps, where the output of one step goes into the next like a factory line, is called a pipeline.

Step 1: make every letter small. “Hello” becomes “hello”. Now “War” and “war” are the same. This is called lowercasing. Whether a letter is capital (upper case) or small (lower case) is called its case.

Step 2: remove punctuation. Punctuation means marks such as . , ! ? : ; and quotes. Removing them stops “good.” and “good” from counting as different words.

Step 3: cut the text into words. The computer cuts the text at each space. This is called tokenization, and each piece is a token. In this chapter a token is one word. (In a later lecture, on large language models, a token can be part of a word: “one word need not equal one token”. For example, “unbelievable” is cut into “un”, “believ” and “able”. The exam sometimes asks about this difference between tokens and words.)

Once the text is cut into tokens, you can ask two different questions. How many tokens are there? And how many different words are there? The list of different words is called the vocabulary. “the cat saw the dog” has 5 tokens, but “the” appears twice, so the vocabulary has 4 words.

Step 4: drop the very common little words. Words like “the”, “of”, “and” and “is” appear in every text. They rarely help you tell texts apart. These are called stop words. The computer uses a ready-made list of them, a stop-word list, and deletes every token on the list. The course uses the list from NLTK, a free toolbox for working with text in Python (a programming language). Here is the trap: NLTK’s English stop-word list also contains the word “not”.

Step 5: drop numbers. Tokens made only of digits, such as “101”, are deleted, if you don’t need them.

Step 6 (optional): shrink words to a base form. “Studies” and “study” should probably count as one word. There are two ways to do this:

  • Chop the ending off by fixed rules. This is called stemming. Example: “studies” → “studi”. The result may not be a real word. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • Look the word up and return its dictionary form. This is called lemmatization. Examples: “studies” → “study”, “was” → “be” (as verbs). [Not in course files — general knowledge]

The course notebook uses two NLTK tools for this. PorterStemmer is a well-known stemming tool. WordNetLemmatizer(pos="v") is the lemmatization tool. “pos” stands for part of speech (noun, verb and so on), and pos="v" tells the tool to treat each word as a verb.

The notebook asks two questions: which method gives the smaller vocabulary, and which gives tokens you can still read? Usually stemming gives a smaller but less readable vocabulary. [Not in course files — general knowledge]

Here is the whole standard pipeline, as the course writes it: “lowercase → remove punctuation → tokenize → drop stop words → drop numbers → (stem or lemmatize)”.

How the slides define each step. The slides show each step with a small Python tool. Three of them appear in the table below, so here is what they do first:

  • string.punctuation is a ready-made list of punctuation marks.
  • text.split() cuts text at the spaces.
  • word.isnumeric() asks “is this token made only of digits?”

The examples also use curly brackets, like {"hello", "world"}. In Python, curly brackets hold a set: a collection of items in no particular order.

In the table, each row is one cleaning step. The middle column is the slide’s definition. The right column is the slide’s example, showing the text before (left of the arrow) and after (right of the arrow).

Step Slide definition Slide example
Lowercasing “Convert all text to lowercase to ensure uniformity.” "Hello World!" → "hello world!"
Removing punctuation “Strip out punctuation marks using string.punctuation.” "hello world!" → "hello world"
Tokenization “Split text into individual words (tokens) using text.split().” "hello world" → {"hello", "world"}
Removing stop words “Eliminate common words (e.g.,”the”, “and”).” {"this", "is", "a", "test"} → {"test"}
Removing numbers “Discard tokens that are purely numeric using word.isnumeric().” {"room", "101"} → {"room"}

Keeping neighbouring words together. Counting single words loses the order of the words. “Dog bites man” and “man bites dog” use the same words in a different word order, but single-word counts look identical. A method that only counts single words and ignores their order is called bag of words (more on it in the chapter on the document-term matrix).

One fix: count short runs of neighbouring words as one item. A run of n neighbouring words is called an n-gram:

  • A 1-gram is a single word.
  • A 2-gram, also called a bigram, is a pair of neighbouring words. The slide’s example: “all the, the words, words in, …”.
  • A 3-gram is three words in a row: “all the words, the words in, …”.

The slide’s point: n-grams “Can handle”low unemployment” versus “high unemployment”“. Single words would split”low” from “unemployment”. The pair keeps them together. So n-grams keep a little bit of word order.

Searching is also a choice. Counting how often a word appears looks neutral. It is not. Three choices change the number you get:

  • Part of a word, or whole word? A search for the letters “war” anywhere is called a substring search. A substring is a piece of text inside a longer text, so it also finds “toward”. A search that only counts “war” when it stands alone as a word is a whole-word match. The edge where a word starts or ends is called a word boundary.
  • Case. Does “War” count as “war”? “Ignore case” means yes.
  • Length. A long speech mentions most words more often than a short one. Dividing each count by the length of the text, for example “mentions per 1,000 words”, makes long and short texts fair to compare. This is called normalising by document length.

Researchers often track one number over time to sum something up, such as “war mentions per 1,000 words, year by year”. That number is an index. The direction it moves over time, up or down, is its trend.

A decision about how you measure that changes the answer you get is called a measurement choice. The course puts it like this: “A text search is a measurement choice: substring vs whole word, case, and normalising by document length can change both the level and the trend of an index.” In plain words: the way you search changes how big the numbers are, and even whether they seem to go up or down over time.

The main lesson. The exact question your study tries to answer is your research question. The course’s rule: “Preprocessing should follow the research question.” Every time you switch on a cleaning step, ask: did I delete something my question needs?

Walk-through example

Example 1: the Ford “not good” trap. In 1975, President Ford said in his State of the Union speech: “I must say to you that the state of the Union is not good.” Let’s clean the part “the state of the Union is not good.” by hand.

  1. Lowercase: “the state of the union is not good.”
  2. Remove punctuation (the full stop): “the state of the union is not good”
  3. Cut into tokens: the, state, of, the, union, is, not, good. That is 8 tokens. “the” appears twice, so there are 7 different words. The vocabulary size here is 7.
  4. Remove stop words. NLTK’s English list contains “the”, “of”, “is” and also “not”. Drop all of them, and 3 tokens are left: state, union, good.

The sentence said “not good”. After cleaning it says “good”. A bad message turned into a good one, only because “not” sat on a stop-word list.

Now try pairs instead (2-grams), on the 8 tokens from step 3. With 8 tokens in a row there are 7 neighbouring pairs, because each token except the last pairs with the one after it: “the state”, “state of”, “of the”, “the union”, “union is”, “is not”, “not good”. The pair “not good” survives as one item, so the meaning is kept.

Example 2: a cleaner that deletes the important parts. A second course notebook, from Practical Day 1, tests its own cleaner on three sentences. (A notebook is a file that mixes code and notes. It is split into blocks called cells. The result stored after the code was run is the saved output.) This cleaner does three things:

  • It lowercases everything.
  • It keeps only alphabetic words (made only of letters, no digits or symbols) that are at least 3 letters long.
  • It removes stop words.

In the table, each row is one test sentence. The left column is the original sentence. The right column is what the cleaner left behind, taken from the notebook’s saved output.

Original sentence After cleaning
Inflation fell from 8% to 3%. inflation fell
The US economy is not growing. economy growing
Banks bank on lower interest rates. banks bank lower interest rates

Let’s work out the first row in words. “Inflation” and “fell” are letters only and long enough, so they stay. “From” is a stop word, so it goes. “8%” and “3%” contain a digit and a symbol, so they are not alphabetic and go. “To” has only 2 letters, so it goes. What is left: “inflation fell”.

What went wrong, row by row:

  • Row 1: the numbers vanished. But the numbers were the main economic information.
  • Row 2: “not” vanished, so the meaning flipped from “not growing” to “growing”. “US” vanished too.
  • Row 3: “interest rates” survived, but only as two separate words, not as one idea.

The notebook’s conclusion is the main lesson again: “Preprocessing should follow the research question.”

Example 3: the case trap. NLTK’s stop-word list is written all in small letters. If you skip lowercasing, “The” with a capital T is not on the list, so it is not removed. And “The” and “the” now count as two different words, so the vocabulary grows.

Example 4: the “war” search trap. Here is a test sentence of our own, 13 words long: “War came. We moved toward the warm south, but the war went on.” Let’s count “war” three ways. In the table, each row is one search method. The middle column shows which words it matched (the matched letters are in bold). The right column is the count. The counts were checked in Python.

The first method, written .count("war") in Python, counts the letters “war” anywhere. The second, written \bwar\b, counts “war” only as a whole word (\b marks a word boundary). The third is a whole-word search that also ignores case.

Search method What it matches Count
Substring, like .count("war") toward, warm, war 3
Whole word \bwar\b war 1
Whole word, ignore case War, war 2

Only the last one is right. The sentence contains the word “war” twice: once at the start with a capital W, once near the end. The substring search finds 3 because it wrongly counts “toward” and “warm”, and misses “War” because of the capital. The plain whole-word search finds only 1, because it misses the capital “War”.

The notebook warns about the same problem with “oil”, which also matches “soil”, “toil” and “spoil”.

There is a third fix: divide by document length. State of the Union speeches from the 1940s to the 1970s were much longer. Longer speeches give higher raw counts. So raw counts can create a fake trend, as if presidents in those decades cared more about war, when they only talked longer.

What preprocessing is good at, and where it breaks.

  • Good at: making the same word count as the same word. Counts become fair, and the vocabulary gets smaller.
  • Good at: removing junk that carries no meaning for your question.
  • Breaks when: a cleaning step deletes the very thing you care about, like “not”, numbers such as “8%”, or “US”.
  • Breaks when: you search sloppily, so “war” also matches “toward”, or long speeches look “more about war” only because they are longer.

Reading the course code

These five lines come from the course’s first interactive notebook, from its helper functions (small, reusable pieces of code that each do one job, such as “count this word”). The exam has not asked students to write code. It helps to recognise what each line does.

pattern = r"\w*" + word + r"\w*"     # whole_word=False: substring search
pattern = r"\b" + word + r"\b"       # whole_word=True: word boundaries
text = text.translate(str.maketrans("", "", string.punctuation))
tokens = [t for t in tokens if t not in STOPS]
tokens = [stemmer.stem(t) for t in tokens]

Lines 1 and 2 build a pattern, also called a regular expression: a small search rule written in code. The text after # on each line is a comment for humans; the computer ignores it.

  • Line 1: the substring pattern. \w* means “any letters here, or none”, before and after the word. So searching for “war” also catches “toward”.
  • Line 2: the whole-word pattern. \b means “word boundary”, so it only matches “war” as a whole word.
  • Line 3: deletes every punctuation mark listed in string.punctuation.
  • Line 4: keeps only the tokens that are not in the stop-word list, which the code calls STOPS. The code comment warns: “STOPS is all lowercase!” That is the case trap from Example 3.
  • Line 5: replaces each token by its Porter stem (the stemming tool from earlier). The other option is lemmatizer.lemmatize(t, pos="v"), which uses lemmatization instead.

The notebook has no saved outputs. When run, a later cell would show a “ladder” table: the number of tokens and the vocabulary size after each extra cleaning step.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

This topic shows up mostly as True/False items. Two examples:

  • “Removing stop words never changes the meaning of a sentence” (False). Ford’s “not good” becomes “good”.
  • “N-grams can distinguish ‘low unemployment’ from ‘high unemployment’” (True). The pair keeps “low” and “unemployment” together.

In the reflection question (2025 Block 5, where you think through a real business problem), your cleaning choices are a strong pitfall (hidden trap) to discuss. For example, say you measure whether customer survey answers are positive or negative. The positive or negative mood of a text is its sentiment. Deleting “not” would turn negative answers into positive ones.

In 2025 Q2(c), on Boolean search. A Boolean search is a keyword search with AND, OR and NOT, like “oil AND price NOT olive”. This chapter helps there. A keyword search needs whole-word matching (so “war” does not match inside “toward”). It also needs length normalisation (dividing by text length), so long texts do not win only by being long.

A likely short question. First, two terms. An earnings call is a phone meeting where a company’s bosses talk to investors about its results. A sentiment index tracks the mood of texts as one number over time. The question: “You build a sentiment index from earnings calls. Which preprocessing step would you switch off, and why?”

Model answer I would not remove stop words with the standard list, because it contains “not”. Removing it turns “growth is not strong” into “growth strong” and flips the sentiment (as in Ford’s “not good” example, Interactive 1). I might also keep numbers, since they can carry the main economic information (Practical Day 1). Preprocessing should follow the research question, not be applied on autopilot.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: The usual stop-word list deletes “not”, and that flips the meaning: “not strong” becomes “strong”. So do not use that list here. Numbers may matter too, so keep them. Pick cleaning steps that fit your question instead of running them out of habit.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • The cleaning steps (the pipeline) in the right order: lowercase, remove punctuation, tokenize, drop stop words, drop numbers, then stem or lemmatize.
  • At least one real course example of cleaning going wrong: Ford’s “not good” (deleting “not” leaves “good”), or “The US economy is not growing” → “economy growing”.
  • The rule that cleaning choices should follow your research question (what you are trying to find out).
  • For search, the three choices: substring vs whole word (does “war” count inside “toward”?), case (does “War” equal “war”?), and per-length normalisation (dividing counts by text length).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Saying stop-word removal is “always safe”. It can delete “not” and flip the meaning.
  • Saying that keeping “not” fully fixes a bag of words (a method that only counts words). It does not: word order is still lost.
  • Mixing up stemming and lemmatization. Stemming chops word endings by fixed rules (“studies” → “studi”). Lemmatization finds the dictionary form (“studies” → “study”).
  • Treating raw keyword counts as comparable across texts of very different length. A long report mentions “war” more than a short note, even if it cares less about war.

Key terms to use

  • preprocessing: cleaning text before counting it
  • lowercasing: turning every capital letter into a small one
  • punctuation removal: deleting commas, full stops and similar marks
  • tokenization: splitting text into single words
  • token: one word or piece after splitting
  • stop words: very common little words, often deleted
  • stemming: chopping word endings by fixed rules
  • lemmatization: turning words into their dictionary form
  • n-gram / bigram: neighbouring words kept together; bigram is two
  • vocabulary: the list of different words in the texts
  • word boundary: where a word starts and ends
  • substring: a piece of text inside a longer word
  • measurement choice: a decision that changes what you measure
  • normalise by document length: divide counts by how long the text is

Quick self-test

  1. True or false: “In the course notebooks, removing English stop words can turn ‘is not good’ into ‘good’.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Stop words are common little words that the computer is told to delete. In the class code, does that deletion also wipe out “is” and “not”, so only “good” is left?

    True. Why: The standard English stop-word list (from NLTK, a Python toolkit for text) includes “not”. So “is not good” loses both “is” and “not”, and a complaint now reads like praise. It is like a censor blacking out “not” in “I do not agree”.

  2. True or false: “Searching with "war" in text counts only the word ‘war’.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: "war" in text is a line of Python code that checks whether the letters w-a-r appear anywhere in a text. Does it find only the real word “war”?

    False. Why: It looks for those letters anywhere, even inside other words (a substring search). So “toward” and “warm” also match. It is like searching for “cat” and getting “education”. The fix is \bwar\b, where \b means “edge of a word”, so only the whole word counts.

  3. True or false: “A 2-gram model keeps some information about word order.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A 2-gram is a pair of neighbouring words treated as one unit, like “low unemployment”. If you count pairs instead of single words, do you keep some sense of which word came next to which?

    True. Why: Counting single words splits “low” and “unemployment” apart. Counting pairs keeps “low unemployment” glued together, so you know “low” came right before “unemployment”. You keep a small piece of the order, not the whole sentence.

  4. True or false: “If you do not lowercase, the vocabulary gets smaller.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Lowercasing means turning every capital letter into a small one. The vocabulary is the list of different words the computer sees. If you skip lowercasing, does that list get shorter?

    False. Why: It gets longer. Without lowercasing, “The” and “the” look like two different words to the computer, like counting “Apple” and “apple” as two different fruits.

  5. Explain in 2–5 sentences: “You build a sentiment index from earnings calls. Which preprocessing step would you switch off, and why?”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: An earnings call is a company meeting where the bosses talk about results. A sentiment index is a score for how positive or negative they sound. Which cleaning step would you turn off, and why?

    Answer: use the model answer in “What the exam asks, and how to answer” above. Why: The standard stop-word list deletes “not”, which flips negative statements into positive ones. Numbers can carry the key economic facts, so you may keep them too. The choice of steps should come from the research question.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • State of the Union: the yearly speech in which the US president reports to Congress. Example: Ford’s 1975 speech.
  • preprocessing: tidying raw text before you count anything. Example: lowercasing and removing punctuation.
  • string: what programmers call a piece of text. Example: “hello world”.
  • pipeline: a fixed chain of steps, where each step’s output goes into the next. Example: lowercase → remove punctuation → tokenize.
  • lowercasing: turning every capital letter into a small letter. Example: “Hello” becomes “hello”.
  • case: whether letters are capital (upper case) or small (lower case). Example: “ignore case” treats “War” and “war” the same.
  • punctuation: marks such as . , ! ? : ; and quotes. Example: the “!” in “Hello World!”.
  • tokenization / token: cutting text into pieces; each piece is a token. Example: “hello world” → “hello”, “world”. In a later lecture a token can be part of a word, like “un” in “unbelievable”.
  • vocabulary: the list of different words in your texts. Example: “the cat saw the dog” has 5 tokens but a vocabulary of 4 words.
  • stop words: very common words often removed because they appear everywhere. Example: “the”, “and”, “is”.
  • stop-word list: a ready-made list of stop words. Example: the NLTK list, which includes “not”.
  • NLTK: a free Python toolbox for working with text. Example: it holds the stop-word list, stemmer and lemmatizer used here.
  • Python: a programming language. Example: all course notebooks are written in it.
  • stemming: cutting word endings off by fixed rules. Example: “studies” becomes “studi”.
  • PorterStemmer: a well-known stemming tool in NLTK. Example: it turns “studies” into “studi”.
  • lemmatization: replacing a word by its dictionary form. Example: “studies” becomes “study”, “was” becomes “be”.
  • WordNetLemmatizer and pos=“v”: NLTK’s lemmatization tool; pos=“v” tells it to treat each word as a verb. Example: “was” → “be”.
  • set (curly brackets { }): a collection of items in no particular order. Example: {“hello”, “world”}.
  • word order: the sequence in which words appear. Example: “dog bites man” vs “man bites dog”.
  • bag of words: counting words while ignoring their order. Example: “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” give the same counts.
  • n-gram: a group of n neighbouring words used as one item. Example: 1-gram “low”, 2-gram (bigram) “low unemployment”, 3-gram “all the words”.
  • substring: a piece of text found inside a longer text. Example: “war” is a substring of “toward”.
  • whole-word match / word boundary: a search that only counts a word standing alone; the boundary is the edge of a word, written \b in code. Example: \bwar\b skips “toward”.
  • pattern (regular expression): a small search rule written in code. Example: \w* means “any letters here, or none”.
  • normalise by document length: dividing a count by how long the text is. Example: “mentions per 1,000 words”.
  • index: one number tracked over time that sums something up. Example: war mentions per 1,000 words, year by year.
  • trend: the direction a number moves over time. Example: an index that goes up year after year has an upward trend.
  • measurement choice: a decision about how you measure that changes the answer. Example: whether “toward” counts as “war”.
  • research question: the exact question your study tries to answer. Example: “Did presidents talk about war more in some decades?”
  • alphabetic: made only of letters, with no digits or symbols. Example: “economy” is alphabetic, “8%” is not.
  • notebook / cell / saved output: a notebook mixes code and notes; a cell is one block in it; saved output is the stored result of running it. Example: the Practical Day 1 cleaning table is a saved output.
  • helper function: a small, reusable piece of code that does one job. Example: a function that counts one word in a speech.
  • sentiment / sentiment index: sentiment is the positive or negative mood of a text; a sentiment index tracks it as one number over time. Example: a monthly mood score for company calls.
  • earnings call: a phone meeting where a company’s bosses talk to investors about its results. Example: a bank’s quarterly results call.
  • Boolean search: a keyword search with AND, OR and NOT. Example: “oil AND price NOT olive”.

Sources: Lecture_bow_cosine_tfidf.pdf (Lecture 2a) slides 6, 7, 12; Lecture 7, slides 13 and 29 (tokens vs words); GRA4164_Interactive_1_Text_as_data.ipynb cells 4, 7–16, 27; practical_day_1.ipynb cells 7–10; 2025 exam Q2(c) and Block 5

3. The bag-of-words assumption and the document-term matrix

Exam priority: ★★★ High — asked directly in 2025 Q2(a) (5 points)

Why this exists

A newspaper has 50,000 old articles. It wants to find all the ones about the economy, or see which articles are alike. A computer can add, compare and sort numbers. It cannot do any of that with words. “Inflation” is not a number.

The course says it like this: “Computers do not inherently understand words, and we cannot directly apply mathematical operations to them.” And: “Words need to be transformed into numerical representations for analysis.” In plain words: before a computer can work with text, every text has to become a list of numbers.

So we need one fixed way to turn every article into a row of numbers, with the same columns for every article. Then the computer can line the articles up and compare them. This chapter shows the simplest way to do that, and the table it produces.

The idea in everyday words

The big picture. Cut a sentence into single words with scissors and throw them into a bag. Shake the bag. You can still count how many times “data” is in there. But you can no longer read the sentence. “Dog bites man” and “man bites dog” give exactly the same bag.

That is the whole method. Here it is step by step.

Step 1: decide what one “document” is. One piece of text you count words for is called a document. The whole collection of documents is the corpus. The course says: “Corpus = all words, sentences and documents”.

A document does not have to be a full article. The course says a document “Can be a sentence, a day, an article, a paragraph, etc.” You pick the size that fits your question. If you want to compare days, all articles from one day can be one document. What you choose as one document is called the document unit.

Step 2: clean the text and cut it into words. You tidy the text first: make letters small, remove punctuation, and often drop very common words like “the” and “and” (called stop words). Then you cut the text into single words. Each piece is called a token.

Step 3: make the word list. Write down every different word that appears anywhere in your corpus. This list is the vocabulary. Each item on the list is called a term. A term is usually one word. Sometimes it is a pair of words, as you will see below.

Step 4: draw a table. One row for each document. One column for each term in the vocabulary. A table filled only with numbers is called a matrix. A row goes across. A column goes down. One box where a row and a column meet is a cell (also called an element or entry).

Step 5: fill each cell with a count. The cell says how many times this term appears in this document. That number is the count.

The finished table is called the document-term matrix, or DTM for short: documents in the rows, terms in the columns, counts in the cells.

Step 6: forget the word order. Only the counts are kept. Which word came first is lost. That is the “bag”: the words are thrown in a bag and shaken. This way of turning text into numbers is called bag-of-words.

Every method takes some things as true to keep life simple. Such a starting belief is called an assumption. The bag-of-words assumption is that word order does not matter. In the course’s words, the words “are treated individually”, and: “The word sequence does not matter!” Because each word is counted on its own, the surrounding words (the context) are not used.

Step 7: notice the zeros. The vocabulary holds every word used in any document. But each single document uses only a few of them. So most cells are 0. A table that is mostly zeros is called sparse. The opposite, a table mostly filled with non-zero numbers, is called dense. The course gives two facts about real DTMs: “Typically sparse (many zeros)” and “Typically LARGE (millions of documents, hundred-of-thousands unique terms)”.

A fix for word order. You can make the columns pairs of neighbouring words instead of single words. A run of n neighbouring words is called an n-gram. A single word is a 1-gram. A pair is a 2-gram. A 2-gram column like “low unemployment” keeps a bit of word order, so it can tell “low unemployment” from “high unemployment”. The choice of what one column stands for (one word, or a word pair) is called the term unit.

Walk-through example

Part 1: a tiny DTM by hand. Take three very short documents. The first two come from the bag analogy; the third is our own.

  • Doc A: “dog bites man”
  • Doc B: “man bites dog”
  • Doc C: “dog barks”

First, the vocabulary: every different word, in alphabetical order. That is barks, bites, dog, man. So there are 4 words, and the table gets 4 columns. There are 3 documents, so the table gets 3 rows.

How to read the table below: each row is one document. Each column is one word from the vocabulary. Each cell is “how many times this word appears in this document”.

Document ↓ / Word → barks bites dog man
Doc A 0 1 1 1
Doc B 0 1 1 1
Doc C 1 0 1 0

Let’s work out one cell out loud. Take row Doc C, column “dog”. Doc C is “dog barks”. “dog” appears once, so the cell is 1. Next to it, take row Doc C, column “man”. “man” does not appear in “dog barks”, so the cell is 0.

Two things to notice:

  • Rows A and B are exactly the same: 0, 1, 1, 1. The table cannot tell “dog bites man” from “man bites dog”. That is the price of ignoring word order.
  • Count the zeros: 1 in row A, 1 in row B, 2 in row C. That makes 4 zeros out of 12 cells (3 rows times 4 columns), already one third. With a real vocabulary of thousands of words, almost every cell is 0. That is what “sparse” means.

Part 2: the course’s own DTM. The slides show the table below. The columns are the words “Using”, “text”, “as” and “data”. The “…” means the real table has more columns and more rows than are shown. Each row is a document, and each cell is “how many times this word appears in this document”.

Documents ↓ / Terms → Using text as data …
Doc1 1 1 2 2 …
Doc2 0 3 0 2 …
Doc3 0 0 5 2 …
… … … … … …

Read one cell by hand: row Doc2, column “text” is 3. That means the word “text” appears 3 times in Doc2.

Now read one whole row. Row Doc1 is 1, 1, 2, 2, and so on. An ordered list of numbers like this is called a vector. So each document becomes one vector. The slide calls the whole table \(C\), and calls row 1 \(c_1\). The small 1 written below the line is an address: “row 1”. The slide writes it like this:

\[c_1 = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 1 & 2 & 2 & \dots \end{bmatrix}\]

The square brackets hold the list of numbers in row 1.

We need two more letters to talk about the size of the table. We write \(n\) for the number of documents (rows) and \(p\) for the number of different terms in the vocabulary (columns). The picture below draws the same table as a grid.

The grid above: rows = documents (\(n\) of them), columns = vocabulary terms (\(p\) of them), each cell = a count. The dashed box is one row, the vector \(c_1\) for Doc1. The faded zeros hint at sparsity.

Part 3: how sparse a real DTM is. One course notebook (Practical Day 1) built a DTM for 72 speeches. Its cells hold tf-idf scores instead of plain counts: a re-weighted version of the counts that makes rare, telling words count more (it has its own chapter). Here only the zeros matter.

  • The table’s shape was (72, 8538). That means 72 rows (one per speech) and 8,538 columns (one per term).
  • So it has \(72 \times 8{,}538 = 614{,}736\) cells.
  • Only 89,284 of those cells are not zero.

Work it out: \(89{,}284 / (72 \times 8{,}538) \approx 14.5\%\) of the cells are filled. So about 85% of the cells are zero.

Part 4: one corpus, many possible DTMs. The same texts can give different tables. You make two choices: (i) the document unit (what one row is) and (ii) the term unit (what one column is). The course shows three set-ups. In the table below, each row is one set-up. The “Rows” column says what becomes a row of the DTM. The “Columns” column says what becomes a column.

Choice Rows Columns
Document level, 1-gram Doc1, Doc2, Doc3 Using, text, as, data
Sentence level, 1-gram Sen1, Sen2, Sen3 Using, text, as, data
Document level, 2-gram Doc1, Doc2, Doc3 “Using text”, “text as”, “as data”

For example, at sentence level each row is one sentence. Sentence 1 is “Using text as data is new to most economists.” It contains each of the four words once, so its row is 1, 1, 1, 1. Sentence 2 is “However, it is a growing field.” It contains none of them, so its row is 0, 0, 0, 0.

The course also shows that one corpus can be split by sentence, by article, or by day (one day can hold many articles). Its message: the research question should decide what counts as a document.

What bag-of-words is good at, and where it breaks.

  • Good at: turning any text into numbers in a fast, simple and repeatable way.
  • Good at: questions where word counts are enough, such as “how often does this article mention inflation?”
  • Breaks when: order matters. “Good, not bad” and “bad, not good” become the same bag, and “dog bites man” equals “man bites dog”.
  • Breaks when: the table gets huge. Thousands of columns and few rows make later statistics unreliable (more on this in the code section).

The formula, explained

You have now seen the idea: the whole corpus becomes one table with \(n\) rows and \(p\) columns, and each row is the list of word counts for one document. The course writes this with a few letters.

First, the raw texts. The course writes: “\(D\) is the raw data”; “\(D_i\) is document \(i\) in \(D\) for \(i = 1, \dots, n\)”. In plain words: \(D\) is the whole pile of texts. \(D_1, D_2, \dots, D_n\) are text number 1, text number 2, and so on up to the last one, number \(n\). The letter \(i\) stands for “any document number”.

Then the table. The size of a table, written “rows by columns”, is called its dimension. Read the sign “\(\times\)” as “by”. Our dog example is \(3 \times 4\): 3 rows by 4 columns.

\[C \ \text{ has dimension } \ n \times p, \qquad c_i = \begin{bmatrix} c_{i1} & c_{i2} & \dots & c_{ip} \end{bmatrix}\]

  • \(C\) = the document-term matrix (the whole table).
  • \(n\) = how many documents we have (the number of rows).
  • \(p\) = “the length of the vocabulary”: how many different terms we have (the number of columns).
  • \(c_i\) = row \(i\): the list of counts for document \(i\). It is the slide’s \(c_1\) from the walk-through, written for any row.
  • \(c_{ij}\) = one cell: how many times term \(j\) appears in document \(i\). The two small letters below the line are an address, “row \(i\), column \(j\)”. So \(c_{i1}\) is the count of the first term, and \(c_{ip}\) is the count of the last term.

Read aloud: “The corpus becomes a table \(C\) with \(n\) rows, one per document, and \(p\) columns, one per vocabulary term; cell \(c_{ij}\) counts how often term \(j\) appears in document \(i\).”

The slide’s own definition uses the same letters. A “numerical array” is programmer talk for a table of numbers.

  • “\(C\) is \(D\) represented as a numerical array with dimension \(n \times p\), where \(p\) is the length of the vocabulary”
  • “Elements of \(C\) are usually counts of tokens in \(D\): words, phrases, etc.” (each cell holds a count)
  • “\(c_i\) of \(C\) is a numerical vector with counts of tokens in row \(i\) in \(C\)” (one row of the table, written as a list of numbers)

For the exam you need to understand this and be able to say “\(n \times p\), where \(p\) is the vocabulary size”. The 2025 exam had no calculations.

Reading the course code

These three lines come from the course’s first interactive notebook. The exam has not asked students to write code. It helps to recognise what each line does.

vec = CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1, NGRAM_MAX), min_df=MIN_DF, stop_words=STOP_WORDS)
X = vec.fit_transform(docs["rawtext"])
share_zero = 1 - X.nnz / n_cells

CountVectorizer is a ready-made Python tool (from a toolbox called scikit-learn) that builds a DTM of counts for you. The words in capitals (NGRAM_MAX, MIN_DF, STOP_WORDS) are settings the student fills in. docs["rawtext"] is the column of the notebook’s table of speeches that holds the raw text.

  • Line 1 sets up the counting machine. Its settings: ngram_range=(1, 2) would add word pairs as extra columns. min_df=5 keeps only words found in at least 5 speeches. stop_words="english" drops stop words.
  • Line 2: fit_transform means “learn the vocabulary, then build the table” in one command. The result X is the DTM: one row per speech, one column per term. It is stored in a sparse format: a space-saving way to store a mostly-zero table by writing down only the cells that are not 0.
  • Line 3: nnz is short for “number of non-zeros”, the count of cells that are not 0. n_cells is the total number of cells. So X.nnz / n_cells is the share of filled cells, and 1 minus that is the share of zeros.

No outputs are saved. Running it would show the share of zeros is very high. The notebook asks you to notice three things:

  • Columns grow more slowly than rows, because new speeches reuse old words.
  • Bigrams (word pairs) add many columns and even more zeros.
  • min_df throws out rare words, typos and names.

The notebook’s warning. The next notebook uses this table to predict GDP growth (how fast a country’s total economic output grows from one year to the next). The method is a regression: it finds how one number moves with other numbers, and gives each column a weight. But there are only about 70 speeches and thousands of columns. With far more columns than rows, written \(p \gg n\) (the sign \(\gg\) means “much bigger than”), the regression overfits. It fits the 70 known speeches perfectly but predicts new ones badly, like memorising last year’s exam answers without understanding them. That is why text regressions need regularisation: a brake that stops the regression giving big weights to too many columns (a later lecture covers it).

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025 Q2(a), 5 points, asked exactly this: what is the underlying assumption of bag-of-words, and what is a document-term matrix? The official marking guide wanted two things:

  • Word occurrences are treated as independent (each word is counted on its own), and context (the surrounding words) is not modelled.
  • Documents in rows, tokens (words) in columns, counts as the entries.

Expect True/False items too:

  • “In a bag-of-words model the order of words matters” (False).
  • “A DTM is typically dense” (False). Dense means mostly non-zero; a DTM is mostly zeros.

Here is the full answer to the 2025 question: “What is the bag-of-words assumption, and what is a document-term matrix?”

Model answer The bag-of-words assumption is that word order does not matter: each word is treated individually, as if the words were thrown into a bag, so context is not modelled. A document-term matrix stores the corpus as numbers: each row is a document, each column is a term from the vocabulary, and each cell counts how often that term appears in that document. Its dimension is \(n \times p\) (\(n\) documents, \(p\) terms). It is typically very large and sparse (mostly zeros), because each document uses only a small part of the vocabulary.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Bag-of-words only counts words and forgets their order. The document-term matrix is the table of those counts: one row per text, one column per word. The table is huge and mostly zeros, because each text uses only a few of all the words.

What a top-grade answer must include

  1. The assumption: word order (sequence) does not matter, and each word is treated on its own, so context (the surrounding words) is lost.
  2. The DTM (document-term matrix): documents in rows, terms (words) in columns, counts in the cells. Its size is \(n\) documents by \(p\) words (\(n \times p\)), where \(p\) is the vocabulary size (the number of different words).
  3. One consequence: the table is usually sparse (mostly zeros) and large.
  4. A one-line example (“dog bites man” counts the same as “man bites dog”), or the fix: n-grams (neighbouring words kept together) keep “low unemployment” apart from “high unemployment”.
  5. Bonus: what counts as one document (a sentence, an article, a day) is your choice, driven by your research question (the question your study tries to answer).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Answering only half: the assumption but not the DTM, or the other way round.
  • Mixing up rows and columns (rows = documents, columns = words).
  • Writing only “it counts words”, with no table size and no mention that word order is ignored.
  • Calling the DTM dense (mostly filled). It is sparse (mostly zeros).
  • Forgetting that the vocabulary size (\(p\)) is usually much bigger than the number of words in any one document.

Key terms to use

  • bag-of-words assumption: word order ignored; only counts matter
  • word order / sequence ignored: which word came first is lost
  • document-term matrix: documents down, words across, counts inside
  • rows = documents: each line of the table is one text
  • columns = terms: each column is one word
  • counts: how many times a word appears
  • \(n \times p\): \(n\) documents by \(p\) words
  • vocabulary: the list of all different words
  • sparse: most cells in the table are zero
  • large: many rows and very many columns
  • corpus: the whole collection of texts
  • document unit: what counts as one “document”
  • n-grams: neighbouring words kept together as one unit

Quick self-test

  1. True or false: “A document-term matrix has dimension \(n \times p\), where \(p\) is the vocabulary size.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A document-term matrix is a table of word counts. “Dimension \(n \times p\)” means it has \(n\) rows and \(p\) columns. The vocabulary size is the number of different words across all your texts. Is the number of columns equal to the number of different words?

    True. Why: Each document gets one row (\(n\) documents, \(n\) rows). Each different word gets one column (\(p\) words, \(p\) columns). Think of a class register: one row per pupil, one column per lesson.

  2. True or false: “With 1-grams, ‘the dog bites the man’ and ‘the man bites the dog’ get the same row in the DTM.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “1-grams” means counting single words one at a time. A row in the DTM (document-term matrix) is the list of word counts for one text. Do these two sentences end up with identical counts?

    True. Why: Both have “the” twice and “dog”, “bites” and “man” once each. Counting single words is like tipping the words into a bag and shaking it: the order is gone. The slide says “The word sequence does not matter!” Only 2-grams or longer (pairs like “dog bites”) would tell the two sentences apart.

  3. True or false: “A document must always be a full article.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: In text analysis, a “document” is one unit you count words for, so one row in the table. Must that unit always be a whole article?

    False. Why: You choose the unit to fit your question, like choosing to count your steps per hour or per day. The slide says a document “Can be a sentence, a day, an article, a paragraph, etc.”

  4. True or false: “Most cells in a DTM are zero.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A cell is one box in the table: how often one word appears in one document. Are most of the boxes 0?

    True. Why: The table has a column for every word used anywhere in all the texts, but each text uses only a few of them. Picture a receipt that lists every product in the shop: most lines would say 0. The slide says “Typically sparse (many zeros)”.

  5. Explain in 2–5 sentences (2025 Q2a style): “What is the bag-of-words assumption, and what is a document-term matrix?”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Two parts. What does the bag-of-words method assume about text? And what is the table of word counts it produces? (This exact question came up in 2025, for 5 points.)

    Answer: use the model answer in “What the exam asks, and how to answer” above. Why: It answers both halves. The assumption: order is ignored and context is lost. The table: rows are documents, columns are terms, cells are counts, size \(n \times p\), and mostly zeros.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • document: one unit of text in the corpus. Example: a sentence, an article, a paragraph or one day of news.
  • corpus: the full collection of texts you study; the slide writes it as \(D\). Example: 50,000 newspaper articles.
  • \(D_i\): document number \(i\) in the corpus. Example: \(D_2\) is the second document.
  • document unit / term unit: what you choose as one row, and as one column. Example: rows = days, columns = word pairs.
  • stop words: very common words that are often removed. Example: “the”, “and”.
  • token: one piece of cut-up text, here one word. Example: “dog barks” has 2 tokens.
  • vocabulary: the list of all different terms in the corpus; its length is written \(p\). Example: barks, bites, dog, man (\(p = 4\)).
  • term: one item in the vocabulary, usually a word, sometimes a word pair. Example: “dog” or “low unemployment”.
