  • matrix: a table of numbers with rows and columns. Example: a spreadsheet with only numbers in it.
  • row / column / cell / element: a row goes across, a column goes down, a cell (element, entry) is one box where they meet. Example: row Doc C, column “dog” holds 1.
  • count: how many times something appears. Example: “text” appears 3 times in Doc2.
  • document-term matrix (DTM): the table with one row per document, one column per term, and counts in the cells; the slide calls it \(C\). Example: the dog/man table.
  • bag-of-words: treating a text as a pile of word counts, ignoring order. Example: “dog bites man” = “man bites dog”.
  • assumption: something a method takes as true to keep things simple. Example: “word order does not matter”.
  • context: the words around a word that help fix its meaning. Example: “not” before “good”.
  • sparse / dense: sparse means mostly zeros; dense means mostly non-zero numbers. Example: a DTM is sparse.
  • n-gram / 1-gram / 2-gram: a group of \(n\) neighbouring words used as one term. Example: 1-gram “low”, 2-gram “low unemployment”.
  • vector: an ordered list of numbers. Example: one DTM row, such as (0, 1, 1, 1).
  • \(c_i\) and \(c_{ij}\): \(c_i\) is row \(i\) (all counts for document \(i\)); \(c_{ij}\) is one cell (the count of term \(j\) in document \(i\)). Example: in the slide table, row Doc2, column “text” holds 3.
  • subscript: the small letter or number written below the line, used as an address. Example: the 1 in \(c_1\) means “row 1”.
  • dimension, \(n \times p\): the size of a table, \(n\) rows by \(p\) columns; read “\(\times\)” as “by”. Example: the dog table is \(3 \times 4\).
  • numerical array: programmer talk for a table (or list) of numbers. Example: the DTM.
  • tf-idf: a re-weighted version of the counts that makes rare, telling words count more. Example: “inflation” weighs more than “said”.
  • CountVectorizer: a ready-made Python tool (from scikit-learn) that builds a DTM of counts. Example: line 1 of the course code.
  • min_df, ngram_range, stop_words: settings of that tool. Example: min_df=5 keeps words found in at least 5 documents; ngram_range=(1, 2) adds word pairs; stop_words="english" drops common words.
  • fit_transform: “learn the vocabulary, then build the table” in one command. Example: line 2 of the course code.
  • nnz: short for “number of non-zeros”, the count of cells that are not 0. Example: 89,284 in the 72-speech table.
  • sparse format: storing a mostly-zero table by writing down only the non-zero cells. Example: how X is kept in memory.
  • regression: a method that finds how one number moves with other numbers, giving each a weight. Example: GDP growth predicted from word counts.
  • GDP growth: how fast a country’s total economic output grows from one year to the next. Example: “the economy grew 2% this year”.
  • overfit: learning the noise in the examples by heart, so new data is predicted badly. Example: memorising last year’s exam answers.
  • \(p \gg n\): many more columns than rows; \(\gg\) means “much bigger than”. Example: thousands of words, about 70 speeches.
  • regularisation: a brake that stops a regression giving big weights to too many columns. Example: needed for the GDP-growth regression.

Sources: Lecture_bow_cosine_tfidf.pdf (Lecture 2a) slides 2, 4, 5, 8–17, 20; GRA4164_Interactive_1_Text_as_data.ipynb cells 17–20; practical_day_1.ipynb cell 14; 2025 exam Q2(a) with the official marking guide

4. Normalising the DTM: raw counts, row normalisation, binary, tf-idf

Exam priority: ★★★ High — asked directly in 2025 Q2(b) (5 points); idf calculations possible

Why this exists

A news website wants to tag each article with its most telling words, so readers can find, say, “articles about inflation”. To do this, a computer first counts how often each word appears in each article. It keeps the counts in one big table: one row per article, one column per word. Each cell says how many times that word appears in that article.

Those plain counts mislead in two ways.

  1. Long articles win automatically. A long article uses almost every word more often than a short one, only because it is long. The course uses the yearly speeches of US presidents as its example. Truman’s 1946 speech has 27,722 words. His 1949 speech has 3,397. The 1946 speech will have bigger counts for nearly every word, whatever it is about.
  2. Common words win automatically. Words like “the”, “said” or “government” have big counts in almost every text. They tell you nothing about what makes this one text special.

So before we use the counts, we adjust them. This chapter shows four ways to do it: keep the counts as they are, turn them into shares, turn them into yes/no, or weight them by how rare the word is.

The idea in everyday words

An everyday picture first. You want to know which student “talks most about football”. Student A wrote 10 pages and mentions football 10 times. Student B wrote 1 page and mentions it 5 times. If you count mentions, A wins. But per page, B talks about football far more: 5 times per page against A’s 1. And if every student mentions “school”, that word is useless for telling the students apart. The four methods below fix exactly these two problems.

A few basic words. A document is one text: an article, a speech, an essay. The corpus is the whole collection of documents you are studying. A token is one word as it appears in a text, counting repeats: “data data text” has 3 tokens. The table of counts (one row per document, one column per word, each cell a count) is called the document-term matrix, or DTM for short. “Term” means word, and “matrix” means a table of numbers.

Changing all the numbers in the table in a fixed way, so that documents become fairer to compare, is called normalising the DTM. Another name for such a change is a transformation. It is like turning test scores into percentages so that tests with different maximum scores can be compared.

Way 1: keep the plain counts. These are the raw counts: the numbers in the table before any change. This is the easiest option, but long documents and common words win.

Way 2: turn counts into shares. Take one document’s row. Add up all its counts. That total is the document’s number of tokens, called its document length. Now divide every count in the row by that total. Each cell then says “what share of this document is this word”. A share (or proportion) is a part of a whole: 3 out of 5 is 0.6, which is 60%. After this step every row adds up to 1, that is, 100%. This method is called row normalisation, because you adjust each row by its own total. Now long and short documents compare fairly. In the football picture, Student B wins.

Way 3: turn counts into yes/no. Replace every count above 0 with a 1. Leave the zeros as 0. A cell now only answers “does the word appear in this document at all?” A value that can only be 0 or 1, like a light switch, is called binary. This removes the effect of how many times a word is repeated: using “war” once or fifty times both give 1.

Way 4: weight each count by how rare the word is. This uses two ingredients.

  • How often the word appears in this document. This is called the term frequency, or tf. In the course’s main formula it is the plain count.
  • How rare the word is across the corpus. First count how many documents contain the word at least once. This number is the document frequency. Careful: it counts documents, not uses. A word used 50 times in one document has a document frequency of 1. Next, divide the total number of documents by the document frequency. With 3 documents, a word found in only 1 of them gives 3 ÷ 1 = 3. A word found in all 3 gives 3 ÷ 3 = 1. Last, press the “log” button on a calculator.

What is the log button? The natural log, written ln, is a calculator button that shrinks big numbers. You only need three facts about it. First, ln 1 = 0. Second, bigger numbers give bigger results. Third, the results grow slowly: ln 3 ≈ 1.1, ln 10 ≈ 2.3, ln 100 ≈ 4.6. So a word that is 100 times rarer gets a weight of about 4.6, not 100.

The number you get from the log button is the word’s rarity weight. Its name is inverse document frequency, or idf. “Inverse” means “the other way round”: it goes up when the document frequency goes down. Fewer documents with the word means a bigger weight.

Multiply the two ingredients and you get tf-idf: term frequency times inverse document frequency. In plain words: “how often the word is used here” times “how rare the word is overall”. A word found in every document gets total ÷ total = 1, and ln 1 = 0. So its tf-idf is 0, however often it is used.

What tf-idf achieves. A word that is common in this document but rare in the others is called a distinctive word: it tells you what this document is about. Small grammar words like “the”, “of” and “and” carry little meaning about the topic. They are called function words, and they appear almost everywhere. Tf-idf pushes distinctive words up and pushes words found everywhere down. A course notebook puts it in one line: “Raw counts describe the language; tf-idf describes the document.” (A notebook here is a file used in class that mixes Python computer code with its results. Python is a programming language.)

What the lecture slides say each method is for. The slides give the reason for normalising in their own words: “long documents will have higher counts just because they are longer. We might want to control for this”. The table below collects the four methods. Each row is one method. The columns say what a cell becomes, why you would use the method, and the slides’ own comment on it.

Method What the cell becomes Why you would use it The slides’ comment
Raw counts the count itself simplest “Simple representation but sensitive to document length.”
Row normalisation count ÷ total tokens in the document removes dependence on document length “Mitigates the impact of document length differences.” (The slide lists this share under the name “Term Frequency (TF)”.)
Binary 1 if the word appears, else 0 removes dependence on how many times a word is used “Ignores frequency; focuses on term occurrence.”
Tf-idf count × rarity weight down-weights words common everywhere, up-weights distinctive words “Highlights terms that are significant in a document but rare in the corpus.”

In plain words: “sensitive to document length” means the numbers change a lot when a text is longer. “Mitigates” means “reduces”. “Term occurrence” means “whether the word occurs at all”.

The slides also explain tf-idf in three short lines: “Rare terms: High IDF → More significant if term appears in a document.” “Common terms: Low IDF → Less impact on distinguishing documents.” “Balance: TF-IDF balances term frequency with uniqueness.” And they name two uses:

  • “Feature Selection: Drop terms with TF-IDF below a threshold.” Feature selection means keeping only the useful columns (words) and dropping the rest. A threshold is a cut-off line: drop every word whose score is under some number you choose.
  • “Weighting: Apply TF-IDF scores to emphasize important terms in models.” Weighting means giving some words more importance than others in later calculations.

Where each method breaks.

  • Tf-idf boosts words that are rare for boring reasons. In one of Trump’s speeches, for example, it ranks names of guests and officials near the top, because no other speech mentions them.
  • Binary throws away useful “how much” information.
  • Different computer programs use slightly different tf-idf formulas, so their numbers differ. The walk-through below shows one example.

Walk-through example

The table we start from. The lecture slides show a tiny DTM. We pretend its 3 documents and 4 words are the whole corpus. Each row is a document (Doc1, Doc2, Doc3). Each column is a word (“Using”, “text”, “as”, “data”). Each cell is a raw count. For example, row Doc1, column “as” holds 2: the word “as” appears 2 times in Doc1. We add one extra column at the right, the row total. It is the document length: all the counts in that row added up.

Document ↓ / Word → Using text as data row total (document length)
Doc1 1 1 2 2 6
Doc2 0 3 0 2 5
Doc3 0 0 5 2 7

Doc1’s total is 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 = 6. So Doc1 has 6 tokens.

All the numbers below are worked out from this table, using the natural log, and were checked in Python.

Way 2: shares (row normalisation). Divide each count by its row total. Doc2’s counts are 0, 3, 0, 2, and its total is 5. The cell for “text” becomes 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6. In words: 60% of Doc2 is the word “text”. Doing this for every cell gives the next table. Rows and columns are the same as before. Each cell is now the share of the document’s tokens that are this word.

Document ↓ / Word → Using text as data
Doc1 0.167 0.167 0.333 0.333
Doc2 0 0.6 0 0.4
Doc3 0 0 0.714 0.286

For Doc1, 1 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.167 and 2 ÷ 6 ≈ 0.333. Each row now adds up to 1.

Way 3: yes/no (binary). Every count above 0 becomes 1. Rows and columns are the same. Each cell is now 1 if the word appears in the document at all, and 0 if it does not.

Document ↓ / Word → Using text as data
Doc1 1 1 1 1
Doc2 0 1 0 1
Doc3 0 0 1 1

Doc3 uses “as” 5 times and Doc1 uses it 2 times. Both cells become 1. The difference between 5 and 2 is gone.

Way 4: tf-idf, the version on the slides. We work out one rarity weight per word, then multiply.

Step 1: document frequency. For each word, look down its column in the first table and count the documents with a count above 0. “Using” is only in Doc1, so its document frequency is 1. “data” is in all three, so its document frequency is 3.

Step 2: idf. Divide the number of documents (3) by the document frequency, then take the natural log. In the next table, each row is a word. The columns show the steps: the document frequency, the division, and the final idf.

Word documents containing it 3 ÷ that number idf = ln of that result
Using 1 3 1.099
text 2 1.5 0.405
as 2 1.5 0.405
data 3 1 0

For “Using”: 3 ÷ 1 = 3, and ln 3 ≈ 1.099. For “data”: 3 ÷ 3 = 1, and ln 1 = 0.

Step 3: multiply each count by its word’s idf. Rows are documents, columns are words, and each cell is now a tf-idf score.

Document ↓ / Word → Using text as data
Doc1 1.099 0.405 0.811 0
Doc2 0 1.216 0 0
Doc3 0 0 2.027 0

Three cells worked out in words:

  • Doc1, “Using”: Doc1 uses “Using” once, and its idf is 1.099. So 1 × 1.099 = 1.099.
  • Doc3, “as”: Doc3 uses “as” 5 times, and its idf is ln 1.5 ≈ 0.4055. So 5 × 0.4055 ≈ 2.027. (5 × 0.405 gives 2.025; the small gap is only rounding.)
  • Every “data” cell: “data” has idf 0, so each of its cells is 0, however big the count.

What happened: “data” is in every document, so its whole column becomes 0. A word found everywhere cannot help tell documents apart. “Using” is in only one document, so it gets the biggest weight per use. That is the whole point of tf-idf.

Way 4 again: the version in scikit-learn. scikit-learn is a free Python toolbox for data analysis used in the course. Its tf-idf tool is called TfidfVectorizer. Its counting tool is called CountVectorizer. A software default is the setting a tool uses if you do not choose one yourself. A course notebook explains what scikit-learn does by default: “By default, scikit-learn uses smoothed inverse document frequencies and normalizes each document vector to length one (L2 normalization).” That sentence describes two extra steps.

Extra step 1: smoothing. Smoothing is a small tweak to the idf formula. It adds 1 in a few places, so that no word gets a weight of exactly 0. Another course notebook says: “scikit-learn adds 1 to every idf, so no word is weighted down to exactly zero”. The exact smoothed formula is: take (1 + number of documents) ÷ (1 + document frequency), take the natural log, and add 1. In symbols, with \(n\) for the number of documents and \(d_j\) for the document frequency of word \(j\): \(idf_j = \ln\frac{1+n}{1+d_j} + 1\). [Not in course files — general knowledge]

The next table uses this smoothed formula on our 3 documents. Each row is a word. The columns are its document frequency and its smoothed idf.

Word documents containing it smoothed idf = ln((1 + 3) ÷ (1 + that number)) + 1
Using 1 \(\ln(4/2) + 1 = 1.693\)
text 2 \(\ln(4/3) + 1 = 1.288\)
as 2 \(\ln(4/3) + 1 = 1.288\)
data 3 \(\ln(4/4) + 1 = 1.000\)

“data” now gets 1, not 0.

Extra step 2: L2 normalisation. A document vector is a document’s row of numbers, seen as a single object. You can picture it as an arrow, or as the instructions for a walk: “1.693 steps in the ‘Using’ direction, 1.288 steps in the ‘text’ direction”, and so on. The L2 length of the row is the straight-line distance from where the walk starts to where it ends. You find it the way Pythagoras finds the long side of a right-angled triangle: square each number (multiply it by itself), add the squares up, and take the square root. The square root is the number that, multiplied by itself, gives the number inside: \(\sqrt{9} = 3\). L2 normalisation then divides every number in the row by this length, so that the row’s new length is exactly 1.

Doc1 worked out. First multiply each count by the smoothed idf: 1 × 1.693 = 1.693 for “Using”, 1 × 1.288 = 1.288 for “text”, 2 × 1.288 = 2.575 for “as”, and 2 × 1 = 2 for “data”. Next find the row’s length: \(\sqrt{1.693^2 + 1.288^2 + 2.575^2 + 2^2} = 3.893\). Then divide each weight by 3.893. For “Using”: 1.693 ÷ 3.893 ≈ 0.435. Doc2 and Doc3 are done the same way.

The result is the next table. Rows are documents, columns are words. Each cell is the scikit-learn tf-idf score: smoothed idf, with each row rescaled to length 1.

Document ↓ / Word → Using text as data
Doc1 0.435 0.331 0.661 0.514
Doc2 0 0.888 0 0.460
Doc3 0 0 0.955 0.297

Notice that “data” is no longer 0. A stop-word list is a list of common words, like “the”, that you delete before counting. Because of the smoothing, a notebook warns that “the can survive tf-idf without a stop-word list” in scikit-learn. As the notebook says: “Software defaults are modelling choices too.” In plain words: the settings you leave untouched still change your results.

The course’s own scikit-learn example. A course notebook runs scikit-learn on three short sentences:

  1. “Inflation and interest rates rose.”
  2. “Interest rates fell as inflation eased.”
  3. “Employment and wages rose.”

The computer works out the scores. You will not do this by hand, and the exam won’t ask you to. What matters is how to read them: a bigger score means the word is more telling for that sentence.

  • In sentence 2, the words found only there (“as”, “eased”, “fell”) get 0.46. The words that also appear in sentence 1 (“inflation”, “interest”, “rates”) get less: 0.349.
  • In sentence 3, “employment” and “wages” (found only there) get 0.563. “and” and “rose” (also in sentence 1) get less: 0.428.
  • In sentence 1, all five words also appear in one other sentence. So they all get the same weight. Because the row’s length must be 1, each of the five equal scores is \(1/\sqrt{5} = 0.447\).

The pattern: rarer words get more weight.

The formula, explained

The slides write the three simple transformations side by side. Here, \(x\) stands for the new, adjusted numbers.

\[x_i = c_i \qquad\qquad x_i = c_i / m_i, \ \text{ with } \ m_i = \sum_j c_{ij} \qquad\qquad x_{ij} = 1_{c_{ij} > 0}\]

  • \(i\) = which document (document 1, 2, 3, …).
  • \(j\) = which word, or term (word 1, 2, 3, …).
  • \(c_{ij}\) = the count: how many times word \(j\) appears in document \(i\). It is one cell of the DTM.
  • \(c_i\) = the whole row of counts for document \(i\).
  • \(x_i\), \(x_{ij}\) = the new row, or the new cell, after the change.
  • \(m_i\) = the document length: the total number of tokens in document \(i\).
  • \(\sum\) (the Greek letter sigma, used as a sum sign) = “add these all up”. \(\sum_j c_{ij}\) means “add up the counts over all words \(j\) in row \(i\)”.
  • \(1_{c_{ij} > 0}\) = an indicator: a little switch that is 1 when the condition written under it is true (the count is above 0) and 0 when it is false.

Read aloud: “Raw counts keep each row as it is. Row normalisation divides each row by its total number of tokens. Binary sets each cell to 1 if the word appears and 0 if it does not.”

The slides then call tf-idf “Even more common”. Its formula:

\[tf_{ij} = c_{ij} \qquad\qquad idf_j = \log\left(\dfrac{n}{d_j}\right), \quad d_j = \sum_i 1_{\{c_{ij} > 0\}} \qquad\qquad \mathrm{tf\text{-}idf}_{ij} = tf_{ij} \times idf_j\]

Or in one line:

\[\mathrm{tf\text{-}idf}_{ij} = tf_{ij} \times idf_j = c_{ij} \times \log\left(\frac{n}{d_j}\right)\]

  • \(tf_{ij}\) = the term frequency of word \(j\) in document \(i\). Here it is the plain count \(c_{ij}\).
  • \(n\) = “Total number of documents.”
  • \(d_j\) = “Number of documents containing term \(j\)” (the document frequency). The formula \(\sum_i 1_{\{c_{ij} > 0\}}\) builds it: for each document, the switch gives 1 if the word is there and 0 if not. Adding the switches up over all documents counts the documents that contain the word.
  • \(\log(n/d_j)\) = the rarity weight, \(idf_j\). If the word is in all documents, \(n/d_j = 1\) and \(\log 1 = 0\). If it is in only one document, \(n/d_j = n\), the biggest possible weight.
  • \(\mathrm{tf\text{-}idf}_{ij}\) = the final score for word \(j\) in document \(i\).

Read aloud: “The tf-idf of word \(j\) in document \(i\) is how often the word appears in that document, times the log of the total number of documents divided by the number of documents that contain the word.”

Will the exam want the formula? In 2025 there were no calculations. But a top-grade answer gives the idf formula, \(idf_j = \log(n/d_j)\), and says what \(n\) and \(d_j\) mean. So learn to write that one. A small calculation is possible.

Two details to get right.

  • The slide writes only “log”, without saying which kind, and has no +1 smoothing. Write the formula exactly as the slide does. If you work out a number, say which log you use. The kind of log is called its base: the natural log, log base 10, and so on. Different bases give different numbers but the same ranking of words. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • The slides contradict themselves twice. First, the formula slide says \(tf_{ij} = c_{ij}\), the raw count. But the summary slide says TF “Normalizes raw counts by the total number of terms in the document”, which is the share \(c_{ij}/m_i\) (row normalisation). In the exam: write the tf-idf formula with \(tf_{ij} = c_{ij}\). If you mention TF as a share, call it row normalisation and say both versions appear on the slides. Second, a later slide says tf-idf can “downplay the importance of very rare or common words”. But the slide that explains idf says rare terms get a high idf. Go with that one: rare = high idf.

Reading the course code

The exam has not asked students to write code. This section only helps you recognise what the course notebook does. Here are two lines from it, slightly simplified:

Vectorizer = TfidfVectorizer if WEIGHTING == "tfidf" else CountVectorizer
X = Vectorizer(stop_words=STOP_WORDS, max_df=MAX_DF).fit_transform(speeches["rawtext"])
  • Line 1 picks the tool. If a setting called WEIGHTING says “tfidf”, it uses TfidfVectorizer, which gives tf-idf scores (smoothed idf, rows rescaled to length 1). Otherwise it uses CountVectorizer, which gives raw counts.
  • Line 2 builds the table, X, from the raw text of all 222 speeches. stop_words=STOP_WORDS deletes the words on a stop-word list first. max_df drops words found in more than a given share of the documents. For example, max_df=0.5 drops words found in more than half the speeches. The notebook calls this “a crude version of the idf idea”: like idf, it pushes aside words that are everywhere, but bluntly.

The notebook has no saved results for these lines. Run on Lincoln’s 1862 speech, raw counts without stop-word removal would put function words such as “the” at the top. With tf-idf, words special to that speech would rise. Another notebook shows the catch: tf-idf can also promote rare names. Trump’s 2018 speech has “justin”, “ho” and “ryan” among its top words, which are names of guests and officials.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025 Q2(b), 5 points: describe three ways to normalise the DTM, and the reason for each. In plain words: name three ways to adjust the word-count table so texts compare fairly, and say why each one helps.

The official marking guide gave marks for:

  • Row normalisation (divide each count by the text’s length) → removes the effect of length.
  • Binary (1 if the word appears, 0 if not) → removes the effect of how many times it appears.
  • Tf-idf (word counts re-weighted so rare words count more) → gives less weight to common words and more to distinctive ones.

Model answer Row normalisation divides each count by the total number of tokens in the document (\(x_i = c_i/m_i\)), so long documents do not get high counts only because they are long. Binary coding sets a cell to 1 if the word appears and 0 otherwise (\(x_{ij} = 1_{c_{ij}>0}\)), which removes the dependence on how often a word is repeated. Tf-idf multiplies the count by \(\log(n/d_j)\), where \(n\) is the number of documents and \(d_j\) the number of documents containing the word. This down-weights words that appear everywhere (weight 0 if in all documents) and up-weights words that are distinctive for a document.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Row normalisation turns counts into shares of the text, so a long text does not win only by being long. Binary records only whether a word is there, not how often. Tf-idf boosts words that are special to one text and shrinks words that are everywhere. A word found in every document ends up with weight 0.

Likely True/False item: “A term that occurs in all documents gets idf = 0.”

Model answer True (under the slide formula).

What this answer is saying, in plain words: With the slide formula, a word in all \(n\) documents gets \(\log(n/n) = \log 1 = 0\). In scikit-learn, with its +1 smoothing, it would not be 0.

Likely True/False item: “Rare terms get a low idf.”

Model answer False.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: It is the other way round. Rare words get a high idf, because few documents contain them.

Possible small calculation with the formula \(idf = \log(n/d_j)\). None appeared in 2025. Question 4 of the self-test below shows what one would look like.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • All three methods by name: row normalisation, binary, tf-idf. For each one, give its formula or a one-line description, AND its reason.
  • Why normalise at all: the slides say “long documents will have higher counts just because they are longer”.
  • For tf-idf, its two parts: term frequency (how often the word is in this document) × inverse document frequency (how rare the word is across documents). Give the formula \(idf_j = \log(n/d_j)\) and say what the letters mean: \(n\) is the number of documents, \(d_j\) is the number of documents that contain word \(j\). Then give the effect: a word in every document gets weight 0, and rare words get a high weight.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Naming three methods but giving no reason. Half the marks are for the “why”.
  • Giving only two methods when three are asked.
  • Saying tf-idf “removes rare words”. It does the opposite: it boosts them.
  • Defining \(d_j\) as “how often the term appears in total”. It is the number of documents that contain the word.
  • Mixing up the slides’ TF (term frequency, which on the formula slide is the raw count) with row normalisation (count divided by length) without saying which one you mean.

Key terms to use

  • normalisation: adjusting counts so texts compare fairly
  • raw counts: plain word counts, nothing adjusted
  • row normalisation: each count divided by text length
  • document length: total number of words in a text
  • binary / indicator: 1 if the word appears, else 0
  • term frequency: how often a word is in a text
  • inverse document frequency: score that is high for rare words
  • document frequency \(d_j\): number of documents containing word j
  • tf-idf: word counts re-weighted so rare words count more
  • distinctive vs common words: special to one text vs used everywhere
  • smoothing: a small tweak, like adding 1, avoiding zero problems
  • L2 normalisation: rescaling each row so its length is 1
  • feature selection: keeping only the most useful words
  • weighting: giving some words more importance than others

Quick self-test

  1. “Under the slide formula, a word in every document gets idf = 0.” True or false?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Idf is a word’s rarity score: high if few documents use the word, low if many do. The slide formula is \(\log(n/d_j)\), where \(n\) is the number of documents and \(d_j\) is how many of them contain the word. If a word is in every document, is its score 0?

    True. Why: If the word is in all \(n\) documents, the formula becomes \(\log(n/n) = \log 1 = 0\). A word that every text uses tells you nothing about any one text, like the word “student” in a pile of student essays. Watch out: scikit-learn (the Python toolbox used in class) adds 1 to the formula, so there the score is not 0.

  2. “Binary representation keeps information on how often a word is used.” True or false?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: In the binary table each cell is only 1 (the word appears) or 0 (it does not). Does that still record how many times the word was used?

    False. Why: Binary is a tick box: present or absent. Saying “war” once or fifty times both give a 1. The slides say it “Ignores frequency; focuses on term occurrence”.

  3. “Rare terms receive a high idf.” True or false?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A rare term is a word that only a few documents use. Do such words get a high rarity score (idf)?

    True. Why: Rare words are what set a text apart, like a fingerprint. Fewer documents with the word means a bigger \(n/d_j\), so a bigger log. The slides say “Rare terms: High IDF”.

  4. “A corpus has \(n = 100\) documents; the word ‘inflation’ appears in 10 of them, 4 times in document 7. Using natural log, what is its tf-idf in document 7?”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The collection has 100 texts. “Inflation” is in 10 of them, and appears 4 times in text number 7. Tf-idf = the count in this text × the rarity score (idf). “Natural log” is the ln button on a calculator.

    Answer: \(idf = \ln(100/10) = \ln 10 = 2.303\); tf-idf \(= 4 \times 2.303 = 9.21\).

    Why: First the rarity score: 100 texts divided by the 10 that use the word is 10, and ln 10 is 2.303. Then multiply by how often the word is in text 7: 4 × 2.303 = 9.21.

  5. “Describe three ways to normalise the DTM and why.” (Explain in 2–5 sentences; this is the 2025 Q2(b) style.)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Name three ways to adjust the word-count table so texts compare fairly, and say why each one helps.

    Answer: Row normalisation (divide by document length) removes the effect of length. Binary (1 if the word appears, 0 if not) removes the effect of repetition. Tf-idf (count × \(\log(n/d_j)\)) down-weights words found everywhere, giving weight 0 to a word in all documents, and up-weights distinctive words. The full model answer, word for word, is in the exam section above.

    Why: These are the three methods and reasons the official marking guide rewards. Each method needs its “why” to earn full marks.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • document: one text in the collection. Example: one speech.
  • corpus: the whole collection of texts. Example: all 222 presidential speeches.
  • token: one word as it appears, counting repeats. “data data text” has 3 tokens.
  • document-term matrix (DTM): the table of counts, one row per document and one column per word. A cell of 2 means “this word appears twice in this document”.
  • normalise / transformation: changing the numbers in a fixed way so they become fairer to compare. Like turning test scores into percentages.
  • raw counts: the plain counts in the DTM, before any change.
  • document length (\(m_i\)): the total number of tokens in document \(i\). Doc1 in the example has 6.
  • \(\sum\) (sigma, the sum sign): “add these all up”. \(\sum_j\) means “add over all words \(j\)”.
  • share / proportion: a part of a whole. 3 out of 5 = 0.6 = 60%.
  • row normalisation: dividing every count in a row by that row’s total, so each row adds up to 1. Doc2’s “text” becomes 3 ÷ 5 = 0.6.
  • binary: only two values, 0 or 1, like a light switch. “as” used 5 times becomes 1.
  • indicator (\(1_{c_{ij} > 0}\)): a switch that is 1 when the condition is true (the count is above 0) and 0 when it is false.
  • term frequency (tf): how often a word appears in one document. On the formula slide it is the raw count; the summary slide describes it as a share.
  • document frequency (\(d_j\)): how many documents contain word \(j\) at least once, not the total number of uses. “data” in the example has 3.
  • \(n\): the total number of documents. 3 in the example.
  • log / natural log (ln): a calculator button that shrinks big numbers. ln 1 = 0, ln 3 ≈ 1.1, ln 10 ≈ 2.3, ln 100 ≈ 4.6.
  • base of a log: which kind of log you use (natural log, log base 10, and so on). Different bases give different numbers but the same ranking of words. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • inverse document frequency (idf): the rarity weight, \(\log(n/d_j)\). “Inverse” because it goes up when the document frequency goes down. “Using” in the example gets 1.099.
  • tf-idf: term frequency times inverse document frequency: a count multiplied by a rarity weight. Doc3’s “as” gets 5 × 0.405 ≈ 2.027.
  • distinctive word: a word common in this document but rare in others, so it tells you what the document is about. Example: “eased” in “Interest rates fell as inflation eased.”
  • function words: small grammar words like “the”, “of”, “and” that carry little topic meaning.
  • stop-word list: a list of common words, like “the”, deleted before counting.
  • Python / notebook: a programming language; a class file mixing Python code with its results.
  • scikit-learn: a free Python toolbox for data analysis used in the course. TfidfVectorizer is its tf-idf tool; CountVectorizer is its counting tool.
  • software default: the setting a tool uses if you don’t choose one yourself.
  • smoothing / smoothed idf: a small tweak (adding 1 in a few places, as in scikit-learn) so that no word gets a weight of exactly 0. “data” gets 1 instead of 0.
  • document vector: one row of the table seen as a single object, which you can picture as an arrow.
  • square root (\(\sqrt{\ }\)): the number that, multiplied by itself, gives the number inside. \(\sqrt{9} = 3\).
  • L2 length / L2 normalisation: the length of a row seen as an arrow (square each number, add them up, take the square root, as in Pythagoras); L2 normalisation divides the row by this length so its length becomes 1. Doc1’s length is 3.893.
  • max_df: a setting that drops words found in more than a given share of documents. max_df=0.5 drops words in more than half of them.
  • feature selection: keeping only the useful columns (words) and dropping the rest.
  • threshold: a cut-off line. “Drop terms below a threshold” means drop the ones with a score under some chosen number.
  • weighting: giving some words more importance than others in later calculations.

Sources: Lecture_bow_cosine_tfidf.pdf (Lecture 2a) slides 10, 16–19, 24; GRA4164_Interactive_1_Text_as_data.ipynb cells 21–24, 27; practical_day_1.ipynb cells 5, 11, 12, 15

5. Comparing documents: Euclidean distance vs cosine similarity

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q3(d) asked for a drawing of high vs low cosine similarity; cosine is reused for word embeddings (Lectures 6 and 8)

Why this exists

You read a news article, and the website shows “More articles like this”. How does the computer pick them? It needs one number that says “how alike are these two articles?” Then it can show the articles with the best numbers.

The catch: a long article and a short article on the same topic look very different if you only count words. The long one has bigger counts for everything, only because it is longer. We want a measure that looks at the mix of words, not at the size of the article. This chapter compares two ways of measuring how alike two documents are. One gets fooled by length. The other does not.

The idea in everyday words

An everyday picture first. Take two recipes for the same cake: one for 4 people and one for 12. The big recipe uses three times as much of everything. If you compare the amounts, the two lists look far apart. But the mix is identical: same ingredients, same proportions. A good similarity measure should say “same recipe”, not “different amounts”. Cosine similarity asks “same recipe?”, not “same amount?”.

How a document becomes numbers. A document is one text, such as an article or a speech. A computer counts how often each word appears in each document. It keeps the counts in a table: one row per document, one column per word, and each cell is a count. This table is called the document-term matrix, or DTM (“term” means word, “matrix” means a table of numbers). Sometimes the counts are first re-weighted so that rare, telling words count more and words found everywhere count less. That version is called tf-idf. Either way, each document ends up as one row of numbers.

How a row of numbers becomes an arrow. Keep it to two words so you can draw it, say “good” and “bad”. Draw a graph with two axes, the two reference lines of a graph: one going right for “count of bad” and one going up for “count of good”. The corner point where both axes are 0 is called the origin. A document with good = 2 and bad = 1 becomes an arrow that starts at the origin and ends at the point 1 step right and 2 steps up.

An ordered list of numbers like this, such as (2, 1), is called a vector. You can always draw a vector as an arrow from the origin. A document’s row, seen as a vector, is called a document vector. The slides write it with a little arrow on top: \(\vec{d_1}\) means “the vector of document 1”. The graph where these arrows live, with one axis per word, is called a vector space (the slides say “vector space diagram”). Each axis is one dimension. Two words give a flat picture with 2 dimensions. A real vocabulary has thousands of words, so thousands of dimensions. Nobody can draw that, but a computer can still do the same sums.

The slides put the idea like this: “Two documents are similar if their vectors are similar” … “BUT: How to measure similarity?” There are two options.

Option 1: measure the gap between the arrow tips. Put a ruler between the tips of two arrows and read off the distance. This straight-line ruler distance is called the Euclidean distance. The problem: a long document has bigger counts, so its arrow is longer and its tip sits far out. It ends up far from a short document even if the two talk about the same things in the same mix.

Option 2: measure the angle between the arrows. Ignore how long the arrows are. Only ask how far apart they point. The amount two arrows point apart is their angle, measured in degrees. It is written \(\theta\), the Greek letter “theta”. Two arrows pointing the same way have an angle of 0 degrees, whatever their lengths. Same direction means the same mix of words. A score that ignores length like this is called length-invariant: making the document longer or shorter does not change it.

To turn the angle into a score, use the cosine button on a calculator. It turns an angle into a number: 0 degrees gives 1, and a right angle (90 degrees) gives 0. The cosine of the angle between two document arrows is the cosine similarity. A score of 1 means the arrows point the same way. A score of 0 means they are at a right angle. “At a right angle” has a name: orthogonal. For word counts, orthogonal means the two documents share no words at all.

How the computer works out the cosine without measuring angles. It uses three small steps.

  1. Multiply the matching numbers of the two documents, word by word, and add the results up. This is called the dot product. For (2, 1) and (4, 2): 2 × 4 + 1 × 2 = 10. It is big when both documents use the same words a lot.
  2. Find the length of each arrow (also called its norm): square each number (multiply it by itself), add the squares up, and take the square root (the number that, multiplied by itself, gives what is inside: \(\sqrt{9} = 3\)). This is Pythagoras’ rule for the long side of a right-angled triangle.
  3. Divide the dot product by the two lengths multiplied together. Dividing by the lengths is what removes the effect of document length.

The slides say the result is “bounded between -1 and 1”: it can never go below −1 or above 1.

What each measure is good at, and where cosine breaks.

  • Cosine ignores document length, so a long and a short text on the same topic look alike.
  • Cosine finds “the most similar documents” fast, which is what search and “more like this” boxes need. Euclidean distance, in contrast, grows with document length.
  • Cosine breaks when two texts share words but make opposite arguments. It only sees which words overlap, not what the text means.
  • Cosine also breaks when shared names, writing style or time period make texts look alike although the topic differs.

A real research example: “Tf-idf and cosine similarity can be enough!” The lecture shows a published study by Engle, Giglio, Kelly, Lee & Stroebel (2020), “Hedging climate change news”, in The Review of Financial Studies, a top academic journal in finance. (The slide title says “Hedging Climate Risk”.) The researchers collected a “climate change vocabulary from a corpus of seventy-four authoritative climate change texts” (a corpus is a collection of texts). The biggest words in it were climate, change, carbon, emissions and greenhouse. They then built a WSJ Climate Change News Index. WSJ is the Wall Street Journal, a business newspaper. An index here is one number per period of time that tracks how much the news talks about a topic. Their index runs from 1984 to 2017 and peaks at events such as the Kyoto Protocol, the 2009 Copenhagen conference and the Paris Agreement (big international climate agreements and meetings). The method compares each Wall Street Journal article’s tf-idf vector with the tf-idf vector of the climate vocabulary using cosine similarity. [Not in course files — general knowledge] The point of the slide: a published finance paper needed nothing fancier than the tools in this chapter.

Walk-through example

Part 1: three made-up reviews, by hand. These are our own small example. We count each review on two words, “good” and “bad”. In the table below, each row is a review, each column is a word, and each cell is how many times that word appears in that review.

Review ↓ / Word → good bad
A: “good good bad” 2 1
B: review A written twice 4 2
C: “bad bad good” 1 2

One cell out loud: row B, column “good”. Review A has “good” 2 times. B is A written twice, so 2 × 2 = 4.

Euclidean distance, A to B. Subtract the counts word by word: 4 − 2 = 2 for “good”, and 2 − 1 = 1 for “bad”. Square the differences: 4 and 1. Add them: 5. Take the square root: \(\sqrt{5} \approx 2.24\).

Euclidean distance, A to C. Differences: 2 − 1 = 1 and 1 − 2 = −1. Squares: 1 and 1. Sum: 2. Square root: \(\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41\).

So Euclidean distance says C is closer to A than B is. That feels wrong: B says exactly what A says, only twice.

Cosine, A and B. Dot product: 2 × 4 + 1 × 2 = 8 + 2 = 10. Length of A: \(\sqrt{2 \times 2 + 1 \times 1} = \sqrt{5} \approx 2.236\). Length of B: \(\sqrt{4 \times 4 + 2 \times 2} = \sqrt{20} \approx 4.472\). Multiply the lengths: 2.236 × 4.472 ≈ 10. Cosine = 10 ÷ 10 = 1. Same direction: a perfect match.

Cosine, A and C. Dot product: 2 × 1 + 1 × 2 = 4. Both lengths are \(\sqrt{5}\), and \(\sqrt{5} \times \sqrt{5} = 5\). Cosine = 4 ÷ 5 = 0.8. Similar, but less so.

Cosine gets it right: B is the same review, only longer.

Part 2: the example from the lecture slides. The slides use two words, called “Term a” and “Term b” (the slides suggest, for example, “Term a = {good}, and Term b = {bad}”). They give three documents, \(d_1\), \(d_2\) and \(d_3\), each as two numbers. The slides do not say which number belongs to which term. We read each pair as (Term b, Term a), because that matches the slides’ drawing, where Term b runs to the right and Term a runs up.

In the table below, each row is a document. The two columns are its values for the two terms. One cell out loud: row \(d_1\), column Term a, holds 2: document 1 uses Term a 2 units’ worth.

Document Term b (to the right) Term a (up)
\(\vec{d_1}\) 1.5 2
\(\vec{d_2}\) 0.75 0.75
\(\vec{d_3}\) 2 0.75

The slides describe them in words: \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) “use the terms \(a\) and \(b\) in roughly the same proportion, while \(d_3\) uses term \(b\) much more frequently”. \(d_1\) is only a longer document than \(d_2\).

Step 1: Euclidean distances (subtract, square, add, take the square root).

  • \(d_1\) to \(d_2\): \((1.5 - 0.75)^2 + (2 - 0.75)^2 = 0.5625 + 1.5625 = 2.125\), and \(\sqrt{2.125} = 1.458 \approx\) 1.46
  • \(d_1\) to \(d_3\): \((1.5 - 2)^2 + (2 - 0.75)^2 = 0.25 + 1.5625 = 1.8125\), and \(\sqrt{1.8125} = 1.346 \approx\) 1.35

By Euclidean distance, \(d_3\) looks closer to \(d_1\). The slides name this as a “Potential issue”: the distance from \(d_1\) to \(d_2\) comes out bigger because \(d_1\) “is a longer document and therefore uses all terms more frequently”. They add: “This issue is avoided by using the Cosine similarity measure (bounded between -1 and 1, where 1 (-1) is perfectly similar and 0 is orthogonal).”

Step 2: the length of each arrow. This will be the bottom of the cosine fraction. The symbol \(\|\vec{d_1}\|\) means “the length of the arrow \(\vec{d_1}\)”.

  • \(\|\vec{d_1}\| = \sqrt{1.5^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{6.25} = 2.5\)
  • \(\|\vec{d_2}\| = \sqrt{0.75^2 + 0.75^2} = \sqrt{1.125} = 1.061\)
  • \(\|\vec{d_3}\| = \sqrt{2^2 + 0.75^2} = \sqrt{4.5625} = 2.136\)

Step 3: dot products (multiply matching numbers, then add). This will be the top of the fraction.

  • \(\vec{d_1} \cdot \vec{d_2} = 1.5 \times 0.75 + 2 \times 0.75 = 1.125 + 1.5 = 2.625\)
  • \(\vec{d_1} \cdot \vec{d_3} = 1.5 \times 2 + 2 \times 0.75 = 3 + 1.5 = 4.5\)

Step 4: divide the top by the bottom. Here \(\cos\theta_{12}\) means “the cosine of the angle between documents 1 and 2”.

  • \(\cos\theta_{12} = 2.625 / (2.5 \times 1.061) = 2.625 / 2.652 = 0.990 \approx\) 0.99
  • \(\cos\theta_{13} = 4.5 / (2.5 \times 2.136) = 4.5 / 5.340 = 0.843 \approx\) 0.84

By cosine, \(d_2\) is more similar to \(d_1\). The two measures disagree, and cosine is right: \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) have the same mix, and \(d_1\) is only longer.

A check that length does not matter for cosine (our own check). Double \(d_2\) to (1.5, 1.5), as if the same document were written twice. Its cosine with \(d_1\) stays 0.99. But its Euclidean distance to \(d_1\) changes from 1.46 to 0.50.

The picture below shows the same example. On the left, the dashed lines are the ruler distances between the arrow tips. On the right, the marked angles are what cosine looks at.

Left: Euclidean distance is the dashed line between arrow tips (\(d_1\)–\(d_2\) = 1.46, \(d_1\)–\(d_3\) = 1.35). Right: cosine looks at the angle. The small arc between \(d_1\) and \(d_2\) gives cos = 0.99; the larger shaded angle between \(d_1\) and \(d_3\) gives cos = 0.84. Redrawn from the lecture slides.

Part 3: back to a real word-count table. The lecture’s tiny DTM has 3 documents and 4 words: “Using”, “text”, “as”, “data”. Doc2’s row is (0, 3, 0, 2): it uses “text” 3 times and “data” 2 times. Doc3’s row is (0, 0, 5, 2): it uses “as” 5 times and “data” 2 times. The slides pick out these two rows as the pair to compare.

  • Dot product: the only word both use is “data”, so the sum is 2 × 2 = 4 (every other pair has a 0 in it).
  • Lengths: \(\sqrt{3^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{13} = 3.606\) and \(\sqrt{5^2 + 2^2} = \sqrt{29} = 5.385\).
  • Cosine: \(4 / (3.606 \times 5.385) = 4 / 19.416 = 0.206\). Not very similar.

Now use tf-idf instead of raw counts, with the formula from the lecture slides. Tf-idf gives a weight of 0 to any word found in every document, because such a word cannot tell documents apart. “data” is in all three documents, so it gets weight 0. That was the only word Doc2 and Doc3 shared, so their dot product becomes 0 and the cosine becomes 0: they share no distinctive words. (Our own illustration, checked in Python.)

The formula, explained

Both formulas come from the lecture slides. First, Euclidean distance:

\[d(\vec{d_1}, \vec{d_2}) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{2} (d_{1,i} - d_{2,i})^2}\]

  • \(d(\vec{d_1}, \vec{d_2})\) = the Euclidean distance between document 1 and document 2.
  • \(i\) = which word. In the slide example there are 2 words, so \(i\) goes from 1 to 2.
  • \(d_{1,i}\) = the number for word \(i\) in document 1. The small letters below are an address: “document 1, word \(i\)”.
  • \(\sum_{i=1}^{2}\) (the Greek letter sigma, used as a sum sign) = “add up over all words, from word 1 to word 2”.

Read aloud: “Subtract the two documents’ numbers word by word, square each difference, add them up, and take the square root.”

Second, cosine similarity:

\[\cos\theta_{12} = \frac{\vec{d_1} \cdot \vec{d_2}}{\left\|\vec{d_1}\right\| \left\|\vec{d_2}\right\|} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_{1,i}\, d_{2,i}}{\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_{1,i}^2}\ \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} d_{2,i}^2}}\]

  • \(\vec{d_1}, \vec{d_2}\) = the two documents as vectors: their rows in the DTM, or their tf-idf rows.
  • \(\cos\theta_{12}\) = the cosine of the angle \(\theta\) between the two arrows.
  • \(\vec{d_1} \cdot \vec{d_2} = \sum_i d_{1,i}\, d_{2,i}\) = the dot product: multiply matching numbers and add them up.
  • \(\|\vec{d_1}\| = \sqrt{\sum_i d_{1,i}^2}\) = the length of arrow 1.
  • Dividing by both lengths removes the effect of document length.
  • \(n\) = careful here. In this sum, \(n\) is the number of terms (dimensions), which is 2 in the slide example. Elsewhere in the course, \(n\) means the number of documents. The slide reuses the same letter for something different.

Read aloud: “The cosine similarity of two documents is their dot product divided by the product of their lengths; it is 1 when they point the same way and 0 when they share no terms.”

About the range. The slide says cosine is “bounded between -1 and 1”. Counts and tf-idf weights are never negative, so for DTM rows the cosine is in practice between 0 and 1. [Not in course files — general knowledge] In a True/False item, answer by the slide’s wording.

Will the exam want the formula? In 2025 there were no calculations, but a small calculation like the slide example is possible. A top-grade written answer gives the cosine formula and its range, so learn to write it.

Reading the course code

The exam has not asked students to write code. This section only helps you recognise what the course notebook does. (A notebook is a class file that mixes Python computer code with its results; Python is a programming language.) The notebook takes one speech, called the query: the document you start from when you ask “what is most like this one?” Here the query is Trump’s 2018 speech. The code finds the five speeches most similar to it.

scores = cosine_similarity(tfidf_matrix[query_row], tfidf_matrix).ravel()
scores[query_row] = -1
top = np.argsort(-scores)[:5]
  • Line 1: cosine_similarity works out the cosine between the query speech and every speech in the tf-idf table. ravel flattens the result into one simple list of scores, one per speech.
  • Line 2: sets the query speech’s score with itself to −1. A speech always has cosine 1 with itself, so without this it would come out as its own best match.
  • Line 3: argsort sorts the scores and gives back the positions in order. Putting a minus sign in front of the scores makes it sort from highest to lowest. [:5] keeps the top 5.

The notebook’s saved results are below. Each row is one of the five most similar speeches. The column is its cosine similarity with Trump 2018.

Speech Cosine with Trump 2018
Trump_2017 0.516
Obama_2013 0.445
Obama_2014 0.443
Obama_2015 0.438
Obama_2012 0.427

The nearest speeches share the speaker and the era. So the notebook asks: are we detecting theme, style, era or speaker? Its warning: “Cosine similarity measures overlap in the chosen representation. It is not evidence that the speeches make the same argument.” In plain words: a high cosine means the speeches use similar words, as counted in this table. It does not prove they say the same thing.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025 Q3(d): “Make a graph illustrating” high vs low cosine similarity. This question sat in the block on word embeddings: lists of numbers that stand for single words, taught in later lectures. It was placed there because word vectors are compared with the same cosine. Draw this:

Our own drawing for the exam answer. Vectors used: A = (1, 3), B = (0.7, 1.6), C = (3, 0.3) as (term b, term a). Computed cosines: A–B = 0.996 (angle 5.2°), A–C = 0.409 (angle 65.9°).

Model answer Checklist for the hand drawing (from the 2025 evaluation guideline, plus what makes it top-grade): two labelled axes (count of term a, count of term b); every vector starts at the origin; two vectors pointing almost the same way (small angle, high cosine); one vector pointing a very different way (large angle, low cosine); mark the angles θ; write cos θ ≈ 1 and “low”; make one of the similar arrows shorter, to show that length does not matter.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Draw a graph with one word on each axis. Draw arrows from the corner. Two arrows point nearly the same way (that pair has a high cosine). One arrow points off in a very different direction (low cosine). Mark the angles. Make one of the close pair shorter, to show that only direction counts.

Explain question (likely): “Why does the course prefer cosine similarity to Euclidean distance for comparing documents?” (2–5 sentences.)

Model answer Euclidean distance measures the straight-line gap between the tips of two document vectors, so a long document is far from a short one even if they use words in the same proportions. Cosine similarity measures only the angle between the vectors, by dividing the dot product by both lengths, so document length drops out. In the slide-22 example, Euclidean distance wrongly says \(d_3\) is closer to \(d_1\) (1.35 vs 1.46), while cosine correctly says \(d_2\) is more similar (0.99 vs 0.84). Cosine is 1 for identical direction and 0 for orthogonal (no shared terms).

What this answer is saying, in plain words: The ruler gap punishes long texts, even when they talk about the same things. The angle looks only at direction, meaning the mix of words, so length does not matter. In the slide example (Part 2 of the walk-through above), the ruler picks the wrong document as closest and the angle picks the right one.

Likely True/False item: “Euclidean distance is unaffected by document length.”

Model answer False.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: The ruler gap between arrow tips grows when a document gets longer, because its arrow gets longer.

Likely True/False item: “Cosine similarity of 0 means the documents are orthogonal.”

Model answer True.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: A cosine of 0 means the arrows are at a right angle (90 degrees), which is what orthogonal means.

Also possible: a small calculation like the slide example. And in a reflection question, where you suggest a method for a real task, cosine on tf-idf is a good way to “find the most similar documents”, as the slides put it. For example, you could use it to group similar survey answers.

What a top-grade answer must include

For the drawing:

  • Labelled axes.
  • Arrows (vectors) that start from the origin (the corner point where both axes are 0).
  • Two arrows with a small angle between them (cosine near 1), and one with a large angle (low cosine).
  • The angles marked.

In words:

  • Cosine measures the angle between document vectors (each document drawn as an arrow of word counts), so it ignores length.
  • Euclidean distance measures the gap between the arrow tips, and it grows with document length (the slides’ “potential issue”).
  • Give the formula and the range. The slide says −1 to 1: 1 = perfectly similar, 0 = orthogonal (at right angles).
  • Give a course example: the Engle et al. 2020 climate index.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Drawing dots instead of arrows from the origin.
  • Drawing the “similar” pair with a large angle but tips close together. That shows a small Euclidean distance, not a high cosine.
  • Forgetting to label the axes.
  • Saying a longer document is less similar under cosine. Length does not matter for cosine.
  • Saying cosine 0 means “opposite”. 0 means orthogonal: the documents share no words. −1 would be opposite [Not in course files — general knowledge]. Word counts are never negative, so for them cosine cannot go below 0.

Key terms to use

  • vector space: a map where each word is one direction
  • document vector: a document drawn as an arrow of counts
  • Euclidean distance: straight-line gap between the arrow tips
  • cosine similarity: how closely two arrows point the same way
  • angle θ: theta, the angle between two arrows
  • dot product: multiply matching numbers, then add them up
  • vector length / norm: how long the arrow is
  • length-invariant: not changed by how long a text is
  • orthogonal: at right angles; no shared words
  • bounded between −1 and 1: the score always lies from −1 to 1
  • tf-idf + cosine: rarity-weighted counts compared by their angle
  • most similar documents: texts whose arrows point closest together

Quick self-test

  1. “Euclidean distance is unaffected by document length.” True or false?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Picture each document as an arrow that gets longer as its word counts grow. Euclidean distance is the straight-line gap between two arrow tips, as if you measured it with a ruler. Does the gap stay the same no matter how long a document is?

    False. Why: A long document has bigger counts, so its arrow is longer and its tip sits far away, even if it talks about the same things. Think of two people walking in the same direction: one walks 1 km, the other 10 km. Same direction, but far apart. The slides warn that \(d_1\) ends up far from \(d_2\) only because \(d_1\) “is a longer document”.

  2. “Two documents whose word counts are exactly proportional have cosine similarity 1.” True or false?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Exactly proportional” means one document’s counts are a fixed multiple of the other’s, for example every count doubled. Cosine similarity is a score based on the angle between two arrows: 1 means they point exactly the same way. Do such documents score 1?

    True. Why: Doubling every count makes the arrow longer but keeps its direction, like stretching it. Same direction means zero angle, so cosine is 1. Check with the slide numbers: doubling \(d_2\) leaves its cosine with \(d_1\) at 0.99 (our own check).

  3. “A cosine similarity of 0 means the documents share no terms.” True or false?

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Terms” means words. A cosine of 0 means the two arrows sit at a right angle (orthogonal). Does that mean no word appears in both documents?

    True for count or tf-idf vectors. Why: The cosine formula multiplies the two documents’ counts word by word and adds the results up. Counts are never negative, so the only way to get 0 is when no word appears in both. Think of two shopping lists with nothing in common. The slide says “0 is orthogonal”.

  4. “\(\vec{x} = (2, 0)\) and \(\vec{y} = (1, 1)\). Cosine?”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Two arrows: x goes 2 steps along the first axis and 0 along the second; y goes 1 step along each. Cosine = dot product (multiply matching numbers, then add) divided by the two arrow lengths multiplied together.

    Answer: dot product \(= 2 \times 1 + 0 \times 1 = 2\); lengths \(2\) and \(\sqrt{2} = 1.414\); cosine \(= 2 / 2.828 = 0.707\).

    Why: The dot product is 2 × 1 plus 0 × 1, which is 2. Arrow x has length 2. Arrow y has length \(\sqrt{1^2 + 1^2} = \sqrt{2} = 1.414\). So the cosine is 2 divided by (2 × 1.414), which is 0.707: fairly similar, but not the same direction.

  5. “Why does the course prefer cosine similarity to Euclidean distance for comparing documents?” (Explain in 2–5 sentences.)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Why does the course compare documents by the angle between their arrows (cosine) rather than by the ruler gap between their tips (Euclidean distance)?

    Answer: Euclidean distance grows with document length, so a long text looks far from a short one with the same mix of words. Cosine divides by both lengths, so only direction counts. In the slide example, Euclidean distance wrongly picks \(d_3\) as closest to \(d_1\) (1.35 vs 1.46); cosine correctly picks \(d_2\) (0.99 vs 0.84). Cosine is 1 for the same direction and 0 for orthogonal (no shared terms). The full model answer, word for word, is in the exam section above.

    Why: The course’s whole argument is that length should not decide similarity. Cosine removes length; Euclidean distance does not.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • document: one text, such as one article or one speech.
  • corpus: a whole collection of texts. Example: 74 climate change texts.
  • document-term matrix (DTM): the table of word counts, one row per document and one column per word. Doc2’s row (0, 3, 0, 2) means “text” 3 times and “data” 2 times.
  • tf-idf: counts re-weighted so that rare, telling words count more and words found everywhere count less (a word in every document gets 0).
  • vector: an ordered list of numbers, such as (2, 1). You can draw it as an arrow.
  • document vector (\(\vec{d_1}\)): a document’s row of counts (or tf-idf weights), seen as an arrow. The little arrow on top marks it as a vector.
  • vector space / vector space diagram: the graph where these arrows live, with one axis per word.
  • axis (axes): the reference lines of a graph, one going right and one going up.
  • origin: the corner point (0, 0) where the axes meet. Every arrow starts there.
  • dimension: one direction in the graph, which here means one word. Two words give a flat picture; a real vocabulary has thousands.
  • \(d_{1,i}\): the number for word \(i\) in document 1. The small letters are an address.
  • \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\): “add up over all words, from word 1 to word \(n\)”. In the cosine formula, \(n\) is the number of words, not documents.
  • square / square root: squaring is a number times itself (\(3^2 = 9\)); the square root goes back (\(\sqrt{9} = 3\)).
  • Euclidean distance: the straight-line ruler distance between two arrow tips. Reviews A and B: about 2.24.
  • angle, \(\theta\) (theta): how far apart two arrows point, measured in degrees.
  • cosine: a calculator button that turns an angle into a number: 0 degrees gives 1, a right angle (90 degrees) gives 0.
  • cosine similarity (\(\cos\theta_{12}\)): the cosine of the angle between two document arrows. 1 = same direction, 0 = no shared words. Reviews A and C: 0.8.
  • dot product (\(\vec{d_1} \cdot \vec{d_2}\)): multiply matching numbers and add them up. (2, 1) and (4, 2) give 2 × 4 + 1 × 2 = 10.
  • length / norm (\(\|\vec{d_1}\|\)): how long the arrow is: square each number, add them up, take the square root. (1.5, 2) has length 2.5.
  • orthogonal: at a right angle. For word counts it means the two documents share no words.
  • bounded between −1 and 1: the value can never go below −1 or above 1.
  • proportion / mix: how the words are shared out in a document, such as “twice as much good as bad”.
  • length-invariant: not changed by making the document longer or shorter.
  • word embeddings: lists of numbers for single words (later lectures), compared with the same cosine.
  • query: the document you start from when you ask “what is most like this one?”
  • Python / notebook: a programming language; a class file mixing Python code with its results.
  • cosine_similarity, ravel, argsort: Python tools: the first computes cosines, the second flattens a table into one list, the third sorts and returns the positions in order.
  • index (climate news index): one number per period of time that tracks how much the news talks about a topic.
  • WSJ / The Review of Financial Studies: the Wall Street Journal, a business newspaper; and a top academic journal in finance.

Sources: Lecture_bow_cosine_tfidf.pdf (Lecture 2a) slides 8, 10, 20–24; practical_day_1.ipynb cells 12, 15, 16

Part II — Methods built on the bag-of-words

6. The method map: supervised vs unsupervised text methods (L3)

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — you need it to place any method in the right box (and to spot a wrong “learning type” in a True/False statement).

Why this exists

Picture a small online shop with 10,000 customer reviews. The owner wants to know three things:

  • “Are people happy?”
  • “What star rating would this new review get?”
  • “What do people talk about most?”

Nobody can read 10,000 reviews by hand, so a computer has to help. But there are many ways a computer can help, and they need different things from you. Some need a correct answer for every review, such as the star rating the customer gave. Some need a rule that you write yourself. Some need nothing at all and find patterns on their own.

This chapter is a map. It sorts every text method in this part of the course into boxes, using one question: do I already know what should come out? The exam uses this map a lot, mostly in True/False statements that put a method in the right box or the wrong one.

The idea in everyday words

Step 0: the computer turns text into a table of counts.

A computer cannot read the way you do. What it can do is count. So for every text, it counts how often each word appears.

Each single text we study is called a document. One review is a document. So is one speech, one email or one newspaper article.

The counts go into one big table:

  • each row is one document;
  • each column is one word;
  • each cell says how many times that word appears in that document.

For example, in the review “great food, tasty food”, the cell for the word “food” holds 2.

A table of numbers with rows and columns is called a matrix. This particular table is called the document-term matrix (“term” = word). The course writes it with the capital letter \(C\) (for “counts”).

We often need to talk about one row of that table. The course calls the row of document number \(i\) by the name \(c_i\). The small \(i\) is a “which one” tag: \(c_1\) is the first document’s row of counts, \(c_3\) is the third document’s row. So \(c_i\) means “the word counts of document \(i\)”.

Everything in this chapter starts from that table. The question is what we do with it next.

Step 1: ask “do I already know what should come out?”

There are three possible answers. Each one leads to a different box on the map.

Answer A: “Yes, I have the correct answer for every text.”

Sometimes each text comes with its correct answer already stored next to it. A review comes with the stars the customer gave. An email comes marked “spam” or “not spam”. A speech comes with the political party of the speaker.

That stored answer is called a label. Texts that come with their labels are called labelled data. The thing we want to know or guess is called the outcome, and the course writes it with the letter \(y\). So \(y_i\) is the outcome of document number \(i\), for example “document 3 got 4 stars”. When we really have the outcome in our data, we say it is observed.

Here the computer studies the texts and their answers. It learns the link between them, for example “reviews that say ‘great’ tend to get more stars”. A link you can see in real data like this is called an empirical relationship. Then the computer uses that link to guess the answer for new texts it has never seen. The examples it learns from are called the training data.

This is called supervised learning. Think of a student who studies past exams together with the correct answers. The answer sheet “supervises” the learning: it tells the student when they are right or wrong.

Two families live in this box:

  • Regression guesses a number, such as a star rating. Two versions in the course are OLS (the standard way to draw the best straight line through data) and Lasso (a version that drops words that do not help). Chapter 8 explains both.
  • Classification sorts texts into boxes, such as “spam” or “not spam”. The boxes are called classes, and the method that does the sorting is a classifier. The course’s classifier is Naive Bayes, which learns how often each word appears in each class (Chapter 9).

Answer B: “No, I have no answers, but I write the rule myself.”

Sometimes you have no stars, no labels, nothing. But you decide the rule in advance. For example: “make a list of happy words and a list of angry words; for each review, count the happy words and subtract the angry words.”

A hand-made list of words like this is called a dictionary, and this approach is the dictionary method. A close cousin is Boolean search: a search rule built with AND, OR and NOT, like a library search filter (“economy AND uncertainty”). Chapter 7 covers both in detail. Dictionaries are often used to measure sentiment, which means how positive or negative a text sounds.

The course puts these methods in the supervised box too. This is the part that confuses almost everyone, so it gets its own section right below.

Answer C: “No answers, and no rule either.”

Sometimes you have only the texts. You ask the computer to find structure on its own. It notices which words tend to show up together and which documents look alike, and it forms groups. Only afterwards do you look at the groups and give them names.

This is called unsupervised learning. Think of sorting a huge pile of mixed letters with no instructions. You put similar letters together, and only at the end do you name the piles: “bills”, “love letters”, “ads”. Nobody told you what the piles should be.

The main methods here are topic models. A topic is a group of words that tend to appear together, such as {goal, match, team}. A topic model finds the topics and says how much of each topic is in each document. You choose how many topics you want, and the course calls that number \(K\). The two topic models in the course are LSA (Latent Semantic Analysis) and LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation), both in Chapter 10. LSA uses pure table arithmetic. Its main tool is called SVD (singular value decomposition), a maths tool that splits one big table into smaller ones. LDA is instead built on chances (probabilities).

A later lecture adds word embeddings: methods that turn each word into a list of numbers, so that words with similar meanings get similar lists. They are built with neural nets (a flexible kind of computer model) and also with SVD.

A fourth, in-between kind: the answers come from the text itself.

Imagine you take a sentence, hide one word, and ask the computer to guess it. You did not have to label anything by hand, yet there is a correct answer: the word you hid. This is called semi-supervised or self-supervised learning.

This matters later in the course. word2vec (a word-embedding method) and LLMs (large language models, the very large text-predicting models behind chatbots) both learn this way: they guess the next or a hidden word, and the real word is the answer.

The confusing one: why dictionaries count as “supervised”

Here is the puzzle. A dictionary method has no answer column. Nobody gave it star ratings. It learns nothing from data. So why on earth does the course call it “supervised”?

The key is what “supervised” means in this course. It does not mean “we have labelled data”. It means: we know what comes out. There are two ways to know what comes out:

  1. You have the correct answers, and the computer learns the link from them (Answer A).
  2. You wrote the link yourself, so you know it already (Answer B).

To see why the second one counts, we need one more word: function. A function is a fixed rule that turns an input into an output, like a little machine. “Take the number and add 2” is a function: put in 5, out comes 7. The course writes a function as \(f()\). The brackets are where the input goes.

A dictionary method is exactly such a machine:

  • the input is one document’s word counts, \(c_i\);
  • the rule is “count the happy words, subtract the angry words”;
  • the output is a score.

Now the important part. You wrote that rule down before you looked at any data. Every piece of it is visible. Nothing in it is estimated or learned. So if someone hands you any review, you can work out its score with a pencil, and you will get the same score every time. You know the output for every possible input in advance.

The course has a name for this: the function has a known functional form. “Functional form” means the shape of the rule. “Known” means it is fixed and written down by you. The lecture puts it like this: “Although we do not know the outcome, we call these methods supervised because we know the functional form. Thus, if we get some input \(c_i\) to \(f()\), we know what the output will be.”

A useful way to remember it: ask who is in control of what comes out.

  • Supervised with labels: the answer sheet controls it. The computer must match the answers.
  • Dictionary: you control it. You hand the computer the rule, and it follows it exactly. You are the supervisor.
  • Unsupervised: nobody controls it. The computer builds its own groups, and you find out what they mean only afterwards.

Think of a cake recipe you wrote yourself. Nobody taught you with example cakes, but you know exactly what cake comes out. That is a dictionary. Compare a guest who tastes 50 dishes and sorts them into groups that “seem similar”. That is unsupervised.

So what is missing in a dictionary method? The true answer. The thing we really want to measure, such as how happy the writer truly is, is hidden. We can never look it up. Something real but hidden like this is called latent. The course calls the hidden true value of document \(i\) by the name \(v_i\). Our score is only an estimate of it. A small hat on a letter means “our estimate of it”, so the course writes our score as \(\hat v_i\) (say “v-hat”).

Two exam traps come straight from this:

  • “Dictionary methods are unsupervised, because there is no outcome \(y\).” False. There is indeed no \(y\), but the rule is known, so the course calls them supervised.
  • “Dictionary methods are supervised, because we observe the outcome \(y\).” False. Right box, wrong reason. We do not observe \(y\). They are supervised because the rule is known.

[Not in course files — general knowledge] Outside this course, many textbooks use “supervised” only for learning from labelled examples, and would not call a dictionary method “learning” at all. In this exam, follow the course: dictionaries belong in the supervised box, because their function is known.

Walk-through example

Here are three very short reviews:

  • R1: “great food, tasty food”
  • R2: “bad delivery, wasted money”
  • R3: “great food, late delivery”

First, the word-count table. Each row is one review. Each column is one word that appears in the reviews. Each cell says how many times that word appears in that review.

Review great food tasty bad delivery wasted money late
R1 1 2 1 0 0 0 0 0
R2 0 0 0 1 1 1 1 0
R3 1 1 0 0 1 0 0 1

For example, the cell for R1 and “food” is 2, because “food” appears twice in “great food, tasty food”. This is the document-term matrix \(C\). Row R1 is \(c_1\).

Now, what each box on the map would do with these reviews. In the next table, each row is again one review. Each column shows what one branch of the map would produce:

  • column 2: the dictionary score, which is happy words minus angry words;
  • column 3: the answer key, the stars the customer gave, which a supervised method learns from;
  • column 4: the themes an unsupervised method might find.
Review Rule-based (dictionary) score = happy words − angry words Answer key (stars the customer gave), which a supervised method learns from Themes an unsupervised method might find
R1 1 − 0 = +1 5 food
R2 0 − 2 = −2 1 delivery
R3 1 − 0 = +1 4 half food, half delivery

The dictionary column, worked out in words. Our happy list is {good, great}. Our angry list is {bad, wasted}. Review R2 says “bad delivery, wasted money”.

  • Happy words in R2: none. That gives 0.
  • Angry words in R2: “bad” and “wasted”. That gives 2.
  • Score = 0 − 2 = −2.

Nobody learned anything here. We wrote the rule and applied it. That is the “known function” from the section above: anyone with the two lists gets −2 for R2. Notice R3, though. “late” is a complaint, but it is not on our angry list, so the rule misses it. The rule only sees what you put in it.

The stars column. These are real answers from the customers, so this is the answer key. A supervised method would look at all three rows and learn something like “‘great’ goes with high stars; ‘bad’ and ‘wasted’ go with low stars”. Then it can guess the stars for a fourth review it has never seen.

The themes column. This needs no answers and no rule. The computer notices that “food” shows up in R1 and R3, and “delivery” shows up in R2 and R3. So it can form two groups of words: one with “food” and “tasty”, one with “delivery”, “late” and “money”. It then says R3 is a bit of each. The computer does not know what the groups mean. We are the ones who name them “food” and “delivery”.

One task, four methods. Now take a single job, “is this customer review positive?”, and solve it with each box. In the table below, each row is one method. The columns say what you must have before you start, and what you get at the end. This illustration is made up for this guide.

Method What you need What you get
Dictionary A word list (good, great / bad, wasted) Score = number of positive words − number of negative words, per review
Lasso regression 500 reviews with a star score \(y\) A weight for each word (how much that word pushes the stars up or down); predicted stars for new reviews
Naive Bayes 500 reviews labelled “good”/“bad” The chance that a review is “good”, given its words; a class for each new review
LDA / LSA Only the reviews, no labels \(K\) topics (“price”, “delivery”, “staff”…) and each review’s mix of them

Only the last row needs no answer key and no hand-written rule. That is exactly what makes it unsupervised.

What the map is good at, and where it stops.

  • Good: it tells you which family of methods fits the data you actually have. Have answers → supervised. No answers → unsupervised.
  • Good: it protects you from the favourite exam trap. Dictionaries count as supervised, even though there is no answer column.
  • Limit: the map tells you what kind of method fits, not which single method is best.
  • Limit: real projects often mix boxes. For example, you can find topics first and then use them as inputs in a regression (Chapter 10 mentions this).

The formula, explained
