None of these formulas needs to be calculated in the exam. In 2025 the exam had no calculations. But the short labels below appear on the lecture’s map, and knowing what they say helps you answer True/False questions about it.

The course’s own definitions. The lecture defines the boxes in words. Two letters appear in them: \(y\) is the outcome (the answer), and \(x\) is the input you use to guess it, here the word counts. The inputs are called explanatory variables.

  • Supervised: “We know the outcome and the explanatory variables, but need to learn their empirical relationship. Think, e.g., linear regression y = βx + e.”
  • Unsupervised: “We do not know the outcome, but learn relationships in the data (x) directly from the algorithm.”
  • Semi-supervised: “Input (x) and output (y) given by the structure of the training data itself.”

An algorithm is a recipe a computer follows step by step. The supervised definition mentions one formula, so here it is.

Linear regression:

\[y = \beta x + e\]

  • \(y\) = the outcome you want to guess, such as the star rating.
  • \(x\) = an input, such as how many times “great” appears.
  • \(\beta\) (the Greek letter “beta”) = the weight, also called the coefficient: how much one unit of the input changes the guess. If \(\beta = 2\), one more “great” adds 2 to the guess.
  • \(e\) = the error: the part the formula gets wrong, the gap between the guess and the truth.

Read aloud: “the outcome equals a weight times the input, plus whatever the straight line misses.” In supervised learning, the computer uses the answers \(y\) to find a good value for \(\beta\). This is called linear regression, because it draws a straight line. Chapter 8 builds it from zero.

The dictionary rule:

\[\hat v_i = f(c_i) \quad \text{for a known function } f(), \quad v_i \text{ latent}\]

  • \(c_i\) = the word counts of document \(i\) (its row in the table).
  • \(f()\) = the rule you wrote, such as “happy words minus angry words”.
  • \(\hat v_i\) = the score the rule gives: our estimate for document \(i\).
  • \(v_i\) = the true hidden value (for example, the writer’s real mood), which we never see. “Latent” means hidden.

Read aloud: “our estimate for document \(i\) is what we get when we feed its word counts into a rule we wrote ourselves; the true value stays hidden.” The word “known” is the whole reason this sits in the supervised box.

The “given” bar. The next labels use chances. A probability is a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely something is: 0 = never, 1 = certain, 0.5 = a coin flip. The course writes “the chance of A” as \(p(A)\). The vertical bar \(\mid\) is read “given”, so \(p(A \mid B)\) means “the chance of A, given that we know B”.

  • \(p(y_i \mid c_i)\) = “the chance of outcome \(y\), given these words”. This is text regression: it goes from the words to the outcome. Example: the chance of 5 stars, given that the review says “great”.
  • \(p(c_i \mid y_i)\) = “the chance of these words, given the class”. This is Naive Bayes. It goes the other way first: it learns which words each class tends to use. Example: how likely the word “prize” is, given the email is spam. It then uses Bayes’ rule, a rule for flipping the second kind of chance into the first, to guess the class of a new text.
  • \(f(c_i \mid v_i)\) = the words explained by a few hidden factors \(v_i\), using a plain maths function, not a chance. This is LSA. It is table arithmetic, “not a probabilistic model”.
  • \(p(c_i \mid v_i)\) = the chance of these words, given hidden topics \(v_i\). This is LDA. Same goal as LSA, but told as a story in chances: hidden topics produce the words.

Notice which way the bar points. Regression goes from text to outcome (\(y\) given \(c\)). Naive Bayes and the topic models go from the class or topic to the text (\(c\) given \(y\) or \(v\)).

The whole map in one table. Each row is one method from the lecture. The columns give its box, the short label the lecture writes under it, and what that label means in plain words.

Method Branch Slide label In plain words
Boolean / dictionary Supervised \(\hat v_i = f(c_i)\) for known function \(f()\), \(v_i\) treated as latent We write down the rule (word lists, AND/OR) and apply it to each document’s counts to get a score such as sentiment or uncertainty.
Text regression, OLS/Lasso Supervised \(p(y_i \mid c_i)\), \(y_i\) observed Predict an observed outcome from the words.
Naive Bayes Supervised \(p(c_i \mid y_i)\), \(y_i\) observed Learn which words each class produces, then flip it with Bayes’ rule (a rule that turns “chance of these words given the class” into “chance of the class given these words”) to guess the class.
LSA Unsupervised \(f(c_i \mid v_i)\), \(v_i\) latent Find a few hidden factors \(v_i\) that explain the counts; a plain mathematical function, not a probability model.
LDA Unsupervised \(p(c_i \mid v_i)\), \(v_i\) latent Same goal, but as a probability model: hidden topics generate the words.

The whole map as a picture. The lecture draws the map as a family tree, and shows it several times, each time with one branch in red. At the top is NLP (natural language processing: getting computers to work with human language). It splits into the supervised and unsupervised boxes, and each box splits into two families. Under each family is its short label from the table above. “(Lecture 6)” means word embeddings come later in the course.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

Type 1: True/False statements that put a method in a box.

  • “Dictionary methods are unsupervised” → False. The rule is known, so the course calls them supervised.
  • “LDA is an unsupervised method” → True. LDA is the topic model from Chapter 10. It has no answers and no rule; it finds topics on its own.

Type 2: the 2025 statement about LLMs. In 2025, T/F (f) said: “Large Language Models are estimated using unsupervised learning”. The answer was False. The official guideline gives only “False”. The reason is in the course’s lecture on training LLMs: “Training LLMs is often called self-supervised training”. That means the answers come from the text itself: the model guesses the next word, and the real next word is the answer. It is the same trap as above: the statement puts a method in the wrong learning type.

Type 3: the reflection question. This is the open question where you plan your own text study. Say which box your method belongs to. Then say why that fits your data: do your texts come with answers (labels) or not? This shows the examiner good judgement.

Type 4: a short “explain” question. “What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised text methods? Give one example of each.”

Model answer In supervised methods we know the outcome (or the mapping) and learn or apply the link between the text and that outcome, like a regression \(y=\beta x+e\); e.g. Naive Bayes learns from speeches labelled by party to classify new speeches. In unsupervised methods there is no outcome; the algorithm finds structure in the text itself, e.g. LDA finds topics (clusters of words) and each document’s topic mix. Dictionary methods are also counted as supervised: there is no observed outcome, but the researcher fixes the function \(f()\), so the output for any input is known (L3 slide 7).

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Supervised means the computer has answers (or a fixed rule) and learns or applies the link from text to answer, like the straight-line formula “outcome = weight × input + error”. Example: Naive Bayes studies speeches marked with the speaker’s party, then guesses the party of new speeches. Unsupervised means there are no answers, so the computer finds groups of words by itself, like LDA finding topics. Dictionaries still count as supervised, because you write the rule yourself and so you know what comes out for any text.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • One line defining supervised (the computer learns from texts that come with answers) and one line defining unsupervised (no answers; the computer finds groups on its own).
  • The correct box for each method.
  • The reason why dictionaries count as “supervised”: the rule is fixed in advance. The lecture calls this a “known functional form” (you already know the formula that turns a text into a score).
  • Which way each model points:
    • text regression guesses the outcome from the words (\(p(y\mid c)\), “the chance of outcome \(y\) given the words \(c\)”);
    • Naive Bayes describes the words from the class (\(p(c\mid y)\), “the chance of these words given the class”);
    • topic models have no outcome at all. They use a hidden variable instead (latent \(v\), for example a document’s mix of topics, which nobody observes).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Calling dictionaries “unsupervised because there is no \(y\)” (no answer column). The course still puts them in the supervised box, because the rule is known.
  • Mixing up text regression (\(p(y_i\mid c_i)\): guess the outcome from the words) with Naive Bayes (\(p(c_i\mid y_i)\): describe the words given the class).
  • Putting LSA (the table-arithmetic topic model from Chapter 10) in the supervised box because its maths looks a bit like regression maths.

Key terms to use

  • supervised (learns from texts with answers, or a fixed rule)
  • unsupervised (no answers; finds groups by itself)
  • semi-supervised (the answers come from the text itself)
  • latent variable \(v_i\) (hidden thing we never observe directly)
  • known functional form \(f()\) (the text-to-score rule is fixed in advance)
  • document-term matrix \(C\) (table: documents as rows, word counts as columns)
  • \(p(y_i\mid c_i)\) (chance of the outcome, given the words)
  • \(p(c_i\mid y_i)\) (chance of the words, given the class)
  • topic model (finds themes in texts without any answers)

Quick self-test

  1. True/False: “Boolean and dictionary methods are called supervised because we observe the outcome \(y\).”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Boolean and dictionary methods are the “count the keywords on my list” methods. “Supervised” is the box for methods that learn from answers or follow a fixed rule. “Observe the outcome \(y\)” means we have the true answer (like the star rating) in our data. So the statement says: “they are in the supervised box because we have the answers”.

    Answer: False. Why: We do not have the answers. They are in the supervised box for a different reason: the researcher writes the rule (the function \(f()\), the formula from text to score) in advance, so we know exactly what comes out for any text. Think of a recipe you wrote yourself. Nobody taught you with examples, but you know what the cake will be.

  2. True/False: “Text regression models \(p(y_i \mid c_i)\) while Naive Bayes models \(p(c_i \mid y_i)\).”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: \(p(A\mid B)\) reads “the chance of A, given that we know B”. \(y_i\) is the answer for document number \(i\) (its outcome or class). \(c_i\) is that document’s word counts. So the statement says: text regression asks “given these words, what is the outcome?”, while Naive Bayes asks “given this class, how likely are these words?”

    Answer: True. Why: Text regression goes from words to outcome, like guessing a house’s price from its features. Naive Bayes goes the other way first. It learns which words each class tends to use (football fans say “goal” a lot), then uses Bayes’ rule to flip it round and pick the most likely class.

  3. True/False: “LSA is a probabilistic model of how text is generated.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: LSA is a topic model that finds themes by breaking the big word-count table into smaller tables. A “probabilistic model of how text is generated” is a story, told in chances, of how each word got written, such as “pick a topic, then pick a word from that topic”. Does LSA tell such a story?

    Answer: False. Why: LSA is pure table maths. It summarises the table but gives no chance-based story of how the words came about. That is why the lecture writes it with a plain function \(f(c_i\mid v_i)\) and not with a probability \(p\), and calls it “not a probabilistic model”. It is like a map that summarises a city without explaining how the city was built. LDA is the topic model that does tell the story.

  4. Explain (2–5 sentences): “What is the difference between supervised and unsupervised text methods? Give one example of each.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Explain the two boxes of the map, and name one method from each box.

    Answer: the model answer in “What the exam asks, and how to answer” above. Why: In short: supervised = we know what comes out (answers to learn from, or a rule we wrote), e.g. Naive Bayes on speeches labelled by party; unsupervised = no answers, the computer finds groups itself, e.g. LDA topics; and dictionaries are supervised because their function is known.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • NLP (natural language processing): getting computers to work with human language. A spell checker or a translation app is NLP.
  • document: one piece of text we study: one review, one speech, one email, one newspaper article.
  • word count: how many times a word appears in a document. In “great food, tasty food”, the count of “food” is 2.
  • matrix: a table of numbers with rows and columns, like a spreadsheet.
  • document-term matrix (\(C\), DTM): the word-count table. Rows are documents, columns are words, each cell is how often that word appears in that document.
  • \(c_i\): the row of the table that belongs to document number \(i\). The little \(i\) is a “which one” tag: \(c_3\) is the third document’s row.
  • method / algorithm: a recipe a computer follows step by step, like a cooking recipe.
  • outcome (\(y\)): the thing you want to know or guess, such as star rating or party. \(y_i\) is the outcome of document \(i\).
  • observed: we actually have it in our data. The stars a customer gave are observed.
  • explanatory variables (\(x\)): the inputs you use to make the guess. Here, the word counts.
  • label / labelled data / answer key: the correct answer stored next to each text, like “spam” written on an email. Labelled data = texts that come with their answers.
  • supervised: in this course, “we know what comes out”: either the computer learns from examples that come with answers, or it follows a rule you wrote. Like a student who studies past exams together with the correct answers.
  • unsupervised: no answers and no rule; the computer finds groups on its own. Like sorting a pile of mixed photos into piles that look alike, then naming the piles.
  • semi-supervised / self-supervised: the answers come from the text itself. Hide a word in a sentence and ask the computer to guess it: the hidden word is the answer.
  • training data: the examples the computer learns from, like the practice exams.
  • empirical relationship: a link you see in real data, such as “reviews with ‘great’ tend to get more stars”.
  • linear regression, \(y = \beta x + e\): a straight-line formula. The outcome \(y\) equals a weight \(\beta\) times an input \(x\), plus an error \(e\) for what the line misses. Chapter 8 builds it from zero.
  • \(\beta\) (beta), weight, coefficient: the number that says how much one input matters. If \(\beta = 2\), one more “great” adds 2 to the guess.
  • \(e\) (error): the part the formula gets wrong, the gap between guess and truth.
  • function, \(f()\): a fixed rule that turns an input into an output, like “take the number and add 2”.
  • known functional form: the rule is written down in advance, so for any input you know the output. That is why dictionaries count as “supervised”. Example: “happy words minus angry words” gives R2 a score of −2, for anyone who applies it.
  • latent / latent variable \(v_i\): hidden; something real we cannot see directly, like a writer’s mood or a hidden theme.
  • \(\hat v_i\) (v-hat): a hat on a letter means “our estimate of it”. \(\hat v_i\) is our best guess of the hidden \(v_i\).
  • Boolean search: a search rule built with AND, OR and NOT, like a library search filter.
  • dictionary method: you write lists of words (happy words, angry words) and count hits.
  • sentiment: how positive or negative a text sounds.
  • regression: a method for guessing a number from inputs (Chapter 8).
  • OLS (ordinary least squares): the standard way to draw the best straight line through points (Chapter 8).
  • Lasso: a regression that charges a fee for big weights so that useless words drop out (Chapter 8).
  • classification / classifier / class: sorting things into boxes. The boxes are the classes (“spam”, “not spam”); the method that sorts is a classifier (Chapter 9).
  • Naive Bayes: a classifier that learns how often each word appears in each class, then picks the most likely class (Chapter 9).
  • probability: a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely something is. 0 = never, 1 = certain, 0.5 = a coin flip.
  • \(p(y_i\mid c_i)\): read the bar “\(\mid\)” as “given”. “The chance of outcome \(y\) given these words.” Example: the chance of 5 stars given the review says “great”.
  • \(p(c_i\mid y_i)\): the reverse: “the chance of these words given the class”. Example: how likely the word “prize” is, given the email is spam.
  • Bayes’ rule: a rule for flipping the second kind of chance into the first (Chapter 9).
  • topic: a group of words that tend to show up together, like {goal, match, team}.
  • topic model: an unsupervised method that finds topics and says how much of each topic is in each document (Chapter 10).
  • \(K\): the number of topics you ask for.
  • LSA (Latent Semantic Analysis): a topic method that uses pure table arithmetic (Chapter 10).
  • LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation): a topic method built on chances (Chapter 10).
  • SVD (singular value decomposition): the maths tool LSA uses to split a big table into smaller ones (Chapter 10).
  • word embeddings / neural nets: later methods (Lecture 6) that turn each word into a list of numbers so that similar words get similar lists.
  • word2vec / LLM (large language model): word2vec is a word-embedding method; an LLM is a very large text-predicting model, like the one behind a chatbot. Both learn by guessing hidden words.
  • T/F: a True/False exam question.

Sources: Lecture 3 “Bag-of-words based methods” (Lecture_bow_based_methods.pdf), slides 4–7 (tree on slide 4, repeated on slides 6, 13, 21 and 30; definitions on slide 5; dictionaries as “supervised” on slide 7), 13, 21, 30, 43 (“not a probabilistic model”); Interactive Notebook 2, cell 21; LLM training lecture (Lecture_llm_trainingandfinetuning.pdf), slide 4 (“self-supervised training”); 2025 exam T/F (f); the shop-review illustrations are made up for this guide, with method labels from slides 4–30.

7. Boolean and dictionary methods: EPU, sentiment dictionaries, and their weaknesses (L3)

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q2(c) (5 points, Boolean search + EPU) and 2025 T/F (h) (dictionaries and polysemy).

Why this exists

Economists wanted to measure how worried people are about what the government will do to the economy: new taxes, budget fights, new rules. There is no thermometer for that kind of worry. But newspapers write about it every day.

Three researchers, Baker, Bloom and Davis, had an idea. Count how many newspaper articles each month talk about this kind of worry, and track that number over time. When the count goes up, worry is going up.

A company could do the same with customer emails, for example by counting how many mention “refund” or “cancel”. A shop could score each review as happy or unhappy by counting happy and unhappy words.

This chapter is about the most basic way to turn text into a number: pick the words, count them, and adjust for size. The lecture says it is “by far the most used approach in economics and finance” and “very simple, just counting and normalizing”.

The idea in everyday words

Step 1: decide what you want to measure. For example, worry about government policy, or how positive a review is.

The thing you want is usually something real that you cannot see directly. Nobody can look up “how worried the country is” or “how happy this customer truly is”. Something real but hidden like this is called a latent concept. Policy here means what the government decides to do: taxes, rules, budgets, interest rates.

Step 2: write down the words that signal it. For worry: “uncertain”, “uncertainty”. For a happy review: “good”, “great”. A word you search for is a keyword. Your hand-made list of keywords is called a dictionary (or word list). Each time a word in the text matches a word on your list, that is one hit. So “bad” in a review is one hit for the unhappy list.

Step 3: choose the type of rule. There are two flavours.

  • A Boolean rule says which mix of words a document must contain. You join words with three little connecting words, called Boolean operators:

    • AND: both parts must be present. “uncertainty AND economy” needs both words in the same article.
    • OR: at least one part is enough. “uncertain OR uncertainty” is happy with either word.
    • NOT: this part must be absent.

    A document either passes the rule or it does not. This is exactly like a shop website filter: “shoes AND red AND NOT sandals”. Using such a rule on a pile of texts is called a Boolean search.

  • A dictionary rule uses two (or more) word lists, for example positive words and negative words. You count the hits on each list and combine them, for example “positive hits minus negative hits”. This is like a teacher’s marking sheet with a column of “good words” and a column of “bad words”: tick every match, and score the essay as ticks in one column minus ticks in the other.

Step 4: run the rule over every document and count. Each single text is called a document: one article, one review, one speech. For a Boolean rule you count how many documents pass. For a dictionary you work out each document’s score.

To do this, the computer first counts how often each word appears in each document. It keeps the counts in a big table: one row per document, one column per word, and each cell says how many times that word appears in that document. This table is called the document-term matrix. The row for document number \(i\) is written \(c_i\) (“the word counts of document \(i\)”). The small \(i\) is a “which one” tag: \(c_3\) is the third document’s row.

Step 5: make the counts fair. A newspaper that prints twice as many articles will get about twice as many hits, even if nobody is more worried. So you divide by the total number of articles. For a dictionary score, you divide by the number of words in the text, so a long speech does not look more emotional only because it is long. Dividing by size to make numbers fair to compare is called normalising. The result, a part divided by the whole, is a share. For example, 4 worried articles out of 200 is a share of 0.02.

Step 6 (optional): rescale so that “normal” = 100. You take the average (add the numbers and divide by how many there are) over some chosen period, and rescale so that this average month equals 100. Then a month at 150 means “50% more than a normal month”. One number that tracks something over time and is rescaled to be easy to read is called an index, like a price index. A list of values in time order, one per month or year, is a series or time series.

Why the course calls this “supervised”. The course sorts text methods into boxes. “Supervised” in this course means “we know what comes out”. Here nobody hands us the correct answers: the true worry or true mood stays hidden. But we wrote the rule ourselves, before seeing any data. Nothing in the rule is learned from the data. So if someone gives us any document, we can work out its score with a pencil, and we always get the same score. A fixed rule that turns an input into an output is called a function, written \(f()\). Because we wrote it ourselves, it is a known function. That known rule is why the course calls dictionary and Boolean methods “supervised” (Chapter 6 explains the whole map).

The course writes this in a short line. The hidden true value for document \(i\) is called \(v_i\). Our score is only an estimate of it, and a small hat on a letter means “our estimate of”, so our score is \(\hat v_i\) (“v-hat”). The lecture says: \(v_i\) “represents some latent concept, e.g., the sentiment or political uncertainty, and \(f(c_i)\) is a known function giving an estimate \(\hat v_i\).” In plain words: feed a document’s word counts into our fixed rule, and out comes our guess of the hidden thing. Sentiment (or tone) means how positive or negative a text sounds.

The two flavours side by side. The lecture compares them in a table. Each column is one flavour. Each row is one step of the recipe. Two names appear in it:

  • General Inquirer: a ready-made, general-purpose list of positive and negative words.
  • Loughran and McDonald (2011): a word list made specially for finance texts.

The sign “#” means “number of”. So \(\#W^{pos}\) is the number of positive words in a text, and \(\#W^{neg}\) the number of negative words.

Dictionary-based technique Boolean-based technique
Step 1 Use general dictionaries (e.g. General Inquirer, a ready-made general-purpose word list) or make your own (e.g. Loughran and McDonald (2011) for finance) Define words of interest, e.g. uncertainty, uncertainties, …
Step 2 List of positive words: good, great, …; list of negative words: bad, wasted, … Use logical operators: AND, OR, NOT
Step 3 Count, normalise and compute, e.g., the difference \(\#W^{pos} - \#W^{neg}\) Search for criteria: “uncertainty” OR “uncertainties”
Step 4 — Count and normalise

The course’s Boolean example: the EPU index. Baker, Bloom and Davis (2016) built the Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) index. It measures how much US newspapers write about uncertainty over economic policy. The lecture describes it like this:

“Index reflects scaled monthly counts of articles containing ‘uncertain’ or ‘uncertainty’, ‘economic’ or ‘economy’, and one or more policy relevant terms: ‘regulation’, ‘federal reserve’, ‘deficit’, ‘congress’, ‘legislation’, or ‘white house’. The series is normalized to mean 100 from 1985–2009 …”

Let’s unpack that. “Scaled monthly counts” means the number of matching articles each month, made fair for size. “Normalized to mean 100 from 1985–2009” means rescaled so that the average month between 1985 and 2009 equals 100. The articles come from 10 major US newspapers: USA Today, Miami Herald, Chicago Tribune, Washington Post, LA Times, Boston Globe, SF Chronicle, Dallas Morning News, NY Times, Wall Street Journal.

So an article counts only if it has at least one uncertainty word, at least one economy word and at least one policy word, all in the same article. The 2025 exam guideline sums this up as “key words political, economy, and uncertainty and all terms need to occur in a document for a count to happen”.

The lecture shows a chart of the index over time. It spikes at Black Monday, Gulf Wars I and II, 9/11, Lehman/TARP, the Euro crisis and the Debt Ceiling Dispute (the highest, about 275). [Not in course files — general knowledge: Black Monday was the 1987 stock-market crash; Lehman/TARP refers to the 2008 collapse of the Lehman Brothers bank and the US rescue plan; the Debt Ceiling Dispute was a 2011 US budget fight.] So the index jumps exactly when you would expect people to be worried, which suggests it measures something real.

Does counting words really work? The lecture gives three pieces of evidence.

  • Tetlock et al. (2008): counting positive and negative words in news predicts firms’ stock returns (how much their share prices go up or down, in %).
  • Sharpe et al. (2017): they scored the tone of the Greenbook forecasts. These are Federal Reserve staff forecasts [Not in course files — general knowledge]. The Federal Reserve is the US central bank, the bank that sets a country’s interest rates [Not in course files — general knowledge]. A forecast is a prediction about the future. The question was whether the words in the forecasts tell you more than the numbers in them about GDP growth (how fast the country’s total production grows, in %). They do. To measure this, they use a score called adjusted \(R^2\): a number from 0 to 1 for how much of the ups and downs in GDP growth a model explains (0 = nothing, 1 = everything; higher is better). “Adjusted” adds a small charge for using extra inputs [Not in course files — general knowledge: the exact meaning of “adjusted”]. Looking 4 quarters ahead (a quarter is three months, so this is one year ahead), adjusted \(R^2\) rises from 0.25 (forecast only) to 0.36 (with Tonality) and 0.41 (with Trend Tonality).
  • Born et al. (2014): the tone of central banks’ Financial Stability Reports (reports where a central bank says how safe it thinks the financial system is) moves stock markets.

General word lists vs finance word lists. The General Inquirer is built for everyday text. Loughran and McDonald (2011) built a finance list because, as the course notebook says, general dictionaries “misclassify finance text (liability, tax, cost are not negative in a 10-K)”. A 10-K is a firm’s annual report. [Not in course files — general knowledge: a 10-K is the annual report US listed firms file with the SEC.] In everyday talk, “liability” sounds bad. In a company report it is a normal accounting word for money the firm owes. An everyday list still marks it as negative, so the score comes out wrong.

Walk-through example

Part 1: which articles count?

Here are four made-up articles, all from one month. In the table, each row is one article. The middle three columns ask one yes/no question each:

  • U: does it contain an uncertainty word (“uncertain” or “uncertainty”)?
  • E: does it contain an economy word (“economic” or “economy”)?
  • P: does it contain a policy word (regulation, federal reserve, deficit, congress, legislation, white house)?

The last column gives the verdict. An article counts only if all three answers are “yes”.

Article (toy text) U: uncertain/-ty E: economic/economy P: policy term Counts as EPU?
A1 “Congress fights over the deficit; uncertainty about the economy grows.” yes (uncertainty) yes (economy) yes (congress, deficit) yes
A2 “Economic uncertainty rises as oil prices jump.” yes yes no no
A3 “The White House is uncertain about new legislation on stadiums.” yes no yes no
A4 “The Federal Reserve says the economy faces uncertain times.” yes yes yes (federal reserve) yes

Let’s go through A1 slowly: “Congress fights over the deficit; uncertainty about the economy grows.”

  • Uncertainty word? Yes: “uncertainty”.
  • Economy word? Yes: “economy”.
  • Policy word? Yes: “congress” and “deficit”.

Three yeses, so A1 counts.

Now A2: “Economic uncertainty rises as oil prices jump.” It has an uncertainty word and an economy word, but no policy word. Because the rule uses AND, one “no” is enough to fail. So A2 does not count. It is clearly about economic uncertainty, but with no policy word it is not policy uncertainty. The AND makes the rule strict.

A3 fails too: it has no economy word. A4 passes. So 2 of the 4 articles count.

Part 2: making it fair across months.

Newspapers print different numbers of articles each month, so the raw count is divided by the total number of articles. [Not in course files — general knowledge: Baker et al. scale the count by the total number of articles in the same newspaper and month; the slide only says “scaled monthly counts”.] Then the series is rescaled so that its average over the base period is 100 (the slide’s “normalized to mean 100”).

The numbers below are made up. Each row is one month. The columns are the steps of the calculation:

  • “EPU articles” = how many articles passed the rule that month;
  • “All articles” = how many articles the newspapers printed that month;
  • “Share” = EPU articles ÷ all articles;
  • “Index” = that month’s share ÷ the average share × 100.
Month EPU articles All articles Share Index = share ÷ average share × 100
1 4 200 0.02 0.02 / 0.03 × 100 = 66.7
2 10 250 0.04 133.3
3 3 100 0.03 100.0

Worked out in words for month 1:

  • Month 1 had 4 EPU articles out of 200. Share = 4 ÷ 200 = 0.02, which is 2 in every 100 articles.
  • Month 2: 10 ÷ 250 = 0.04. Month 3: 3 ÷ 100 = 0.03.
  • The average share over the three months is (0.02 + 0.04 + 0.03) ÷ 3 = 0.09 ÷ 3 = 0.03.
  • Month 1’s index = 0.02 ÷ 0.03 × 100 = 66.7.

So month 1 was a calm month, about a third below normal. Month 2 has the most uncertainty. Notice why normalising matters. In raw counts, month 2 (10 articles) would look more than three times as bad as month 3 (3 articles). In shares it is only \(0.04 / 0.03 \approx 1.33\) times as high.

Part 3: a dictionary score.

Take the review “good food but bad service and wasted time”. Our lists are: happy {good, great}, unhappy {bad, wasted}.

  • Length: the review has 8 words.
  • Happy hits: 1 (“good”).
  • Unhappy hits: 2 (“bad”, “wasted”).
  • Score = (1 − 2) ÷ 8 = −0.125.

Numbers like −0.125 are hard to read, so the course multiplies by 1,000. That gives −125 per 1,000 words. The review comes out negative.

Now a text from the lecture itself, called Doc1, with the same two lists. Doc1 contains “good”, “great”, “bad” and “wasted”: 2 happy hits and 2 unhappy hits. The course notebook cuts the text into separate words with a small piece of code (explained in “Reading the course code” below), and counts 74 words. So the score is 1,000 × (2 − 2) ÷ 74 = 0. The text comes out neutral, even though it is quite positive about the course and only worried about “the investment”. The count cannot see what the words are about.

Part 4: where it goes wrong.

Before the table, three words you need:

  • Polysemy: one word with several meanings. “Apple” the fruit or the company. “Bank” by a river or a bank for money.
  • Synonym: different words with the same meaning, like “unsure” and “uncertain”.
  • Negation: a “not” or “no” that flips the meaning. “No crisis” is good news, but a plain count only sees “crisis”.

These methods also treat each text as a bag-of-words: a bag of loose words with their order thrown away. So “dog bites man” and “man bites dog” look the same.

In the next table, each row is one weakness. The columns say what it means and give an example from the course.

Weakness What it means Example
Very subjective Someone chooses the words; another person would choose others Notebook 2 Q1: swap the 5+5 baseline words for your own and see how much the index changes
Need to know what to search for You can only find what you thought of in advance EPU misses an article that says “doubt about tax policy and the outlook”
Polysemy Same word, different meanings in different contexts; a count cannot tell them apart “liability” (negative in daily speech, neutral in a 10-K); “apple” the fruit vs the company (2025 Q3b guideline)
Synonyms Different words, same meaning; missing ones are not counted “unsure”, “doubt” are not in the EPU uncertainty list
Negation Bag-of-words ignores order, so “no crisis” counts as “crisis” see below
One word can be the index A very frequent word dominates the hits Notebook 2 takeaway: “one frequent word (here war) can be the index. Always look at which words produce the hits.”

“Subjective” means it depends on the person choosing. Two researchers would pick different word lists, and get different answers.

Negation, worked out. The course notebook has a simple fix: skip a hit when the word right before it is one of not, no, never, without, nor.

Take the sentence “there was no crisis and no war only growth”. It has 9 words. The positive list contains “growth”. The negative list contains “crisis” and “war”.

  • Without the fix: 1 positive hit (“growth”) and 2 negative hits (“crisis”, “war”). Score = 1,000 × (1 − 2) ÷ 9 = −111.1. The sentence sounds bad.
  • With the fix: “crisis” and “war” both come right after “no”, so they are skipped. That leaves 1 positive hit and 0 negative hits. Score = 1,000 × (1 − 0) ÷ 9 = +111.1. Now it sounds good, which is right.

The notebook calls this “a crude but common fix”. “Not a crisis” would still count as negative, because the word right before “crisis” is “a”, not “not”.

What it’s good at, and where it breaks.

  • Good: easy to understand, explain and check. You can always see which words gave the score.
  • Good: cheap and fast, even on millions of articles.
  • Breaks: it only finds the words you thought of. “Doubt about tax policy” is missed, because “doubt” is not on the list.
  • Breaks: it cannot read context. One word with two meanings (“apple”), or a “no” in front (“no crisis”), fools a plain count.

The formula, explained

The EPU rule, as a formula. In words first: an article counts only if it has at least one uncertainty word, at least one economy word and at least one policy word.

\[\underbrace{(\text{uncertain OR uncertainty})}_{\text{U}}\ \text{AND}\ \underbrace{(\text{economic OR economy})}_{\text{E}}\ \text{AND}\ \underbrace{(\text{regulation OR federal reserve OR deficit OR congress OR legislation OR white house})}_{\text{P}}\]

  • The curly bracket under each group is a name tag. U, E and P stand for the uncertainty, economy and policy groups.
  • Inside each bracket, OR means “any one of these words is enough”.
  • Between the brackets, AND means “every group must be present”.
  • All three groups must appear in the same article.

Read aloud: “an article counts if it has an uncertainty word, and an economy word, and a policy word.” In the exam you do not need the symbols. Write the three groups (Economy, Policy, Uncertainty) and give one or two example words for each.

The tone formula. In words first: take the happy-word hits minus the unhappy-word hits, divide by the length of the text, and multiply by 1,000 to get a score per 1,000 words.

\[\text{tone}_i = \frac{\#W^{pos}_i - \#W^{neg}_i}{\text{number of words in document } i}\times 1000\]

  • \(i\) = which document we are scoring (document number \(i\)).
  • \(\#W^{pos}_i\) = how many words in document \(i\) are on the positive list. (“#” = “number of”; the lecture writes \(\#W^{pos}\).)
  • \(\#W^{neg}_i\) = how many are on the negative list.
  • Dividing by the number of words = normalising for length, so a long speech does not look more emotional only because it is long.
  • \(\times 1000\) = “per 1,000 words”, only to make the numbers readable.

Read aloud: “the tone of a document is its positive hits minus its negative hits, per 1,000 words.”

For Doc1 from the walk-through:

\[\text{tone} = 1000\times\frac{\#\text{pos} - \#\text{neg}}{\#\text{words}} = 1000\times\frac{2-2}{74} = 0\]

The exam might ask you to describe this recipe in words. It has not asked you to calculate it. Knowing the formula helps you explain why normalising matters.

Reading the course code

The exam has not asked students to write code. But the course notebook builds the dictionary like this, and it helps to recognise it:

POSITIVE = ["prosperity","growth","peace","progress","success"]
NEGATIVE = ["war","crisis","unemployment","debt","inflation"]
HANDLE_NEGATION = False
  • Line 1 makes a list called POSITIVE with five happy words.
  • Line 2 makes a list called NEGATIVE with five unhappy words.
  • Line 3 is a switch: a setting you turn on (True) or off (False). Here the negation fix from the walk-through is turned off.

These three lines are the dictionary. The notebook then scores each US State of the Union speech (the US president’s yearly speech to Congress [Not in course files — general knowledge]) with 1000*(pos-neg)/n_words, which is the tone formula above.

To count words, the notebook uses re.findall(r"[a-z]+", ...). This is a short piece of Python code that pulls out every run of letters as one word. That word-cutting rule is called a tokeniser, and each piece it cuts out is a token.

The notebook then shows a scoreboard. It gives the correlation between your version and the baseline index (the notebook’s original version). Correlation says how closely two series move together: near 1 = they rise and fall together, near 0 = no link. The scoreboard also lists which words produce the hits. The notebook has no saved outputs. When run, it would show a time series (one value per year, in time order) of State of the Union tone, and a list of the words behind most hits. The notebook hints that “war” dominates.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025 Q2(c), worth 5 points: “Describe what is meant by a Boolean search-based method in NLP. Use a concrete example discussed in this course.” (NLP = natural language processing, getting computers to work with human language.)

Model answer A Boolean method starts from the documents (the document-term matrix), picks keywords of interest and combines them with logical operators (AND, OR, NOT) into a search rule; we then count the documents that satisfy the rule and normalise the count (e.g. by the total number of articles). The course example is the Economic Policy Uncertainty index of Baker et al. (2016): a newspaper article counts if it contains “uncertain” or “uncertainty”, AND “economic” or “economy”, AND at least one policy term such as “congress”, “deficit” or “white house”. The monthly counts from 10 US newspapers are scaled and normalised to mean 100 over 1985–2009, and the index spikes at events like 9/11 and the debt-ceiling dispute. The method is simple and transparent, but subjective: it only finds the words you thought of, and cannot handle synonyms or polysemy.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: You pick some words, join them with AND, OR, NOT into a search rule, count how many articles match, and divide by the total so months can be compared fairly. The EPU index does this with US newspapers: an article counts only if it has an uncertainty word, an economy word and a policy word. The final numbers are scaled so their average is 100, and they jump at big shocks like 9/11. The method is easy to understand, but it only finds the exact words you chose, so it misses other words with the same meaning and is fooled by words with two meanings.

2025 T/F (h): “Dictionary-based methods allow you to capture polysemy in text well” → False. Polysemy means one word with several meanings, like “bank” (river bank or money bank). The lecture lists it as a problem for dictionaries.

The reflection question (the open question about customer survey texts). A sentiment dictionary (a list of happy words and unhappy words) is an obvious first method. But name the pitfalls:

  • Loughran–McDonald-style domain issues: a word can mean something else in a special field. For example, “liability” is a normal word in a company report, not bad news.
  • Negation: “not good” contains “good”.
  • Subjectivity: the word list depends on the researcher’s own choices.

What a top-grade answer must include

For Q2(c), go through these steps in order:

  1. Start from the documents (or the document-term matrix, the word-count table).
  2. Choose keywords (a dictionary, i.e. your fixed word list).
  3. Combine them with the logical operators AND, OR, NOT.
  4. Count the documents (or words) that match the rule.
  5. Normalise: divide by the number of articles or words, so a month with more news does not look bigger only because there was more news. The EPU index is also rescaled so its average is 100.
  6. Give the EPU example with its three word groups (economy, policy, uncertainty), which must all appear in the same article.

A top answer also adds one weakness: the word choice is subjective (depends on the researcher), synonyms (different words with the same meaning) are missed, and polysemy (one word, several meanings) confuses it.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Forgetting normalisation (dividing by the total). The 2025 guideline says “Think about normalization issues”.
  • Saying an EPU article needs only one of the words. It needs one word from each of the three groups.
  • Inventing your own example when the question asks for an example from the course.
  • Claiming dictionaries handle polysemy (one word, several meanings) or synonyms (several words, one meaning) well.

Key terms to use

  • Boolean operators (AND, OR, NOT) (words that combine search terms)
  • keyword list / dictionary (the fixed list of words you count)
  • count and normalise (count matches, then divide by the total)
  • Economic Policy Uncertainty (EPU) index (monthly newspaper measure of policy uncertainty)
  • Baker, Bloom and Davis (2016) (the economists who built the EPU index)
  • General Inquirer (an older, general-purpose positive/negative word list)
  • Loughran and McDonald (2011) (word list made for finance reports)
  • tone = positive − negative (happy-word count minus unhappy-word count)
  • polysemy (one word, several meanings)
  • synonyms (different words, same meaning)
  • negation (“not” flips the meaning of a word)
  • subjective (depends on the researcher’s own choices)

Quick self-test

  1. True/False: “Dictionary-based methods allow you to capture polysemy in text well.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Dictionary methods count words from a fixed list. Polysemy means one word has several meanings, like “bank” (river or money). The statement says these methods handle such words well.

    Answer: False. Why: A dictionary only sees the spelling of a word, never its meaning. It counts “bank” the same way in “river bank” and “bank loan”. It is like a metal detector that beeps at bottle caps and coins alike.

  2. True/False: “An article enters the EPU count if it contains ‘uncertainty’ and ‘economy’, even without a policy term.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The EPU index counts newspaper articles about economic policy uncertainty. The statement says an article is counted if it has an uncertainty word and an economy word, even with no policy word (like “congress” or “deficit”).

    Answer: False. Why: The rule joins the groups with AND, so the article needs one word from each of the three groups: uncertainty, economy and policy. It is like a cake that needs flour, eggs and sugar: two out of three is not the cake.

  3. True/False: “Boolean/dictionary methods are by far the most used approach in economics and finance.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Are the “count the keywords” methods the most common way economists and finance researchers study text?

    Answer: True. Why: The lecture says so directly. They are popular because they are simple and transparent: anyone can see which words were counted.

  4. True/False: “General-purpose sentiment dictionaries work well for 10-K reports.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A general-purpose sentiment dictionary is an everyday list of positive and negative words, built for normal text. 10-K reports are the yearly reports that US companies must publish. The statement says the everyday list works well on these reports.

    Answer: False. Why: In company reports, words like liability, tax and cost are normal business words, not bad news. The everyday list still marks them as negative, so the score is wrong. That is why Loughran and McDonald built a special word list for finance. It is like reading a medical test that comes back “positive” as good news, when in medicine it often is not.

  5. Explain (2–5 sentences): “Describe a Boolean search method with a course example.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Explain how a keyword search with AND, OR, NOT works, and use the example from the lectures (the EPU index).

    Answer: the model answer in “What the exam asks, and how to answer” above. Why: In short: pick keywords, join them with AND, OR, NOT, count the articles that match, and divide by the total; the EPU index needs an uncertainty word, an economy word and a policy word in the same article, is scaled to an average of 100, and spikes at big shocks; it is simple but subjective, and misses synonyms and polysemy.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • Boolean search: a search rule made of words joined by AND, OR and NOT. Like a shop website filter: “shoes AND red AND NOT sandals”.
  • Boolean operators: the joining words AND, OR, NOT.
  • AND: both parts must be present. “uncertainty AND economy” needs both words in the same article.
  • OR: at least one of the parts is enough. “uncertain OR uncertainty” is happy with either.
  • NOT: this part must be absent. “shoes AND NOT sandals” drops any page with “sandals”.
  • document: one piece of text we study, such as one article or one review.
  • document-term matrix: the word-count table. Rows are documents, columns are words, each cell is a count.
  • \(c_i\): the word counts of document number \(i\); \(c_3\) is the third document’s row.
  • dictionary (word list): a hand-made list of words that signal something, like a list of happy words.
  • keyword: a word you search for.
  • hit: one match between the text and your list. “bad” in a review is a hit for the unhappy list.
  • normalise: make numbers fair to compare by dividing by size. 4 bad reviews out of 10 is worse than 4 out of 1,000.
  • share: a part divided by the whole. 4 EPU articles out of 200 = a share of 0.02.
  • average (mean): add the numbers and divide by how many there are. The average of 0.02, 0.04 and 0.03 is 0.03.
  • index: one number that tracks something over time, rescaled so it is easy to read, like a price index.
  • “normalized to mean 100”: rescaled so the average month in the chosen period (1985–2009) equals 100. Then 200 means “twice as much as normal”.
  • series / time series: a list of values in time order, one per month or year.
  • EPU (Economic Policy Uncertainty) index: the Baker, Bloom and Davis measure: the scaled monthly count of newspaper articles that mention uncertainty AND the economy AND policy.
  • policy: what the government decides to do (taxes, rules, budgets, interest rates).
  • latent concept: something real but hidden that we cannot measure directly, like worry or mood.
  • function, \(f()\): a fixed rule that turns an input into an output, like “take the number and add 2”.
  • \(f(c_i)\), known function: the fixed rule (our word lists and counting) applied to document \(i\)’s word counts \(c_i\). Known = written by us in advance, so anyone gets the same score.
  • supervised (in this course): “we know what comes out”, either from answers or from a rule we wrote. Dictionaries are supervised because their rule is known.
  • \(v_i\): the hidden true value for document \(i\), such as its real mood.
  • \(\hat v_i\): the hat means “our estimate”. It is the number our rule gives for the hidden concept in document \(i\).
  • sentiment / tone: how positive or negative a text sounds.
  • per 1,000 words: the score scaled up so it reads like “−125 for every 1,000 words”, which is easier to read than −0.125.
  • \(\#W^{pos}\), \(\#W^{neg}\): “#” means “number of”. The number of positive words and the number of negative words.
  • General Inquirer: a ready-made, general-purpose list of positive and negative words.
  • Loughran and McDonald (2011): a word list made for finance texts.
  • 10-K: the annual report a US listed company must publish.
  • polysemy: one word, several meanings. “Apple” the fruit or the company; “liability” (a bad thing in daily talk, a neutral accounting item in a company report).
  • synonym: different words with the same meaning, like “unsure” and “uncertain”.
  • negation: a “not” or “no” that flips the meaning. “No crisis” is good news, but a plain count sees “crisis”.
  • subjective: depends on the person choosing. Two researchers would pick different word lists.
  • bag-of-words: treating a text as a bag of loose words, ignoring their order. “Dog bites man” and “man bites dog” look the same.
  • token / tokeniser: a token is one word-piece of a text; the tokeniser is the rule that cuts the text into tokens.
  • re.findall(r"[a-z]+", ...): a piece of Python code that pulls out every run of letters as one word.
  • stock returns: how much a share price went up or down, in %.
  • forecast: a prediction about the future, such as next year’s growth.
  • GDP growth: how fast a country’s total production grew, in %. Used as “how well the economy is doing”.
  • quarter: three months. “4 quarters ahead” = one year ahead.
  • \(R^2\) / adjusted \(R^2\): a score from 0 to 1 for how much of the ups and downs in the outcome a model explains. 0 = nothing, 1 = everything. “Adjusted” adds a small charge for using extra inputs. [Not in course files — general knowledge: the exact meaning of “adjusted”.]
  • central bank / Federal Reserve: the bank that sets a country’s interest rates; the Federal Reserve is the US one. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • Financial Stability Report: a report where a central bank says how safe it thinks the financial system is.
  • correlation: how closely two series move together. Near 1 = they rise and fall together; near 0 = no link.
  • baseline index: the starting version you compare your own version with.
  • switch (HANDLE_NEGATION = False): a setting you turn on (True) or off (False) in the code.
  • \(\underbrace{\ \cdots\ }_{U}\) (the curly bracket under the formula): a name tag for a group of words. U, E and P stand for the uncertainty, economy and policy groups.
  • NLP (natural language processing): getting computers to work with human language, like a spell checker.

Sources: Lecture 3 “Bag-of-words based methods” slides 6–12 (slide 7: “by far the most used approach”, latent concept and known function; slide 8: dictionary vs Boolean table, EPU recipe in the figure note and EPU chart; slides 8–11: Tetlock, Sharpe, Born evidence, adjusted \(R^2\) on slide 10; slide 12: weaknesses), slide 32 (Doc1); Interactive Notebook 2 cells 4 (tone function, negation fix), 7 (×1000 tone formula), 8 (word lists), 9, 10 (Q1, finance misclassification), 31 (takeaway on “war”); 2025 exam evaluation guidelines, Q2(c), 1(h) and Q3b.

8. Text regressions and regularisation (Lasso, Ridge, λ, cross-validation) (L3, Interactive 2)

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 T/F (e) (“regularization … help overcome the curse of dimensionality” → True) and very likely T/F or short questions on λ and cross-validation.

Why this exists

Here are three real problems.

  • An economist wonders whether the words a US president uses in the yearly State of the Union speech say anything about how the economy is doing. (The State of the Union is the president’s big speech to Congress each year. [Not in course files — general knowledge])
  • A shop wants to guess a review’s star rating, from 1 to 5, from the words in the review.
  • An investment fund wants to guess how a share price will move, from today’s news.

All three have the same shape. You have a pile of texts. Each text comes with one number. You want a recipe that reads a new text and guesses its number.

This chapter builds that recipe in four steps. First, the basic tool for guessing a number. Second, why that tool breaks when the inputs are words. Third, the fix. Fourth, how to check honestly whether the recipe works.

The idea in everyday words

Step 1: guessing a number by drawing a line through dots.

Forget text for a moment. Say you run an ice-cream stand. Every day you write down two numbers: the temperature and how many ice creams you sold. Now draw a chart. Each day becomes one dot. How far right the dot sits is the temperature. How high up it sits is the sales. On hot days the dots sit higher, so the cloud of dots slopes upwards.

Now take a ruler and draw one straight line through the middle of the cloud, as close to all the dots as you can. Tomorrow will be 25 degrees? Go along the bottom to 25, go up to the line, and read off the sales. That is your guess.

That is all a regression is: predicting a number by drawing the best line through points.

Some names for the parts:

  • The number you want to guess (ice-cream sales) is the outcome. It is usually written \(y\).
  • The number you guess from (temperature) is the input. It is also called the explanatory variable, the regressor or the feature. It is usually written \(x\).

A straight line is fully described by two numbers.

  • The intercept is where the line sits when the input is 0. It is the starting value of the guess.
  • The slope, also called the coefficient, is how steep the line is. It says how much the guess goes up when the input goes up by one.

For example, “guess = 20 + 3 × temperature” has intercept 20 and slope 3. Each extra degree adds 3 ice creams to the guess.

Step 2: which line is “best”?

For each dot, measure the gap between the real value and the line’s guess. This gap is the miss. It is also called the error or the residual.

Next, square each miss, which means multiply it by itself. This does two useful things. The minus sign disappears, so a miss of −2 and a miss of +2 both become 4. And big misses count extra: a miss of 3 becomes 9.

Add up all the squared misses. The total says how badly the line fits. This total is called the loss. The best line is the one with the smallest total. This recipe for picking the line is called ordinary least squares, or OLS. “Least squares” means “the smallest total of squared misses”. A computer finds this line instantly.

Step 3: more than one input.

A guess can use several inputs at once, for example temperature and whether it is a weekend. Each input then gets its own coefficient. The guess becomes:

guess = intercept + (input 1 × its coefficient) + (input 2 × its coefficient) + … for every input.

It is still called a regression, and OLS still picks the coefficients by making the total of squared misses as small as possible.

Step 4: words as inputs.

To use words as inputs, turn each text into numbers. The usual way is to count how many times each word appears. Each single text (one speech, one review) is called a document. Put the counts in a table:

  • one row per document,
  • one column per word,
  • each cell = how many times that word appears in that document.

This table is called the document-term matrix, or DTM. Now each word column is one input, with its own coefficient. A word with a positive coefficient pushes the guess up each time it appears. A word with a negative coefficient pushes it down. A regression whose inputs are the word columns is a text regression.

Sometimes the plain counts are swapped for smarter word weights, such as tf-idf. Tf-idf gives a high weight to a word that is frequent in this document but rare in the other documents. The regression works the same way either way.

The method learns from texts whose right number is already known. Learning from examples with known answers is called supervised learning.

The lecture slides describe the goal in symbols as \(p(y_i \mid c_i)\). Read it like this. The small \(i\) is the document’s number (document 1, document 2, …). \(y_i\) is the outcome of document \(i\). \(c_i\) is document \(i\)’s row of word counts. The upright bar “\(\mid\)” is read “given”. The letter \(p(\cdot)\) stands for probability: a number from 0 to 1 for how likely something is. (This is not the \(p\) for “number of words” that comes up below.) So \(p(y_i \mid c_i)\) means “how likely each value of this document’s outcome is, given its word counts”: what to expect for the outcome, given the words. In practice the slides say it is usually estimated through the conditional expectation, written \(E[y_i \mid c_i]\). That is the average outcome you would expect for a document with these word counts: in other words, the best guess of \(y\) given the words.

The slides also mention one simple approach that does work: pick a few word columns you care about (for example, the count of “good” in course reviews) and run ordinary OLS on those few columns only.

Step 5: why using all the words breaks OLS.

Call the number of documents \(n\) and the number of different words \(p\). In the course notebook, there are about 70 State of the Union speeches (69 speech–year pairs, from 1948 to 2018). Each speech is paired with that year’s GDP growth, which is how fast the economy grew, in %. But the speeches together contain thousands of different words. So \(n\) is about 70 and \(p\) is in the thousands. This is written \(n \ll p\), read “\(n\) is much smaller than \(p\)”.

Why is that a problem? Every coefficient is an unknown number that the computer must choose. Every document gives one fact to check the choice against. With more unknowns than facts, there are endless answers. It is like being asked “find two numbers that add up to 10”: 3 and 7 works, 1 and 9 works, 4.5 and 5.5 works, and so on forever.

So with thousands of words and 70 speeches, the computer can always find coefficients that hit every training speech exactly, and it can do so in endless different ways. A perfect fit sounds great. But it is memorising, not learning. On a new speech the guess is bad. This is called overfitting: the model memorises the training examples, including their random noise, and then guesses badly on new ones.

The cause has a name. Each input column counts as one dimension. Thousands of word columns make the problem high-dimensional. The trouble that comes with far more columns than rows is called the curse of dimensionality, or the “\(n \ll p\) problem”. The slides put it like this: “Typically \(n \ll p\), thus we have more explanatory variables than observations of the outcome (more unknowns than equations). Thus, we cannot apply linear regression directly.” (“Linear regression” here means the line-fitting regression, OLS.)

Step 6: the fix is to charge a fee.

Analogy Imagine guessing the price of a house from 70 sales, but you are allowed to use 5,000 features (colour of the door, name of the dog…). With enough features you can explain the 70 prices exactly, yet you will predict the next house badly. Regularisation is a strict budget: every feature you use costs money, so you only keep the few that pay for themselves.

In the regression, this budget works as a fee. Every coefficient that is not zero now costs something, and bigger coefficients cost more. The total the computer tries to make small is no longer “squared misses”. It becomes “squared misses + fee”. So the computer only gives a word a big coefficient if that word cuts the misses by more than its fee.

Adding this fee is called regularisation, or penalisation. The fee itself is the penalty. The way the fee pulls coefficients towards zero is called shrinkage.

There are a few versions of the fee. The slides call them “Lasso and friends”.

  • Lasso charges by the size of each coefficient, ignoring its minus sign. It can push many coefficients to exactly zero. Those words drop out, so you get a short, readable list of the words that matter.
  • Ridge charges by each coefficient squared. It shrinks coefficients towards zero but never exactly to zero, so it keeps every word. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • Elastic net is a mix of the two.

The slides sum up: “Text regressions are high-dimensional problems. Thus, we need penalization methods or dimension reduction.” Dimension reduction means squeezing the thousands of word columns into a few summary columns first, and then running the regression on those. Two named ways are PCA and Partial Least Squares. (PCA is the same squeezing idea that this guide’s chapter on LSA covers.) The slides also list non-linear methods: GLMs, regression trees and random forest. These are methods that allow curves and if-then rules instead of one straight line [Not in course files — general knowledge].

Step 7: how big should the fee be? Meet λ.

The fee rate is written \(\lambda\), the Greek letter “lambda”. It works like a dial.

  • \(\lambda = 0\): no fee at all. You are back to plain OLS. The slides warn: “With λ = 0 we get standard OLS. This is typically not what we do with text data!”
  • Small \(\lambda\): a tiny fee, so the model can still overfit.
  • Big \(\lambda\): a huge fee, so every coefficient is pushed to zero. The slides: “high values of λ shrink coefficients to zero”. The model then ignores all words and guesses the average every time.

The right setting is somewhere in between. But where?

Step 8: choosing λ by testing on hidden data.

Hide part of the data from the model. Let it learn from the rest. Then see how well it guesses the hidden part. The part it learns from is the training set. The hidden part is the test set, also called held-out data. Do this for several values of \(\lambda\) and keep the one that guesses the hidden data best. This is cross-validation, a form of out-of-sample testing (“out-of-sample” = measured on data the model never saw).

The course notebook uses 5-fold cross-validation. It cuts the speeches into 5 equal groups, called folds. It trains on 4 groups and guesses the 5th. Then it repeats, so each group is guessed once by a model that never saw it. In the notebook’s words: “split the speeches into 5 groups, train on 4, predict the 5th, repeat… \(R^2 = 0\) means ‘no better than predicting the average’.” (\(R^2\) is a score for how good the guesses are; the next step explains it.)

The slides name a second way to choose \(\lambda\): information criteria, such as AIC and BIC. These are scores computed on the training data that reward good fit but charge for every extra coefficient [Not in course files — general knowledge]. Because they use the training data itself, they are in-sample (“in-sample” = measured on the data the model learned from).

Step 9: judging the result with \(R^2\).

The usual score for a regression is \(R^2\) (say “R squared”). It measures how much of the ups and downs in the outcome the guesses explain.

  • \(R^2 = 1\): perfect guesses.
  • \(R^2 = 0\): no better than always guessing the average.
  • \(R^2\) below 0: worse than always guessing the average.

You can measure \(R^2\) on the training documents (in-sample \(R^2\)) or on hidden documents (cross-validated or out-of-sample \(R^2\)). When there are far more words than documents, the in-sample \(R^2\) is close to 1 almost always, because the model can memorise. So it proves nothing. Only the cross-validated \(R^2\) is honest. The walk-through below shows a striking test of this, the placebo test.

What it’s good at, and where it breaks.

  • Good: it can use all the words at once and lets the data decide which ones matter.
  • Good: Lasso pushes most coefficients to exactly zero, so you get a short, readable list of the words that matter.
  • Good: cross-validation gives an honest score on texts the model has never seen.
  • Breaks: with few texts (about 70 speeches), even the best model may predict poorly. The honest score can be near zero or below.
  • Breaks: the result depends on the fee \(\lambda\). A different \(\lambda\) gives a different list of words.

Walk-through example

All numbers in Parts 1 to 3 are toy numbers made up for this explanation.

Part 1: one word, one straight line.

Three speeches. In the table below, each row is one speech. The middle column is how many times the word “growth” appears in that speech (the input). The last column is that year’s GDP growth in % (the outcome). So the cell “3” in row 3 means “speech 3 says ‘growth’ three times”.

Speech count of “growth” GDP growth (%)
1 1 2
2 2 4
3 3 5

Let us score two candidate lines.

Line B: “guess = 2 × count”. Speech 1: 2 × 1 = 2. The real value is 2, so the miss is 0. Speech 2: 2 × 2 = 4. Real 4, miss 0. Speech 3: 2 × 3 = 6. Real 5, miss 1. The squared misses are 0, 0 and 1. Total = 1.

Line C: “guess = 1 + count”. Speech 1: 1 + 1 = 2, miss 0. Speech 2: 1 + 2 = 3, real 4, miss 1. Speech 3: 1 + 3 = 4, real 5, miss 1. The squared misses are 0, 1 and 1. Total = 2.

Line B beats line C, because 1 is smaller than 2. OLS does this for every possible line at once and finds the very best one. Here it is about “guess = 0.67 + 1.5 × count”. Its guesses are about 2.17, 3.67 and 5.17. Its misses are about −0.17, 0.33 and −0.17. Squared and added, the total is about 0.17, smaller than both B and C.

How to read the best line: the intercept 0.67 is the guess for a speech that never says “growth”. The slope 1.5 says each extra “growth” adds 1.5 to the guessed GDP growth.

Part 2: more words than speeches, and why the line method breaks.

Now there are 3 speeches (\(n = 3\)) and 4 words (\(p = 4\)). In the table, each row is a speech. The columns “word 1” to “word 4” hold how many times each word appears in that speech. The last column, \(y\), is the outcome (GDP growth, %). For example, row 2 says: speech 2 uses word 2 once and word 4 once, and that year’s growth was 5.

Speech word 1 word 2 word 3 word 4 \(y\)
1 1 0 0 1 2
2 0 1 0 1 5
3 0 0 1 1 1

The model has no intercept here. Its guess for a speech is:

guess = (coefficient 1 × count of word 1) + (coefficient 2 × count of word 2) + (coefficient 3 × count of word 3) + (coefficient 4 × count of word 4).

In symbols: \(y_i = \beta_1 c_{i1}+\beta_2 c_{i2}+\beta_3 c_{i3}+\beta_4 c_{i4}\). Here \(\beta\) (the Greek letter “beta”) stands for a coefficient, so \(\beta_1\) is word 1’s coefficient. \(c_{i1}\) is the count of word 1 in speech \(i\).

So there are 4 coefficients to choose, and only 3 speeches to check them against. The next table lists three different choices. Each row is one candidate set of four coefficients. The third column shows that candidate’s guesses for speeches 1, 2 and 3. The last column is the candidate’s total size: add up its four coefficients, ignoring minus signs. (The size of a number ignoring its minus sign is its absolute value, written with straight bars: \(\lvert -1 \rvert = 1\).)

Candidate \(\beta_1,\beta_2,\beta_3,\beta_4\) Predictions for speeches 1–3 \(\sum_j\lvert\beta_j\rvert\)
A 2, 5, 1, 0 2, 5, 1 8
B 1, 4, 0, 1 2, 5, 1 6
C 0, 3, −1, 2 2, 5, 1 6

(The symbol \(\sum\), the Greek capital “sigma”, means “add up”. \(\sum_j\lvert\beta_j\rvert\) means “add up the sizes of all the coefficients”.)

Let us check a few cells by hand.

  • Candidate A, speech 2 (counts 0, 1, 0, 1): 2 × 0 + 5 × 1 + 1 × 0 + 0 × 1 = 5. The real \(y\) is 5. A perfect hit.
  • Candidate B, speech 1 (counts 1, 0, 0, 1): 1 × 1 + 4 × 0 + 0 × 0 + 1 × 1 = 2. The real \(y\) is 2. Also perfect.
  • Candidate C, speech 3 (counts 0, 0, 1, 1): 0 × 0 + 3 × 0 + (−1) × 1 + 2 × 1 = 1. The real \(y\) is 1. Also perfect.
  • Candidate C’s total size: 0 + 3 + 1 + 2 = 6 (the −1 counts as 1).

Three very different sets of coefficients, and every one predicts all three speeches exactly. In fact there are infinitely many perfect fits. So OLS, which is the method with no fee (\(\lambda = 0\)), has no single answer. The data cannot tell us which candidate is “true”, so the perfect fit tells us nothing.

Part 3: the fee picks a winner.

Now add the Lasso fee. In this example it is:

fee = (number of speeches) × \(\lambda\) × (total size of the coefficients).

Compare two extreme candidates.

  • Candidate A (the perfect fit above). Its squared misses add up to 0. Its total size is 8, so its fee = 3 × \(\lambda\) × 8 = \(24\lambda\).
  • Candidate Z sets every coefficient to 0. It ignores the words and always guesses the average of the outcomes: (2 + 5 + 1) ÷ 3 = 8 ÷ 3 ≈ 2.67. (In the formula this starting value is the intercept, written \(\alpha\), the Greek letter “alpha”. Candidate A has \(\alpha = 0\).) Z’s misses are 2 − 2.67 = −0.67, 5 − 2.67 = 2.33 and 1 − 2.67 = −1.67. Squared, that is about 0.44, 5.44 and 2.78, a total of about 8.67. Its coefficients are all zero, so its fee is 0.

The next table compares their totals (squared misses + fee). Each row is one value of \(\lambda\). The middle columns are each candidate’s total at that \(\lambda\). The last column says which of the two has the smaller total, and so is preferred.

λ A: loss + penalty Z: loss + penalty Preferred of these two
0 0 + 0 = 0 8.67 A (OLS: fit at any cost)
0.1 0 + 2.4 = 2.4 8.67 A
1 0 + 24 = 24 8.67 Z (all coefficients zero)

Worked out in words for \(\lambda = 1\): A’s fee is 24 × 1 = 24, and its misses add 0, so A costs 24. Z costs 8.67. Z is cheaper, so Z wins. For \(\lambda = 0.1\): A’s fee is 24 × 0.1 = 2.4, which is cheaper than Z’s 8.67, so A wins.

So the size of the fee decides how much the model is allowed to use the words. As \(\lambda\) grows, the fee wins and coefficients are pushed to zero. The real Lasso answer lies somewhere between such extremes. The table only shows the direction of the trade-off.

Part 4: the honest score, in-sample versus cross-validated.

The course notebook reports two \(R^2\) scores for its text regression of GDP growth on the speeches. In the next table, each column is one of the two scores, and each row asks one question about it.

In-sample \(R^2\) Cross-validated \(R^2\)
Measured on the speeches the model was trained on speeches the model did not see
With \(p \gg n\) close to 1 almost always (the notebook’s own question says “an R² close to 1”) the honest number; can be near or below 0
What it tells you almost nothing whether the words really predict GDP

(\(p \gg n\) is the same as \(n \ll p\): far more words than speeches.)

Part 5: the placebo test, or the student who memorised 70 random answers.

Picture a teacher who gives a student 70 questions. But the “answers” on the sheet were drawn out of a hat. They are random and have nothing to do with the questions. The student memorises all 70. Next day the teacher asks the same 70 questions, and the student scores 70 out of 70.

Does that prove the student understands the subject? No. There was nothing to understand, because the answers were random. The student memorised, nothing more. The honest test is to ask 10 new questions. On those, the student does no better than guessing.

The course notebook runs exactly this test on the regression. A switch called PLACEBO = True shuffles the GDP growth numbers between years. Now each speech is paired with some other year’s growth, at random. These are the answers from the hat: the words cannot contain information about them. A fake test like this, where the outcome is scrambled on purpose, is called a placebo test.

What happens?

  • In-sample \(R^2\) stays near 1. With thousands of word columns and about 70 speeches, the model can memorise 70 random numbers, like the student memorising 70 random answers.
  • Cross-validated \(R^2\) collapses. On speeches it has not seen, the model has nothing real to go on, like the student facing new questions.

So if the model can get a near-perfect in-sample fit even on nonsense, a near-perfect in-sample fit on the real data proves nothing either. The notebook’s takeaway: “In text regression the in-sample R² is meaningless when p ≫ n — even a scrambled target gets a near-perfect fit. Judge text models on data they have not seen.”

The business lesson from the notebook: if a vendor shows you a text model with “R² = 0.95”, your first question is “in-sample or out-of-sample?”

The formula, explained

The slides write the Lasso as one formula. Here is the idea first, in words: choose the intercept and coefficients that make “how badly we miss” plus “the fee for big coefficients” as small as possible.

\[\min\Big\{\, l(\alpha,\beta) + n\lambda \sum_{j=1}^{p} \omega_j\,|\beta_j| \,\Big\}\]

The miss part is spelled out like this. In words: the miss total is the sum of squared gaps between each real outcome and the model’s guess, and the guess is the starting value plus each word’s value times its coefficient.

\[l(\alpha,\beta) = \sum_{i=1}^{n} (y_i - \eta_i)^2 \quad\text{and}\quad \eta_i = \alpha + x_i'\beta\]

Each symbol:

  • \(\min\{\cdot\}\) = “choose \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) to make everything inside the bracket as small as possible”.
  • \(l(\alpha,\beta)\) = the loss: how badly the model fits. Here it is the total of squared misses, exactly as in OLS.
  • \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\) = “add this up for document 1, document 2, … up to document \(n\)”.
  • \(y_i\) = the real outcome of document \(i\) (for example, GDP growth in the year of speech \(i\)).
  • \(\eta_i\) (the Greek letter “eta”) = the model’s guess for document \(i\).
  • \(\alpha\) = the intercept, the starting value of the guess.
  • \(x_i = f(c_i)\) = the inputs of document \(i\). This is either its plain row of word counts \(c_i\) from the document-term matrix, or a changed version of it such as tf-idf weights. (The slides say “e.g., the identity”, which means “no change: use the counts as they are”.)
  • \(\beta_j\) = the coefficient of word \(j\). The slides: “The object of interest is β, one for each column in x”.
  • \(x_i'\beta\) = short for “multiply each of document \(i\)’s inputs by its coefficient, and add them all up”.
  • \(n\) = the number of documents (rows). \(p\) = the number of words (columns).
  • \(\lambda\) = the overall penalty: how expensive big coefficients are. \(\lambda = 0\) gives standard OLS.
  • \(\omega_j\) (the Greek letter “omega”) = a variable-specific cost: an extra weight on word \(j\)’s fee, so different words can be charged differently. In text analysis it is typically scaled by each word’s sample standard deviation, which measures how much that word’s count varies from document to document. This is called “rare feature upweighting”.
  • \(|\beta_j|\) = the size of coefficient \(j\), ignoring its minus sign (absolute value). Using absolute values is what lets Lasso set coefficients exactly to zero.
  • \(\sum_{j=1}^{p}\) = “add this up for word 1, word 2, … up to word \(p\)”.

Read aloud in one sentence: “Choose the intercept and the word coefficients to minimise the squared prediction errors plus a penalty that is λ times the (weighted) total size of all the coefficients.”

When the outcome is yes/no. For a yes/no outcome (for example, spam or not), the misses are scored with a different formula, the logistic loss:

\[l(\alpha,\beta) = -\sum_{i=1}^{n} \big(\eta_i y_i - \log(1 + e^{\eta_i})\big)\]

Two new symbols appear. \(\log\) is the logarithm, a function that turns multiplying into adding (\(\log(a \times b) = \log a + \log b\)); it grows slowly, so big numbers become small ones. \(e\) is a fixed number, about 2.718, and \(e^{\eta_i}\) means \(e\) raised to the power \(\eta_i\) (for \(\eta = 2\), that is \(e \times e \approx 7.39\)). You only need to know that this formula exists for yes/no outcomes; the fee part stays the same.

Ridge. The slides only name Ridge and Elastic net as members of the “Lasso family” and give no formula for them. [Not in course files — general knowledge: Ridge uses squared coefficients, \(\sum_j \beta_j^2\), instead of \(|\beta_j|\). It shrinks coefficients towards zero but never exactly to zero, so it keeps all words. Lasso can set some exactly to zero, so it also selects words. Elastic net mixes the two.]

Will the exam ask you to write it? The 2025 exam had no calculations. But the top-grade answer for “why regularise?” names the penalty \(n\lambda\sum_j\omega_j|\beta_j|\), so learn that part well enough to write it down and explain it in words. You will not need to compute with it.

Reading the course code

The exam has not asked students to write code. This section is only so that the notebook makes sense to you.

model = make_pipeline(TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english", min_df=MIN_DF),
                      Ridge(alpha=ALPHA))
cv = KFold(n_splits=5, shuffle=True, random_state=0)
pred = cross_val_predict(model, texts, y, cv=cv)

(Simplified from the course notebook.) The tools come from scikit-learn, a popular Python toolbox for these methods.

  • Lines 1–2 build a pipeline: a chain of steps run in order. Step one turns each speech into tf-idf word weights.
