While doing so it drops English stop words (very common words like “the” and “and”) and words found in fewer than MIN_DF = 5 speeches (min_df = “minimum document frequency”). Step two fits a Ridge regression on those weights.
  • Watch the names. In scikit-learn, alpha is the penalty strength: the slides’ λ. It is not the slides’ intercept α. The notebook says “ALPHA sets how hard it shrinks”, and suggests trying values from 0.01 to 100.
  • Line 3 (KFold) cuts the data into 5 folds. shuffle=True mixes up the order of the speeches first. random_state=0 fixes the random mixing, so you get the same folds each time you run it.
  • Line 4 (cross_val_predict) goes through the folds one by one. For each fold it trains on the other 4 and guesses this one. The result is an out-of-sample guess for every speech. Then r2_score(y, pred) gives the cross-validated \(R^2\).

No outputs are saved in the notebook. Running it would print about 69 speeches for \(n\), thousands of word columns for \(p\), an in-sample \(R^2\) near 1 for small ALPHA, a much lower cross-validated \(R^2\), and a bar chart of the 8 most positive and 8 most negative word coefficients. Note that the notebook uses Ridge, while the slides write the Lasso formula. Both are penalised regressions.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025 exam, True/False (e): “In text regressions usage of regularization techniques help overcome the curse of dimensionality.”

Model answer — True. A text regression predicts a number (like GDP growth) from word counts. Regularization means adding a penalty that keeps the word weights small. The curse of dimensionality is the problem of having far more columns (words) than rows (documents), so the model can fit anything.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: with far more words than documents, the model can bend itself to fit anything. The fee on big word weights stops that, so yes, regularisation helps.

Likely variants of this question:

  • “With λ = 0 the Lasso equals OLS” → True. λ (the strength of the penalty dial) at 0 means no penalty, so you are back to OLS (ordinary least squares, the plain line-fitting regression).
  • “A high in-sample R² proves the text predicts the outcome” → False. R² (a 0-to-1 score of how well the model fits) measured in-sample (on the same documents the model learned from) proves nothing.
  • “λ is chosen by cross-validation” → True. Cross-validation means testing on documents held back from training.
  • “Text regressions typically have n ≫ p” → False. It is \(n \ll p\): the number of documents (\(n\)) is much smaller than the number of words (\(p\)).

Likely short question: “Why do we need regularisation in text regressions, and how is the penalty chosen?” (2–5 sentences)

Model answer — In a text regression the regressors are the columns of the document-term matrix, so we usually have far more words than documents (\(n \ll p\)), i.e. more unknowns than equations, and OLS cannot be estimated or fits the training data perfectly but meaninglessly (the curse of dimensionality). Penalised regressions such as Lasso add a cost \(n\lambda\sum_j\omega_j|\beta_j|\) for large coefficients, which shrinks most of them towards zero (Lasso sets some exactly to zero), so only informative words keep weight; λ = 0 gives back OLS. The penalty λ is chosen by cross-validation: estimate the model on training data for different λ values and pick the one that predicts held-out test data best (or use an information criterion such as AIC/BIC).

What this answer is saying, in plain words: in a text regression every word is an input, so there are far more inputs than documents, and plain regression either breaks or fits the training data perfectly without learning anything real. Lasso and similar methods add a fee for big word weights, so most weights shrink towards zero and only the useful words keep weight; with no fee (λ = 0) you are back to plain regression. To pick the fee, you try several values, train on part of the data, and keep the value that predicts the held-back part best. AIC and BIC are fit scores that charge for every extra weight, and can be used instead.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • \(n \ll p\): there are far more word columns than documents. Then OLS (plain line-fitting) fails: there are more unknowns than equations, so it fits the data perfectly but meaninglessly.
  • Penalised regression adds a fee for big weights: \(n\lambda\sum_j\omega_j|\beta_j|\). In words: take the size of each word’s weight (\(|\beta_j|\)), multiply by that word’s own cost factor (\(\omega_j\)), add them all up, and multiply by λ and by the number of documents \(n\).
  • λ (the strength of the penalty dial) controls shrinkage (how hard the weights are pushed towards zero). λ = 0 gives back OLS.
  • Lasso (one type of penalised regression) sets some weights to exactly zero, so those words drop out.
  • Choose λ by cross-validation on held-out data (documents kept aside during training). Judge the model on out-of-sample \(R^2\) (fit on documents it has not seen), not in-sample \(R^2\) (fit on the documents it learned from).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Writing \(n \gg p\) (more documents than words). It is the other way round.
  • Saying λ = 0 is “maximum penalty”. It is no penalty at all.
  • Confusing the code’s alpha (in the scikit-learn library, alpha is the penalty dial λ) with the intercept \(\alpha\) on the slides (the starting value of the prediction).
  • Trusting in-sample \(R^2\) (the score on the training documents).
  • Claiming Ridge sets weights to exactly zero. It only shrinks them; Lasso is the one that sets some to zero.

Key terms to use

  • document-term matrix as regressors (word counts used as model inputs)
  • \(n \ll p\) (far fewer documents than words)
  • curse of dimensionality (too many columns, model fits anything)
  • overfitting (memorises training data, fails on new data)
  • penalised / regularised regression (regression with a fee for big weights)
  • Lasso (penalty that can set weights exactly zero)
  • Ridge (penalty that shrinks weights but keeps all)
  • Elastic net (a mix of Lasso and Ridge)
  • penalty λ (dial for how strong the fee is)
  • rare feature upweighting (\(\omega_j\)) (each word gets its own penalty cost)
  • shrinkage (pushing weights towards zero)
  • cross-validation (repeatedly test on held-back documents)
  • train/test split (learn on one part, test on another)
  • out-of-sample \(R^2\) (fit score on unseen documents)
  • placebo test (shuffle the answers; honest score should collapse)
  • dimension reduction (PCA, PLS) (squeeze many word columns into a few)

Quick self-test

  1. “In text regressions, regularisation helps overcome the curse of dimensionality.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A text regression predicts a number from word counts. Regularisation means adding a fee for big word weights. The curse of dimensionality is having far more words (columns) than documents (rows). Does the fee help with that problem?

    Answer: True. Why: With thousands of words and only a few dozen documents, the model can bend itself to fit anything. The fee forces it to keep most weights small, so only words that really matter keep a big weight. It is like a packing limit for a trip: you can only bring what you really need. This was question (e) on the 2025 exam.

  2. “With λ = 0, the penalised regression on the slides becomes standard OLS.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: λ is the strength of the penalty dial. OLS (ordinary least squares) is the plain regression with no penalty. If you turn the dial to 0, do you get plain regression back?

    Answer: True. Why: The fee is λ times the size of the weights. If λ is 0, the fee is always 0, so only the fit counts, and that is exactly OLS. Like a speed camera switched off: it is still there, but it never charges you.

  3. “In Lasso, high values of λ make coefficients larger.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Lasso is a regression with a fee for big weights. Coefficients are the word weights. λ is the strength of the fee. The statement says a stronger fee makes the weights bigger.

    Answer: False. Why: A higher fee makes big weights more expensive, so the model shrinks them, and with a high enough λ they become zero. It is like a tax on luggage weight: the higher the tax, the less you pack.

  4. “If a Ridge regression of a shuffled (placebo) target on word counts gives an in-sample R² near 1, the words are informative.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Ridge is a regression with a fee for big weights. The target is the number we try to predict (here GDP growth). “Shuffled (placebo)” means we mixed up the target values randomly between years, so the words cannot possibly hold real information about them. In-sample R² near 1 means the model fits the documents it learned from almost perfectly. The statement says this perfect fit proves the words are useful.

    Answer: False. Why: With far more words than documents (p ≫ n), the model can fit almost any target, even a random one. A student given 70 questions with random answers can memorise them and score 100% on those same questions, but that proves memorising, not understanding; the honest test is new questions. Only out-of-sample R² (the score on documents the model has not seen) counts.

  5. “Why do we need regularisation in text regressions, and how is the penalty chosen?” (Explain in 2–5 sentences.)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Why do we add a fee for big word weights, and how do we decide how strong that fee should be?

    Answer: write the model answer from “What the exam asks” above. Its three beats: far more words than documents (\(n \ll p\)), so plain OLS breaks or fits meaninglessly; Lasso-type methods add a fee \(n\lambda\sum_j\omega_j|\beta_j|\) that shrinks weights (λ = 0 gives back OLS); λ is picked by cross-validation (or AIC/BIC). Why: those three beats are the problem, the fix, and how to set the fix, which is exactly what the question asks for.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • regression: a method for guessing a number (the outcome) from other numbers (the inputs) by finding the best formula, often a straight line. Example: guessing ice-cream sales from the temperature.
  • text regression: a regression where the inputs are the word counts of each document. Example: guessing GDP growth from a speech’s words.
  • document: one single text in the collection. Example: one speech.
  • document-term matrix (DTM): the word-count table: rows = documents, columns = words, cells = counts. Example: a cell of 3 = “this speech says this word 3 times”.
  • outcome (\(y\)): the number we want to guess, such as GDP growth or a star rating. \(y_i\) is the outcome of document \(i\).
  • explanatory variable / regressor / feature / input (\(x\)): an input used to make the guess. In text regression, each word column is one input.
  • \(x_i = f(c_i)\): the inputs of document \(i\). Either its raw row of word counts \(c_i\), or a changed version of it (like tf-idf weights).
  • supervised: learning from examples whose right answer is known. Example: speeches paired with that year’s growth.
  • \(p(y_i\mid c_i)\) and conditional expectation \(E[y_i\mid c_i]\): what to expect for the outcome given the word counts; the average outcome for documents with these counts, i.e. the best guess.
  • intercept (\(\alpha\), alpha): the starting value of the guess when every input is 0. Example: the 20 in “20 + 3 × temperature”.
  • coefficient / slope (\(\beta\), beta): how much the guess changes when an input goes up by one. \(\beta_j\) belongs to word \(j\). Example: the 3 in “20 + 3 × temperature”.
  • prediction / guess (\(\eta_i\), eta): the model’s guess for document \(i\): intercept plus each input times its coefficient.
  • \(x_i'\beta\): short for “multiply each of document \(i\)’s inputs by its coefficient and add them all up”.
  • miss / error / residual: the gap between the real outcome and the guess. Example: real 5, guess 6, miss 1.
  • squared error: the miss times itself. A miss of 2 becomes 4, a miss of −2 also becomes 4.
  • loss (\(l(\alpha,\beta)\)): the total of how badly the model fits. Here, the total of squared misses.
  • \(\sum\) (sigma): “add up”. \(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\) means “add this up for document 1, 2, … up to \(n\)”.
  • \(\min\{\cdot\}\): “choose the numbers that make this as small as possible”.
  • objective: the total you are trying to make as small as possible (here, loss + fee).
  • OLS (ordinary least squares): the standard way of choosing the coefficients: make the total of squared misses as small as possible, with no fee.
  • \(n\) and \(p\): \(n\) = number of documents (rows); \(p\) = number of words (columns).
  • \(n \ll p\) (and \(p \gg n\)): “\(n\) is much smaller than \(p\)”: far fewer documents than words. Example: 70 speeches, thousands of words.
  • more unknowns than equations: more numbers to choose (coefficients) than facts to pin them down (documents). Like being asked for two numbers that add to 10: there are endless answers.
  • dimension / high-dimensional: each input column is one “dimension”. Thousands of word columns = high-dimensional.
  • curse of dimensionality: the trouble that comes with too many input columns compared with data rows: perfect but meaningless fits.
  • overfitting: a model that memorises the training examples, including their noise, and so guesses badly on new ones. Like a student who memorises last year’s answers and fails a new exam.
  • regularisation / penalisation: adding a fee for big coefficients, so the model only uses words that really help.
  • penalty: the fee itself. Example: \(24\lambda\) for candidate A in the walk-through.
  • \(\lambda\) (lambda): the fee rate. \(\lambda = 0\) = no fee (plain OLS). Bigger \(\lambda\) = bigger fee, more coefficients pushed to zero.
  • shrinkage: coefficients getting pulled towards zero by the fee.
  • absolute value \(\lvert\beta_j\rvert\): the size of a number ignoring its minus sign. \(\lvert -3\rvert = 3\).
  • Lasso: the version whose fee uses absolute values. It can set coefficients to exactly zero, so it also picks words.
  • Ridge: the version whose fee uses squared coefficients. It shrinks them but keeps every word. [Not in course files — general knowledge, as in the Ridge note in the formula section]
  • Elastic net: a mix of Lasso and Ridge.
  • \(\omega_j\) (omega), variable-specific cost: an extra weight on each word’s fee, so words can be charged differently.
  • standard deviation: how much a number varies around its average. Counts that jump around a lot have a big standard deviation.
  • rare feature upweighting: setting each word’s extra weight \(\omega_j\) using its standard deviation.
  • yes/no outcome and logistic loss: when the outcome is yes/no (spam or not), the misses are scored with a different formula, the logistic loss.
  • log: the logarithm, a function that turns multiplying into adding; \(\log(a \times b) = \log a + \log b\). It grows slowly: big numbers become small ones.
  • \(e\) (in \(e^{\eta_i}\)): a fixed number, about 2.718, that appears in growth formulas. \(e^{\eta}\) is \(e\) raised to the power \(\eta\) (for \(\eta = 2\), that is \(e \times e \approx 7.39\)).
  • tf-idf: a word weight that is high for words that are frequent in this document but rare in the other documents.
  • stop words: very common words like “the”, “and”, “of”, usually removed.
  • min_df: “minimum document frequency”: drop words that appear in fewer than this many documents. Example: MIN_DF = 5.
  • dimension reduction (PCA, Partial Least Squares): squeezing thousands of word columns into a few summary columns before running the regression. PCA is the same idea as LSA, covered in its own chapter of this guide.
  • non-linear methods (GLMs, regression trees, random forest): methods that allow curves and if-then rules instead of one straight line. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • training set / test set: the part of the data the model learns from, and the hidden part used to check it.
  • cross-validation: choosing λ by repeatedly training on part of the data and checking guesses on the hidden part.
  • fold / 5-fold: the data is cut into 5 equal groups (folds). Train on 4, test on the 5th, and repeat 5 times so every group is tested once.
  • in-sample / out-of-sample: in-sample = measured on the data the model trained on; out-of-sample = measured on data it never saw.
  • held-out data: data kept aside and not used for training.
  • \(R^2\): a score for how much of the ups and downs in the outcome the guesses explain. 1 = perfect; 0 = “no better than always guessing the average”; below 0 = worse than that.
  • cross-validated \(R^2\): the \(R^2\) measured on held-out data only, the honest one.
  • placebo test: a fake test where the outcome is shuffled on purpose, so the words cannot really predict it. If the model still “fits”, the fit is fake. Like a student memorising 70 random answers.
  • information criteria (AIC, BIC): scores computed on the training data that reward good fit but charge for every extra coefficient. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • pipeline: a chain of steps run in order: first turn text into numbers, then fit the regression.
  • scikit-learn / Ridge(alpha=…): a popular Python toolbox for these methods. Its alpha setting is the fee λ, not the intercept.
  • KFold, shuffle, random_state: the code that cuts the data into folds, mixes up the order first, and fixes the random mixing so you get the same result each time you run it.
  • GDP growth / State of the Union: GDP growth = how fast the economy grew, in %. The State of the Union is the US president’s yearly speech to Congress. [Not in course files — general knowledge]

Sources: Lecture 3 slides 13–20 and 34; Interactive Notebook 2 cells 11–14 and 31 (code simplified from cells 12–13); 2025 exam T/F (e).

9. Naive Bayes classification (L3, Interactive 2)

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 T/F (g) (“Naive Bayes … great for … two continuous variables” → False); the mechanics (Bayes’ rule, “naive”, Laplace smoothing) are a likely T/F or short question.

Why this exists

Your inbox gets 200 emails a day, and 50 of them are junk (“You won a prize! Click here!”). You want a program that moves the junk to a spam folder before you see it.

You also have a big pile of old emails that you already marked “spam” or “not spam”. Can the computer learn from that pile, and then sort new emails by itself?

Naive Bayes is one of the oldest and most basic ways to do this. The same idea can sort political speeches by party, or reviews into good and bad.

The idea in everyday words

Sorting into boxes, not guessing a number.

Some tasks ask you to guess a number, like next year’s economic growth (2.37%). The standard tool for that is a regression: it predicts a number by drawing the best line through points on a chart. Other tasks ask you to put something into one of a few boxes: spam or not spam, Democrat or Republican, good review or bad review. Sorting into boxes is called classification. The method that does the sorting is a classifier. Each box is a class, or category. Think of a post office sorting letters by city.

Two words for these two kinds of answer:

  • A continuous outcome is a number that can take any value, like 2.37% growth or a person’s height.
  • A categorical outcome is one of a fixed set of boxes, like spam / not spam.

The lecture slides put it like this: regression (for example OLS, the standard line-fitting method) “works best for continuous outcome variables”. For categorical outcomes, such as “good versus bad, spam versus not spam, etc.”, “it is more common and better to apply classification methods”. Naive Bayes is one such classification method.

A quick word on chances.

Naive Bayes works with chances, also called probabilities. A probability is a number from 0 to 1 for how likely something is. \(P(\text{rain}) = 0.3\) means a 30% chance of rain. The notation \(P(A \mid B)\) means “the chance of A, given B”. The upright bar “\(\mid\)” is read “given”. For example, \(P(\text{umbrella} \mid \text{rain})\) is how likely you are to carry an umbrella when it rains.

How a doctor would do it.

Analogy A doctor guessing between a cold and the flu. They know how common each illness is right now (the prior) and how often each symptom appears with each illness (the likelihoods). For a patient with a fever and aching muscles, they multiply “how common the illness is” by “how typical each symptom is for it” and choose the larger. “Naive” means the doctor treats every symptom as independent evidence, even though fever and aches often come together.

Naive Bayes does the same thing, with words playing the role of symptoms.

How it works, step by step.

  1. Collect labelled examples. Gather old emails that already carry the right box, “spam” or “not spam”. The box written next to each example is its label. This labelled pile is the training set: the examples the model learns from.
  2. Count how common each class is. If 1 in 4 old emails was spam, then before reading a new email, your starting guess is “1 in 4 chance it is spam”. This starting guess is called the prior: how common a class is before you read the document.
  3. For each class, count each word. “prize” might be common in spam and rare in normal mail; “meeting” the other way round. Turn these counts into shares: out of all the words in spam emails, what share is “prize”? This share is the likelihood of the word in that class: how typical the word is for that class.
  4. Fix the zero problem. If a word never appeared in spam, its share would be 0. One zero wipes out the whole score, because anything times 0 is 0. So we pretend every word was seen one extra time in every class. This fix is called Laplace smoothing.
  5. Score a new email for each class. Start from the prior, and multiply by the share of each word in the email. Here we treat every word as separate evidence, as if the words did not affect each other. This simplification is the “naive” part.
  6. Pick the winner. The class with the bigger score wins. To turn the scores into chances that add up to 100%, divide each score by the total of all the scores. This is called normalising. The chance of a class after reading the document is called the posterior. In short: prior + evidence from the words → posterior.
  7. Why “Bayes”. Bayes’ rule is the bit of probability that lets us flip the question. We learned “how likely are these words, if the email is spam?” Bayes’ rule turns that into “how likely is it spam, given these words?”
  8. Test it fairly. Check it on emails that were not in the training pile. That separate pile is the test set. Compare with a lazy rule such as “always say not spam”.

The course notebook sums it up nicely: “Naive Bayes learns, for each party, the odds of every word, and lets the words vote.” (Odds here means how much more often a word shows up for one party than for the other.)

Why the name, in the slides’ own words.

  • “It is called ‘Naive’ because it operates under the bag-of-words assumption and assumes that the words in a document are independent.” The bag-of-words assumption treats a document as a loose bag of words: word order does not matter, only the counts. Independent means that, once you know the class, knowing one word tells you nothing about the next word. (The full name is conditional independence: independent given the class.)
  • “It is called ‘Bayes’ because it applies the Bayes rule to make inference.” Inference means drawing a conclusion from the data; here, deciding the class.

Despite being so basic, the slides say it “works very well for categorizing documents”, has a long history in NLP (natural language processing, the field of getting computers to handle text), and “is usually regarded as a good starting point”. The slides also name other classifiers, Support Vector Machines, logistic regression and neural networks. These are other, more complex sorting methods; they are named but not taught here.

What it’s good at, and where it breaks.

  • Good: fast, and needs only counting.
  • Good: easy to see which words push a document towards each class.
  • Breaks: it only sorts into categories (spam / not spam). It cannot guess a number like GDP growth (how fast the economy grew, in %). This was tested on the 2025 exam.
  • Breaks: the “words are independent” idea is false in real text (“New” is often followed by “York”). Also, a test set that shares people or time periods with the training set makes the accuracy look better than it is. Part 2 of the walk-through shows how.

Walk-through example

Part 1: sorting one new text by hand.

The situation. Four short texts are already sorted into two classes, called a and b. Think of them as two people’s notes. A fifth text is new, and we must decide its class. In the table, each row is one text. The middle column is the text itself. The last column is its class; “?” means unknown.

Doc Words Class
1 (train) growth high trump a
2 (train) trump rocket man a
3 (train) trump trump trump a
4 (train) trump inflation norway b
5 (test) inflation norway high ?

Documents 1–4 are the training set. Document 5, “inflation norway high”, is the one to sort. Naive Bayes works like a detective with two questions:

  1. How common is each class in general?
  2. How typical are the new text’s words for each class?

Question 1: how common is each class? (the prior)

3 of the 4 training texts are class a, and 1 of the 4 is class b. So class a starts with 3/4 and class b with 1/4. Before reading a single word, class a looks more likely, because it is more common.

Question 2: how typical is each word for each class? (the likelihood)

First, count all the words in each class. One word occurrence is called a token. So “trump trump trump” is 3 tokens of 1 word.

  • Class a has 9 tokens in total (3 texts × 3 words): trump 5, growth 1, high 1, rocket 1, man 1.
  • Class b has 3 tokens: trump 1, inflation 1, norway 1.

The list of different words seen in training is the vocabulary. Here it has 7 words: growth, high, trump, rocket, man, inflation, norway. The vocabulary size is written \(p\), so \(p = 7\).

Now take each word of the new text and ask, for each class: what share of this class’s tokens is this word?

One fix first. Class a never uses “inflation”, so its share would be 0 out of 9. Multiplying by 0 would kill class a’s score because of one missing word. So we pretend every word was seen one extra time in every class. That is the “+1” of Laplace smoothing. There are 7 different words, and each gets one extra sighting, so each class’s total also goes up by 7. Class a’s total becomes 9 + 7 = 16, and class b’s becomes 3 + 7 = 10.

In the next table, each row is one word of the new text. For each class there are two columns: how many times the word appeared in that class, plus 1; and that number divided by the class’s new total (16 for a, 10 for b), which is the word’s share in the class.

New word (rows) Times in class a, +1 Share in a Times in class b, +1 Share in b
inflation 0 + 1 = 1 1/16 1 + 1 = 2 2/10 = 1/5
norway 0 + 1 = 1 1/16 1 + 1 = 2 2/10 = 1/5
high 1 + 1 = 2 2/16 = 1/8 0 + 1 = 1 1/10

Read one cell in words: “high” appears once in class a. Add 1 to get 2. Divide by class a’s total of 16. So the share of “high” in class a is 2/16 = 1/8.

Put it together: the score. Score = how common the class is × how typical each word is, all multiplied:

  • Class a: 3/4 × 1/16 × 1/16 × 1/8 = 3/8192 ≈ 0.000366
  • Class b: 1/4 × 1/5 × 1/5 × 1/10 = 1/1000 = 0.001

Working out class a in words: 3/4 × 1/16 = 3/64. Then 3/64 × 1/16 = 3/1024. Then 3/1024 × 1/8 = 3/8192. For class b: 1/4 × 1/5 = 1/20. Then 1/20 × 1/5 = 1/100. Then 1/100 × 1/10 = 1/1000.

Both numbers are tiny, because you multiply lots of small fractions. That is normal. Only which one is bigger matters. Class b’s score is bigger (about 2.7 times class a’s), so the new text goes to class b.

Turning scores into percentages. Add the two scores: 0.000366 + 0.001 = 0.001366. Each class’s share of that total is its chance, the posterior. Class b: 0.001 ÷ 0.001366 ≈ 0.73, or 73%. Class a: 0.000366 ÷ 0.001366 ≈ 0.27, or 27%. The two add up to 100%, as chances should.

The one-sentence intuition. “trump” is the typical class-a word, but document 5 has no “trump”. Its words “inflation” and “norway” were seen only in the class-b text, and that evidence outweighs class a’s head start of 3/4.

Why “naive”. It scores each word separately and multiplies, as if the words had nothing to do with each other, ignoring order and phrases. That is a simplification, but it works surprisingly well, which is why spam filters have used it for years.

Why smoothing matters. Try it without the +1 and +7. Then the chance of “inflation” in class a is 0/9 = 0, so class a’s product is 0. And the chance of “high” in class b is 0/3 = 0, so class b’s product is 0 too. Both classes score zero, and we cannot decide. One unseen word wipes out all the other evidence. Smoothing prevents that.

A warning about the slide. The lecture slide prints the two scores as ≈ 0.00004 and ≈ 0.0001. These are about 10 times too small; the exact values are 0.000366 and 0.001. Both are off by the same factor, so the ratio between them, the normalised 0.27 / 0.73 and the winning class “b” are all still correct. In the exam, write the correct values (0.000366 and 0.001), or write the fractions 3/8192 and 1/1000.

Part 2: checking a classifier on real speeches.

The course notebook trains Naive Bayes to guess a US president’s party from the words of their State of the Union speech (the president’s yearly speech to Congress). How do we know if it is any good?

Accuracy against a lazy baseline. Accuracy is the share of test documents put into the right class: 70 right out of 100 = 70%. But 70% is not impressive if 65% of the test speeches belong to one party anyway, because “always guess that party” would already score 65% (illustrative numbers). The rule “always guess the biggest class” is the majority-class baseline. A real model must beat it. The notebook compares its accuracy with “always guessing the bigger party”.

How you split decides what accuracy means. Splitting means choosing which speeches go into training and which into testing. The notebook tries two ways. In the next table, each row is one way of splitting. The middle column says what ends up in the test set. The last column says what can go wrong.

Split What goes into the test set Problem
"random" a random quarter of the speeches the same president appears in training and test, so the model can recognise the president and era (names, events) rather than the party: information leaks from train to test
"by_president" (GroupShuffleSplit) a random quarter of the presidents every test speech is by a president the model never saw: an honest test of party

When information from the test set sneaks into training like this, it is called data leakage. Holding out whole groups (here, all speeches by some presidents) is a grouped split.

The notebook’s takeaway: “How you choose the test data decides what the accuracy means. A random split rewards a Naive Bayes model that recognises presidents and eras; holding out whole presidents reveals how little of that is party.”

It also warns that “one split proves little”, so it repeats the experiment over 20 random seeds. A random seed is the starting number for the computer’s random choices: the same seed gives the same split, a new seed gives a new split.

The business version: a complaint-email flagger trained on a random split of last year’s mail may fail on next year’s mail.

The formula, explained

You have now done the whole method by hand. The slides write the same steps as a chain of formulas. In 2025 the exam had no calculations, so you mainly need to understand these. A short posterior calculation like the walk-through is a possible question, though, and the estimation formulas below are exactly the recipe you used.

New symbols first:

  • \(d\) = the document we want to sort.
  • \(v\) or \(v_k\) = a class (“class number \(k\)”; in the example, \(a\) or \(b\)).
  • \(c_{ij}\) = the count of word \(j\) in document \(i\). So \(c_{i1},\dots,c_{ip}\) is the document’s full row of word counts.
  • \(\arg\max\) = “the choice that gives the biggest value”. If a scores 0.000366 and b scores 0.001, the argmax is b.

Line 1, Bayes’ rule. In words: the chance of class \(v\) after reading document \(d\) equals how likely the document is under that class, times how common the class is, divided by how likely the document is overall.

\[P(v\mid d) = \frac{P(d\mid v)P(v)}{P(d)} \qquad\text{(Bayes' rule: posterior = likelihood × prior / data)}\]

Line 2. In words: the predicted class is the one with the largest of these chances. That winner is called the MAP class (maximum a posteriori: “the highest posterior”), written \(v_{map}\).

\[v_{map} = \arg\max \frac{P(d\mid v)P(v)}{P(d)} \qquad\text{(pick the most probable class)}\]

Line 3. In words: treat the document as its list of word counts, and drop the bottom part \(P(d)\), because it is the same for every class.

\[v_{k,map} = \arg\max P(c_{i1},\dots,c_{ip}\mid v_k)P(v_k) \qquad\text{(document = its words; } P(d) \text{ dropped)}\]

Line 4, the naive step. In words: the chance of seeing all the words together is taken to be the chance of each word on its own, multiplied together.

\[P(c_{i1},\dots,c_{ip}\mid v_k) = P(c_{i1}\mid v_k)\times\dots\times P(c_{ip}\mid v_k) \qquad\text{(the "naive" independence step)}\]

Line 5, the finished classifier. In words: for each class, multiply how common the class is by the chance of each word in that class, and pick the class with the largest result.

\[v_{k,nb} = \arg\max P(v_k)\,\prod_j P(c_{ij}\mid v_k) \qquad\text{(Multinomial Naive Bayes classifier)}\]

What each part means:

  • \(P(v_k)\) = the prior: how common class \(k\) is before reading the document.
  • \(P(c_{ij}\mid v_k)\) = the likelihood of word \(j\) in class \(k\).
  • \(P(d\mid v)\) = how likely this document’s words are, if it came from class \(v\).
  • \(P(v\mid d)\) = the posterior: the chance of class \(v\) after reading the document.
  • \(P(d)\) = the overall chance of seeing this document. It is dropped because it is the same for every class, so it does not change which class wins.
  • \(\prod\) (capital “pi”) = “multiply all of these together”, over all words in the document, in the same way \(\sum\) means “add all of these”. The slide writes a capital \(\Pi\).
  • Multinomial Naive Bayes is the name of this word-count version of Naive Bayes.

Once \(P(d)\) is dropped, the scores are no longer exact chances, so people write \(\propto\), “proportional to”, instead of \(=\). It means “equal up to a common scaling”: we skip dividing by the same number for every class, because it does not change the winner.

How the numbers are estimated: “simple counting”. A hat on a letter, as in \(\hat P\), means “estimated from the data”.

In words: the prior of a class is the share of training documents that belong to it.

\[\hat P(v_k) = \frac{doccount(V = v_k)}{n} = \frac{n_k}{n}\]

In words: the chance of word \(j\) in class \(k\) is how often it appears in that class (plus 1), divided by the total number of words in that class (plus the vocabulary size).

\[\hat P(c_{\cdot j}\mid v_k) = \frac{count(c_{\cdot j}, v_k) + 1}{\sum count(c, v_k) + p}\]

  • \(n_k\) = the number of training documents in class \(k\); \(n\) = all training documents. In the example, \(n_a = 3\) and \(n = 4\), so the prior is 3/4.
  • \(count(c_{\cdot j}, v_k)\) = how many times word \(j\) appears in all class-\(k\) documents together. The dot in \(c_{\cdot j}\) means “across all documents”.
  • \(\sum count(c, v_k)\) = the total number of tokens in class-\(k\) documents (9 for class a in the example).
  • \(p\) = vocabulary size, the number of different words (7 in the example).
  • \(+1\) and \(+p\) = Laplace smoothing “to avoid zeros”: pretend every word was seen once more in every class.

Read aloud in one sentence: “Pick the class whose share of training documents, times the smoothed frequency of each of the document’s words in that class, is largest.”

The big picture, as the slides summarise it. We know the classes of the training documents (\(V^{train}\)) and observe their word counts (\(C^{train}\)). We learn \(p(c^{train}\mid v^{train})\), the chance of the words given the class. “Via Bayes rule we can use this to predict \(p(v^{test}\mid c^{test})\)”, the chance of the class given the words, for the test documents. So Naive Bayes models \(p(c_i\mid y_i)\), words given outcome. That is the reverse of text regression, which models \(p(y_i\mid c_i)\), outcome given words.

Reading the course code

The exam has not asked students to write code. This section is only so that the notebook makes sense to you.

vec = CountVectorizer(stop_words="english", min_df=5, token_pattern=r"[a-zA-Z][a-zA-Z]+")
Xtr = vec.fit_transform(train.rawtext)
nb  = MultinomialNB().fit(Xtr, train.party)
acc = nb.score(vec.transform(test.rawtext), test.party)
tilt = nb.feature_log_prob_[0] - nb.feature_log_prob_[1]

(Simplified from the course notebook.)

  • Line 1 makes a word counter (CountVectorizer). It drops English stop words (very common words like “the” and “and”) and keeps only words found in at least 5 speeches (min_df=5, “minimum document frequency”). The token_pattern part says a word is two or more letters in a row.
  • Line 2 learns the vocabulary from the training speeches only, and builds their document-term matrix (the word-count table: one row per speech, one column per word). “Fit” means “learn from this data”.
  • Line 3 fits Multinomial Naive Bayes (MultinomialNB). This does the counting shown above: priors and smoothed likelihoods. Scikit-learn’s default smoothing is the same add-one (Laplace) idea. [Not in course files — general knowledge: MultinomialNB has a smoothing parameter alpha that defaults to 1.]
  • Line 4 gives the accuracy: the share of test speeches given the right party.
  • Line 5 computes each word’s “tilt”. feature_log_prob_ stores the log chance of each word in each party. (A log, or logarithm, is a function that turns multiplying into adding. The difference of two logs compares how many times bigger one chance is than the other.) So line 5 is log P(word | party 0) − log P(word | party 1). Positive = “more Democratic”, negative = “more Republican”. The notebook lists the top 12 of each. For the toy data above, the tilt of “trump” towards class a is \(\log(3/8) - \log(1/5) \approx 0.63\), because P(trump | a) = (5+1)/(9+7) = 3/8 and P(trump | b) = (1+1)/(3+7) = 1/5.

There are no saved outputs. When run, it would print the test accuracy next to the majority-class baseline, the test presidents, and the most party-typical words. With a random split, the notebook hints these are often names and events.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025 exam, True/False (g): “The Naive Bayes Classifier is great for capturing the relationship between two continuous variables.”

Model answer — False. Naive Bayes is a classifier for a categorical outcome (an answer that is one of a few groups, like “spam / not spam” or “party a / party b”), and it works on word counts. Continuous variables are numbers that can take any value, like height or GDP growth.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Naive Bayes sorts things into boxes. Linking two numbers is a different job, done by regression.

Likely variants:

  • why it is called “naive” and why “Bayes”;
  • what Laplace smoothing (adding 1 to every word count) does;
  • regression (guessing a number) vs classification (guessing a group);
  • a short posterior calculation (working out the chance of each class for a new document) like the walk-through;
  • the evaluation trap: a random split vs a grouped split (keeping all speeches by one person on the same side of the train/test line).

Likely short question: “How does Naive Bayes classify a document, and why is it called ‘naive’ and ‘Bayes’?” (2–5 sentences)

Model answer — From labelled training documents, Naive Bayes estimates the prior share of each class (\(n_k/n\)) and, for each class, the probability of each word (its smoothed frequency among all words in that class, with +1/+p Laplace smoothing so unseen words do not give zero). For a new document it multiplies the class prior by the probabilities of all the document’s words and picks the class with the largest result. It is “Bayes” because it uses Bayes’ rule to turn \(p(\text{words}\mid\text{class})\) into \(p(\text{class}\mid\text{words})\), and “naive” because it uses the bag-of-words assumption that words are independent given the class. It is for categorical outcomes (spam/not spam), not continuous ones.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: first it learns from documents that already have their correct group: how common each group is, and how often each word shows up in each group (with 1 added to every count so nothing is zero). For a new document, it multiplies the group’s share by the chances of all the document’s words, and picks the group with the biggest result. “Bayes” is the rule that flips “how likely are these words in this group?” into “how likely is this group, given these words?”. “Naive” is the simplifying belief that words do not depend on each other; and it sorts into groups, it does not predict numbers.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • The outcome is categorical (a group label, not a number).
  • From labelled training data (documents that come with their correct class), learn the chance of the words given the class (\(p(c\mid v)\)). Then flip it with Bayes’ rule to get the chance of the class given the words (\(p(v\mid c)\)).
  • “Naive” = the bag-of-words assumption (word order is ignored) plus the assumption that words are independent given the class (each word is treated as if it tells you nothing about the other words).
  • The prior (how common each class is before reading the document) is \(n_k/n\): the number of training documents in class \(k\) divided by all training documents.
  • The likelihood is the smoothed share of that word among all words in the class.
  • Laplace smoothing adds 1 to each word count (top of the fraction) and \(p\), the number of different words in the vocabulary, to the bottom. This avoids zero chances.
  • Choose the class with the highest posterior (the chance of the class after reading the document).
  • Evaluate on held-out data (documents the model did not learn from) and compare with a baseline (a dumb rule such as always guessing the biggest class). Hold out whole groups (e.g. all speeches by one president) to avoid leakage (test information sneaking into training).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Using Naive Bayes for continuous outcomes (numbers like GDP growth).
  • Saying “naive because it is simple”. It is naive because of the independence assumption (words treated as unrelated given the class).
  • Forgetting smoothing, or adding 1 to the bottom of the fraction instead of \(p\) (the number of different words).
  • Forgetting the prior (how common each class is).
  • Stopping at the raw products (before dividing by their total) without saying which class wins.
  • Reporting accuracy from a random split as proof that the model learned “party”. It may have only learned names and events of each president.

Key terms to use

  • classification (guessing which group a document belongs to)
  • categorical outcome (answer is a group, not a number)
  • Bayes’ rule (formula that flips “words given class” round)
  • prior (how common each class is beforehand)
  • likelihood (how typical these words are for a class)
  • posterior (chance of a class after reading the words)
  • maximum a posteriori (argmax) (pick the class with the highest posterior)
  • conditional independence (words treated as unrelated within a class)
  • bag-of-words assumption (word order is ignored; only counts matter)
  • Multinomial Naive Bayes (the word-count version of Naive Bayes)
  • Laplace smoothing (add 1 so no chance is zero)
  • training/test data (learn on one part, check on another)
  • accuracy (share of documents classified correctly)
  • majority-class baseline (always guess the most common class)
  • data leakage (test information sneaking into training)
  • grouped split (keep each group wholly in train or test)

Quick self-test

  1. “The Naive Bayes classifier is great for capturing the relationship between two continuous variables.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Naive Bayes is a method that sorts documents into groups. Continuous variables are numbers that can take any value, like height and weight. The statement says Naive Bayes is good at linking two such numbers.

    Answer: False. Why: Naive Bayes is built to pick a group (a categorical outcome, like “spam” or “not spam”), using word counts. Linking two numbers is a job for regression. It is like using a letter-sorting machine to measure parcels: wrong tool. This was question (g) on the 2025 exam.

  2. “Naive Bayes is called naive because it assumes the words in a document are independent (bag-of-words).” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Independent” means each word is treated as if it tells you nothing about the other words in the document. Bag-of-words means we ignore word order and only count words, as if the words were shaken up in a bag. Is that the reason for the name “naive”?

    Answer: True. Why: In real text, words clearly depend on each other (“New” is often followed by “York”). Pretending they do not is a naive (overly simple) assumption, hence the name. It still works well in practice.

  3. “Laplace smoothing adds 1 to every word count so that unseen words do not give zero probability.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: If a word never appeared in a class’s training documents, its chance for that class would be 0. Because Naive Bayes multiplies all word chances together, one 0 makes the whole result 0. The statement says Laplace smoothing fixes this by adding 1 to every count.

    Answer: True. Why: Adding 1 to every count means no word ever has a chance of exactly 0. To keep the shares adding up properly, you also add \(p\) (the number of different words in the vocabulary) to the bottom of each fraction. Think of it as giving every word one free “starter” sighting, so one missing word cannot veto all the other evidence.

  4. “Using the four training documents from the walk-through, classify a new document containing only ‘trump’.” (Calculation)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Use the small four-document example from the walk-through. Class a has 3 of the 4 training documents and 9 words in total, 5 of them “trump”. Class b has 1 document with 3 words, 1 of them “trump”. There are 7 different words overall. Which class does a new document that says only “trump” belong to?

    Answer: a: \(\tfrac34\times\tfrac{5+1}{9+7} = \tfrac34\times\tfrac38 = 0.281\); b: \(\tfrac14\times\tfrac{1+1}{3+7} = \tfrac14\times\tfrac15 = 0.05\). Normalised: a ≈ 0.85, b ≈ 0.15 → class a.

    Why: For each class, multiply how common the class is (the prior: 3/4 or 1/4) by the smoothed chance of “trump” in that class (count + 1, divided by the class’s word total + 7). Class a scores 0.281 and class b scores 0.05. Dividing each by their sum (0.281 + 0.05 = 0.331) gives chances of about 85% for a and 15% for b, so the document goes to class a. That makes sense: “trump” is the typical class-a word, and class a is also the more common class.

  5. “How does Naive Bayes classify a document, and why is it called ‘naive’ and ‘Bayes’?” (Explain in 2–5 sentences.)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Walk through the steps Naive Bayes uses to put a document in a group, and explain both parts of its name.

    Answer: write the model answer from “What the exam asks” above. Its beats: learn priors (\(n_k/n\)) and smoothed word chances (+1/+p) from labelled documents; multiply prior × word chances and pick the biggest; “Bayes” = Bayes’ rule flips words-given-class into class-given-words; “naive” = bag-of-words, words independent given the class; for categorical, not continuous, outcomes. Why: those beats cover both halves of the question, the steps and the name.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • regression: guessing a number by drawing the best line through points. Example: guessing GDP growth from word counts.
  • classification / classifier: sorting things into boxes; the classifier is the method that does the sorting. Like a post office sorting letters by city.
  • class / category: one of the boxes, such as “spam” or “Democrat”. Written \(v_k\) (class number \(k\)), or \(a\) and \(b\) in the example.
  • categorical vs continuous: categorical = a fixed set of boxes (spam / not spam). Continuous = a number that can take any value (2.37% growth).
  • label / labelled data: the correct class written next to each training document. Example: “spam” next to an old email.
  • training set / test set: the training set is the labelled pile the model learns from. The test set is a separate pile kept aside to check how well it sorts.
  • probability / chance, \(P(\cdot)\): a number from 0 to 1 for how likely something is. \(P(\text{rain}) = 0.3\) = 30% chance of rain.
  • \(P(A\mid B)\): “the chance of A, given B”. \(P(\text{umbrella}\mid\text{rain})\) = how likely you carry an umbrella when it rains.
  • document \(d\): the text we want to sort. Example: “inflation norway high”.
  • prior, \(P(v_k)\): how common a class is before you read the document. If 3 of 4 documents are class a, the prior for a is 3/4.
  • likelihood, \(P(c_{ij}\mid v_k)\): how likely a word is to show up in a class. “prize” has a high likelihood in spam.
  • posterior, \(P(v\mid d)\): the updated chance of a class after reading the document. Prior + evidence → posterior. Example: 73% for class b.
  • \(P(d)\): the overall chance of seeing this document. It is the same for every class, so it can be dropped when comparing.
  • Bayes’ rule: the rule that flips “chance of words given class” into “chance of class given words”: posterior = likelihood × prior ÷ \(P(d)\).
  • \(\propto\) (“proportional to”): “equal up to a common scaling”. We skip dividing by the same number for every class, because it does not change the winner.
  • \(\arg\max\): “the choice that gives the biggest value”. If a scores 0.000366 and b scores 0.001, the argmax is b.
  • MAP, \(v_{map}\) (maximum a posteriori): the class with the highest posterior chance, the winner.
  • naive / independence / conditional independence: treating each word as separate evidence, as if knowing one word tells you nothing about the next once you know the class.
  • bag-of-words assumption: a document is a loose bag of words; order does not matter. “dog bites man” = “man bites dog”.
  • \(\prod\) (capital pi): “multiply all of these together”, like \(\sum\) means “add all of these”.
  • \(c_{ij}\): the count of word \(j\) in document \(i\).
  • token: one word occurrence. “trump trump trump” is 3 tokens of 1 word.
  • vocabulary, \(p\): the list of different words seen in training. In the example, \(p = 7\).
  • Multinomial Naive Bayes: the version of Naive Bayes that works with word counts.
  • Laplace smoothing (+1 / +p): add 1 to every word’s count in every class, and add the vocabulary size \(p\) to the bottom, so no chance is ever exactly zero. Example: “inflation” in class a becomes (0+1)/(9+7) = 1/16.
  • normalise: divide each score by the total so the chances add up to 1.
  • estimate, hat (\(\hat P\)): a value worked out from the data. \(\hat P(a)\) = our estimated prior for class a.
  • inference: drawing a conclusion from the data.
  • odds: how many times more likely one thing is than another. In the notebook’s quote, how much more a word belongs to one party than the other.
  • NLP (natural language processing): the field of getting computers to handle human language.
  • Support Vector Machines, logistic regression, neural networks: other, more complex classifiers, named on the slides but not taught here.
  • accuracy: the share of test documents sorted into the right class. 70 right out of 100 = 70%.
  • majority-class baseline: the lazy rule “always guess the biggest class”. A real model must beat it.
  • data leakage: when information from the test set sneaks into training, so the test score looks better than it should.
  • random split vs grouped split (GroupShuffleSplit): a random split picks test documents at random. A grouped split holds out whole groups (for example, all speeches by some presidents).
  • random seed: the starting number for the computer’s random choices. Same seed = same split; new seed = new split.
  • log / log probability: the logarithm, a function that turns multiplying into adding. The difference of two logs compares how many times bigger one chance is than the other.
  • CountVectorizer, fit, MultinomialNB, feature_log_prob_: Python tools that count words, learn from training data, run Naive Bayes, and store the log chance of each word in each class.
  • stop words / min_df: very common words (“the”, “and”) that are removed / drop words seen in fewer than this many documents.
  • document-term matrix: the word-count table: one row per document, one column per word.

Sources: Lecture 3 slides 21–29 (example on slides 24 and 26, formulas on slide 25, summary on slide 27); Interactive Notebook 2 cells 15–20 and 31 (code simplified from cell 17); 2025 exam T/F (g).

10. Topic models: LSA via SVD and LDA (L3, Interactive 2, Practical day 1)

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q2(d) (5 points: what topic models are, two methods, intuition and difference); slide 43’s “LSA is not probabilistic” is a natural T/F.

Why this exists

A newspaper archive holds 50,000 articles, and nobody has tagged them by subject. A central-bank researcher has years of meeting notes and wants to know what the members talk about, and how that changes over time. A company has 5,000 open answers to a customer survey. Reading all of it by hand would take months.

In each case you want the computer to do two things by itself:

  1. find the themes in the pile, without anyone naming them in advance;
  2. say how much of each theme is in each text.

Nobody gives the computer a list of themes. Nobody gives it example answers either. A method that does this is called a topic model. “Topic” is the method’s word for a theme.

Because no answers or labels are supplied, topic models are unsupervised: the method finds the structure on its own. The lecture says a topic model finds out what texts are about “in a parsimonious (unsupervised) manner”. Parsimonious means using as few pieces as possible to explain a lot.

The idea in everyday words

Step 1: turn the texts into a word-count table. A computer cannot read. So first, every text becomes a row of counts.

  • Each row is one document (one article, one speech, one survey answer).
  • Each column is one word.
  • Each cell says how many times that word appears in that document. For example, a football report’s row might say “goal: 3, match: 2, stock: 0”.

This table is called the document-term matrix, or DTM. (“Matrix” is maths for a table of numbers. “Term” means word.) The course calls it \(C\), for counts. We write \(n\) for the number of documents (the rows) and \(p\) for the number of different words (the columns). The table’s size is written \(n \times p\), read “n by p”. Most cells are zero, because most words do not appear in most documents. A table that is mostly zeros is called sparse.

Step 2: the trick. Words of one theme appear in the same documents. “goal” and “match” tend to show up in the same articles. So do “stock” and “market”. If an article contains “goal”, it probably contains “match” too. That is the whole trick: a topic is a cluster of words that tend to appear together. A real example from the lecture is {motor, toyota, nissan, vehicl, car, auto…}. (“vehicl” is a stem: a word cut back to its root, so “vehicle” and “vehicles” both count as “vehicl”.) A topic model hunts for groups of words whose counts rise and fall together from document to document.

Step 3: one text can mix several themes. The lecture’s example is a news article about a Nissan car factory hit by a volcano. It is part “Motor”, part “Natural disasters” and part “Outlook”. So a document is a mixture of topics, in different amounts.

Analogy Think of a smoothie bar. Each smoothie (a document) is a mix of a few base fruits (the topics): say 70% strawberry and 30% banana. Each fruit has its own taste over many flavour notes (the words). You only get to taste the finished smoothies. A topic model works out what the base fruits must be and each smoothie’s recipe.

Step 4: you choose how many themes you want. This number is called \(K\). Ask for \(K = 2\) and you get 2 themes; ask for \(K = 6\) and you get 6. The computer does not know the “right” number. You pick it. \(K\) is usually far smaller than the number of words: maybe 6 themes instead of 10,000 words. In symbols this is written \(K \ll p\), where “\(\ll\)” means “much smaller than”.

Each theme the computer finds is also called a component or a factor. All three words mean “one hidden theme”. The themes are latent, which means hidden: we never see a theme directly, only the words it leaves behind.

Why squeeze 10,000 word columns into a handful of themes? There are four reasons.

  1. Easier to understand. You look at 6 themes, not 10,000 words.
  2. Less noise. The word-count table is large and sparse. The theme table is small and dense (few zeros). Random one-off words get washed out.
  3. It might catch synonyms and polysemy. Synonyms are different words with the same meaning, like “good” and “fine”. Polysemy is one word with several meanings, like “check”.
  4. It helps a later regression. A regression is a method that predicts a number (say, sales) from a set of input columns. A regression that uses the theme shares as its inputs is called a second-stage regression. Each column of a table is one dimension. With 10,000 word columns there are too many inputs for the number of examples, and the regression cannot learn reliably. This problem is called the curse of dimensionality. Summarising many columns with a few is called dimension reduction, and it avoids the problem.

Step 5, way 1: LSA. A maths procedure squeezes the table. The first method is called LSA, short for Latent Semantic Analysis. (“Semantic” means “to do with meaning”.) LSA hands the word-count table to a standard maths procedure that squeezes the table into its few main patterns.

Think of a school report with ten grades per student. A teacher could summarise each student with two scores instead: “how strong overall” and “maths-type subjects versus language-type subjects”. Two numbers per student instead of ten, and you lose little. The squeezing procedure does the same for the word-count table. It finds the few patterns that describe the table best, and gives every document and every word a score on each pattern.

This squeezing procedure has a name: SVD, short for Singular Value Decomposition. (“Decomposition” means splitting something into parts.) SVD is a procedure the computer runs. Nobody does it by hand, and the exam will not ask you to.

What comes out that you need to read:

  • A table called \(F\), for factors. One row per document, one column per theme. Each cell is that document’s score on that theme. Its size is \(n \times K\).
  • A table called \(L\), for loadings. One row per word, one column per theme. Each cell says how strongly that word belongs to that theme. Its size is \(p \times K\).
  • One importance number per theme, called its singular value. The themes come out sorted, most important first.

Documents about similar things end up with similar rows in \(F\). Words about similar things end up with similar rows in \(L\).

SVD actually finds as many patterns as the table allows. You keep only the \(K\) most important ones and throw the rest away as noise. Cutting off the rest is called truncation.

There is a second standard procedure that gives the same themes: PCA, short for Principal Components Analysis. PCA finds the few directions in which the data vary the most. The lecture describes LSA as “Principal Components Analysis (PCA) applied to text”. It can be computed with PCA or with SVD: “Same results, but differences in implementation” (implementation = how the computer carries it out).

One feature of LSA matters a lot for the exam. Its scores are plain numbers. They can be negative, and they do not add up to anything in particular. So they are not shares and not chances.

Step 6, way 2: LDA. A story of how documents are written. The second method is called LDA, short for Latent Dirichlet Allocation. (Dirichlet is the name of a mathematician [Not in course files — general knowledge].) LDA works with probabilities. A probability is a chance written as a number from 0 to 1: 0 means never, 1 means certain, 0.5 means half the time. A list of chances for all the possible outcomes adds up to 1, the way shares add up to 100%. Such a list is called a distribution (or a probability vector). For example, (0.50, 0.40, 0.05, 0.05) is a distribution over four words.

LDA imagines that every article was written by a writer following this recipe:

  1. “Pick the overall theme of an article by randomly giving it a distribution over topics.” For example: this article will be 80% finance and 20% football.
  2. For each word:
    • 2.1 “From the topic distribution chosen in 1., randomly pick one topic”. Picture a spinning wheel that lands on “finance” 80% of the time and “football” 20% of the time.
    • 2.2 “Given that topic, randomly choose a word from this topic.” Each topic has its own list of word chances. The finance list might give “stock” a 50% chance.

Repeating step 2 gives one document that mixes several topics with different weights. Repeating steps 1 and 2 gives a whole collection of documents. A collection of documents is called a corpus.

A model that tells a step-by-step story of how the data could have been produced is called a generative model. Nobody thinks real writers work like this. But the story has the right shape: in LDA, “Topics are distributions of words” and “Documents are distributions of topics”. That is why LDA is “seen as a more plausible generative model for text” (plausible = believable).

The computer then runs the story backwards. It only sees the finished word counts. It asks: which topic word lists, and which topic mix for each article, would best explain the counts we actually see? In the lecture’s words: “Assign words to topics and assign topics to documents such that the fit of the Document-term matrix becomes as good as possible”. Working out these unknown numbers from the data is called estimation.

Step 7: LDA’s starting assumption. Before it sees any data, LDA assumes that each document has only a few main topics, and each topic has only a few main words. What you assume before seeing the data is called a prior. LDA’s prior is a Dirichlet prior. A Dirichlet distribution is a way of drawing a random list of shares that add up to 1. The pattern it pushes towards, “most shares near zero, a few big ones”, is called sparsity. Two dials control it:

  • \(\alpha\) (the Greek letter alpha) controls the document side. Lower \(\alpha\) means each document has fewer main topics.
  • \(\beta\) (the Greek letter beta) controls the topic side. Lower \(\beta\) means each topic has fewer main words.

(This \(\beta\) is LDA’s topic dial. It is not the \(\beta\) used elsewhere in the course for regression coefficients.)

Step 8: LDA starts from a random guess. To run the story backwards, the computer starts from a random guess and improves it, round after round. Doing something round after round is called iterative. The two methods the lecture names for this are variational Bayes (Blei et al. 2003) and Gibbs sampling (Griffiths and Steyvers 2004). Both start from a guess and improve it step by step, many times [Not in course files — general knowledge: this description of the two methods]. The starting point of the random guess is set by a number called the random seed. Same seed, same result. A different seed can give different topics. So a careful analyst runs LDA again with a different seed and trusts the themes that come back both times.

Step 9: you name the themes yourself. The computer only hands you lists of words with numbers. You look at each theme’s top words and give it a name, such as “finance” or “football”. The names are your interpretation.

Step 10: how the two ways differ. Now the lecture’s key line makes sense: “LSA is not a probabilistic model (non-parametric), and not seen as a plausible generative model for text!” A probabilistic model is one where every number is a chance between 0 and 1, and the chances in a group add up to 1. LSA’s numbers are not chances, and LSA tells no story of how the words were written. “Non-parametric” here means it does not assume any probability model with settings to estimate. LSA is pure table arithmetic. LDA is a chance story.

Choosing \(K\). The lecture says: “Ad-hoc or based in out-of-sample testing (marginal likelihood)! For LSA one can look at the variance explained (λ)”. In plain words:

  • ad hoc = chosen by judgement;
  • out-of-sample testing = holding back some texts, fitting the model on the rest, then checking how well the model explains the held-back texts. The marginal likelihood is how probable the held-back texts are under the fitted model; higher means the model explains new texts better [Not in course files — general knowledge];
  • for LSA, you can look at how much of the table each theme accounts for. The lecture calls this the “variance explained” and writes it with the Greek letter λ (lambda). The walk-through below shows it with real numbers.

Why people trust LDA, and where it is used. LDA is popular because it sorts texts “in much the same manner as humans would do” (Chang et al. 2009). Hansen et al. (2018) used topics as data to study the discussions of the FOMC, the US central bank’s committee that sets interest rates [Not in course files — general knowledge: what the FOMC is]. Before using topics as data like this, you should show that the results do not hinge on one lucky seed. The lecture also names three extensions of LDA: dynamic, supervised and correlated topic models.

Good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: no labels and no word lists are needed. It finds themes on its own.
  • Good: it shrinks thousands of word columns into a few theme columns, which you can then use as inputs in a regression.
  • Breaks: you must choose \(K\) yourself, and the names of the themes are your own interpretation.
  • Breaks: LDA can give different themes with a different random seed. LSA’s numbers can be negative, so they cannot be read as shares.

Walk-through example

Part A: LSA on four tiny documents.

Here is a word-count table made up for this guide. Each row is one document (d1 to d4). Each column is one word. Each cell is how many times that word appears in that document. For example, the cell in row d1, column “stock” is 3: the word “stock” appears 3 times in document d1.

Doc stock market goal match
d1 3 2 0 0
d2 2 3 0 0
d3 0 0 3 2
d4 0 1 2 3

A person can see the themes at a glance. d1 and d2 talk about stock and market: finance. d3 and d4 talk about goal and match: football. d4 also has one stray “market”. The question is whether the computer can find this split by itself, without being told.

We hand the table to SVD. (It was run with numpy, a maths toolbox for the programming language Python.) The computer works these numbers out; you never do this by hand, and the exam won’t ask you to. What matters is how to read them.

The importance numbers (singular values). SVD finds four patterns in this table and gives each one an importance number:

\[s = (5.285,\ 4.780,\ 1.273,\ 0.778)\]

Here \(s\) stands for “singular values”, listed from most to least important. A bigger number means the pattern describes more of the table. Here is a plain way to see how much. Square every count in the table and add them up: \(9 + 4 + 4 + 9 + 9 + 4 + 1 + 4 + 9 = 53\). Now square each importance number: \(5.285^2 \approx 27.93\), \(4.780^2 \approx 22.85\), \(1.273^2 \approx 1.62\) and \(0.778^2 \approx 0.61\). These four add up to the same 53 [Not in course files — general knowledge: that the squared singular values add up to the sum of the squared counts]. So each squared importance number is that pattern’s slice of the table. The first two patterns together take \(27.93 + 22.85 = 50.78\) out of 53, which is about 96%. The last two take only about 4%. So keeping \(K = 2\) themes is a natural choice, and the last two are treated as noise.

This share has a name: variance explained. Variance means how much numbers spread out around their average. “Variance explained” is how much of that spread a pattern accounts for. In the lecture’s version, the variance explained by pattern number \(l\) is written \(\lambda_l\) (the Greek letter lambda) and works out here as \(9.31,\ 7.62,\ 0.54,\ 0.20\). (Each is the squared importance number divided by \(n - 1 = 3\), where \(n = 4\) documents. For example, \(27.93 / 3 = 9.31\).) Strictly, “variance” needs centred columns, meaning each column has its own average subtracted so it averages zero. Our toy table skips that step, but the ranking idea is the same: the first two patterns matter, the last two hardly do.

The table \(F\) (factors): one row per document, one column per kept theme. Each cell is that document’s score on that theme.

\(F\) comp. 1 comp. 2
d1 2.504 2.485
d2 2.616 2.389
d3 2.411 −2.560
d4 3.000 −2.100

(“comp.” is short for component, which means theme.)

The table \(L\) (loadings): one row per word, one column per kept theme. Each cell says how strongly that word belongs to that theme.

\(L\) comp. 1 comp. 2
stock 0.456 0.536
market 0.568 0.439
goal 0.474 −0.520
match 0.495 −0.500

How to read theme 1. Every number in the comp. 1 column is positive, for documents and for words. So theme 1 does not split anything. It is roughly “how many words in total”. d4 has the most words (6 against 5 for the others) and the highest score, 3.000.

How to read theme 2: a scale with two ends. Picture theme 2 as a line with a finance end (+) and a football end (−). Every document and every word gets a spot on that line.

  • The sign (+ or −) tells you which side something is on.
  • The size tells you how strongly it belongs there. A number near zero would mean “in the middle, not clearly either”.

Now read the documents in \(F\). d1 = 2.485 and d2 = 2.389 are positive: they sit on the finance side. d3 = −2.560 and d4 = −2.100 are negative: they sit on the football side. d3 is the most clearly football document. d4, which also contains one finance word (“market”), sits a little less far out on the football side.

Then read the words in \(L\). stock = 0.536 and market = 0.439 are positive: finance words. goal = −0.520 and match = −0.500 are negative: football words. The computer has found the same split as you did by eye, for documents and for words, and nobody told it which words were about money.

So theme 2 is the finance vs football contrast. Documents on the same subject have similar rows of \(F\); words on the same subject have similar rows of \(L\).

A warning about signs. SVD software may flip the sign of a whole theme. The finance end could come out negative and football positive. That changes nothing: only the split matters, not which end is called plus. (In this example, theme 1 came out all negative and was flipped to positive.)

Rebuilding one cell by hand. \(F\) and \(L\) together can rebuild the original table, approximately. To rebuild one cell, take the document’s row in \(F\) and the word’s row in \(L\), multiply them number by number, and add. Let’s rebuild d1’s count of “stock”.

  • d1’s row in \(F\) is (2.504, 2.485). stock’s row in \(L\) is (0.456, 0.536).
  • Theme 1: \(2.504 \times 0.456 = 1.142\).
  • Theme 2: \(2.485 \times 0.536 = 1.332\).
  • Add them: \(1.142 + 1.332 = 2.474\), about 2.47.

The real count was 3. It is close but not exact, because we threw away the two smallest patterns. That gap is the “noise” we dropped. The table rebuilt from only the 2 kept themes is called the rank-2 approximation.

What LSA’s numbers are not. The entries of \(F\) and \(L\) are unrestricted: negative values appear, and the rows do not add up to 1. So they are scores, not shares or chances. That is a key difference from LDA.

Synonyms and polysemy in \(L\). The lecture shows rows of \(L\) for three words, with their scores on the first two themes. Synonyms “might load heavily on the same topic”: “good” = [10 1 …] and “fine” = [10 1 …] have the same pattern. A polysemous word has “associations with multiple topics”: “check” = [5 5 …] scores on two themes at once.

Part B: LDA, mixing two topics.

LDA’s numbers are chances, so they read differently. Here are two made-up topics over the same four words. Each row is one topic. Each column is one word. Each cell is the chance that, when the writer is using this topic, the next word is this word. So each row adds up to 1. The rows are called \(\theta_1\) and \(\theta_2\) (\(\theta\) is the Greek letter theta, used for a topic’s word list).

Topic stock market goal match
\(\theta_1\) finance 0.50 0.40 0.05 0.05
\(\theta_2\) football 0.05 0.05 0.50 0.40

For example, the cell in row “finance”, column “stock” is 0.50: when the writer uses the finance topic, half of the words are “stock”.

Now take one document that is 80% finance and 20% football. We write its topic mix as \(\mathbf v_i = (0.8, 0.2)\), where \(i\) names the document. Its chance for each word is a blend of the two rows: 0.8 of the finance row plus 0.2 of the football row. We call the blended list \(\mathbf q_i\).

Work out “stock” by hand. \(0.8 \times 0.50 + 0.2 \times 0.05 = 0.40 + 0.01 = 0.41\).

Work out “goal” by hand. \(0.8 \times 0.05 + 0.2 \times 0.50 = 0.04 + 0.10 = 0.14\). So in this document we expect about 14 words in every 100 to be “goal”.

The full blended list:

stock market goal match
\(\mathbf q_i\) 0.41 0.33 0.14 0.12

The four numbers add up to 1, as chances must. Compare this with LSA: every number here is a share between 0 and 1, never negative.

Part C: what the \(\alpha\) dial does. This is a general illustration, not from the slides. The computer drew random topic mixes for imaginary documents with 3 topics, from a Dirichlet distribution (using numpy with random seed 1; a seed is the starting number for the computer’s random draws, explained in Step 8 above). Each draw is one document’s three topic shares, which add up to 1.

  • With \(\alpha = 0.1\) (low), the draws were (0.00, 1.00, 0.00), (0.06, 0.00, 0.94) and (0.99, 0.00, 0.00). Each document is dominated by one topic.
  • With \(\alpha = 10\) (high), the draws were (0.29, 0.29, 0.43), (0.21, 0.36, 0.44) and (0.18, 0.49, 0.33). Each document is an even mixture.

So a low \(\alpha\) gives sparse, “one main topic” documents; a high \(\alpha\) gives evenly mixed ones.

The formula, explained

1. SVD: the exact split (LSA).

In words: any word-count table can be rebuilt exactly as three tables multiplied together: one for documents, one for how important each pattern is, and one for words.

\[\underbrace{C}_{n\times p} = \underbrace{U}_{n\times n}\ \underbrace{S}_{n\times p}\ \underbrace{V'}_{p\times p}\]

  • \(C\) = the document-term matrix: \(n\) documents in rows, \(p\) words in columns.
  • The small labels under each letter give the table’s size, rows × columns.
  • \(U\) = the document table, one row per document. The lecture calls it a “unitary matrix (orthogonal, \(UU' = I\))”. Orthogonal means its columns point in completely separate directions, so they share no information. \(U'\) (“U prime”) is \(U\) flipped so rows become columns. \(I\) is the identity matrix: the “do-nothing” table with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere. Multiplying by it changes nothing, like multiplying a number by 1. So \(UU' = I\) is the maths way of saying the columns do not overlap.
  • \(S\) = “a diagonal matrix of singular values \(s_i\)”. A diagonal matrix is all zeros except on the line from top-left to bottom-right. The numbers on that line are the importance numbers, largest first.
  • \(V'\) = the word table, flipped so there is one column per word. It is also unitary (orthogonal).

Read aloud: “any document-term matrix can be written exactly as a document matrix times a diagonal importance matrix times a word matrix.”

2. Truncation: keep only \(K\) patterns.

In words: keep only the \(K\) biggest patterns, so the three tables become much smaller and rebuild the original table approximately.

\[\underbrace{C}_{n\times p} \approx \underbrace{U}_{n\times K}\ \underbrace{S}_{K\times K}\ \underbrace{V'}_{K\times p}\]

  • \(\approx\) = “is approximately equal to”.
  • \(U\) now keeps only its first \(K\) columns, \(S\) only its first \(K\) importance numbers, and \(V'\) only its first \(K\) rows.

The two tables you read come from these pieces:

\[F = U_{1:K}S_{1:K} \qquad L = V_{1:K}\]

  • The subscript \(1{:}K\) means “the first \(K\) columns only”.
  • Factors \(F\) (\(n\times K\)): the document table times the importance numbers. The lecture calls it “the prevalence of the common components in each document”, meaning how much of each theme each document has. Similar documents have similar factor rows.
  • Loadings \(L\) (\(p\times K\)): the word table. The lecture calls it “the importance of each factor for each word”. Similar words have similar loading rows.
  • The columns of \(F\) are orthogonal: the themes are unrelated to each other. The first theme captures the most variance, the second the next most, and so on.
  • PCA and SVD give the same factors. The lecture writes this as \(F = XV = US\), where \(X\) is the data table PCA works on.

Read aloud: “keep the \(K\) biggest patterns; the document scores are \(F\), the word scores are \(L\), and multiplying them back rebuilds the table approximately.”

3. Variance explained (for choosing \(K\) in LSA).

In words: a pattern’s share of the table’s spread is its importance number squared, divided by the number of documents minus one.

\[\lambda_l = \frac{s_l^2}{n-1}\]

  • \(l\) = which pattern (1 for the first, 2 for the second, and so on).
  • \(s_l\) = the importance number (singular value) of pattern \(l\).
  • \(n\) = the number of documents.
  • \(\lambda_l\) = the variance explained by pattern \(l\). It falls as \(l\) rises, because the patterns come out sorted.

Read aloud: “the variance explained by pattern \(l\) is its singular value squared, divided by \(n\) minus one.” (If you meet a \(\lambda\) elsewhere in the course, it may mean something else.)

4. LDA: words drawn from a blend of topics.

In words: each document’s word counts are drawn at random from one list of word chances, made by blending the topics’ word lists using the document’s own topic shares.

\[\mathbf{c}_i \sim MN(\mathbf{q}_i, m_i), \qquad \mathbf{q}_i = v_{i1}\boldsymbol\theta_1 + v_{i2}\boldsymbol\theta_2 + \dots v_{ik}\boldsymbol\theta_k = \mathbf{v}_i\boldsymbol\Theta\]

  • \(i\) = which document.
  • \(\mathbf{c}_i\) = the word counts of document \(i\): its row of the DTM.
