  • \(\sim\) = “is drawn at random from”.
  • \(MN(\cdot)\) = the multinomial distribution: \(m_i\) separate draws of a word from the vocabulary, with chances \(\mathbf{q}_i\). (Item 5 below explains it with an urn.)
  • \(m_i = \sum_j c_{ij}\) = the document’s length: its counts added up over all words \(j\). (\(\sum\) means “add all of these up”.)
  • \(\mathbf{q}_i\) = document \(i\)’s chance of each word: the blended list from Part B.
  • \(v_{il}\) = the share of document \(i\) devoted to topic \(l\). Each document’s shares add up to 1: \(\sum_{l} v_{il} = 1\). These are the topic weights. All of them stacked together form the table \(V\).
  • \(\boldsymbol\theta_l\) = topic \(l\): a list of chances over all \(p\) words that adds up to 1, \(\sum_{j} \theta_{lj} = 1\).
  • \(k\) = the number of topics (the same number as \(K\)).
  • \(\boldsymbol\Theta\) = all the topics stacked together.

Read aloud: “each document’s words are drawn from a blend of the topics’ word distributions, blended with that document’s topic weights.”

The lecture’s punchline: “a probabilistic topic model is just a factor model for multinomial data!” That means LDA has the same two-table shape as LSA. The topic weights \(V\) play the role of LSA’s factors \(F\). The topics \(\Theta'\) (all topic word-lists side by side, one column per topic) play the role of LSA’s loadings \(L\), “but, here, the matrix entries are probabilities”: each row of \(V\) sums to one, and each column of \(\Theta'\) sums to one. The lecture also says LDA “combines the factor model assumption for multinomial data with a Dirichlet prior” (Blei et al. 2003).

5. The multinomial building block: an urn.

In words: the multinomial gives the chance of getting a particular set of counts when you draw several times from the same set of chances.

An urn holds 8 “true”, 3 “false” and 9 “maybe” balls: 20 in total. You draw 6 balls with replacement, meaning each ball goes back into the urn after it is drawn. What is the chance of getting exactly 2 “true”, 1 “false” and 3 “maybe”?

\[P(2\text{ true}, 1\text{ false}, 3\text{ maybe}) = \frac{6!}{2!\,1!\,3!}(8/20)^2(3/20)^1(9/20)^3 = 60\times0.16\times0.15\times0.091125 \approx 0.131\]

  • The “!” is a factorial: multiply down to 1. \(6! = 6\times5\times4\times3\times2\times1 = 720\), \(2! = 2\), \(3! = 6\), \(1! = 1\).
  • \(\frac{6!}{2!\,1!\,3!} = 720/12 = 60\) is the number of different orders in which those balls can come out.
  • \((8/20)^2 = 0.16\) is the chance of “true” twice; \(3/20 = 0.15\) is the chance of “false” once; \((9/20)^3 = 0.091125\) is the chance of “maybe” three times.

Read aloud: “number of possible orders, times the chance of one such order.” (The slide’s formula is missing the “=” sign and uses commas where products are meant; write it with products.) With more than 2 outcomes and only 1 draw (like picking one single word), the multinomial becomes the categorical distribution, “the one we typically use in NLP” (NLP = natural language processing, the study of computers and text).

6. The Dirichlet dials and their usual values.

  • \(Dir(\alpha)\) = the prior on \(v_i\), the document’s topic weights: “lower values of α will give fewer topics a high probability in each document”.
  • \(Dir(\beta)\) = the prior on \(\theta_l\), the topics: “lower values of β will give fewer words higher probability in the topic distributions”.
  • The lecture’s benchmark values are “β = 0.01 and α = 50/k”, where \(k\) is the number of topics. The lecturer has also used “β = 200/N and α = 50/k” (\(N\) is not defined on the slide).

The Dirichlet is the many-outcome version of the Beta distribution, which draws a random share between 0 and 1 for two outcomes. It is also the conjugate prior of the multinomial: it fits the multinomial so neatly that the maths stays easy. That makes Bayesian estimation (combining a prior with the data to get updated beliefs) convenient.

Notation warning. The lecture’s plate diagram (a box-and-arrow picture of the LDA story) uses other letters: it calls the document–topic mix \(\theta_m\) and the topic–word list \(\varphi_k\) (\(\varphi\) is the Greek letter phi). The LDA formula above calls them \(v_i\) and \(\theta_l\). In the exam, use the formula’s notation (\(v_i\), \(\theta_l\)) and say what each symbol means.

Will the exam want these formulas? In 2025 the exam had no calculations. You will not be asked to compute an SVD or a multinomial. But writing \(C \approx U_K S_K V_K'\) and saying “documents’ topic weights sum to one” makes a Q2(d) answer stronger. Understand all of them; be ready to write the truncated SVD.

Side by side: LSA vs LDA. Rows = features; columns = the two methods. In the second row, \(f(c_i\mid v_i)\) means “a plain function linking the counts to the theme scores”, and \(p(c_i\mid v_i)\) means “a probability of the counts given the topic weights”. (The bar “\(\mid\)” is read “given”.)

Feature LSA (via SVD/PCA) LDA
What it is Matrix decomposition: PCA applied to the DTM Probabilistic generative model: factor model for multinomial data + Dirichlet prior
Slide label \(f(c_i\mid v_i)\) — a function \(p(c_i\mid v_i)\) — a probability model
Document side Factors \(F = U_{1:K}S_{1:K}\) (\(n\times K\)), any real numbers Topic weights \(V\) (\(n\times K\)), probabilities, each row sums to 1
Word side Loadings \(L = V_{1:K}\) (\(p\times K\)), any real numbers Topics \(\Theta'\) (\(p\times K\)), probabilities, each column sums to 1
Topics are Orthogonal components, ordered by variance explained Distributions over words; all words in all topics with different probability
Generative story? No — “not a probabilistic model … not seen as a plausible generative model for text” Yes — pick topic mix, then for each word pick topic, then word
Sparsity control None built in Dirichlet α (topics per document) and β (words per topic)
Estimation SVD — exact, one answer Variational Bayes or Gibbs sampling — iterative, starts from a random seed, so results can change with the seed
Choosing K Variance explained \(\lambda_l = s_l^2/(n-1)\) Ad hoc or out-of-sample marginal likelihood
Synonyms / polysemy Synonyms load on the same component; a polysemous word loads on several Same idea: a word can have high probability in several topics
Shared ground Both are unsupervised; both explain the \(n\times p\) DTM with \(K \ll p\) latent factors; both treat a topic as a cluster of words and a document as a mix of topics ← same

Reading the course code

The exam has not asked students to write code. This section only helps you recognise what the course notebooks did.

The seed-stability check (Interactive Notebook 2, simplified).

vec = CountVectorizer(stop_words="english", max_df=MAX_DF, min_df=5)
X = vec.fit_transform(texts)
run_a = LatentDirichletAllocation(n_components=N_TOPICS, random_state=SEED).fit(X)
run_b = LatentDirichletAllocation(n_components=N_TOPICS, random_state=SEED+1).fit(X)
match = cosine_similarity(run_a.components_, run_b.components_).max(axis=1)
  • Line 1 sets up the word counter. It drops stop words (very common words like “the” and “and”). max_df=MAX_DF drops words that appear in more than MAX_DF = 90% of speeches (too common). min_df=5 drops words that appear in fewer than 5 speeches (too rare). LDA uses raw counts, not tf-idf. (tf-idf is a re-weighted word score, high for words that are frequent in one text but rare elsewhere.) The course says: “We supply word counts, not the TF-IDF matrix”. Plain counts fit LDA’s multinomial model, which is a model of counts.
  • Line 2 builds the word-count table (the DTM) for the speeches given after 1945.
  • Lines 3–4 fit LDA twice, with \(K\) = N_TOPICS topics (6 by default). random_state is the random seed: run A uses SEED, run B uses SEED+1, a different starting point. In the notebook’s words, LDA “starts from a random guess (SEED) and improves it”.
  • Line 5: components_ is where the tool stores each topic’s word weights, one row per topic. For each topic from run A, the line finds the most similar topic from run B. “Similar” is measured by cosine similarity: a score of how alike two lists of numbers are, where 1 means the identical pattern.

No outputs are saved in the notebook. When run, it would show a best-match score for each topic plus the average, and a table of the top 8 words per topic. The notebook asks whether the topics with a match below about 0.8 are the hard-to-name ones. Its takeaway: “LDA topics depend on the seed and on K. Topics that reappear across runs deserve more trust than those that do not.”

LDA on US presidents’ speeches (Practical day 1).

LdaModel(corpus=corpus, id2word=dictionary, num_topics=6, passes=5, random_state=42)
  • Gensim is a Python toolbox for topic models, and LdaModel is its LDA tool.
  • num_topics=6 asks for \(K = 6\) topics. random_state=42 fixes the seed. passes=5 means it goes through all the speeches 5 times.
  • The data: 72 State of the Union speeches (the US president’s yearly speech to Congress [Not in course files — general knowledge: what this speech is]) and 6,241 words. That is after filter_extremes(no_below=3, no_above=0.8), Gensim’s version of min_df/max_df: it drops words that appear in fewer than 3 speeches or in more than 80% of them.

What came out: readable themes such as Cold War/Europe (soviet, europe…), budget (spending, deficit, taxes…) and Iraq/terror (weapons, saddam, hussein…). Most speeches got topic shares near 0 or 1. For example, Truman’s 1946–1949 speeches each got about 1.000 on one topic. So the mixtures were very “peaky”, and the topics tracked the vocabulary of each era (the word “tonight” shows up in 4 topics).

Lines worth quoting in the exam:

  • “We supply word counts, not the TF-IDF matrix. We choose the number of topics; the model does not discover a uniquely correct number”
  • “Names are your interpretations; they are not labels supplied by LDA”
  • “A fixed seed makes one run reproducible; it does not establish that the topics are stable.”

One more trap: topic numbers can change between seeds. What is “Topic 1” in one run may be “Topic 4” in the next. So compare the words and the documents, not the topic numbers.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025 Q2(d), worth 5 points: “what is meant by topic models? Mention at least two methods for estimating topics and the underlying intuition and difference/similarity of these methods.”

Model answer (official 2025 marking guideline): “In NLP topics are basically clusters of words. Articles/documents are assumed to consist of different topics, with different weights. SVD for matrix decomp and LDA for probabilities.”

What this answer is saying, in plain words: a topic is a group of words that appear together; each document is a blend of topics in different amounts; SVD (used in LSA) splits the word-count table into patterns, while LDA describes topics with chances.

A full answer that earns all the points:

Model answer A topic model is an unsupervised method that explains what texts are about: topics are clusters of words that tend to occur together, and each document is a mixture of topics with different weights, so the large \(n\times p\) document-term matrix is summarised by \(K \ll p\) latent factors. LSA applies the singular value decomposition \(C = USV'\) to the DTM and keeps the \(K\) largest components, giving document factors \(F = U_KS_K\) and word loadings \(L = V_K\); it is a pure matrix decomposition, with unrestricted values and no probabilistic story. LDA is a probabilistic generative model: each document draws a distribution over topics, and each word is drawn by first picking a topic and then a word from that topic’s word distribution, with Dirichlet priors encouraging sparsity. So both decompose the DTM into document–topic and topic–word parts, but in LDA these are probabilities (rows/columns sum to one), which makes it a more plausible model of how text is generated.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: A topic model finds themes without any answers: a topic is a group of words that often appear together, and each document is a blend of a few topics. LSA does this with table maths: it breaks the big word-count table into a few main patterns and keeps the biggest ones, giving a score for each document and a weight for each word. LDA instead tells a chance-based story: each document has a topic mix, and every word is written by first picking a topic, then picking a word from that topic. Both end up with “documents → topics” and “topics → words”, but only LDA’s numbers are real shares that add up to one.

Likely True/False statements:

  • “LSA is a probabilistic generative model” → False. LSA is table maths with no chance-based story of how words get written.
  • “In LDA each document’s topic weights sum to one” → True. Each document’s topic mix is a set of shares, like 70% sport + 30% money.
  • “Lower α in LDA gives each document fewer dominant topics” → True. α is the dial for how spread out a document’s topics are.
  • “LDA always gives the same topics regardless of the random seed” → False. The random seed is the starting point of the computer’s random guessing; a different start can give different topics.

The reflection question (the open question about customer survey answers): LDA is a strong method for “what do customers talk about”. Name two pitfalls: choosing \(K\) (the number of topics, which you must pick yourself) and seed instability (topics can change from run to run).

What a top-grade answer must include

For Q2(d), cover these four parts:

  1. The idea. Topics are clusters of words that tend to appear together. Each document is a mix of topics with different weights. It is unsupervised (no answers needed). It summarises the big word-count table (\(n\times p\) DTM: \(n\) documents by \(p\) words) with a small number of topics (\(K \ll p\), far fewer topics than words).
  2. LSA. It runs SVD/PCA (a standard way to break a table into a few main patterns) on the DTM: \(C \approx U_K S_K V_K'\), meaning the table is roughly rebuilt from \(K\) patterns. This gives factors \(F\) (a documents × topics table of scores) and loadings \(L\) (a words × topics table of weights). The values can be any number, even negative, and there are no probabilities.
  3. LDA. It is probabilistic. A topic is a set of chances over words; a document is a set of chances over topics (so the rows/columns add up to 1). It tells a story of how each word is generated. Dirichlet priors (settings that push the model towards few topics per document and few main words per topic) give sparsity (most shares near zero, a few big).
  4. One clear sentence on how they differ and how they are alike: “Both decompose the DTM into document–topic and topic–word parts; LSA does it as a matrix factorisation, LDA as a probability model.”

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Naming the methods without the intuition: topics = clusters of words, documents = mixtures of topics.
  • Calling LSA probabilistic. Its numbers are scores, not chances.
  • Saying LDA needs labelled data (texts with answers). It does not; it is unsupervised.
  • Mixing up α (the document–topic dial: how many topics per document) and β (the topic–word dial: how many main words per topic).
  • Forgetting that \(K\) (the number of topics) must be chosen by you, and that LDA results depend on the seed (the random starting point).
  • Feeding tf-idf (re-weighted word scores) into LDA. LDA models plain word counts.

Key terms to use

  • topic model: finds themes in texts without answers
  • latent topics: hidden themes, never observed directly
  • unsupervised: no answers or labels needed
  • dimension reduction (\(K \ll p\)): summarise many words with few topics
  • Latent Semantic Analysis (LSA): topic model built on table maths
  • PCA: finds the few main patterns in a table
  • Singular Value Decomposition \(C = USV'\): splits the table into three simpler tables
  • truncation: keep only the \(K\) biggest patterns
  • factors \(F\): each document’s score on each topic
  • loadings \(L\): each word’s weight in each topic
  • variance explained: how much of the table a pattern captures
  • Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA): topic model built on chances
  • generative model: a story of how the words were written
  • multinomial distribution: chances of counts from repeated draws
  • topic weights \(v_i\): document \(i\)’s mix of topics
  • topic–word distribution \(\theta_l\): chances of each word in topic \(l\)
  • Dirichlet prior α and β: dials for how concentrated the mixes are
  • sparsity: only a few topics or words dominate
  • Gibbs sampling: step-by-step random guessing that estimates LDA
  • number of topics \(K\): how many topics you ask for
  • random seed: the starting point of the random guessing
  • polysemy: one word, several meanings
  • synonyms: different words, same meaning

Quick self-test

  1. “LSA is not a probabilistic model and is not seen as a plausible generative model for text.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: LSA is the topic model that breaks the word-count table into smaller tables. A “probabilistic model” works with chances. A “plausible generative model” is a believable story of how each word in a text came to be written. The statement says LSA is neither of these.

    Answer: True. Why: LSA is pure table maths. Its numbers can be any value, even negative, so they cannot be chances, and they tell no story of how words were written. It is like a summary of a book’s word list, not a story of how the author wrote it.

  2. “In LDA, each row of the document–topic matrix sums to one.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: LDA is the chance-based topic model. The document–topic matrix is a table with one row per document and one column per topic, showing how much of each topic is in each document. The statement says the numbers in each row add up to 1.

    Answer: True. Why: Each row is a document’s topic mix written as shares, like a pie chart: 0.7 sport + 0.3 money = 1. The slices of one pie always make a whole pie.

  3. “In LDA, a higher α gives each document fewer high-probability topics.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: α is a dial in LDA that controls how spread out each document’s topic mix is. “Fewer high-probability topics” means each document is mostly about one or two topics. The statement says turning α up makes documents more focused.

    Answer: False. Why: It is the other way round. A lower α gives more sparsity: each document is dominated by a few topics. A higher α spreads each document over many topics. Think of α as how much a cook mixes the ingredients: low α gives a dish with one or two main flavours, high α gives a stew of everything.

  4. “Running LDA twice with different random seeds always gives exactly the same topics.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: LDA finds topics by guessing randomly and improving step by step. The random seed is the starting point of that random guessing. The statement says changing the starting point never changes the topics.

    Answer: False. Why: Different starting points can lead to different topics, and so can a different number of topics (\(K\)). Think of two people sorting the same pile of photos: they may end up with slightly different piles. So trust the topics that show up again and again across runs.

  5. “What is a topic model? Describe two methods and how they differ.” (Explain in 2–5 sentences.)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Say what topic models do, then explain LSA and LDA and the difference between them.

    Answer: the full model answer under “What the exam asks, and how to answer” above, word for word. Why: it covers all four parts the marker looks for: the idea (topics = word clusters, documents = mixtures), LSA (SVD, \(F\) and \(L\), any numbers), LDA (chance story, Dirichlet priors) and one sentence on how they differ and are alike.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • topic: a group of words that tend to appear together, like {goal, match, team}.
  • topic model: an unsupervised method that finds topics and says how much of each topic is in each document.
  • unsupervised: no answers or labels are given; the method finds the structure itself.
  • parsimonious: using as few pieces as possible to explain a lot.
  • cluster: a group of things that are alike, like a cluster of football words.
  • mixture (of topics): a document made of several topics in different amounts, like a smoothie that is 70% strawberry and 30% banana.
  • latent: hidden; we never see the topics directly, only the words.
  • stem (e.g. “vehicl”): a word cut to its root, so “vehicle” and “vehicles” both become “vehicl”.
  • corpus: a collection of documents, like 72 presidents’ speeches.
  • document-term matrix (DTM, \(C\)): the word-count table, rows = documents, columns = words.
  • matrix: a table of numbers. Its size is written “rows × columns”: \(n\times p\) = \(n\) rows and \(p\) columns.
  • \(n\), \(p\): the number of documents and the number of different words.
  • sparse / dense: a sparse table is mostly zeros (most words do not appear in most documents). A dense table has few zeros.
  • dimension / dimension reduction: each column is a dimension. Dimension reduction = summarising many columns with a few, like 10,000 words into 6 themes.
  • regression / second-stage regression: a method that predicts a number from input columns / a regression that uses the topic shares as its inputs.
  • curse of dimensionality: too many input columns for the number of examples, so a regression cannot learn reliably.
  • synonyms / polysemy: several words with one meaning (“good”, “fine”) / one word with several meanings (“check”).
  • \(K\), and \(K \ll p\): \(K\) is the number of topics (components) you ask for; “\(\ll\)” means “much smaller than”. 6 topics instead of 10,000 words.
  • component / factor: one hidden theme found by the method, like “finance vs football”.
  • LSA (Latent Semantic Analysis): the topic method that applies SVD (or PCA) to the word-count table.
  • SVD (Singular Value Decomposition): the computer’s procedure for squeezing a table into its main patterns; it rewrites any table as three tables multiplied together, \(U\) (documents), \(S\) (importance) and \(V'\) (words).
  • PCA (Principal Components Analysis): a standard method that finds the few directions in which the data vary the most. For text, it gives the same result as SVD.
  • factors \(F\): a table with one row per document saying how much of each theme it has (\(n\times K\)). d1 scores 2.485 on theme 2.
  • loadings \(L\): a table with one row per word saying how strongly it belongs to each theme (\(p\times K\)). “stock” scores 0.536 on theme 2.
  • sign and size of a score: the sign (+ or −) says which end of a theme’s scale; the size says how strongly. −2.560 = strongly on the football end.
  • singular values (\(s\)): the importance number of each pattern, on the diagonal of \(S\), largest first, like 5.285 and 4.780.
  • diagonal matrix: a table that is all zeros except on the line from top-left to bottom-right.
  • orthogonal / unitary matrix: a table whose columns point in completely separate directions, so they share no information.
  • \(U'\), \(V'\) (the prime): the table flipped, so rows become columns.
  • identity matrix \(I\): the “do-nothing” table, with 1s on the diagonal and 0s elsewhere. Multiplying by it changes nothing, like multiplying a number by 1.
  • truncation: keeping only the first \(K\) patterns and dropping the rest.
  • rank-2 approximation: the table rebuilt using only the 2 kept patterns; close to, but not the same as, the original (2.47 instead of 3).
  • unrestricted (values): can be any number, including negative; they need not add up to 1.
  • variance / variance explained (\(\lambda_l\)): variance = how much numbers spread out around their average. Variance explained = how much of that spread a pattern accounts for; here the first two patterns take about 96%.
  • centred columns: each column with its own average subtracted, so it averages zero.
  • LDA (Latent Dirichlet Allocation): the probabilistic topic model.
  • probability: a chance from 0 (never) to 1 (certain); 0.5 = half the time.
  • distribution / probability vector: a list of chances that add up to 1, like (0.50, 0.40, 0.05, 0.05) for four words.
  • probabilistic model: a model where every number is a chance between 0 and 1, and the chances in a group add up to 1.
  • generative model / generative story: a model that tells a step-by-step story of how the text could have been produced.
  • non-parametric (as the lecture uses it for LSA): it does not assume any probability model with settings to estimate.
  • estimation: working out the unknown numbers of a model from the data.
  • \(\theta_l\) (theta), \(\Theta\): topic \(l\)’s list of word chances; \(\Theta\) is all topics stacked together.
  • \(v_{il}\), topic weights, \(V\): the share of document \(i\) that is topic \(l\); each document’s shares add up to 1, like (0.8, 0.2).
  • \(\mathbf q_i\): document \(i\)’s blended list of word chances, like (0.41, 0.33, 0.14, 0.12).
  • \(m_i\): the length of document \(i\) (its total number of words).
  • \(\sim\): “is drawn at random from”.
  • \(\sum\): “add all of these up”.
  • multinomial distribution (\(MN\)): the chances of getting each possible set of counts when you make several draws, like drawing coloured balls from an urn several times.
  • with replacement: each ball goes back into the urn after it is drawn.
  • factorial (\(6!\)): multiply down to 1: \(6! = 6\times5\times4\times3\times2\times1 = 720\).
  • categorical distribution: one single draw from several possible outcomes, like picking one word.
  • NLP: natural language processing, the study of computers and text.
  • prior: what you assume before seeing the data.
  • Dirichlet distribution / Dirichlet prior: a way of drawing a random list of shares that add up to 1. As a prior, it is LDA’s starting assumption about which topic mixes (and word lists) are likely.
  • \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) (in LDA): the two Dirichlet dials. Low \(\alpha\) → each document has few main topics. Low \(\beta\) → each topic has few main words.
  • sparsity (in LDA): most chances are near zero, and only a few are big, like (0.00, 1.00, 0.00).
  • Beta distribution: the two-outcome version of the Dirichlet: a random share between 0 and 1.
  • conjugate prior: a prior that fits the multinomial so neatly that the maths stays easy.
  • Bayesian estimation: combining a prior with the data to get updated beliefs.
  • variational Bayes / Gibbs sampling: two computer methods that start from a guess and improve it step by step, many times. [Not in course files — general knowledge: the “start from a guess and improve” description]
  • iterative: repeated round after round.
  • random seed: the starting number for the computer’s random guess. Same seed = same result; a new seed can give different topics.
  • cosine similarity: a score of how alike two lists of numbers are; 1 = identical pattern.
  • ad hoc: chosen by judgement.
  • marginal likelihood / out-of-sample testing: how probable held-out texts are under the fitted model; higher = the model explains new texts better. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • plate diagram: a box-and-arrow picture of the LDA story.
  • \(\varphi_k\) (phi), \(\theta_m\): the plate diagram’s names for the topic-word list and the document-topic mix.
  • stop words: very common words like “the” and “and”, usually dropped before counting.
  • tf-idf: a word weight, high for words that are frequent here but rare elsewhere. LDA needs plain counts instead.
  • Gensim / LdaModel / passes: a Python toolbox for topic models / its LDA tool / how many times it goes through all the texts.
  • filter_extremes, min_df, max_df: settings that drop words that are too rare or too common.
  • components_: where scikit-learn (another Python toolbox) stores each topic’s word weights.
  • FOMC: the US central bank’s committee that sets interest rates. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • dynamic / supervised / correlated topic models: extensions of LDA named in the lecture.

Sources: Lecture 3 slides 30–59 (topic model aims 31–34; LSA, PCA and SVD 35–38, 42–44; LDA 45–58; choosing K, extensions and Hansen et al. 59–60); Interactive Notebook 2 cells 21–24, 31; practical_day_1.ipynb cells 16–22 (LDA section, from the Part A notes); 2025 exam evaluation guideline Q2(d).

Part III — Learning from prediction: n-grams, neural networks and word embeddings

11. Language models from counting: n-grams, bigram probabilities, smoothing, sampling, temperature, loss and perplexity

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — not asked in 2025, but taught in 2026 and perfect material for True/False and a small calculation.

Why this exists

You type “see you” on your phone, and the keyboard offers “tomorrow” or “soon”. Nobody wrote a rule for every possible sentence. So how does it know? It has seen “tomorrow” and “soon” follow “see you” many times, and it guesses from that.

Much of a text-analysis course turns each text into a word-count table: one row per document, one column per word, and each cell says how often that word shows up. That table is handy, but it throws away the order of the words. It treats a text as a loose bag of words, which is why it is called bag-of-words. A bag of words cannot tell you what comes next. Real language depends on order: after “thank” comes “you” far more often than “banana”.

This chapter builds the smallest possible machine that guesses what comes next, using nothing but counting. The big chatbots (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini) run on the same “guess the next piece” idea, only much bigger.

The idea in everyday words

What we are building. A language model is a machine that guesses what comes next in a text. Your phone’s autocomplete is a small one. A very big one, like ChatGPT, is called an LLM, short for large language model.

What “piece” means. The model works with small pieces of text called tokens. A token can be a whole word, a piece of a word, or a single letter. Real chatbots use pieces of words, called sub-word tokens: “playing” might become “play” + “ing”. The course model is smaller. It works with single letters, called characters (a character is one letter or symbol). A model that guesses one letter at a time is called character-level. The lecture says: “Real LLMs use sub-word tokens (a vocabulary of ∼100k pieces). We use single characters (26 letters + start/end) so the whole model fits on one screen”. Here vocabulary means the full list of tokens the model knows, and “∼100k” means about 100,000.

Guessing the next piece from the pieces before it is called next-token prediction. The lecture defines it as “predicting the next word or token in a sequence given the previous tokens.” Models such as GPT are trained this way. Now the lecture’s opening line makes sense: ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini are, “at their core, next-token predictors trained on trillions of tokens. Today we build the smallest possible one”.

Step 1: collect example text. The pile of example text you learn from is called the corpus (or dataset). In the course, it is a long list of first names.

Step 2: write down every pair of neighbouring letters. In “emma”, the pairs are “e then m”, “m then m” and “m then a”. Two neighbouring tokens are called a bigram (“bi” = two). The lecture defines a bigram as “two consecutive characters that appear together in a text” (consecutive = one right after the other).

Step 3: mark where each name starts and ends. Put a pretend “start” character before each name and a pretend “end” character after it. Now the machine also learns which letters like to begin a name and which like to finish one. These pretend characters are called start and end markers. Different parts of the course write them as <start>/<end>, <S>/<E>, or a dot .. They count as characters too, so “emma” also gives the pairs “start then e” and “a then end”.

Step 4: count, and put the counts in a grid. Count how often each pair shows up. Put the counts in a grid: one row for “the letter I’m on”, one column for “the letter that came next”. Each cell says how often that pair appeared. A grid of numbers is called a matrix, so this one is the count matrix.

Step 5: turn each row into chances. A probability (a chance) is a number from 0 to 1. 0 means never, 1 means certain, 0.5 means half the time, like heads on a coin. To turn a row of counts into chances, add up the row (the row total), then divide every cell by that total. Now the row adds up to 1 and says: “after this letter, here is how likely each next letter is”. Making a row add up to 1 like this is called normalising. A list of chances for every possible outcome that adds up to 1 is called a probability distribution. Think of a weather forecast: 70% dry, 20% rain, 10% snow.

A chance worked out once you already know something is called a conditional probability. “The chance of e, given that we saw h a moment ago” is one. It is written \(P(e \mid h)\), where \(P\) means “probability” and the bar “\(\mid\)” is read “given”.

The model’s name. Our machine looks back exactly one letter. So it is a bigram character-level language model. More generally, a run of \(n\) tokens in a row is an n-gram, and an n-gram model guesses the next token from the \(n-1\) tokens before it. The lecture’s definition: an n-gram model “predicts the next token by calculating the most likely token based on the previous \(n-1\) tokens”. A bigram (\(n = 2\)) looks back one token. A trigram (\(n = 3\)) looks back two.

Step 6: fix the zeros. A pair you never saw gets a chance of zero. That is too harsh: a name with that pair would be called impossible. So pretend you saw every pair one extra time. The lecture: “We fix this with smoothing (add a ‘fake’ count of 1 to every bigram)”. This is called smoothing, and this version is add-one smoothing, also called Laplace smoothing. Think of giving every new restaurant one free good review, so none is marked “impossible”.

Step 7: write a new name. Start at the “start” row. Roll a loaded dice that follows that row’s chances. Write down the letter you get, jump to that letter’s row, and roll again. Stop when you roll “end”. Picking the next letter at random, weighted by the chances, is called sampling.

Why roll a dice instead of always taking the favourite letter? A model that always gives the same answer for the same starting point is called deterministic. The course says: “We don’t want our model to be deterministic.” Always picking the most likely next letter has its own name: greedy decoding. It would write the same name every time.

Step 8: the temperature knob. Before rolling the dice, you can reshape the chances with a knob called temperature, written \(T\). The lecture calls it “the ‘creativity’ setting in LLM interfaces”. Turn it below 1 and the model gets cautious: the favourite letter wins even more often. Turn it above 1 and the model gets adventurous: rare letters get more of a chance.

Step 9: grade the machine. Walk through real names. At each step, look at the chance the model gave to the letter that really came next. A good model gave it a high chance. Squash all of those chances into one “wrongness” score, called the loss. Lower is better. From the loss you get perplexity: roughly how many letters the machine was torn between at each step. The lecture: “roughly how many characters the model is ‘choosing between’ at each step”. Lower is better here too.

The yardstick is a model that knows nothing and gives every possible next character the same chance. This is called uniform guessing, the baseline. On the names, the next character can be any of 26 letters or the end mark: 27 options. A blind guesser is torn between all 27, so its perplexity is 27.

Where the right answers come from. No human labels anything here. The right next letter is already sitting in the text. Learning where the text supplies its own answers is called self-supervised learning. The learning step itself is called training; for this model, training means counting.

Good at / where it breaks.

  • Good: easy to build and easy to understand. You can check every number by hand.
  • Good: it already beats blind guessing by a lot (perplexity 11.6 against 27 on the names).
  • Breaks: it only looks one letter back, so it happily writes “helllo” (you will see why in the walk-through). Looking further back makes the grid explode: with 27 characters, two letters of memory already needs 27 × 27 = 729 rows [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Breaks: a pair it never saw gets chance zero, and that makes the loss endless, unless you smooth.

Walk-through example

Step A: a tiny corpus. Our whole corpus is the word “hello” written twice: “hello hello”. Treat it as two words, each with a start mark in front and an end mark behind.

Step B: list the pairs. One “hello” gives six neighbour pairs: start→h, h→e, e→l, l→l, l→o, o→end. (The arrow means “then”.) That is 4 pairs inside the word plus the start pair and the end pair: 6 bigrams. We have two copies, so we see each pair 2 times.

Bigram (previous → next) Count
<start> → h 2
h → e 2
e → l 2
l → l 2
l → o 2
o → <end> 2

Each row of this table is one pair; the count is how many times it appeared in “hello hello”.

Step C: the count grid. Now arrange the same counts as a grid. Each row is the letter you’re on. Each column is the letter that came next. Each cell is how many times that happened. The last column adds up the row.

On ↓ / Next → h e l o <end> Row total
<start> 2 0 0 0 0 2
h 0 2 0 0 0 2
e 0 0 2 0 0 2
l 0 0 2 2 0 4
o 0 0 0 0 2 2

The row totals say how often each letter appears as the first letter of a pair: h = 2, e = 2, l = 4, o = 2.

Let’s work out one cell out loud: row l, column o. “l then o” happened once in each “hello”, so 2 times. The l row’s total is 4, because l is followed by something four times (twice by another l, twice by o). So the chance of o after l is 2 out of 4 = 0.5. The chance of l after l is also 2/4 = 0.5. The letter l is followed by another l half the time and by o half the time.

After h, e came 2 times out of 2, so its chance is 2/2 = 1: certain. In the lecture’s words: “Whenever ‘h’ appears, it is always followed by ‘e’”.

And the problem case: “q after h” never happened, so its chance is 0 out of 2 = 0. The lecture: “Unseen bigrams get probability zero.”

Step D: write a new word. Start→h is certain, h→e is certain, e→l is certain. At l, it’s a coin flip: half the time o, half the time another l. So the machine might write:

  • “helo”, with chance 0.5 (o at the first l);
  • “hello”, with chance 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25 (l, then o);
  • “helllo”, with chance 0.5 × 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.125 (l, l, then o).

To get the chance of a whole word, multiply the chances of each step. The machine only remembers one letter back, so it cannot keep track of how many l’s it has already written. It even rates “helo” as more likely than “hello”.

Step E: smoothing. Add a pretend count of 1 to every cell. In the course’s full grid there are 28 characters: 26 letters plus start plus end. So the grid is 28 × 28 (28 rows, 28 columns), and the h row gains 28 pretend counts. Its total grows from 2 to 2 + 28 = 30. Now:

  • q after h = (0 + 1)/30 = 1/30 ≈ 0.033. No longer zero.
  • e after h = (2 + 1)/30 = 3/30 = 0.10.

(These two numbers are this guide’s own illustration, computed with Python, a programming language.) Notice how much smoothing changes things when the corpus is tiny: e after h fell from 1 to 0.10. On the course’s real corpus of 32,033 names the counts are large, so the fake 1s matter much less.

Step F: grade it. Score the word “hello” with the unsmoothed grid. Each column below is one step through the word; the number is the chance the model gave to the letter that really came next.

Transition <start>→h h→e e→l l→l l→o o→<end>
Probability 1 1 1 0.5 0.5 1
  • Multiply them: \(1 \times 1 \times 1 \times 0.5 \times 0.5 \times 1 = 0.25\). This is the chance the model gave to the whole real word, called the likelihood.
  • Take the log of each chance. (A log is the reverse of a power. The natural log, written ln, asks “e to what power gives this number?”, where e is a fixed number, about 2.718. So ln 1 = 0, because \(e^0 = 1\), and ln 0.5 ≈ −0.693. The log of any number below 1 is negative.) Adding the logs: 0 + 0 + 0 + (−0.693) + (−0.693) + 0 = −1.386. This sum is the log-likelihood, written \(\ell\). It equals ln 0.25: adding logs carries the same information as multiplying the chances.
  • Divide by the number of steps (\(n = 6\)) and drop the minus sign: loss = 1.386 / 6 = 0.231.
  • Perplexity = \(e^{0.231}\) ≈ 1.26. So the machine is torn between about 1.26 letters per step: nearly sure every time. It only hesitates after l.

(These numbers are also this guide’s own illustration, computed with Python.)

In plain words: loss is a “surprise score”. A higher chance for the real next letter gives a lower loss, never a higher one. Loss measures how surprised the model was when it saw the real letter. If it was sure (chance 1), it isn’t surprised at all, so the loss is 0. The less likely it thought the real letter was, the bigger the surprise, and the bigger the loss.

Chance the model gave the real next letter Its log (ln) Loss for that step (minus sign dropped)
1 (completely sure) 0 0: no surprise
0.5 (a coin flip) −0.69 0.69
1/27 ≈ 0.037 (a blind guess) −3.30 3.30
0.01 (thought it very unlikely) −4.61 4.61: big surprise

Where the confusion comes from: the log of a chance is always zero or negative, and the smaller the chance, the more negative the log. Dropping the minus sign turns those negative numbers into positive surprise scores. So as the chance goes down, the loss goes up. Training tries to push the loss down, which is the same as giving the real letters higher chances.

Step G: the blind guesser. A model that gives each of the 27 possible next characters the same chance, 1/27, gets the same loss at every step: \(-\ln(1/27) = \ln 27 = 3.2958 \approx 3.30\). Its perplexity is \(e^{3.30} = 27\): it is “choosing between” all 27 characters.

Step H: the real names. The course file names.txt holds 32,033 lowercase first names (emma, olivia, ava, …, zzyzx). They use only the letters a–z and are 2 to 15 letters long. For “emma”, the notebook prints the bigrams <S> e, e m, m m, m a, a <E>: 5 bigrams. All the counts go into a 28 × 28 count matrix, called N. Its rows are the current character (<S>, a, …, z), and its columns are the next character (a, …, z, <E>). Some cells always stay at zero, such as anything after the end mark. Each row is divided by its row total, which gives the probability matrix P. The one result the notebook writes out: the most likely first letter is a, with \(P(\langle S \rangle \to a) = 0.14\). In words: 14% of names start with “a”.

Step I: how the course’s models compare. The table below comes from the lecture. Each row is one model. The columns say how many earlier letters the model looks at (its context), its loss, and its perplexity. Two models are from later in the course. A neural network is a machine of many adjustable number-dials that learns from examples. An MLP, short for “multi-layer perceptron” [Not in course files — general knowledge], is a neural network with at least one hidden middle layer.

Model Context (letters looked back) Loss Perplexity
Uniform guessing none 3.30 27
Count-based bigram (Part 1) 1 character 2.45 11.6
Neural network bigram (Part 2) 1 character 2.46 11.7
MLP (Part 3) 5 characters 2.22 9.2

Check: \(e^{2.45} = 11.59\), \(e^{2.46} = 11.70\), \(e^{2.22} = 9.21\). All match.

How to read it. Counting cuts the blind guesser’s 27 options down to about 12. Counting and the neural network learn the same thing (loss 2.45 vs 2.46). The real gain comes from more context: the MLP looks back 5 letters and reaches 2.22. The lecture: “The neural network learns the same thing as counting, but it scales: we can give it more context without the table exploding”.

The formula, explained

1. Bigram probability.

In words: to get the chance of a next letter, count how often that pair appeared, and divide by how often the first letter appeared at the start of any pair.

\[P(c_n \mid c_{n-1}) = \frac{\text{count}(c_{n-1}, c_n)}{\text{count}(c_{n-1})}\]

  • \(c_n\) = the next character, the one we want to predict.
  • \(c_{n-1}\) = the character right before it.
  • \(P(c_n \mid c_{n-1})\) = the probability of \(c_n\) given that we saw \(c_{n-1}\) right before.
  • \(\text{count}(c_{n-1}, c_n)\) = “the number of times the pair of characters \((c_{n-1}, c_n)\) appears in the training corpus.”
  • \(\text{count}(c_{n-1})\) = “the total number of times the character \(c_{n-1}\) appears as the first character of any bigram.”

Read aloud: “The chance that \(c_n\) comes next, given \(c_{n-1}\), is how often the pair appeared, divided by how often \(c_{n-1}\) appeared as a first letter.”

Example from the walk-through:

\[P(e \mid h) = \frac{\text{count}(h, e)}{\text{count}(h)} = \frac{2}{2} = 1.0\]

This is the one most likely to appear on the exam as a small sum. Be ready to write it and use it.

2. Temperature.

In words: raise every chance to the power “one divided by the temperature”, then rescale the results so they add up to 1 again.

\[P_T(c) \propto P(c)^{1/T}\]

  • \(P(c)\) = the model’s probability for character \(c\).
  • \(T\) = the temperature.
  • \(P_T(c)\) = the reshaped probability after the temperature is applied.
  • A power means multiplying a number by itself: \(0.5^2 = 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\). A power of 1/2 means the square root.
  • \(\propto\) = “proportional to”: go up and down together. Here it means: work out the powers first, then divide each by their total so the numbers sum to 1 again.
  • \(T < 1\): sharper, the likely characters dominate (safer, more repetitive). \(T = 1\): the model as estimated. \(T > 1\): flatter, rare characters more likely (more random). \(T \to 0\) (T shrinking towards zero): always pick the top character, which is greedy decoding.

Example (this guide’s illustration, computed with Python): start with three chances, \(P = (0.5, 0.3, 0.2)\). With \(T = 0.5\) the power is \(1/0.5 = 2\), and after rescaling the chances become \((0.66, 0.24, 0.11)\): sharper, the favourite grew. With \(T = 2\) the power is \(1/2\), and they become \((0.42, 0.32, 0.26)\): flatter, the underdogs grew.

Read aloud: “The new chance is the old chance to the power one-over-T, rescaled to add up to one.” Understand it; you are unlikely to need to write it.

3. Log-likelihood and loss.

In words: add up the logs of the chances the model gave to every real next letter in every word (that total is \(\ell\)), then divide by the number of steps and flip the sign to get the loss.

\[\ell \;=\; \sum_{w\in D}\;\sum_{t=0}^{T_w} \log P(c_{t+1}\mid c_t) \qquad\qquad \text{Loss function} = -\frac{\ell}{n}\]

  • \(\sum\) = “add all of these up”. There are two: one over words, one over positions inside each word.
  • \(D\) = the dataset; \(w\) = one word in it. \(w \in D\) reads “every word \(w\) in the dataset”.
  • \(t\) = the position inside the word; \(T_w\) = the last transition in word \(w\). (Here \(T\) is a length, not the temperature.)
  • \(\log P(c_{t+1}\mid c_t)\) = the log of the probability the model gave to the letter that really came next.
  • \(\ell\) = the sum of all these logs = the log-likelihood.
  • \(n\) = the total number of character transitions (steps).

Read aloud: “Add up the log-probabilities of every real next letter, divide by how many there were, and flip the sign.”

Why logs? Multiplying thousands of chances gives a super-tiny number that a computer rounds to zero. Logs turn the product into a sum and avoid this. Why the minus sign? The logs of chances are negative, so \(\ell\) is negative. Flipping the sign turns it into a positive “surprise” score, the negative log-likelihood. The course: “we want to maximize the log likelihood but minimize the loss” (maximise = make as large as possible; minimise = make as small as possible). The loss function is that one number saying how wrong the model is, here the average negative log-likelihood per step.

Why a single zero is a disaster: the log of 0 is minus infinity, written \(-\infty\) (“endlessly negative”). One unseen pair in the test names puts a \(-\infty\) in the sum, and the loss becomes endless. Smoothing prevents that.

4. Perplexity.

In words: take e (about 2.718) to the power of the loss; the answer is roughly how many letters the model is torn between at each step.

\[\text{Perplexity} = e^{\text{Loss}}\]

  • \(e^{x}\) = “e to the power \(x\)”.
  • Loss = the average negative log-likelihood from item 3.

Read aloud: “Perplexity is e to the power of the loss; it says roughly how many characters the model is choosing between at each step.” Lower is better: 27 = clueless (blind guessing), 1 = always sure.

Will the exam want these? In 2025 the exam had no calculations. Here a small sum like \(P(e \mid h) = 2/2\) is possible. Know the bigram formula and “perplexity = \(e^{\text{Loss}}\)” well enough to write them; understand the other two.

Reading the course code

The exam has not asked students to write code. This section only helps you recognise what the notebook does. It is written in Python with PyTorch (written torch), a Python toolkit for building this kind of model, inside a notebook (a document that mixes code and text).

Turning counts into probabilities with smoothing:

P = (N+1).float()            # Add-one (Laplace) smoothing
P /= P.sum(1, keepdim=True)
  • Line 1 adds a fake count of 1 to every cell of the 28 × 28 count matrix N, so no bigram is ever 0. (.float() turns the counts into numbers that can hold decimals. The text after # is a comment for humans.)
  • Line 2 divides every row by its row total. Each row now sums to 1: it is the probability distribution of the next letter.

Sampling instead of always choosing the top letter: torch.multinomial(P[0], 10, replacement=True) is the PyTorch “loaded dice” command. P[0] is the start row. The command draws 10 first letters at random, in proportion to their probabilities. replacement=True means each pick is put back, so the same letter can be drawn again.

Temperature in code: P_T = P ** (1 / T) (** means “to the power”), then the rows are renormalised (made to add up to 1 again).

The loss loop adds torch.log(P[ix1, ix2]) over all transitions. Here ix1 and ix2 are the positions of the current and next character in the grid, so P[ix1, ix2] is the chance of that pair. Then it computes -log_likelihood/n for the loss and torch.exp(...) (e to the power) for perplexity. The notebook has no saved outputs; the lecture reports the result: loss ≈ 2.45, perplexity ≈ 11.6. The notebook also shows that without smoothing, the made-up name “jq” gets log-likelihood \(-\infty\), because \(\log(0) = -\infty\).

What the exam asks, and how to answer

This topic was not asked in 2025. But it is in the 2026 lectures, so we expect True/False or short questions (our prediction). The likely topics:

  • bigram chances (the chance of the next letter given the one before);
  • smoothing (adding pretend counts so nothing is zero);
  • softmax (turning scores into chances, a step used by neural networks);
  • loss and perplexity (how wrong the model is);
  • temperature (the cautious/adventurous knob).

Typical True/False traps:

  • “A bigram conditions on the previous two tokens.” False. “Conditions on” means “looks at before guessing”, and a bigram looks back only one piece.
  • “The n-gram model treats tokens as independent.” False. Independent would mean each piece has nothing to do with the one before. The whole point is that it uses the one before.
  • “Higher temperature makes output more predictable.” False. Turning the knob up makes it more random, not less.

A small sum: for example, the chance of e after h, \(P(e \mid h) = 2/2\).

Links to 2025-style questions: tokens vs words, and “are LLMs (big chatbots) supervised or unsupervised?”. The answer there: next-letter guessing is self-supervised. The text holds its own answers, so no human labels anything.

A likely short question: “What does perplexity measure, and what do the course’s numbers show?” (2–5 sentences)

Model answer Perplexity is \(e^{\text{Loss}}\), where the loss is the average negative log-likelihood of the true next character. It can be read as how many characters the model is “choosing between” at each step, so lower is better. Uniform guessing over 27 characters gives perplexity 27, the count-based bigram 11.6, the neural network bigram 11.7, and the MLP with 5 characters of context 9.2. So counting and the simple neural net learn the same thing, and the gain comes from giving the model more context (L4 slide 9).

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Perplexity tells you roughly how many letters the model is torn between at each step, so smaller is better. Blind guessing is torn between all 27. Counting letter pairs brings that down to about 12, and the simple neural network gets the same. The model that looks back five letters does best, at about 9, so looking further back is what really helps.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • The bigram formula, naming both counts: how often the pair appeared, and how often the first letter appeared at the start of any pair.
  • The “hello hello” example.
  • Why smoothing is needed: a pair never seen gets chance 0. The log of 0 is minus infinity (\(\log 0 = -\infty\)), so the loss becomes endless.
  • Loss = the average negative log-likelihood (the average “surprise” at each real next letter).
  • Perplexity = e to the power of the loss (\(e^{\text{Loss}}\)), compared with blind guessing among 27 characters, which gives 27.
  • The lesson of the comparison table: the neural network does as well as counting, no better, but it can grow to look further back without the table exploding.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Saying a bigram uses the two previous pieces. It uses one.
  • Forgetting the start and end pairs (start→h and o→end).
  • Dividing by the total number of pairs in the whole text. The right number to divide by is how often the first letter appeared at the start of a pair (\(\text{count}(c_{n-1})\)).
  • Saying the neural network bigram is “much better”. Its loss is 2.46 against 2.45 for counting: the same.
  • Getting temperature backwards. Above 1 = more random, below 1 = more cautious.
  • Forgetting the minus sign in the loss. Without it, the loss would be negative and you’d want it big, which is the wrong way round.

Key terms to use

  • next-token prediction: guessing the next piece of text
  • n-gram: guess from the previous n − 1 pieces
  • bigram: two neighbouring pieces; looks back one
  • conditional probability: a chance, given something already known
  • character-level vs sub-word tokens: single letters vs pieces of words
  • add-one (Laplace) smoothing: pretend every pair appeared once more
  • sampling: picking the next letter by weighted dice
  • temperature: knob: cautious below 1, adventurous above
  • greedy decoding: always pick the most likely letter
  • likelihood: chances of the real letters, multiplied together
  • log-likelihood: the logs of those chances, added up
  • negative log-likelihood (loss): average surprise score; lower is better
  • perplexity: roughly how many letters it’s torn between
  • context length: how much earlier text it sees

Quick self-test

  1. “A bigram model predicts the next character from the previous two characters.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A bigram model is the letter-guesser from this chapter. A character is one letter or symbol. Does it look back two letters before guessing the next one?

    Answer: False. Why: “Bi” means two, but the two are the letter you’re on plus the one you’re guessing. So it looks back only one letter. In general, an n-gram looks back n − 1 pieces. It’s like a friend who only remembers the last word you said.

  2. “Without smoothing, a single unseen bigram can make the loss infinite.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Smoothing means adding a pretend count of 1 to every pair. An unseen bigram is a letter pair that never showed up in the training text. The loss is the “how wrong” score. Can one never-seen pair make that score endless?

    Answer: True. Why: A never-seen pair gets chance 0. The loss uses the log of each chance, and the log of 0 is minus infinity (\(\log 0 = -\infty\)). One endless number makes the whole average endless. It’s like a judge who gives a score of “impossible”: one such vote wrecks the whole total.

  3. “Setting the temperature above 1 makes rare characters more likely.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Temperature is the knob that reshapes the chances before the model rolls its dice. Rare characters are letters that normally get a small chance. If you turn the knob above 1, do those letters get picked more often?

    Answer: True. Why: Above 1, the chances get flatter: the favourite loses some of its lead and the underdogs gain. Think of turning up a DJ’s “surprise me” setting: less-played songs come on more often.

  4. “A model with loss 3.30 on 27 characters is doing better than random guessing.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The loss is the “how wrong” score, lower is better. The model chooses among 27 characters (26 letters plus an end mark). Is a score of 3.30 better than picking letters blindly?

    Answer: False. Why: Blind guessing, giving each of the 27 characters the same chance, gives a loss of exactly ln 27 ≈ 3.30 (perplexity 27). So 3.30 is blind guessing, not better. It’s like scoring 25% on a test with four answer options per question: that’s what you’d get by guessing with your eyes closed.

  5. “What does perplexity measure, and what do the course’s numbers show?” (Explain in 2–5 sentences.)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Say what the perplexity number means, then use the course’s comparison table (blind guessing, counting, neural network, MLP) to say what we learn.

    Answer: the model answer under “What the exam asks, and how to answer” above, word for word. Why: it gives the definition (\(e^{\text{Loss}}\)), the reading (“choosing between” so many characters, lower is better), all four numbers (27, 11.6, 11.7, 9.2) and the lesson (more context is what helps).

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • language model: a machine that guesses what comes next in a text. Your phone’s autocomplete is a small one.
  • LLM (large language model): a very big next-token guesser, such as ChatGPT, Claude or Gemini.
  • token: one small piece of text the model works with. It can be a letter, a word, or a piece of a word.
  • character / character-level: a character is a single letter or symbol. A character-level model guesses one letter at a time instead of one word at a time.
  • sub-word token: a piece of a word, such as “play” and “ing” in “playing”. Big chatbots use about 100,000 such pieces.
  • vocabulary: the full list of tokens the model knows. Here: 26 letters plus start and end.
  • next-token prediction: guessing the next piece of text from the pieces before it, like finishing a friend’s sentence.
  • bag-of-words: treating a text as a bag of loose words. You count each word and ignore the order. That’s what gives the word-count table (rows = documents, columns = words).
  • corpus / dataset: the pile of example text you learn from. In the course: 32,033 first names.
  • training: the learning step, where the model looks at examples and sets its numbers. For this model, training means counting.
  • probability (chance): a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely something is. 0 = never, 1 = certain, 0.5 = half the time, like heads on a coin.
  • conditional probability: a chance worked out once you already know something. “The chance of e, given that we saw h a moment ago.” The bar “|” in \(P(e \mid h)\) is read “given”.
  • n-gram: a run of n tokens in a row. An n-gram model guesses the next token from the n − 1 tokens before it.
  • bigram: two neighbouring tokens, like “h then e”. A bigram model looks back one token.
  • trigram: three neighbouring tokens. A trigram model looks back two tokens.
  • start and end markers (<start>, <end>, <S>, <E>, .): pretend characters put before and after each word, so the model learns which letters begin and end names.
  • matrix / count matrix: a grid of numbers with rows and columns. The count matrix N has one row per current letter, one column per next letter, and each cell counts how often that pair appeared.
  • row total / normalise: add up a row, then divide every cell by that total, so the row adds up to 1. “Renormalise” means doing it again after the numbers changed.
  • probability distribution: a list of chances for every possible outcome that adds up to 1. Like a weather forecast: 70% dry, 20% rain, 10% snow.
  • smoothing / add-one (Laplace) smoothing: pretending you saw every pair one extra time, so nothing gets a chance of exactly zero. Like giving every new restaurant one free review so it isn’t marked “impossible”.
  • sampling: picking the next letter at random, weighted by the chances, like rolling a loaded dice.
  • deterministic: always giving the same answer for the same starting point. The opposite of random.
  • greedy decoding: always picking the most likely next letter, never rolling the dice.
  • temperature (T): a knob that reshapes the chances before you roll. Below 1 = cautious, the favourite wins more often. Above 1 = adventurous, rare letters get more of a chance.
  • proportional to (∝): “goes up and down together with”. In the temperature formula: work out the powers first, then rescale so they add up to 1.
  • power / exponent: how many times you multiply a number by itself. \(0.5^2 = 0.5 \times 0.5 = 0.25\). A power of 1/2 means the square root.
  • e: a fixed number, about 2.718, that shows up all over maths. \(e^{x}\) means “e to the power x”.
  • log (logarithm), ln: the reverse of a power. ln asks “e to what power gives this number?” So ln 1 = 0 and ln 0.5 ≈ −0.693. The log of a number below 1 is negative. \(\log_2\) asks the same question with 2 instead of e.
  • likelihood: the chance the model gave to the real text, found by multiplying the chances of each real next letter. For “hello” in our example: 0.25.
  • log-likelihood (ℓ): the sum of the logs of those chances. Adding logs carries the same information as multiplying the chances, but avoids super-tiny numbers.
  • negative log-likelihood: the log-likelihood with its sign flipped, so it becomes a positive “surprise” score. Lower = less surprised.
  • loss / loss function: one number that says how wrong the model is. Here it’s the average negative log-likelihood per step. Training tries to make it small.
  • minimise / maximise: make as small as possible / make as large as possible.
  • −∞ (minus infinity): “endlessly negative”. The log of 0 is −∞, so a single zero chance makes the loss endless.
  • sum (Σ): the sign for “add all of these up”.
  • perplexity: e to the power of the loss. Roughly “how many letters the model is torn between at each step”. 27 = clueless, 1 = always sure.
  • uniform guessing (baseline): giving each of the 27 characters the same chance, 1/27. It’s the “knows nothing” yardstick you compare against.
  • context / context length: the text the model looks at before it guesses. A bigram’s context is 1 letter; the MLP’s is 5 letters.
  • neural network: a machine of many adjustable number-dials that learns from examples (next chapter).
  • MLP: short for “multi-layer perceptron” [Not in course files — general knowledge]: a neural network with at least one hidden middle layer (next chapter).
  • softmax: a step that turns a list of scores into chances that add up to 1 (used by neural networks).
  • self-supervised: learning where the text gives its own answers. The right next letter is already sitting in the text, so no human has to label anything.
  • notebook / Python / PyTorch (torch): a notebook is a document that mixes code and text; Python is the programming language; PyTorch is a Python toolkit for building this kind of model.
  • torch.multinomial: the PyTorch command that rolls the loaded dice: it draws random picks according to the chances you give it.

Sources: Lecture 4 “Introducing next token prediction” (Larsen), slides 2–9 (LLMs as next-token predictors 2; tokens vs characters 3; bigrams and “hello” 4, 6; bigram formula 5; temperature 7; loss/perplexity comparison table 9); notebook Predict_the_next_token_part1.ipynb (cells 0–45: names and “emma” bigrams 12; count matrix 20–22; smoothing 27; first-letter probability and sampling 30–37; temperature 38–39; loss 41, 43; uniform baseline 42; “jq” and \(-\infty\) 44–45); Part 2 notebook cell 33 (comparison table); dataset names.txt; exam prediction from _exam_prep_work/exam_blueprint.md.

12. Neural network basics you need: one-hot vectors, weights, softmax, loss, gradient descent, backpropagation

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — the one-hot vector was 2025 Q3(c); softmax, loss and training words come back in the transformer and LLM questions.

Why this exists

Think of the keyboard on your phone. You type “see you” and it suggests “tomorrow”. Or think of your email inbox, which quietly moves spam into a separate folder. Nobody sat down and wrote a rule for every possible message. The rules would never end.

One simple way to make guesses like this is counting. Say you want to guess the next letter of a first name. You take a long list of names and count how often each letter comes after each other letter. After “q” you almost always saw “u”, so you guess “u”.

Counting works, but it has two problems.

  • It only remembers a little. If you count “which letter follows which letter”, the machine remembers one letter back. To remember two letters back, you need a count for every pair of letters followed by every letter. With 27 symbols (26 letters plus a dot that marks the start or end of a name), one letter of memory needs 27 × 27 = 729 counts. Two letters of memory need 27 × 27 × 27 = 19,683. Every extra letter multiplies the table by 27 again. It grows out of control.
  • Many jobs aren’t about counting at all, like spotting spam.

What we want is a machine that learns a pattern from examples on its own, without anyone writing the rules. A neural network is that machine. It matters in this course because the word-map method called word2vec (the next chapter) and the big chatbots are built from exactly the parts in this chapter.

The idea in everyday words

A machine of many small dials. Picture a big box covered in small dials, like the knobs on a sound mixing desk. Numbers go in at one end. Numbers come out at the other end. Each dial decides how much one incoming number counts: turn it up and that number matters more, turn it down and it matters less. Such a dial is called a weight. There is also one extra dial that adds a fixed amount no matter what comes in, like a shop that adds the same delivery fee to every order. That one is called the bias. All the weights and biases together are the network’s parameters: everything it learns.

At first the dials are set at random, so the guesses are bad. Then the machine learns like this:

  1. Show it one example, and let it make a guess.
  2. Compare the guess with the right answer. Measure how wrong it was with one number.
  3. For every dial, work out which way to turn it so the guess would have been a little less wrong.
  4. Turn every dial a small step in that direction.
  5. Repeat with many examples, many times.

After thousands of small nudges, the guesses get good. That is the whole idea. The rest of this section gives names to each piece.

Words must become numbers first. The machine only handles numbers, and words and letters aren’t numbers. So we turn each word into a row of 0s with a single 1 in that word’s own slot. Say the machine knows only three words: cat, dog, car. Give each word a slot, in that order. Then “cat” becomes 1, 0, 0. “Dog” becomes 0, 1, 0. “Car” becomes 0, 0, 1. Think of a row of light switches where only one is turned on. This row of numbers is called a one-hot vector. (“Vector” means a list of numbers in a row. “One-hot” means exactly one of them is “on”.) The full list of words the machine knows is its vocabulary, and the slides write its size with the letter \(p\). A one-hot vector always has \(p\) numbers.

Inside the box: small calculators. The box is made of many tiny calculators. Each one does the same three things:

  1. It takes its incoming numbers and multiplies each one by its own dial (its weight).
  2. It adds all of these up, plus the bias. This total is the weighted sum, written \(z\). A school grade works the same way: exam × 0.6 + project × 0.4.
  3. It pushes the total through a squashing rule, so the result stays in a useful range. This rule is the activation function. A common one is the sigmoid, which squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1. Big numbers come out close to 1, very negative numbers close to 0, and 0 comes out as exactly 0.5.

One such tiny calculator is called a neuron (also neural unit or node).

Neurons are stacked in layers. A layer is a group of neurons working side by side. The outputs of one layer are the inputs of the next.

  • The input layer is where the numbers come in. It does no calculation, so it usually isn’t counted.
  • The hidden layers sit in the middle. They’re “hidden” because you never see their numbers directly. Each one finds useful in-between patterns in the input on its own. A useful piece of information about the input is called a feature (for example “does the word end in -ing?”). Patterns the network finds by itself, which nobody named, are called latent features (“latent” means hidden).
  • The output layer is the last one. It gives the final answer.

A network with one hidden layer is called a two-layer network: the hidden layer plus the output layer, because the input layer isn’t counted. If every neuron in one layer is linked to every neuron in the next, the network is fully connected. If numbers only flow one way, from input to output, with no loops back, it is feed-forward. Using many hidden layers is called deep learning.

A link to an older method. There is a classic method called logistic regression. It takes a weighted sum and squeezes it into a chance, the same way one neuron does. So the last layer of a network that turns scores into chances works like logistic regression. A deep network is like layer after layer of these small judges, each passing its verdict to the next. The difference: in logistic regression a human picks the inputs by hand. In a network, the earlier layers work out by themselves which useful summaries of the input to build.

From raw scores to chances. Suppose the job is to guess the next letter. The output layer gives one raw number for each possible letter, for example 2.0, 1.0 or −3.5. These raw numbers are called scores or logits. They can be any size, even negative. We’d rather have chances (probabilities): numbers between 0 and 1 that add up to 1, where 0.7 means “70% likely”. A step called softmax does this. It makes every score positive, then divides each one by the total. The biggest score gets the biggest chance, but every option keeps some chance.

Measuring “how wrong”. The one number that says how wrong the guess was is the loss (also cost function). In this course it works like this: look at the chance the machine gave to the right answer. If that chance was high, the loss is small. If it was low, the loss is big. The exact rule is “minus the log of the chance given to the right answer, averaged over all examples”. It’s called negative log-likelihood or cross-entropy. (The “log” is explained with numbers in the walk-through below.) Training means making this loss as small as possible.

Which way to turn each dial. For each dial, you want to know: if I turn this dial up a tiny bit, does the loss go up or down, and by how much? That answer is the dial’s gradient. It points “uphill”, towards a bigger loss. The method that works out the gradient for every dial at once is backpropagation. It traces the error backwards from the output, through each layer, to every dial.

Turning the dials. Now turn every dial a small step in the opposite direction to its gradient, so the loss goes down. This is gradient descent. Picture walking down a foggy hill: you can’t see the bottom, so you feel which way the ground slopes and take a step downhill. The size of each step is the learning rate. Too small, and learning is slow. Too big, and you overshoot.

Backpropagation and gradient descent are two different jobs. Backpropagation works out the directions. Gradient descent uses them to turn the dials.

Repeating. One full pass through all the training examples is an epoch. Often the machine doesn’t look at all examples before each step. It takes a small random handful, called a mini-batch, works out the gradients from those, and takes a step. This is stochastic gradient descent (SGD) (“stochastic” means “random”). It’s faster and a bit noisier.

What can go wrong, and why networks took off. A network can learn its training examples by heart instead of the general pattern, like memorising last year’s exam answers without understanding them. This is overfitting. Tricks against it are called regularisation. One such trick is dropout: during training, switch off some random neurons each time, so the network can’t lean on any single one. (How dropout works is [Not in course files — general knowledge].) Networks also need huge numbers of small multiplications. A GPU (a graphics chip) can do thousands of these at the same time.

Neural networks are not new; the lectures say they have a long history. They became popular partly thanks to newer developments: stochastic gradient descent, dropout and regularisation (better learning, less overfitting), and GPU computing.

Analogy Tuning an old radio in the dark. You turn the knob a little, listen whether the noise got better or worse, and turn it further in the better direction. The loss is the noise; gradient descent is the “turn a little in the better direction” rule; backpropagation is working out, for each of thousands of knobs at once, which direction is “better”.

Walk-through example

We’ll go through seven small steps. Every number is shown and worked out.

Step 1: one neuron, by hand. One input comes in: the number 2. Its dial (weight) is set to 0.5. The bias is 1. These are made-up numbers for practice.

  • Weighted sum: bias + weight × input = 1 + 0.5 × 2 = 1 + 1 = 2.
  • Now squash it with the sigmoid. The sigmoid rule is “1 divided by (1 + \(e^{-z}\))”, where \(z\) is the weighted sum. Here \(e\) is a fixed number, about 2.718, a bit like π is a fixed number about 3.14. \(e^{-2}\) means “1 divided by \(e\) twice”, which is about 0.135.
  • So: 1 ÷ (1 + 0.135) = 1 ÷ 1.135 ≈ 0.88.

The output, 0.88, sits between 0 and 1, so you can read it as a chance: 88%.

Step 2: a one-hot vector picks out a row. Use the three-word vocabulary from before: cat, dog, car. Here are their one-hot vectors. Each row is one word. Each column is one slot in the vocabulary. A cell is 1 if that slot belongs to the word, and 0 otherwise.

Word slot “cat” slot “dog” slot “car”
cat 1 0 0
dog 0 1 0
car 0 0 1

Now take a grid of dials, called \(W\). A grid of numbers with rows and columns, like a small spreadsheet, is called a matrix. This one has one row per word and two columns, so each word owns two numbers. The numbers are made up. People describe a grid’s size as “rows × columns”, so this is a 3 × 2 matrix.

\(W\) column 1 column 2
row for cat 0.9 0.2
row for dog 0.8 0.3
row for car 0.1 0.9

Written the way maths books write it:

\[W = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.2 \\ 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.1 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix} \quad\begin{matrix}\leftarrow \text{cat}\\ \leftarrow \text{dog}\\ \leftarrow \text{car}\end{matrix}\]

Now we combine dog’s one-hot vector (0, 1, 0) with \(W\). This combining is called matrix multiplication. The rule: for each column of \(W\), multiply the vector’s numbers by that column’s numbers, one pair at a time, and add up.

  • Column 1: 0 × 0.9 + 1 × 0.8 + 0 × 0.1 = 0 + 0.8 + 0 = 0.8.
  • Column 2: 0 × 0.2 + 1 × 0.3 + 0 × 0.9 = 0 + 0.3 + 0 = 0.3.

\[(0,\;1,\;0)\,W = \big(0{\times}0.9 + 1{\times}0.8 + 0{\times}0.1,\;\; 0{\times}0.2 + 1{\times}0.3 + 0{\times}0.9\big) = (0.8,\;0.3)\]

The answer, (0.8, 0.3), is exactly dog’s row of \(W\). Every 0 wipes out a row. The single 1 keeps one row. So the one-hot vector doesn’t change anything. It only picks something out of the grid. That’s why it’s also called a selection vector. The course notebook says the same: “for one-hot input this simply picks out row x of W”.

The lecture writes the same thing the other way round. It stores the grid on its side (rows and columns swapped), with one column per word. It calls that grid \(W^1\), of size \(K \times p\): \(K\) rows (how many numbers each word owns) and \(p\) columns (one per word). Then the one-hot vector picks out a column instead of a row. Same idea. In an exam answer about word2vec, use the lecture’s version: the one-hot vector selects a column of \(W^1\).

Step 3: softmax on three scores. Say the network gives three raw scores (logits) for three possible next characters: 2, 1 and 0. Softmax does two things.

  1. It takes \(e\) to the power of each score. \(e^2 = 2.718 \times 2.718 = 7.389\). \(e^1 = 2.718\). \(e^0 = 1\) (anything to the power 0 is 1). These are always positive. The total is 7.389 + 2.718 + 1 = 11.107.
  2. It divides each one by the total. Character 1: 7.389 ÷ 11.107 = 0.665.

In the table below, the columns are the three characters, and each row is one step of the calculation.

Character 1 Character 2 Character 3 Sum
Score \(z\) 2 1 0
\(e^{z}\) 7.389 2.718 1.000 11.107
Softmax \(= e^{z}/\text{sum}\) 0.665 0.245 0.090 1.000

Read the last row as chances: 66.5%, 24.5% and 9.0%. The biggest score got the biggest chance. Every chance is positive. They add up to 1.

Step 4: the loss. Say the true next character was character 1. The network gave it the chance 0.665. The loss for this example is “minus the log of 0.665”.

What is a log? The natural log, written ln, answers the question “\(e\) to what power gives this number?”. For example, ln 1 = 0, because \(e^0 = 1\). For any number below 1, the answer is negative. So “minus ln” of a chance is always 0 or positive.

  • Here: −ln 0.665 = 0.41.
  • If the network had given the truth 0.9: −ln 0.9 ≈ 0.11 (small loss).
  • If it had given the truth only 0.1: −ln 0.1 ≈ 2.30 (big loss).

Confident and right means a small loss. Giving the truth a low chance means a big loss. Averaging this over all examples gives the negative log-likelihood.

Step 5: one nudge. Take one dial, currently set to 2.0. Backpropagation tells us its gradient is 0.5. That means turning this dial up would push the loss up. So we turn it down. With a learning rate of 1, the new value is:

old value − learning rate × gradient = 2.0 − 1 × 0.5 = 1.5.

This is a made-up illustration. Then the same happens for every dial, for every example, many times.

Step 6: the course’s first network. The course notebook builds a network that guesses the next character of a first name. It uses 27 characters: the 26 letters plus a dot ., which stands for both “start of name” and “end of name”.
