  • It is “a single linear layer (a 27×27 weight matrix, no hidden layer) followed by a softmax”. In words: each character comes in as a one-hot vector of 27 numbers. A grid of 27 × 27 = 729 dials turns it into 27 scores, one per possible next character. Softmax turns these into chances. That grid is “the same size as the count table from part 1” (the counting method from “Why this exists”).
  • From the name “emma” it builds 5 training examples. Each example is “this character comes in, this one should come next”:
Example Character that comes in Character that should come next
1 . e
2 e m
3 m m
4 m a
5 a .
  • After training, its loss is 2.46, against 2.45 for plain counting. In the notebook’s words: “exp(W) normalized row-wise is close to the count table P”. In plain words: if you turn the learned dials into chances, you get almost the same table you would get by counting.

A warning about the course files: the notebook’s subtitle says “neural network with one hidden layer”, but its text, its code and the lecture slides say no hidden layer. Write “no hidden layer” in the exam.

Step 7: a deeper network (the MLP). A network with at least one hidden layer is called an MLP. The course’s next notebook builds one for the same job.

  • Each of the 27 characters gets its own 10 learned numbers. Such a short list of learned numbers that stands for a character or word is called an embedding (the next chapter is all about these). These numbers sit in a grid called C, of size 27 × 10.
  • It looks at the five previous characters. Five characters × 10 numbers each = 50 numbers going in.
  • These go into a hidden layer of 300 neurons. Their squashing rule is tanh, which works like the sigmoid but gives outputs from −1 to 1.
  • Then come 27 output scores, then softmax and the cross-entropy loss.
  • It trains on mini-batches of 32 examples for 200,000 steps.
  • The names are split 80/10/10: 80% to learn from (the train set), 10% and 10% held back for checking (the dev and test sets). The loss measured on held-back examples, which the network never learned from, is the validation loss.
  • Validation loss: 2.22. Perplexity: 9.2. Perplexity is \(e\) to the power of the loss (\(e^{2.22} \approx 9.2\)). Roughly, the network is “torn between about 9 characters” at each guess. Lower is better.

How many dials does this network have? The file doesn’t print it, so this is my own count:

Part Size Dials
Character embeddings C 27 × 10 270
Weights into the hidden layer 50 × 300 15,000
Biases of the hidden layer one per neuron 300
Weights into the output layer 300 × 27 8,100
Biases of the output layer one per output 27
Total 23,697

\[270 + 15{,}000 + 300 + 8{,}100 + 27 = 23{,}697\]

What these numbers show: good points and weak points.

  • Good: the network learns the pattern from examples on its own. Nobody has to write rules or hand-pick the inputs.
  • Good: it grows gracefully. Giving it more memory doesn’t blow up a table: the MLP with 5 characters of memory reaches loss 2.22, against 2.45 for counting.
  • Weak: with the same information, it’s no smarter than counting (2.46 vs 2.45 for the one-character version).
  • Weak: it needs lots of data and computing power, and it can overfit. GPUs help with the computing; dropout and regularisation help against overfitting.

The formula, explained

Inside one neuron. You’ve already done this by hand in Step 1. Here it is in the lecture’s symbols:

\[z = b + wx, \qquad a = f(z), \qquad a = \sigma(z) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-z}}, \qquad a = \text{softmax}(z) = \frac{e^{z_j}}{\sum e^{z_j}}\]

  • \(x\) = the inputs (the numbers coming in).
  • \(w\) = the weights: how much each input counts.
  • \(b\) = the bias: a baseline amount added on top.
  • \(z\) = the weighted sum, a raw score.
  • \(f\) = the activation function, the squashing rule.
  • \(a\) = the neuron’s output.
  • \(\sigma\) (the Greek letter “sigma”) = the sigmoid. It squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1, for example \(\sigma(0) = 0.5\).
  • \(e\) = the fixed number about 2.718.
  • \(\sum\) (a capital Greek “sigma”) = “add all of these up”.
  • softmax: take \(e\) to the power of each score \(z_j\) and divide by the sum over all scores. The slide uses the same letter \(j\) above and below the line. It means “this score, divided by the sum over all scores”. You may write \(\sum_k e^{z_k}\) in the bottom part to be clear.

Read aloud: “Each neuron takes a weighted sum of its inputs plus a bias and pushes it through an activation function.”

A two-layer network with a softmax output. Now stack two layers. A small raised number such as \(W^1\) is a label meaning “of layer 1”, not a power.

\[h^1 = \sigma(W^1 h^0 + b^1), \qquad h^2 = W^2 h^1 + b^2, \qquad y = \text{softmax}(h^2)\]

  • \(h^0 = x\) = the input vector (the list of numbers coming in).
  • \(W^1, b^1\) = the weights and biases of layer 1.
  • \(h^1\) = the hidden layer’s outputs, also called its “activations”.
  • \(W^2, b^2\) = the weights and biases of layer 2.
  • \(h^2\) = the output scores.
  • \(W^l\) = the weight grid of any layer \(l\). It is a \(j^l \times k^{l-1}\) matrix: one row per neuron in this layer (\(j\) of them) and one column per output of the layer before (\(k\) of them). It links the \(j\) neurons of layer \(l\) to the \(k\) activations of layer \(l-1\).
  • \(y\) = the final output: a chance for each possible answer (each “class”).

Read aloud: “Weight the inputs, squash them into hidden features, weight those features into scores, and turn the scores into probabilities with softmax.”

Will the exam ask you to write these? In 2025 the exam had no calculations. You should understand both lines and be able to say them in words. Writing the one-neuron line (\(z = b + wx\), \(a = f(z)\)) can make a definition answer stronger.

Reading the course code

The exam has not asked students to write code. This is only so you recognise the steps. Here is the whole first network in the course notebook (Step 6): one guess, the loss, and one training step.

H = xs_onehot @ W                                          # picks out row x of W
output = torch.exp(H) / torch.exp(H).sum(1, keepdim=True)  # softmax
loss = -output[torch.arange(len(ys)), ys].log().mean()     # negative log-likelihood
loss.backward()                                            # backpropagation
W.data -= lr * W.grad                                      # gradient descent step

The code uses PyTorch, a Python toolkit for neural networks. The @ sign means matrix multiplication.

  • Line 1: multiply the one-hot inputs by the grid of dials. Because each input is one-hot, this only looks up a row of W. Those rows are the raw scores (logits).
  • Line 2: softmax. Take \(e\) to the power of each score and divide by the row’s total. Now each row holds chances for the 27 possible next characters.
  • Line 3: for each example, take the chance given to the true next character, take its log, average, and flip the sign. This is the same loss the counting method uses: minus the average log-chance of the truth (written \(-\ell/n\) there, where \(\ell\) is the total of the log-chances and \(n\) the number of examples).
  • Line 4: .backward() runs backpropagation. PyTorch works out how the loss would change if each dial moved a little (the gradient). It stores the answer in .grad.
  • Line 5: move every dial a small step against its gradient. lr is the learning rate. This line is repeated: the notebook first runs 10 steps with learning rate 1, then 1,000 steps with learning rate 15.

The notebook has no saved outputs. Its summary table gives the final loss ≈ 2.46.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025, Q3(c) (2.5 points): what a one-hot vector is, and how word2vec (the word-map method of the next chapter) uses it in its first layer. In word2vec, the word fed in is called the target word, and \(x_t\) is its one-hot vector. \(W^1\) (the target embedding matrix) is the grid holding one column of \(K\) numbers per word, and \(h^1_t\) is the result of the first layer. “\(K\)-dimensional” means “\(K\) numbers long”. “No activation and no bias” means this layer has no squashing rule and no added baseline. The model answer, also given in the next chapter:

Model answer “A one-hot vector is a \(p \times 1\) vector of zeros with a single 1 at the word’s position in the vocabulary. In word2vec the target word enters as a one-hot vector \(x_t\). The first layer computes \(h^1_t = W^1 x_t\) with no activation and no bias, so \(x_t\) just selects the column of \(W^1\) belonging to that word: a ‘selection vector’. That column is the word’s \(K\)-dimensional embedding, and \(W^1\) (the target embedding matrix) is what word2vec learns.”

What this answer is saying, in plain words: A one-hot vector is a list as long as the word list, all 0s except a 1 in the word’s own slot. word2vec feeds each word in this way. Multiplying it by the first grid of dials, with no squashing and no bias, picks out that word’s own column, exactly as in Step 2. That column of \(K\) numbers is the word’s embedding, and learning this grid is the whole point of word2vec.

Likely True/False items:

  • “A softmax output layer makes a neural network like logistic regression.” True. Logistic regression turns a weighted sum into a chance; a network ending in softmax does the same in its last layer.
  • “The input layer is counted as a layer.” False. The input layer only passes numbers in, so it isn’t counted.
  • “The neural network bigram has a hidden layer.” False. (“Bigram” means “pair of neighbouring characters”: it’s the course’s first network from Step 6, which guesses the next character from one character.) It has no hidden layer.

Likely explain question: “How is a neural network trained, and why did neural networks become popular?”

Model answer With the current weights the network makes a prediction, and a cost function (e.g. negative log-likelihood) measures how far it is from the truth. Backpropagation computes how the cost changes with each weight, and gradient descent moves every weight a small step in the direction that lowers the cost. This is repeated many times over the data. Neural networks became popular partly thanks to stochastic gradient descent, dropout and regularisation (better learning, less overfitting), and GPU computing (L6 slide 19).

What this answer is saying, in plain words: The network makes a guess with its current dials, and one score says how wrong the guess was. Backpropagation works out which way each dial should turn, and gradient descent turns them all a small step that way. You repeat this many times. Networks took off thanks to faster learning from small random handfuls of examples, tricks against memorising, and graphics chips that do many sums at once.

The training words also come back in the transformer and chatbot questions: gradient descent (turning the dials downhill), backpropagation (working out which way to turn each dial), cross-entropy (the “how wrong” score) and epoch (one full pass through the examples).

What a top-grade answer must include

  • For one-hot: “vector of length \(p\) (vocabulary size), all zeros except a 1 at the word’s index”. In words: a list as long as the word list, all 0s except a 1 in the word’s own slot. Plus: “multiplying it by a weight matrix selects one row/column = that word’s vector (a selection vector)”. In words: multiplying it by the grid of dials picks out only that word’s own row or column.
  • For softmax: it “turns scores into positive probabilities that sum to 1”.
  • For training: “minimise a cost function; backpropagation computes gradients; gradient descent updates weights; repeat”. In words: make the “how wrong” score small; backpropagation works out which way to turn each dial; gradient descent turns them a small step; do it again and again.
  • For why networks got popular: SGD (learning from small random handfuls of examples), dropout and regularisation (tricks against memorising), and GPUs (graphics chips that do many sums at once).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Saying a one-hot vector “counts how often a word appears”. That describes a row of the word-count table (one row per document, one column per word, each cell a count). A one-hot vector only marks which word it is.
  • Saying softmax picks the single biggest value. It gives a chance to every option: a whole list of chances that adds up to 1.
  • Mixing up backpropagation and gradient descent. Backpropagation works out the directions (the gradients). Gradient descent uses them to turn the dials.
  • Saying neural networks are popular because they are “new”. The lecture says they have a “long history”, and that the rise in popularity is “partly due to newer developments”: SGD, dropout and regularisation, and GPUs.

Key terms to use

  • one-hot vector (all 0s, one 1 for the word)
  • selection vector (one-hot used to pick one row)
  • weights (dials saying how much each input counts)
  • bias (a fixed baseline nudge added on)
  • neural unit (one small calculator inside the network)
  • activation function (the squashing rule after the sum)
  • sigmoid (squeezes any number between 0 and 1)
  • softmax (turns scores into chances adding to 1)
  • logits (raw scores before softmax)
  • hidden layer (middle layer you never see directly)
  • fully connected (every unit linked to every next unit)
  • feed-forward (numbers flow one way, no loops)
  • deep learning (networks with many hidden layers)
  • cost/loss function (one “how wrong” score to shrink)
  • negative log-likelihood (minus log of the truth’s chance)
  • gradient descent (turn dials a step downhill)
  • learning rate (how big each step is)
  • backpropagation (works out which way each dial goes)
  • stochastic gradient descent (steps using small random handfuls of examples)
  • dropout (randomly switching off units while training)
  • regularisation (tricks that stop memorising)
  • GPU (chip doing thousands of sums at once)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “Multiplying a one-hot vector by a weight matrix returns the sum of all rows of the matrix.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A one-hot vector is a list of 0s with a single 1 in one word’s slot. A weight matrix is a grid of dials with one row per word. When you multiply the two, do you get all the rows added together?

    False. Why: Every 0 wipes out its row, and the single 1 keeps one row. So you get only that one row (or column), the one where the 1 sits. It’s like a row of light switches with only one on: only that one lamp lights up.

  2. T/F: “A deep neural network can be seen as layer after layer of logistic regression classifiers.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A deep neural network is one with many middle layers. Logistic regression is a classic method that adds up weighted inputs and squeezes the result into a chance. A classifier is something that sorts items into groups. Is a deep network like many of these stacked on top of each other?

    True. Why: Each layer does a weighted sum and then a squashing step, which is what logistic regression does. Stack them, and each layer feeds the next, like a relay of small judges each passing their verdict on.

  3. T/F: “The input layer is counted when we call a network with one hidden layer a two-layer network.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The input layer is where the numbers come in. A hidden layer is a middle layer. A network with one middle layer is called “two-layer”. Is the input layer one of those two?

    False. Why: The input layer does no calculation, so it usually isn’t counted. The two layers are the hidden layer and the output layer. It’s like a front door: you don’t count it as a room of the house.

  4. T/F: “Softmax outputs always sum to 1.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Softmax is the step that turns a list of raw scores into chances. Do those chances always add up to exactly 1?

    True. Why: Softmax makes each score positive (\(e\) to the power of the score), then divides each one by the total of all of them. Anything divided by its own total adds up to 1, like slices of one pizza always making one whole pizza.

  5. Explain (2–5 sentences): “How is a neural network trained, and why did neural networks become popular?”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Describe the learning loop (guess, measure how wrong, work out directions, nudge, repeat) and give the reasons networks took off.

    Answer: With the current weights the network makes a prediction, and a cost function (e.g. negative log-likelihood) measures how far it is from the truth. Backpropagation computes how the cost changes with each weight, and gradient descent moves every weight a small step in the direction that lowers the cost. This is repeated many times over the data. Neural networks became popular partly thanks to stochastic gradient descent, dropout and regularisation (better learning, less overfitting), and GPU computing (L6 slide 19).

    Why: This is the loop from “The idea in everyday words”: guess, score the guess, find which way each dial should go, turn them a small step, repeat. The popularity part names the three developments the lecture gives, rather than “they are new”.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • neural network: a machine of many small adjustable dials that turns input numbers into output numbers and learns by nudging the dials after each wrong guess.
  • weight (w, W): one dial. It says how much one input counts. A big weight is like turning up the volume on that input.
  • bias (b): a baseline nudge added on top, whatever the inputs are. Like a shop that adds a fixed delivery fee to every order.
  • parameters: all the weights and biases together: everything the network learns.
  • input / output: the numbers you feed in / the numbers that come out.
  • neuron / neural unit / node: one small calculator inside the network. It adds up its weighted inputs plus the bias, then squashes the result.
  • weighted sum (z): multiply each input by its weight and add it all up. Like a course grade: exam × 0.6 + project × 0.4.
  • activation function (f): the squashing rule a neuron applies to its weighted sum, so the output stays in a useful range.
  • sigmoid (σ): an activation function that squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1. Sigmoid of 0 is 0.5; big numbers get close to 1.
  • tanh: a squashing rule like sigmoid, but its outputs run from −1 to 1. [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • softmax: turns a list of raw scores into chances that are all positive and add up to 1. The biggest score gets the biggest chance. Scores 2, 1, 0 become 0.665, 0.245, 0.090.
  • logits / scores: the raw numbers a network gives before softmax. They can be any size, even negative.
  • probability (chance): a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely something is. 0.665 = 66.5%.
  • e, exponentiate: e is a fixed number, about 2.718. To exponentiate a score z means to work out \(e^{z}\), which is always positive. \(e^2 = 7.389\).
  • vector: a list of numbers in a row, like (0.8, 0.3). Its length is how many numbers it holds.
  • matrix: a grid of numbers with rows and columns, like a spreadsheet.
  • matrix multiplication (@, \(xW\)): a way to combine a list with a grid: for each column, multiply the list’s numbers by the column’s numbers one by one and add up.
  • size notation (\(K \times p\), \(27 \times 27\)): “rows × columns”. A 3 × 2 grid has 3 rows and 2 columns.
  • “stored on its side” (transposed): the same grid with rows and columns swapped.
  • one-hot vector: a list as long as the vocabulary, all 0s except one 1 in the word’s own slot. Like a row of light switches with only one turned on. With cat, dog, car: dog = (0, 1, 0).
  • selection vector: another name for a one-hot vector when it’s used to pick one row (or column) out of a grid.
  • vocabulary (p): the list of all words (or characters) the model knows.
  • embedding: a short list of learned numbers that stands for a word or letter (next chapter). In the MLP, each character gets 10 such numbers.
  • layer: a group of neurons that work side by side. The outputs of one layer feed the next.
  • input layer: where the numbers enter. It does no calculation, so it usually isn’t counted.
  • hidden layer: a layer between input and output. “Hidden” because you never see its numbers directly.
  • output layer: the last layer. It gives the final scores.
  • two-layer network: one hidden layer plus the output layer (the input layer isn’t counted).
  • fully connected: every neuron in one layer is linked to every neuron in the next.
  • feed-forward: numbers flow one way only, from input to output, with no loops back.
  • deep learning: using networks with many hidden layers.
  • feature / latent feature: a feature is a useful piece of information about the input (“does the word end in -ing?”). Latent = hidden: patterns the network finds on its own, which nobody named.
  • logistic regression: a classic method that turns a weighted sum into a chance with sigmoid (or softmax for many classes). A network with a softmax output works the same way in its last layer.
  • classifier: something that sorts items into groups, like “spam” or “not spam”.
  • cost function / loss (\(\hat{y}\) vs \(y\)): one number that measures how far the guess \(\hat{y}\) (“y-hat”) is from the truth \(y\). Training tries to make it small.
  • negative log-likelihood / cross-entropy: the loss used here: minus the log of the chance the model gave to the right answer, averaged. A low chance for the truth gives a big loss. Chance 0.665 gives 0.41.
  • log, ln: the reverse of a power: ln asks “e to what power gives this number?” ln 1 = 0; ln of a number below 1 is negative.
  • gradient: for each dial, how much the loss changes if you turn that dial up a tiny bit. It points “uphill”.
  • gradient descent: turning every dial a small step against its gradient, so you walk downhill to a lower loss. Like walking down a foggy hill by always stepping where the ground slopes down.
  • learning rate (lr): how big each step is. Too small = slow. Too big = you overshoot.
  • backpropagation: the method that works out the gradient for every dial at once, by tracing the error backwards from the output through each layer.
  • stochastic gradient descent (SGD): gradient descent that uses a small random handful of examples for each step, instead of all of them. Faster, slightly noisier. [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • mini-batch: that small handful of examples, here 32 at a time.
  • epoch: one full pass through all the training examples.
  • overfitting: memorising the training examples instead of learning the general pattern, like learning last year’s exam answers by heart without understanding them.
  • dropout: during training, switching off some random neurons each time, so the network can’t lean on any single one. It helps against overfitting. [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • regularisation: any trick that keeps the network from overfitting, for example by keeping the weights small. [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • GPU: a graphics chip. It can do thousands of small multiplications at the same time, which is exactly what networks need. [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • train / dev / test split, validation loss: keep most examples to learn from (train) and hold some back to check the model (dev and test). Validation loss is the loss on held-back examples the model didn’t learn from.
  • perplexity: e to the power of the loss: roughly how many options the model is torn between. Loss 2.22 gives about 9.2.
  • bigram: a pair of neighbouring characters or words, like “e” then “m”. A bigram model guesses the next one from the one before.
  • MLP: a neural network with at least one hidden layer. The course’s Part 3 model.
  • PyTorch, .backward(), .grad: PyTorch is a Python toolkit for neural networks. .backward() runs backpropagation, and .grad holds the resulting gradient for each dial.

Sources: Lecture 4 slide 8; Lecture 6 “Neural Networks and Word Embeddings” (Thorsrud) slides 14–19, 21–22; notebooks Predict_the_next_token_part2_nn.ipynb (cells 0–33, incl. 0, 6–14, 19–21, 27–28, 33) and Predict_the_next_token_part3_mpl.ipynb (cells 5–16, incl. 5, 7, 10, 16).

13. Word embeddings: distributional hypothesis, co-occurrence, PMI/PPMI, SVD on PMI, word2vec, vector arithmetic, static vs contextual

Exam priority: ★★★ High — a whole 15-point block in 2025: Q3(a) assumption + PMI matrix, Q3(b) word2vec vs BERT, Q3(c) one-hot in word2vec, Q3(d) cosine drawing, plus a True/False item on SVD on PMI.

Why this exists

You search a website for “automobile”. You’d like it to also find pages that only say “car”. To a computer, though, these are two different strings of letters. Nothing tells it they mean the same thing.

The usual way to turn text into numbers makes this worse. It’s the word-count table: one row per document, one column per word, and each cell says how many times that word appears in that document. Word order is thrown away, so this is also called bag-of-words, and the table is called the document-term matrix (the slides call it \(C\)). In that table, “car” and “automobile” are two separate columns with nothing linking them. The table also ignores the words around each word, its context.

We want the computer to learn which words are close in meaning, without anyone writing a dictionary for it. Word embeddings do exactly that. Researchers then use them to measure things like “how strongly do the news link recession with credit?”, month by month.

The idea in everyday words

A map of meaning. Imagine a map where every word has its own spot, and words with similar meanings sit close together. “Car” sits next to “automobile”. “Apricot” sits next to “pineapple”, far from “computer”.

A spot on a paper map is given by two numbers, like “3 cm across, 5 cm up”. A word’s spot works the same way: it’s a short list of numbers. A list of numbers is called a vector. You can draw a vector as an arrow from the centre of the map to that spot. How many numbers each list has is the number of dimensions. A paper map has 2. Word maps use maybe 100 or 300: you can’t draw that, but a computer handles it fine. The whole “map” where these arrows live is called a vector space.

A word’s spot on this map is its word embedding. The slides sum it up in a slogan: “embedding is location”. The meaning of a word is where it sits.

The clue: the company a word keeps. How can a computer find these spots without a dictionary? By looking at which words a word turns up next to. “Apricot” and “pineapple” both appear near “sugar” and “pinch”. “Digital” and “information” both appear near “computer” and “data”. So apricot should end up near pineapple, and digital near information.

The idea behind this is that words used in similar surroundings have similar meanings. The linguist Firth put it like this in 1957: “You shall know a word by the company it keeps!” This idea is usually called the distributional hypothesis. The slides quote Firth but don’t use that name; the name is the standard one [Not in course files — general knowledge].

Who counts as “company”. The word we’re looking at is the target word. The words near it are its context words. “Near” is set by a window: for example, look 4 words to the left and 4 words to the right. The slides write the window size as \(b\), so \(b = 4\) means 4 words on each side. Two words inside the same window are said to co-occur (appear together). Each time they do is a co-occurrence.

There are two ways to turn “who appears with whom” into spots on the map. One counts. The other plays a guessing game.

Way 1: counting.

  1. Count. Build a big table with one row per word and one column per word. Each cell says how often the row word and the column word appeared together in a window. This is the co-occurrence matrix (the slides call it \(Co\)). If the vocabulary (the list of all distinct words) has \(p\) words, the table has \(p\) rows and \(p\) columns. People write that as “\(p \times p\)” (“p by p”). Note the difference from the word-count table: that one is documents × words, written \(n \times p\) with \(n\) = the number of documents. This one is words × words.
  2. Re-weight with PMI. Raw counts have a problem: very common words like “the” appear next to everything, so they become everybody’s neighbour and tell you nothing. The fix is to ask a fairer question: “Do these two words meet more often than they would by pure luck, given how common each one is?” Think of two people who each visit a café now and then. If both go there often, they’ll bump into each other often by luck alone. That tells you nothing. If two people who rarely go there keep turning up together, that means something. The score that measures “how much more often than luck” is PMI (pointwise mutual information). Above 0 means the words attract each other. 0 means “exactly as often as luck”. Below 0 means they avoid each other.
  3. Set the negatives to 0. Negative PMI scores are hard to trust (the slides call them “strange”), so every negative score is replaced by 0. This version is PPMI (positive PMI).
  4. Squeeze the table. The PMI table is huge (with 20,000 words it has 400 million cells) and mostly zeros, because most pairs of words never meet. A table like that is called sparse: lots of storage, little information per number. So we squeeze it. A maths tool keeps only the few strongest patterns in the table and gives each word a short list of numbers, say 300. Most of these numbers are not zero, so the list is dense. Think of summing up a long survey by a few main themes, and giving each person a score on each theme. The squeezing tool is called SVD (singular value decomposition). Keeping only the strongest few patterns is truncated SVD. The number of patterns you keep is written \(K\) (for example 100 or 300). SVD splits the table into three thinner tables called \(U\), \(S\) and \(V'\). Each word’s row in \(U\), with \(K\) numbers, becomes its embedding. The computer does SVD; you never do it by hand.

The same squeezing tool appears earlier in the course, in a method called LSA, which runs SVD on the word-count table \(C\). The slides put it this way: use SVD, “but now not on C, but on M!”, where \(M\) is the PMI table.

Way 2: predicting (word2vec). The second way uses a small neural network: a machine of many small dials that turns input numbers into output numbers and learns by nudging its dials after every wrong guess. The method is called word2vec (Mikolov et al. 2013, a “game changer”).

The network plays a guessing game with real text. There are two versions:

  • Skipgram: show the network one word and ask it to guess which words appear nearby. “Here’s ‘cat’. Which words would you expect around it?”
  • CBOW: show it the neighbours and ask for the word in the middle. A fill-in-the-blank exercise. (CBOW stands for “continuous bag of words”; the long name is [Not in course files — general knowledge].)

The text itself provides the right answers: the real neighbours. No human has to label anything. When a human gives the right answers, learning is called supervised. When there are no answers at all, it’s unsupervised. When the data supplies its own answers, it’s self-supervised. Word embeddings sit under “unsupervised/self-supervised” in the course.

How does a word enter the network? Networks only handle numbers. So each word becomes a one-hot vector: a list as long as the vocabulary, all 0s, with a single 1 in that word’s own slot. Like a row of light switches with only one turned on.

The first grid of dials in word2vec is called the target embedding matrix, \(W^1\). A matrix is a grid of numbers with rows and columns. \(W^1\) has one column per word. When you multiply a word’s one-hot vector by \(W^1\), all the 0s wipe out the other columns, and only that word’s column comes through. So the one-hot vector works as a selection vector: it selects one column. The selected column is the network’s middle step (its hidden layer). A second grid, the context embedding matrix \(W^2\), turns it into one score per word in the vocabulary. A step called softmax turns those scores into chances (numbers from 0 to 1 that add up to 1): the chance that each word is a neighbour. One full pass through all the training text is an epoch; training runs over the text many times.

Every wrong guess nudges the dials. After training, each word’s column in \(W^1\) is its spot on the map. Learning \(W^1\) is the whole point.

Scoring every word in the vocabulary for every example is slow, because the vocabulary is huge. A shortcut called negative sampling fixes this. For each real (word, neighbour) pair, make 2–5 fake pairs with random words. Then train the network on a simpler yes/no question: “is this pair real or fake?”. A yes/no chance is made with the sigmoid, a rule that squeezes any number into the range 0 to 1. A yes/no model built this way is called logistic regression.

The slides add a word of balance: “Neural Network-based methods might not outperform the simple SVD” (Levy et al. 2015). Counting plus SVD can do as well as word2vec.

Comparing two words. Once every word has an arrow, how do we say two words are similar? We look at the angle between their arrows. If they point almost the same way, the angle is small and the words are similar. If they point in very different directions, they’re not. The score for this is cosine similarity. It runs from −1 to 1; with plain counts (which are never negative) it stays between 0 and 1. Close to 1 means “same direction”, so similar. 0 means “at a right angle”, so unrelated. It ignores how long the arrows are; only the direction matters. The words closest to a given word on the map are its nearest neighbours.

Directions can carry meaning. You can add and subtract word vectors number by number. This is vector arithmetic. The famous example: King − Man + Woman lands near Queen. The step from Man to King is a “royalty” direction; add it to Woman and you reach Queen.

One spot per word, whatever the sentence. word2vec gives every word one fixed spot. “Apple” the fruit and “Apple” the computer company share a single spot. Embeddings like this are static. Newer, bigger language models from 2017/2018, such as BERT (built on a network design called the transformer), give a word a new spot in each sentence, depending on the words around it. These are contextual (context-specific) embeddings.

Analogy You can guess a lot about a stranger from their friends. If someone always hangs around climbers, buys chalk and talks about ropes, they are probably a climber, even if nobody tells you. Word embeddings guess a word’s meaning from the words it keeps company with.

Walk-through example

Step 1: a tiny co-occurrence table. Our whole text (the corpus) is three sentences:

  1. “the cat drinks milk”
  2. “the dog drinks water”
  3. “the car needs fuel”

Rule for this example: two words “appear together” if they’re in the same sentence. So the window is the whole sentence, as in the course notebook. We skip “the”: it’s in every sentence and tells us nothing. Very common words like this are called stop words and are usually removed.

In the table below, each row is a target word (a word we want a spot for). Each column is a context word (a possible neighbour). Each cell is the number of sentences where both words appear.

Target ↓ / Context → drinks milk water needs fuel
cat 1 1 0 0 0
dog 1 0 1 0 0
car 0 0 0 1 1

Two cells out loud:

  • Row dog, column drinks. “Dog” is only in sentence 2, and “drinks” is also in sentence 2. They’re together once, so the cell is 1.
  • Row cat, column water. “Cat” is only in sentence 1, and “water” only in sentence 2. They never meet, so the cell is 0.

Each row is already a rough spot on a map, with 5 numbers: cat = (1, 1, 0, 0, 0), dog = (1, 0, 1, 0, 0), car = (0, 0, 0, 1, 1).

Step 2: cosine similarity by hand. Compare cat and dog. Three small steps:

  • Dot product: multiply the numbers in matching positions and add them up. 1 × 1 + 1 × 0 + 0 × 1 + 0 × 0 + 0 × 0 = 1.
  • Length of each arrow (also called its norm): square each number, add them, take the square root. Cat: √(1 + 1) = √2 ≈ 1.414. Dog: also √2 ≈ 1.414.
  • Cosine = dot product ÷ (length of one × length of the other) = 1 ÷ (1.414 × 1.414) = 1 ÷ 2 = 0.5.

Now cat and car. The dot product is 1 × 0 + 1 × 0 + 0 × 0 + 0 × 1 + 0 × 1 = 0, so the cosine is 0.

So cat is halfway similar to dog (they share “drinks”) and not at all like car. With millions of sentences, this kind of sharing is what pulls related words together.

Step 3: the window on the slides. The slides use a window of \(b = 4\) instead of whole sentences. Take the sentence “Working with text as data is so fun that we can’t stop.” Look 4 words to the left and right of “data”. Inside that window are “text” and “fun”, so those cells get a 1. Here is the slide’s partial table. Rows are target words, columns are context words, and each cell is how often they occur within the window.

Target ↓ / Context → text fun economics stuff bore great
data 1 1 0 0 0 0
cool 0 0 1 1 0 0
after 0 0 0 0 0 1

Step 4: PMI, slowly, with the lecture’s example. The lecture uses four target words and five context words. All the numbers below were recomputed and match the slide.

Table 1: raw co-occurrence counts. Rows are target words. Columns are context words. Each cell is how many times the two co-occurred. I added the row and column totals.

Co computer data pinch result sugar Row total
apricot 0 0 1 0 1 2
pineapple 0 0 1 0 1 2
digital 2 1 0 1 0 4
information 1 6 0 4 0 11
Column total 3 7 2 5 2 19

How to read it: “information” appeared together with “data” 6 times. In total, the table holds 19 co-occurrences (add every cell). “Information” is part of 11 of them (its row total). “Data” is part of 7 (its column total).

Table 2: turning counts into shares. A probability (or chance) is a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely something is. Here we get one by dividing a count by the grand total of 19.

  • The share of all co-occurrences that are one exact pair is the joint probability, written \(p_{ij}\). Information-with-data: 6 ÷ 19 = 0.32. The slides also call this the skipgram probability.
  • The share for one word on its own is its unigram probability: its row total ÷ 19 for a target word (\(p_i\)), or its column total ÷ 19 for a context word (\(p_j\)). Information: 11 ÷ 19 = 0.58. Data: 7 ÷ 19 = 0.37.

Here is every cell divided by 19, rounded to 2 decimals as on the slide. The last column holds \(p_i\) and the last row holds \(p_j\).

\(p_{ij}\) computer data pinch result sugar \(p_i\)
apricot 0.00 0.00 0.05 0.00 0.05 0.11
pineapple 0.00 0.00 0.05 0.00 0.05 0.11
digital 0.11 0.05 0.00 0.05 0.00 0.21
information 0.05 0.32 0.00 0.21 0.00 0.58
\(p_j\) 0.16 0.37 0.11 0.26 0.11

The key step: real share vs luck share. If two words had nothing to do with each other, how often would they land together by luck? Multiply their two shares. This is the same rule as for coins: the chance of two heads is ½ × ½ = ¼. So for information and data: 0.58 × 0.37 = 0.213. Then:

  • Divide the real share by the luck share. This says “how many times more often than luck”.
  • Take the log base 2 of that. The log base 2, written \(\log_2\), answers “2 to what power gives this number?”. \(\log_2 8 = 3\), because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. \(\log_2 1 = 0\). For a number above 1 the answer is positive; for a number below 1, negative. So “more than luck” gives PMI above 0, and “less than luck” gives PMI below 0.

Here is that step for four pairs:

Pair Real share Luck share (one word’s share × the other’s) Times more than luck PMI (\(\log_2\) of that) PPMI
apricot–pinch 1/19 = 0.053 (2/19) × (2/19) = 0.011 4.75 2.25 2.25
digital–computer 2/19 = 0.105 (4/19) × (3/19) = 0.033 3.17 1.66 1.66
information–data 6/19 = 0.316 (11/19) × (7/19) = 0.213 1.48 0.57 0.57
digital–data 1/19 = 0.053 (4/19) × (7/19) = 0.078 0.68 −0.56 0.00

One row in words: apricot and pinch met 1 time out of 19, a share of about 0.053. Apricot makes up 2 of the 19 counts and pinch 2 of the 19, so luck alone would give (2/19) × (2/19) = 4/361 ≈ 0.011. The real share is (1/19) ÷ (4/361) = 361/76 = 4.75 times the luck share. Doubling 1 twice gives 4, so \(\log_2 4.75\) is a bit over 2: it’s 2.25. PMI = 2.25, well above 0. Apricot and pinch meet far more often than luck would explain.

The digital–data row is the other way round. They met less often than luck would give (0.68 times as often), so the PMI is negative, −0.56. PPMI sets it to 0.

Table 3: the full PPMI table (the slides write it \(\tilde{M}_{ij}\)). Rows are target words, columns are context words, and each cell is the PPMI score. A blank cell means the pair never co-occurred (count 0). The log of 0 is undefined, so PPMI treats it as 0.

\(\tilde{M}_{ij}\) computer data pinch result sugar
apricot 2.25 2.25
pineapple 2.25 2.25
digital 1.66 0.00 0.00
information 0.00 0.57 0.47

Where the 0.00s come from (my own computer check): three pairs co-occur less than luck, so their raw PMI is negative: digital–data −0.56, digital–result −0.07, information–computer −0.80. PPMI = max(PMI, 0) clips them to 0.00. (Here max(…, 0) means “take whichever is bigger, the number or 0”, which turns negatives into 0.)

The warning in this table. Apricot appears only twice in the whole table, yet apricot–pinch gets the highest score, 2.25. One lucky meeting between two rare words looks hugely “more than chance”. The slide says: “Rare events, e.g. apricot in context of pinch, get high weight.” The suggested fix is add-one smoothing: add 1 to every count before computing PMI, so rare pairs don’t get extreme scores and zeros disappear.

Step 5: squeezing the PMI table with SVD. With a real vocabulary of, say, \(p\) = 20,000 words, the PMI table \(M\) has 20,000 × 20,000 = 400 million cells. Most pairs never appear together, so most cells are 0. Even in the tiny lecture example, 10 of the 20 cells are empty. So \(M\) is large and sparse, like the word-count table.

Truncated SVD keeps only \(K\) patterns. The computer works these out; you never do this by hand, and the exam won’t ask you to. What matters is how to read the result: each word gets one row of \(K\) numbers in \(U\), for example 100 or 300 numbers. That row is the word’s embedding, its spot on the map. One number alone doesn’t mean much. What matters is how two words’ rows compare: compare them with cosine similarity, and words with similar company come out close to 1.

Step 6: one-hot vectors and word2vec’s first layer. This was 2025 Q3(c), so let’s go slowly.

Take a vocabulary of three words: cat, dog, car. Give each word a slot, in that order. A word’s one-hot vector has a 1 in its own slot and 0 everywhere else. In this table, each row is a word, each column is a slot, and each cell says whether that slot is “on” for that word.

Word slot 1 (cat) slot 2 (dog) slot 3 (car)
cat 1 0 0
dog 0 1 0
car 0 0 1

A one-hot vector does not count anything. Compare it with a row of the word-count table. Say a short document reads “dog dog car”. Its word-count row and the one-hot vector for “dog” look like this (my own illustration):

cat dog car What it tells you
Word-count row for the document “dog dog car” 0 2 1 how often each word appears in a document
One-hot vector for the word “dog” 0 1 0 which word this is, nothing more

Where the training pairs come from. Skipgram makes its training examples from real text. From sentence 1 of Step 1 (“the cat drinks milk”), it makes the pairs (cat, drinks) and (cat, milk). Shown “cat”, the network should give “drinks” and “milk” high chances of being neighbours. The text decides the right answers, which is why this is self-supervised.

The first layer. Each word should get \(K\) = 2 numbers (real models use about 300). So the target embedding matrix \(W^1\) has 2 rows and 3 columns, one column per word. Its size is written \(K \times p = 2 \times 3\). At the start the numbers are random; these are made-up numbers for practice. In the table, each column belongs to one word, and the two cells in it are that word’s two numbers.

\(W^1\) column for cat column for dog column for car
number 1 0.9 0.8 0.1
number 2 0.2 0.3 0.9

Now feed in “dog” as the one-hot vector (0, 1, 0). Multiplying a grid by a list (matrix multiplication) works like this: for each row of the grid, multiply its numbers by the list’s numbers one pair at a time, and add up.

  • Row “number 1”: 0.9 × 0 + 0.8 × 1 + 0.1 × 0 = 0.8.
  • Row “number 2”: 0.2 × 0 + 0.3 × 1 + 0.9 × 0 = 0.3.

In maths writing (\(x_{\text{dog}}\) is dog’s one-hot vector written as a column, and \(h^1\) is the result of the first layer):

\[W^1 = \begin{pmatrix} 0.9 & 0.8 & 0.1 \\ 0.2 & 0.3 & 0.9 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad x_{\text{dog}} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad h^1 = W^1 x_{\text{dog}} = \begin{pmatrix} 0.8 \\ 0.3 \end{pmatrix}\]

The result, (0.8, 0.3), is exactly the dog column. The 1 sits in dog’s slot, so it keeps dog’s column. The 0s wipe out the cat and car columns. That column is dog’s embedding. There’s no squashing rule and no extra added amount (bias) in this layer, so nothing changes it.

With these numbers, cat (0.9, 0.2) and dog (0.8, 0.3) point almost the same way: their cosine is 0.99. Cat and car (0.1, 0.9) do not: their cosine is 0.32. Similar words, similar embeddings. (Both cosines are worked out with the same three steps as in Step 2.)

After the first layer. The second grid, \(W^2\), turns dog’s column into one score per word in the vocabulary. Softmax turns those scores into chances of being a neighbour. The computer does all of this, over millions of pairs; you never do it by hand. If “water” is a real neighbour but got a low chance, the dials (including dog’s column in \(W^1\)) get nudged so it gets a higher chance next time.

Negative sampling in one number. With negative sampling, the network instead looks at the dot product of the target word’s vector and the neighbour’s vector, and turns it into a “real pair” chance with the sigmoid. A real pair with dot product 2 gets the chance 1 / (1 + \(e^{-2}\)) = 0.88 (computer check). Here \(e\) is a fixed number, about 2.718, and \(e^{-2}\) ≈ 0.135. Training pushes real pairs’ dot products up and fake pairs’ dot products down.

Step 7: King − Man + Woman. The lecture’s toy example puts four words on a flat 2-number map: Queen (0.4, 0.9), King (0.5, 0.7), Woman (0.4, 0.3), Man (0.5, 0.1). The first number is how far right the spot is (x), the second how far up (y).

First subtract Man’s two numbers from King’s, one at a time:

\[\text{King} - \text{Man} = (0.5 - 0.5,\; 0.7 - 0.1) = (0.0,\; 0.6)\]

Then add Woman’s numbers to that result, one at a time:

\[(0.0,\; 0.6) + \text{Woman} = (0.0 + 0.4,\; 0.6 + 0.3) = (0.4,\; 0.9) = \text{Queen}\]

King − Man, (0.0, 0.6), is a “royalty” direction: the dashed arrow in the picture. Add it to Woman and you land on Queen. On real data the result is not exactly Queen, but it has “high cosine similarity with Queen”. In this toy example the cosine similarity of the result with Queen is exactly 1.

What it’s good at, and where it breaks.

  • Good: it learns “similar meaning” from raw text alone, with no dictionary. The spots are short lists, so comparing words is quick.
  • Good: directions on the map can carry meaning: King − Man + Woman lands near Queen.
  • Breaks: every word gets one spot, whatever the sentence. “Bank” the river and “bank” the money share a single spot (static embeddings). Newer models like BERT fix this.
  • Breaks: it needs a lot of text. On a small corpus the word arithmetic can fail, and PMI over-rewards rare pairs like apricot–pinch.

The formula, explained

1. PMI. The slides first give an informal version. \(P(\ldots)\) means “the probability of”:

\[\text{PMI}(word_1, word_2) = \log\left(\frac{P(word_1, word_2)}{P(word_1)P(word_2)}\right)\]

  • \(P(word_1, word_2)\) = how often the two words really appear together, as a share.
  • \(P(word_1)P(word_2)\) = how often they would appear together by luck: one word’s share times the other’s.
  • \(\log\) = the log, which turns “more than luck” into a positive number and “less than luck” into a negative one.

The slides then give the formal set. One warning first: the slides use the letter \(p\) for two things. Plain \(p\) is the vocabulary size. \(p\) with small letters below it (\(p_{i,j}\), \(p_i\), \(p_j\)) is a probability.

\[Co_{i,j} = \#pair(i, j \mid b), \qquad p_{i,j} = \frac{Co_{i,j}}{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{p} Co_{i,j}}, \qquad p_i = \frac{\sum_{j=1}^{p} Co_{i,j}}{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{p} Co_{i,j}}, \quad p_j = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{p} Co_{i,j}}{\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{p} Co_{i,j}}\]

\[M_{i,j} = \log_2\left(\frac{p_{i,j}}{p_i p_j}\right), \qquad \tilde{M}_{i,j} = \max\left(\log_2\left(\frac{p_{i,j}}{p_i p_j}\right), 0\right)\]

  • \(p\) = the number of words in the vocabulary, so the table is \(p \times p\).
  • \(i\) = the row = the target word; \(j\) = the column = the context word \(c_j\).
  • \(b\) = the window size (how many words either side count as “together”).
  • \(Co_{i,j}\) = the count of times \(i\) and \(j\) appear within \(b\) words of each other. \(\#pair(i, j \mid b)\) reads “the number of pairs of \(i\) and \(j\), given window \(b\)”.
  • \(\sum\) (the Greek capital “sigma”) = “add all of these up”. \(\sum_{j=1}^{p}\) means “add over all \(p\) columns”. Two of them, \(\sum_{i=1}^{p}\sum_{j=1}^{p}\), means “add every cell in the table”: the grand total (19 in the example).
  • \(p_{i,j}\) = a cell divided by the grand total: the joint probability (“skipgram probability”).
  • \(p_i\), \(p_j\) = a row total or a column total divided by the grand total: how common each word is on its own (“unigram probability”).
  • \(p_i p_j\) = how often they would meet if they were unrelated.
  • \(M_{i,j}\) = PMI. \(\tilde{M}_{i,j}\) (M with a wavy line on top) = PPMI, negatives replaced by 0.

Read aloud: “PMI is the log of how often two words actually appear together, divided by how often they would appear together by pure chance.” Above 0 = they attract; below 0 = they avoid each other.

A difference between course files: the informal slide writes plain “log”, the formal slide uses \(\log_2\), and the course notebook code uses the natural log (written ln: the log that uses the fixed number \(e\) ≈ 2.718 instead of 2). In the exam, write the \(\log_2\) version (the lecture’s example numbers use it). Changing the log base only rescales the scores and never changes the sign [Not in course files — general knowledge].

Will the exam expect you to write this? 2025 asked you to describe the PMI matrix. Writing \(\log_2\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i p_j}\) and explaining it, as the model answer does, earns full marks. A small PMI sum, like the ones in the walk-through, is a likely new question.

2. Truncated SVD on M. The small labels below each letter give its size, rows × columns.

\[\underbrace{M}_{p\times p} \approx \underbrace{U}_{p\times K}\;\underbrace{S}_{K\times K}\;\underbrace{V'}_{K\times p}\]

  • \(M\) = the PMI table, \(p\) rows by \(p\) columns.
  • \(\approx\) = “is approximately equal to”.
  • \(K\) = the number of patterns (dimensions) kept, much smaller than \(p\).
  • \(U\) = one row per word, \(K\) numbers each = the word embeddings (the usual choice).
  • \(S\) and \(V'\) = the other two pieces. The slides call \(US\) (U times S) the “Factors” and \(V'\) the “Loadings”.

Read aloud: “Approximate the huge word-by-word PMI table by three thin matrices, and use each word’s row of U as its short, dense vector.” You only need to understand this; the computer does the SVD.

3. The word2vec layers.

\[\underbrace{h^1_t}_{K\times 1} = \underbrace{W^1}_{K\times p}\;\underbrace{x_t}_{p\times 1}, \qquad \underbrace{h^2_t}_{p\times 1} = \underbrace{W^2}_{p\times K}\;\underbrace{h^1_t}_{K\times 1}, \qquad \underbrace{y_t}_{p\times 1} = \text{softmax}(h^2_t)\]

  • \(t\) = one row of the training data (one target–context pair).
  • \(x_t\) = the one-hot vector of the target word, \(p\) numbers long: “a selection vector”.
  • \(W^1\) = the target embedding matrix, \(K\) rows by \(p\) columns (“our ultimate goal”).
  • \(h^1_t\) = the selected word’s embedding, \(K\) numbers. (The raised 1 and 2 are labels for “layer 1” and “layer 2”, not powers.)
  • \(W^2\) = the context embedding matrix; \(h^2_t\) = a score for every word in the vocabulary.
  • \(y_t\) = the chance of each word being a context word.
  • There is no squashing rule (activation) on the hidden layer and no bias terms. A typical \(K\) is 300. Training goes over the data many times; each pass is one epoch.

Read aloud: “The one-hot vector picks the word’s column out of \(W^1\), \(W^2\) turns that column into a score for every word, and softmax turns the scores into chances of being a neighbour.”

4. Negative sampling. The softmax over all \(p\) words is “computationally expensive since p is large”. So we add fake pairs with outcome 0, typically 2–5 negatives per real pair. The fake words are drawn at random with this rule:

\[P_\alpha(w) = \frac{count(w)^\alpha}{\sum count(w')^\alpha}, \qquad \alpha = 0.75\]

  • \(count(w)\) = how often word \(w\) appears in the text.
  • \(\alpha\) (Greek “alpha”) = 0.75, a power applied to each count. It gives rarer words a slightly better chance of being picked [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • The bottom part adds the same thing up over all words \(w'\), so the chances add to 1.

Similarity is the dot product \(\vec{w}^{\,t} \cdot \vec{w}^{\,c}\) of the target word’s vector (\(t\)) and the context word’s vector (\(c\)). The slides call it “the un-normalized cosine”: a cosine without dividing by the two arrow lengths. The sigmoid turns it into a chance that the pair is real, which is a logistic regression:

\[P(true \mid x) = \frac{1}{1 + e^{-\vec{w}^{\,t} \cdot \vec{w}^{\,c}}}, \qquad L(\theta) = \log\left(\frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}\right) + \log\left(\frac{1}{1+e^{nx}}\right)\]

  • \(P(true \mid x)\) = the chance that the pair is real, given its dot product.
  • \(x\) = the dot product of the target with a real context word; \(nx\) = the dot product with a negative (random) word.
  • \(\theta\) (Greek “theta”) = all the dials being learned. \(L(\theta)\) = the score training tries to make as big as possible.
  • Maximise \(L\): make real pairs’ dot products big and negative pairs’ dot products small.

Example: a real pair with dot product 2 gets \(P(true) = 1/(1+e^{-2}) = 0.88\). You only need to understand these lines, not write them.

5. Cosine similarity.

\[\cos = \frac{a \cdot b}{\lVert a \rVert\,\lVert b \rVert}\]

  • \(a\), \(b\) = the two word vectors.
  • \(a \cdot b\) = their dot product (multiply matching numbers, add up).
  • \(\lVert a \rVert\) = the length (norm) of \(a\): square each number, add, take the square root.

Read aloud: “The dot product of the two arrows, divided by their two lengths: the cosine of the angle between them.” Small angle → close to 1 → similar. It depends on direction, not length. In Step 2 this gave cat–dog = 0.5.

Reading the course code

The exam has not asked students to write code; this is so you recognise the steps. The course notebook builds embeddings by counting, in its own words: “sentence-word matrix -> co-occurrence -> (PMI) -> SVD”.

X = vec.fit_transform(sentences)                  # rows: sentences, columns: words (binary)
C = (X.T @ X).toarray().astype(float)             # C[i, j]: sentences with word i AND j
expected = np.outer(freq, freq) / X.shape[0]      # co-occurrence if words were random
M = np.clip(np.log(C / expected), 0, None)        # PMI, keep only positive surprise = PPMI
vectors = TruncatedSVD(n_components=n_dims).fit_transform(M)

(Lines lightly shortened from the notebook.)

  • Line 1: build a table with one row per sentence and one column per word. Each cell is binary: 1 if the word is in the sentence, 0 if not (not “how many times”). Stop words are removed, and words appearing in too few sentences are dropped with a setting called min_df.
  • Line 2: co-occurrence = how many sentences contain both words. The window here is the whole sentence, not ±b words as on the slides. (Here the code reuses the letter C for this word-by-word table.)
  • Line 3: the count you would expect by luck (the same idea as \(p_i p_j\)).
  • Line 4: log of real ÷ expected = PMI, then clip negatives to 0 = PPMI. np.log is the natural log.
  • Line 5: truncated SVD keeps n_dims numbers per word: the embeddings. A function called cosine_similarity then finds nearest neighbours.

word2vec is trained with gensim, a Python package: Word2Vec(..., vector_size=100, window=5, min_count=10) (100 numbers per word, a window of 5, words appearing fewer than 10 times dropped) and w2v.wv.most_similar(positive=["king","woman"], negative=["man"]) (King − Man + Woman, then list the nearest words). The notebook does not set sg, so gensim uses CBOW by default [Not in course files — general knowledge]. No outputs are saved, so the notebook does not show the answers. Its takeaways say:

  • PMI does for embeddings what tf-idf (an earlier re-weighting of the word-count table that turns down words found in almost every document) did for documents: it removes the “frequent word” noise. Raw counts make common words everybody’s neighbour.
  • You need enough SVD dimensions to hold the structure.
  • Meaning drifts over time: “union meant the Constitution in 1850 and the Soviet Union in 1980” (222 State of the Union speeches, 1791–2018).
  • “Word arithmetic works only for relations the corpus actually contains.” On a small corpus, king − man + woman may fail. That is a point for using pre-trained embeddings (learned by someone else from a huge amount of text) instead of training on your own small business corpus.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

In 2025 this was a whole block worth 15 points.

Q3(a) (5 points): “What is the underlying assumption … and the PMI matrix?”

Model answer “Word embeddings rest on the distributional hypothesis, ‘You shall know a word by the company it keeps’ (Firth 1957): words used in similar contexts have similar meanings, so meaning can be learned from co-occurrence. The PMI matrix is a \(p \times p\) matrix (\(p\) = vocabulary size) with words in rows and context words in columns. Each cell is \(\log_2\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i p_j}\): how much more often word \(i\) appears within \(b\) words of word \(j\) than it would by chance. Negative values are set to 0 (PPMI). The matrix is large and sparse, so we apply truncated SVD and use the rows of \(U\) as dense, \(K\)-dimensional word embeddings.”

What this answer is saying, in plain words: The big idea is that words keeping similar company have similar meanings, so you can learn meaning by seeing which words appear near each other. The PMI table has one row and one column per word. Each cell compares how often two words really meet nearby with how often they’d meet by luck, as in the walk-through’s apricot–pinch row. Negative scores are set to 0, and the huge, mostly-empty table is then squeezed with SVD so each word ends up with a short list of \(K\) numbers: its spot on the map.

Q3(b) (2.5 points), in two sentences at most: how word2vec and BERT embeddings differ.

Model answer “word2vec gives each word one fixed (static) embedding whatever the sentence, so ‘apple’ the fruit and ‘Apple’ the computer company share the same vector. BERT produces context-specific embeddings, so ‘apple’ gets a different vector in ‘I ate an apple’ than in ‘Apple released a new laptop’.”

(The apple example is the one in the 2025 evaluation guideline. “Bank” as river bank vs money bank works the same way [Not in course files — general knowledge].)

What this answer is saying, in plain words: word2vec hands each word one map spot that never changes, so “apple” the fruit and “Apple” the company get the same spot. BERT works out a fresh spot for the word each time, based on the sentence around it.

Q3(c) (2.5 points): what a one-hot vector is, and how word2vec’s first layer uses it.

Model answer “A one-hot vector is a \(p \times 1\) vector of zeros with a single 1 at the word’s position in the vocabulary. In word2vec the target word enters as a one-hot vector \(x_t\). The first layer computes \(h^1_t = W^1 x_t\) with no activation and no bias, so \(x_t\) just selects the column of \(W^1\) belonging to that word: a ‘selection vector’. That column is the word’s \(K\)-dimensional embedding, and \(W^1\) (the target embedding matrix) is what word2vec learns.”

What this answer is saying, in plain words: A one-hot vector is a list as long as the word list, all 0s except a 1 in the word’s slot. word2vec feeds the word in this way. Multiplying it by the first grid of dials (\(W^1\)), with no squashing and no extra nudge, picks out that word’s own column, as with dog’s (0.8, 0.3) in Step 6. That column, \(K\) numbers long, is the word’s spot on the map, and learning that grid is the whole point of word2vec.

Q3(d) (5 points): draw two arrows with high cosine similarity and two with low cosine similarity. How to answer: cosine similarity depends only on the angle between two arrows, not their length. For “high”, draw two arrows from the same starting point that point almost the same way (a small angle; cosine close to 1). For “low”, draw two arrows with a big angle between them, for example a right angle (cosine 0). Label which pair is which and say that the angle, not the length, decides.

2025 True/False: an item on SVD on the PMI matrix. Squeezing the PMI table with SVD is a course method for making word embeddings, so the statement “Word embeddings can be obtained by applying SVD to a PMI matrix” is True (see self-test item 1).

Likely new questions: CBOW vs Skipgram (guess the middle word from its neighbours, or the neighbours from the middle word), negative sampling (training against a few random fake neighbours), PPMI and rare words, King − Man + Woman (word arithmetic), a small PMI sum, and an example of how researchers use embeddings. For that last one, the course gives these examples:

  • Kozlowski et al. (2019), “The geometry of culture”: word embeddings trained on US text for each decade of the 20th century. They measure the cosine similarity between a “class” direction and five cultural directions (beautiful–ugly, educated–uneducated, employed–unemployed, graceful–awkward, fine–coarse). Roughly read from the chart: the looks and manners directions (graceful, fine) fall, while education and employment rise. The meaning of class shifts over time.
  • Labonne & Thorsrud (2023), “Risky news and credit market sentiment”: they define each concept as a sum of word vectors, \(gr_t = recession_t + risk_t\) and \(fc_t = credit_t + leverage_t + funding_t\) (the small \(t\) means “in month \(t\)”). Each month they compute the cosine between the two, \(RNI_t = \frac{gr_t \cdot fc_t}{\lVert gr_t \rVert \, \lVert fc_t \rVert}\). A small angle (vectors pointing the same way) = high RNI; a near right angle = low RNI.
  • Kapfhammer, Larsen & Thorsrud (2020): a “transition risk for Norway” index built with word embeddings, moving with climate-policy events (EU ETS, Paris agreement).
  • Alternatives named on the slides: GloVe; Doc2vec (for whole documents, “an alternative to LDA”, the earlier topic-model method); Word Mover’s Distance.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • For Q3(a): the assumption by name and quote: the distributional hypothesis, “You shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth 1957), meaning words used in similar contexts have similar meanings.
  • The PMI table’s shape: \(p \times p\), words in rows and context words in columns (\(p\) = number of words in the vocabulary).
  • What one cell is: \(\log_2\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i p_j}\), how much more often word \(i\) appears within \(b\) words of word \(j\) than by luck.
  • Negatives set to 0 (PPMI), then truncated SVD on the large, sparse table, with the rows of \(U\) as short, dense, \(K\)-number word embeddings.
  • For Q3(b): static (one fixed vector per word, word2vec) vs context-specific (a new vector in each sentence, BERT), with the apple example, in two sentences at most.
  • For Q3(c): one-hot = \(p \times 1\), all zeros, a single 1 at the word’s position; \(h^1_t = W^1 x_t\) with no activation and no bias selects that word’s column of \(W^1\) (a selection vector); that column is the word’s \(K\)-number embedding, and \(W^1\) is what word2vec learns.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Saying Skipgram guesses the word from its neighbours (its context). That is CBOW. Skipgram goes the other way: it guesses the neighbours from the word.
  • Saying PMI favours common words. It over-rewards rare ones: a rare pair that meets once or twice can get a huge score.
  • Calling the PMI table \(n \times p\) (documents × words, like the word-count table). It is \(p \times p\): words in the rows and words in the columns.
  • Saying word2vec gives a word different spots in different sentences. It gives one fixed spot.
  • Writing three sentences when the question says “max two”.
  • Saying the neural-network maps always beat the counting-plus-SVD maps. Levy et al. (2015) found they might not.
  • Calling word embeddings supervised (learned from human-made labels). They are self-supervised or unsupervised: the text supplies its own answers.

Key terms to use

  • distributional hypothesis (similar company means similar meaning)
  • Firth (1957) (“know a word by its company”)
  • embedding is location (a word’s meaning = its map spot)
  • co-occurrence (two words appearing near each other)
  • window size \(b\) (how many words either side count)
  • \(p \times p\) matrix (words in rows, words in columns)
  • PMI (how much more than chance two words meet)
  • PPMI (PMI with negative scores set to 0)
  • add-one smoothing (add a pretend 1 to every count)
  • large and sparse (huge table, mostly zeros)
  • truncated SVD (squeeze the table to K strongest patterns)
  • matrix \(U\) (SVD output; its rows are word vectors)
  • dense vectors (short lists with few zeros)
  • cosine similarity (angle between two word arrows)
  • word2vec (neural network that learns map spots by guessing)
  • CBOW (guess the middle word from neighbours)
  • Skipgram (guess the neighbours from the middle word)
  • self-supervised (the text supplies its own answers)
  • one-hot / selection vector (all 0s, one 1; picks a column)
  • target embedding matrix \(W^1\) (grid holding each word’s map spot)
  • context embedding matrix \(W^2\) (grid scoring words as possible neighbours)
  • \(K = 300\) (each word gets 300 numbers)
  • negative sampling (train against a few random fake neighbours)
  • static vs contextual (context-specific) embeddings (one fixed spot vs a new spot per sentence)
  • BERT (model giving context-specific spots)
  • transformer (the network design behind BERT and chatbots)

Quick self-test

  1. T/F: “Word embeddings can be obtained by applying SVD to a PMI matrix.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Word embeddings are each word’s short list of numbers, its spot on the meaning map. The PMI matrix is the big words-by-words table that scores how much more often two words meet than by chance. SVD is a way to squeeze a big table down to its few strongest patterns. Can you get the word spots by squeezing that table?

    True. Why: That is one of the two course methods (the other is word2vec). The table is huge and mostly zeros; squeezing it keeps the main patterns and gives each word a short list of numbers. It’s like summing up a long survey with a few key scores per person. The slide says: “Use the SVD … not on C, but on M!”.

  2. T/F: “Skipgram predicts a word from its surrounding words.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Skipgram is one of word2vec’s two guessing games. Surrounding words are the neighbours within the window. Does Skipgram guess the middle word from its neighbours?

    False. Why: That’s the other game, CBOW. Skipgram goes the other way: it sees the middle word and guesses its neighbours. Think of CBOW as a fill-in-the-blank exercise, and Skipgram as “here’s a word, which words would you expect around it?”.

  3. T/F: “PMI gives rare word pairs low weight, so add-one smoothing is not needed.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: PMI scores how much more often two words meet than by luck. Weight means how much a pair counts. Add-one smoothing means adding a pretend 1 to every count. Does PMI give rare pairs small scores, so no fix is needed?

    False. Why: It’s the opposite: PMI gives rare pairs big scores (“PMI gives rare words high weight”). “Apricot” appears only twice, yet apricot–pinch gets the top score in the table, 2.25. One lucky meeting looks hugely “more than chance”. It’s like a café regular you’ve seen once with a stranger: one sighting and you’d wrongly guess they’re best friends. Adding a pretend 1 to every count calms that down.

  4. T/F: “In word2vec, the word ‘bank’ gets the same embedding in ‘river bank’ and ‘bank loan’.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: An embedding is the word’s spot on the meaning map. “Bank” means a riverside in one phrase and a money business in the other. Does word2vec give it one spot for both?

    True. Why: word2vec hands each word one fixed spot, whatever sentence it’s in. It’s like a phone contact list with only one entry for two different people named “Sam”. Models such as BERT fix this by giving a new spot in each sentence.

  5. Calculate: “With the slide-12 counts, compute PMI(digital, computer).”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Use the lecture’s small count table (Table 1 in the walk-through, 19 counts in total) to work out how much more often “digital” and “computer” meet than they would by luck.

    Answer: \(p_{ij} = 2/19\), \(p_i = 4/19\), \(p_j = 3/19\); ratio \(= \frac{2/19}{(4/19)(3/19)} = 38/12 = 3.17\); \(\log_2 3.17 = 1.66\) (matches the slide).

    Why: The pair met 2 times out of 19 (that’s \(p_{ij}\)). “Digital” makes up 4 of the 19 counts (\(p_i\)) and “computer” 3 of the 19 (\(p_j\)). By luck you’d expect them to meet (4/19) × (3/19) of the time. They really met about 3.17 times as often as that. The log base 2 asks “2 to what power gives 3.17?”, and the answer is 1.66. Above 0 means “more than luck”.

  6. Explain (2–5 sentences): “Why does negative sampling make word2vec practical?”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Negative sampling is the shortcut of mixing each real neighbour pair with a few random fake pairs. Why does that make training fast enough to use?

    Answer: In plain word2vec the softmax output must be computed over the whole vocabulary for every training pair, which is expensive because \(p\) is large. Negative sampling instead adds a few (2–5) random “negative” word pairs with outcome 0 for every real pair, drawn by word frequency raised to 0.75. The model then only has to tell real context words from these fakes, a logistic-regression (sigmoid) task on the dot product of the two word vectors. It pushes real pairs’ vectors together and negative pairs’ vectors apart (L6 slides 23–25).

    Why: Without the trick, word2vec must score every word in the whole word list for each example, which is very slow because the list is huge. With the trick, each real neighbour pair is matched with 2 to 5 random fake pairs, and the model only has to say “real or fake?”. It’s a yes/no question, like spotting the one real photo among a few fakes, instead of ranking every photo in the world. Real pairs get pulled closer on the map, and fake pairs get pushed apart.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • bag-of-words / document-term matrix (C): the word-count table: one row per document, one column per word, each cell a count. Word order is thrown away. “dog dog car” gives dog = 2, car = 1.
  • word embedding: a word’s spot on the meaning map: a short list of numbers. Similar words get nearby spots.
  • “embedding is location”: the slides’ slogan: an embedding is a position in space.
  • vector: a list of numbers, like (0.4, 0.9). You can draw it as an arrow from the centre of a map to that point.
  • vector space: the “map” where all these arrows live.
  • dimension: how many numbers each vector has. 2 dimensions = a flat map; 300 dimensions = a map you can’t draw but a computer can handle.
  • dense vs sparse: dense = most numbers are not zero; sparse = almost everything is zero, like a huge spreadsheet with a few filled cells.
  • corpus: the whole collection of text you learn from, like our three sentences.
  • distributional hypothesis: the idea that words used in similar surroundings have similar meanings. “You shall know a word by the company it keeps” (Firth 1957).
  • target word / context word: the target is the word we’re looking at; context words are its neighbours in the window.
  • window (b): how far left and right we look for neighbours. b = 4 means 4 words on each side.
  • co-occurrence: two words appearing near each other.
  • co-occurrence matrix (Co): a word-by-word table counting how often each pair appears together. Rows = target words, columns = context words.
  • \(p \times p\): “p rows by p columns”, where p is the number of words in the vocabulary. Words × words, not documents × words.
  • vocabulary (p): the list of all distinct words the model knows.
  • probability (chance): a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely something is.
  • joint probability (\(p_{ij}\)) / skipgram probability: the share of all pairs that are this exact pair. Information-with-data: 6/19 = 0.32.
  • unigram probability (\(p_i\), \(p_j\)): how common one word is on its own, as a share of the total. Information: 11/19 = 0.58.
  • PMI (pointwise mutual information): the log of “how often two words really appear together” ÷ “how often they would by pure chance”. Above 0 = they attract; below 0 = they avoid each other. Apricot–pinch: 2.25.
  • PPMI (positive PMI): PMI with every negative number replaced by 0. Digital–data: −0.56 becomes 0.
  • log, \(\log_2\), ln: the reverse of a power. \(\log_2 8 = 3\) because 2 × 2 × 2 = 8. ln does the same with the number e (about 2.718). The log of a number above 1 is positive, below 1 negative.
  • max(…, 0): “take whichever is bigger, the number or 0”. It turns negatives into 0.
  • sum (Σ): “add all of these up”.
  • add-one smoothing: add 1 to every count, so rare pairs don’t get extreme scores and zeros disappear.
  • SVD (singular value decomposition): a maths tool that breaks a big table into three smaller tables (U, S, V′) that multiply back to it. Like summarising a long survey by its few main themes.
  • truncated SVD: keeping only the K strongest themes and throwing the rest away, so each word ends up with K numbers.
  • U, S, V′, factors, loadings: the three pieces of SVD. Each word’s row of U is its embedding. “Factors” (US) and “loadings” (V′) are the slides’ names for these pieces.
  • K: the number of dimensions you keep, for example 100 or 300.
  • matrix: a grid of numbers with rows and columns, like a spreadsheet.
  • matrix multiplication: combining a grid with a list: for each row of the grid, multiply matching numbers and add up. A one-hot list picks out one column.
  • LSA: the earlier course method that runs SVD on the document-term matrix C. Here the same tool runs on the PMI matrix M.
  • tf-idf: the earlier re-weighting of the word-count table that turns down words appearing in almost every document. PMI plays a similar role here.
  • stop words: very common words like “the” and “and” that are usually removed.
  • binary: only 0 or 1: “is the word there or not”, not “how many times”.
  • cosine similarity: a score from −1 to 1 for how closely two arrows point the same way. With plain counts (never negative) it stays between 0 and 1. Small angle → close to 1 → similar. It ignores how long the arrows are. Cat–dog in our toy table: 0.5.
  • dot product: multiply two vectors’ numbers in matching positions and add up. Big when the arrows point the same way and are long.
  • length / norm (\(\lVert a \rVert\)): how long an arrow is: square each number, add, take the square root.
  • angle: how far apart two arrows point. 0° = same direction; 90° = unrelated.
  • nearest neighbours (most_similar): the words whose spots are closest to a given word.
  • vector arithmetic: adding and subtracting word vectors number by number, as in King − Man + Woman ≈ Queen.
  • neural network: a machine of many small dials that learns by nudging them after each wrong guess.
  • shallow / two-layered / feed-forward: a small network with one hidden layer, where numbers flow one way from input to output.
  • word2vec: a small neural network that learns word embeddings by playing the “guess the neighbours” game (Mikolov et al. 2013).
  • CBOW (continuous bag of words): the word2vec version that guesses the middle word from its neighbours. Like a fill-in-the-blank exercise. (The long name is [Not in course files — general knowledge].)
  • Skipgram: the opposite version: from the middle word, guess the neighbours. From “the cat drinks milk”: (cat, drinks), (cat, milk).
  • supervised / unsupervised / self-supervised: supervised = a human gives the right answers; unsupervised = no answers at all; self-supervised = the text itself provides the answers (the real neighbours).
  • one-hot vector / selection vector: a list as long as the vocabulary, all 0s except a single 1 at the word’s slot. Multiplying it by a grid picks out that word’s column. With cat, dog, car: dog = (0, 1, 0).
  • target embedding matrix (\(W^1\)): the grid of dials holding one column per word. After training, those columns are the embeddings.
  • context embedding matrix (\(W^2\)): the second grid, used to score every word as a possible neighbour.
  • hidden layer (\(h^1\)): the middle step of the network. In word2vec it’s the chosen word’s embedding.
  • activation / bias: a squashing rule applied after a sum / a fixed amount added on. word2vec’s first layer has neither.
  • softmax: turns a list of scores into chances that are all positive and add up to 1.
  • sigmoid: squeezes any number into a chance between 0 and 1. Dot product 2 gives 0.88.
  • logistic regression: a classic method that turns a score into a yes/no chance with the sigmoid.
  • epoch: one full pass through all the training data.
  • negative sampling: a shortcut for word2vec. Instead of scoring every word in the vocabulary, mix each real pair with 2–5 fake pairs made of random words, and train the network to tell real from fake.
  • α = 0.75: a power applied to word counts when picking the fake words. It gives rarer words a slightly better chance of being picked [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • static vs contextual (context-specific) embeddings: static = one fixed spot per word in every sentence (word2vec); contextual = the spot changes with the sentence (BERT).
  • BERT / transformer: newer, bigger language models (2017/2018) that give each word a spot depending on its sentence. The transformer is the network design behind them.
  • pre-trained embeddings: embeddings someone already learned from a huge amount of text, which you can reuse instead of training on your own small corpus.
  • gensim: the Python package the notebook uses to train word2vec.
  • min_df: a setting that drops words appearing in too few sentences.
  • GloVe, Doc2vec, Word Mover’s Distance: alternatives on the slides: GloVe is another way to learn word embeddings; Doc2vec gives whole documents embeddings; Word Mover’s Distance compares documents using word embeddings [Not in course files — general knowledge].
