  • LDA: the topic-model method from an earlier course chapter; the slides call Doc2vec an alternative to it.

Sources: Lecture 6 “Neural Networks and Word Embeddings” (Thorsrud), slides 2–14, 20–31 (incl. 3–14, 20–31 for definitions, worked PMI example on slide 12, SVD on slide 13, word2vec layers 21–22, negative sampling 23–25, static vs contextual 27, applications 26–31); notebook GRA4164_Interactive_3_Embeddings_and_llms.ipynb (cells 0–27, incl. cells 0, 4, 16, 18); 2025 exam evaluation guideline (Q3).

Part IV — Large Language Models and the Transformer

14. What a Large Language Model is

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 T/F (b) and (f) came straight from this lecture, and it is the base for all of Block 4. (T/F = the exam’s true/false statements, worth 2 points each. Block 4 = the 25-point exam section on Transformers and LLMs.)

Why this exists

You type “What is the capital of Norway?” into ChatGPT. A second later it writes “The capital of Norway is Oslo.”

Nobody wrote that answer in advance. The program is not looking it up in an atlas either. So how can a computer write a fresh, sensible answer to almost any question?

The answer is a program that has read a huge amount of text and learned which bits of text tend to come next. That kind of program is called a Large Language Model, or LLM for short. ChatGPT is a product built on one [Not in course files — general knowledge].

Companies care because an LLM can write, summarise, translate and answer questions. But it also makes mistakes, and it costs money to run. To use one well, you need to know what it is, how it learns, and what it can and cannot “remember”. That is this chapter.

The idea in everyday words

Step 1: it is a guessing machine.

An LLM does one thing, over and over. You give it some text. It guesses the next small bit of text. It adds that bit to the end. Then it guesses again, with the slightly longer text. It stops when the answer is finished.

Think of the word suggestions on your phone keyboard. You type “See you”, and it suggests “tomorrow”. An LLM is that idea, made enormous and very good.

Step 2: the text is cut into pieces, and each piece gets a number.

Computers can only work with numbers, not letters. So before anything else, a tool cuts your text into small pieces. A piece can be a whole word, part of a word, a space or a punctuation mark. Each piece is called a token. The tool that does the cutting is called a tokenizer.

Every token has an ID number, like a barcode in a shop. That number is its token ID. The fixed list of all tokens the model knows is its vocabulary. Think of it as the full box of LEGO pieces the model is allowed to build with.

A token is not always a word. The word “strawberry”, for example, is three tokens: st | raw | berry.

Step 3: the guess is a set of chances.

The model does not pick one word with total certainty. It gives every token in its vocabulary a chance of being next. A chance like this is called a probability. It runs from 0% (impossible) to 100% (certain). All the chances together add up to 100%.

Step 4: inside, it is billions of adjustable knobs.

Picture a giant mixing desk with billions of tiny volume knobs. Each knob is one number. The positions of all the knobs decide which guesses come out. Each of these adjustable numbers is called a parameter, or a weight. Here, the two words mean the same thing.

A set of numbers plus rules that turns an input into an output is called a model. Think of a recipe that turns ingredients into a dish. A model for language, with billions of weights, is a Large Language Model (LLM).

Step 5: it learns by playing “guess the next piece”.

At the start, the knobs are set at random, so the guesses are rubbish. Setting the knobs well by showing the model lots of examples is called training.

The first and biggest training stage works like this. The model reads a stretch of text. The next token is hidden. The model guesses it. Then it checks the real token. The knobs are nudged a tiny bit, so the right token becomes a little more likely next time. This repeats billions of times, over books, websites, code and more. This stage is called pre-training.

Notice who supplies the right answers: the text itself. The real next token is already sitting in the text. Nobody has to mark anything by hand. Learning where the answers come for free from the data is called self-supervised learning.

Analogy Think of a student who learns a language by covering the next word in millions of books with a finger, guessing it, then lifting the finger to check. No teacher marks the answers; the book itself is the answer key. After years of this, the student’s “gut feeling” (the weights) is very good at guessing. When you later ask the student a question, they do not keep learning; they use that gut feeling. Handing them a document to read is like putting a sheet on their desk. Sending them on a training course changes their gut feeling.

Two other kinds of learning matter here, because the exam likes to mix them up:

  • Supervised learning: a person has written the right answer for each example. For example, emails already marked “spam” or “not spam”.
  • Unsupervised learning: there are no right answers at all. The computer only hunts for patterns. For example, sorting customers into groups that nobody named in advance.

Pre-training is neither of these. There is a right answer (the real next token), but no person wrote it. So the course’s word is self-supervised. Calling it “unsupervised” is wrong, and it was a 2025 exam trap.

One side effect: while learning patterns, the model can also store exact bits of its training text, including mistakes, and repeat them later. This is called memorization. The lecture says pre-training “can also memorize examples and errors.”

Step 6: more training turns a text-guesser into a helpful assistant.

After pre-training, the model is good at continuing text, but not yet good at following instructions. So more training stages follow. All the stages after pre-training together are called post-training. The lecture says post-training “develops instruction following, tool use, and reasoning capabilities.” (Tool use and reasoning are explained in Steps 10 and 11.)

The lecture lists the usual stages, in order. It calls them “common ingredients, not a fixed pipeline”, meaning not every model uses every stage:

  1. Pre-training: “Learn to predict tokens from large collections of text, code, and, for some models, other media.”
  2. Continued pre-training / mid-training (when used): “Add targeted data, for example long documents, domain material, or tool interactions.” “Domain material” means texts from one field, like law. “Tool interactions” means records of the model using outside programs (Step 10). In plain words: extra rounds of the same guessing game, on chosen text, to strengthen one skill.
  3. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): “Learn from examples of instructions and desired responses.” People write example questions with good answers, and the model learns from them. Like a new employee studying model answers. This is the supervised step, because humans wrote the answers. More generally, extra training on top of an existing model is called fine-tuning, and it changes the weights.
  4. Preference optimization / reinforcement learning: “Improve responses using preferences or rewards, including verifiable results such as passing code tests.”
    • Preference optimization means showing the model pairs of answers and which one people preferred, so it learns to give the preferred kind.
    • Reinforcement learning (RL) means learning from rewards, like a dog getting a treat for sitting.
    • A reward is a score for an answer. A verifiable result is one a computer can check, like “did the code pass its tests?”.

Step 7: when you use it, the knobs are frozen.

Using a finished model to produce answers is called inference, or answer time. During inference, the weights do not move at all. The program that runs the model on a computer is the inference software.

So the model does not learn from your chat. Training changes the weights. Answering uses fixed weights.

Now the lecture’s own definition makes sense. An LLM is “A learned set of parameters (weights), used with a tokenizer and inference software to generate language.” In plain words: a big pile of learned numbers, plus a tool that cuts text into pieces, plus a program that runs the numbers to write text.

Step 8: the design inside is called a Transformer.

The way the billions of numbers are arranged follows a blueprint. Almost all modern LLMs use the same blueprint, called the Transformer (Chapter 16 explains how it works inside). The lecture says: “Most generative LLMs use the Transformer architecture and predict the next token: a word, word fragment, or other symbol.” (“Generative” means it writes new text. “Architecture” means design.)

A few related words:

  • A layer is one stage of number-crunching. A model built from many layers stacked on top of each other is a deep neural network. “Deep” means many layers.
  • A hidden layer is any layer between the input and the output, so you never see it directly. The lecture says “Hidden layers learn representations of the input.”
  • A representation is the model’s internal list of numbers that sums up what a bit of text means, like a fingerprint of the meaning.
  • A Transformer block is one repeated unit of the Transformer. LLMs stack many of them.

Even in 2026, the core is unchanged. The lecture puts it plainly: “The basic mechanism is unchanged: a Transformer predicting the next token”. What has changed is the size, the training recipes and the software built around the model.

Step 9: everything it “sees” sits in one window.

While answering, the model can only use the text in front of it right now. That text is its context. The maximum amount it can see at once, counted in tokens, is its context window. Think of a desk: only the papers on the desk can be read.

The window holds all of these at once:

  • the system instructions: hidden instructions the app gives the model before your question, like “You are a polite helper”;
  • the conversation so far;
  • any uploaded or searched-for documents;
  • results from outside programs the model asked to run (called tools, see Step 10);
  • the answer being written.

The lecture says the window ranges “from a few thousand to about one million tokens, depending on the model”. It adds: “Everything the model uses at answer time must fit in the window; nothing else is ‘remembered’ unless the application re-inserts it.” Longer contexts cost more and are slower. A big window also “does not guarantee that every detail is used reliably”.

So there are two very different things you can change:

  • what is on the desk right now (the context), and
  • the gut feeling (the weights).

The lecture’s key line: “Uploading a document changes the context. Fine-tuning changes the weights.”

Step 10: adding outside knowledge without retraining.

Often you want the model to use your company’s own documents. There are three common add-ons:

  • Retrieval means searching a collection, say company reports, and fetching the relevant bits.
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means: first search for relevant text, then paste it into the context, so the model can use it. Like handing a student the right page before the question. The lecture: “RAG: add retrieved evidence to context.”
  • Tools are outside programs the model can ask to run, like a calculator, a web search or a database. The lecture: “Tools: run operations outside the model.”
  • An agent is a setup where the model repeats a loop of deciding, using tools and checking, until a task is done. The lecture: “Agents: repeat decisions and tool calls, with permissions and stopping conditions.” (Permissions = what it is allowed to do. Stopping conditions = when it must stop.)

RAG changes the desk, not the gut feeling. The lecture says it again: “Retrieval changes context; fine-tuning changes weights. Neither guarantees accuracy.”

Step 11: thinking longer before answering.

Many current models can write extra hidden working-out before their final answer. This is reasoning at answer time. The lecture says it can help hard tasks “but increases latency and resource use”. Latency means waiting time before the answer arrives. It also warns: “A longer answer or a persuasive explanation does not guarantee correctness.”

Step 12: making huge models cheaper to run.

  • Mixture-of-experts (MoE). The model is split into many “expert” parts, and only a few experts work on each token. The lecture: “only a subset of the parameters is activated for each token.” Think of a hospital where each patient sees two specialists, not all 200 doctors.
  • Quantization. Each weight is stored with fewer digits, so the model takes less computer memory (the space a computer has to hold numbers while it works). How many digits a number is stored with is its precision. The lecture: quantization “stores weights at lower precision, reducing memory needs.” Like rounding 3.14159 to 3.1.
  • Bigger is not always better. The lecture says more parameters “can increase capacity, but performance also depends on data quality, training, and the task,” and “the largest model is not always the best choice.” Smaller models can suit narrow tasks or running on your own machine.

Step 13: getting a model you can run yourself.

Some makers let anyone download the learned numbers. This is called open weights. The lecture: “downloadable model parameters; permissions depend on the license.” A license is the legal terms saying what you may do with something, like the rules in a rental contract. Open weights “do not necessarily include training data or the full training recipe.” So you get the numbers, not the texts the model learned from.

Where do you download them? The lecture slide shows the Hugging Face model hub (“The AI community building the future.”) and the model library of Ollama. A hub is a central meeting place, here a website. The course outline calls Huggingface “the AI community’s open-source hub for Machine Learning and Natural Language Processing”. (Machine Learning = computers learning patterns from data. Open-source = free for anyone to use and share. Natural Language Processing (NLP) = getting computers to work with human language.)

Step 14: four ways a business can use an LLM.

The lecture names four:

  1. Chat application: use it through a website or app, like the ChatGPT site.
  2. API integration: an API (application programming interface) is a doorway that lets your own program send text to the model and get answers back, with no chat window.
  3. Agent: the model loops through a task using tools (Step 10).
  4. Local deployment: run the model on your own computer or company servers instead of someone else’s.

The lecture: “The mode determines the cost structure, where data goes, and who is accountable for errors.”

What it is good at, and where it breaks.

  • Good at: writing, summarising, translating and answering common questions, because it has seen so much text of that kind.
  • Breaks: it writes what sounds likely, not what has been checked. So it can invent facts and references with total confidence. This is called hallucination (Chapter 17 covers it).
  • Breaks: it does not learn from your chat. Once something falls outside the context window, the model has no memory of it.
  • Breaks: it never sees letters or digits one by one, only tokens. So spelling and arithmetic can go wrong (Chapter 15 shows why).

Walk-through example

Example 1: writing one word.

The lecture uses this example. Its numbers are made up for illustration (the slide calls them “illustrative”), but they show the real process.

  1. You type three words: “This course is”.
  2. The tokenizer turns them into three ID numbers: 17, 42 and 9. One token per word here, each with its barcode number.
  3. The model looks at those three IDs. It gives a chance to every token in its vocabulary. Two tokens get most of the chance: “useful” gets 50% and “practical” gets 30%. All the other tokens share the remaining 20%.
  4. Check the sum in words: fifty plus thirty is eighty, plus twenty is one hundred. So all the chance has been handed out, as it must be.
  5. One token is picked. Say it picks “useful”, the most likely one. (Real systems often draw at random, weighted by these chances, so “practical” would sometimes win. [Not in course files — general knowledge])
  6. The text is now “This course is useful”, four tokens long. It goes back in at step 1, and the model guesses the fifth token.

Here is the same loop as a table. Each row is one step of the loop. The middle column says what happens. The right column shows the example’s value at that step.

Step What happens Example
1 Text goes in “This course is”
2 Tokenizer turns it into token IDs 17, 42, 9
3 Model turns IDs into numbers and computes next-token probabilities useful 50%, practical 30%, other tokens 20%
4 One token is selected and appended “This course is useful”
5 Go back to step 1 with the longer text —

Example 1b: the same sentence during training.

Now suppose the training text really says “This course is useful”. The model sees “This course is”. The next token is hidden. The model guesses, and gives “useful” 50%. Then it checks: the real next token is “useful”. So the knobs are nudged to make “useful” a bit more likely next time.

Nobody labelled anything. The sentence held its own answer. That is what self-supervised means.

Example 2: how much of an MoE model works per token.

The lecture gives one real model, DeepSeek-V4-Flash. Its numbers come from the model’s makers:

  • It has 284 billion weights in total.
  • It uses about 13 billion of them for each token. (It is a mixture-of-experts model, so only some experts work each time.)
  • It was pre-trained on more than 32 trillion tokens.

What share of the model works per token? Divide the part used by the total: 13 ÷ 284 = 0.0458. As a percentage, that is about 4.6%.

So for each token, roughly 95% of the model sits idle. That is the point of MoE: a huge model that is cheaper to run per token.

Example 3: does it change the desk, or the gut feeling?

In the table below, each row is something you might do with an LLM. The two columns ask which part of the system it changes: the context (what it reads right now) or the weights (what it learned). A “Yes” in a cell means that action changes that part.

Action Changes the context? Changes the weights?
Upload a PDF to a chat Yes No
RAG: search company reports and paste excerpts in Yes No
Fine-tune on 5,000 labelled support tickets No Yes
Chat with the model for an hour Yes (history is in the window) No (weights are fixed at answer time)

Read the last row slowly. An hour of chatting feels like the model “gets to know you”. But all that happens is that the chat history fills the desk. The weights never move.

Example 4: is this a good business use? (useful for the exam’s business-case question)

The lecture gives a five-point checklist for a good use case: Clear Task, Available Context, Verifiable Results, Manageable Errors, Business Value. In plain words: you know exactly what you want, the model can be given the information it needs, you can check its output, a mistake would not be a disaster, and it is worth the money.

It also gives a risk grid. It asks two questions about any task:

  • How bad is it if the model makes a mistake? (the rows: lower or higher)
  • How hard is it to check the model’s output? (the columns: easier or harder)

Each cell names one example task, and, in quotes, what the lecture says you should do about it.

Consequences of an error ↓ / Difficulty of checking → Easier to check Harder to check
Higher Extract invoice fields for payment — “Validate against original records” Authorize unusual payments — “Require human approval”
Lower Draft marketing copy — “Check before publishing” Summarize feedback — “Ambiguous responses: inspect examples”

Read one cell: top right. Approving unusual payments is costly if wrong, and hard to check. So a human must approve every one.

Reading the course code

This lecture has no code. The related course notebook (a file that mixes short pieces of code with their saved results) is Notebook 4, GRA4164_Interactive_4_A_real_LLM_on_your_laptop.ipynb. It downloads a small open-weight model from Hugging Face and runs it on your own laptop. So it is a live example of “local deployment” and “open weights” from Steps 13 and 14.

The exam has not asked students to write code.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025, true/false (f): “Large Language Models are estimated using unsupervised learning” (“estimated” means trained).

Model answer False.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: the right word is “self-supervised”. The text supplies its own answers: the real next token.

2025, true/false (b): “HuggingFace is a open source hub for Natural Language Processing”

Model answer True.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Hugging Face is a free website where people share AI models. The course outline calls it exactly that, and the lecture slide shows its model hub.

Likely new true/false items:

“RAG updates the model’s weights”

Model answer False.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: RAG looks up documents and pastes the useful bits into what the model reads. It changes only what the model reads, not what it has learned.

“An LLM updates its weights during each conversation”

Model answer False.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: the weights (the huge set of numbers the model learned in training) stay fixed while you chat.

“In an MoE model all parameters are used for every token”

Model answer False.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: a mixture-of-experts model is split into many “expert” parts, and only a few of them work on each token.

“Open weights always include the training data”

Model answer False.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: open weights means you can download the learned numbers, not the texts the model learned from.

“Bigger is always better”

Model answer False.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: more weights can help, but results also depend on data quality, training and the task. Smaller models can suit narrow tasks or running on your own machine.

Likely explain question (2–5 sentences): Why is LLM pre-training called self-supervised, and which training step is supervised?

Model answer In pre-training the model reads large amounts of text and, at each position, predicts the next token; the true next token in the text is the target, and future tokens are hidden from the prediction (Lecture 7, slide 7). Because the labels come from the text itself, no one has to label data by hand, so it is called self-supervised rather than supervised or unsupervised. The supervised step comes later: in supervised fine-tuning (SFT) the model learns from examples of instructions paired with desired responses written by people (slide 9).

What this answer is saying, in plain words: First, the model reads a huge amount of text and keeps guessing the next piece. The real next piece in the text is the right answer, so nobody has to write answers by hand; that is why it is called self-supervised. Later, people write example questions with good answers, and the model learns from those. That later step (SFT) is the supervised one.

In the business-case question (Block 5 of the exam): you can use the four ways to use an LLM (Step 14), the good-use-case checklist and the risk grid (Example 4) to explain where an LLM fits in a business case.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • When you describe how an LLM is trained, use the words “next token” (the next small piece of text) and “self-supervised”. Also say why it is self-supervised: the target (the right answer) is the next token of the text itself, so no human has to label anything.
  • Give the training steps in order: pre-training (reading huge amounts of text and guessing the next token) → (mid-training, an extra in-between round, when used) → SFT (supervised fine-tuning: learning from example questions with answers written by people) → preference optimization/RL (reinforcement learning: rewarding the answers people like better). Name SFT as the supervised step.
  • Explain context vs weights in one sentence, quoting the lecture: “Uploading a document changes the context. Fine-tuning changes the weights.” Context is what the model reads right now (your prompt and any pasted documents). Weights are what it learned in training.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Calling pre-training “unsupervised”. This was the 2025 trap. The right word is “self-supervised”, because the text supplies the right answers.
  • Saying the model “learns from your chat” or “remembers you”. The weights are fixed; only the context (what it is reading right now) changes.
  • Saying RAG or uploading documents “retrains” the model. It only gives the model more to read.
  • Thinking one token = one word. A long word can be split into several tokens (“strawberry” = st | raw | berry).
  • Claiming a bigger model or a longer answer is automatically more correct. The lecture says the largest model is not always the best choice, and “A longer answer or a persuasive explanation does not guarantee correctness.”

Key terms to use

  • next-token prediction: guessing the next piece of text
  • parameters, also called weights: the numbers the model learned
  • Transformer: the design behind most LLMs
  • self-supervised pre-training: learning from raw text, no human labels
  • supervised fine-tuning (SFT): learning from human-written example answers
  • preference optimization / reinforcement learning: rewarding answers people like better
  • context vs weights: what it reads now vs learned
  • inference with fixed weights: using the model without changing it
  • context window, counted in tokens: how much text it reads at once
  • mixture-of-experts (MoE): only a few expert parts work per token
  • quantization: storing the numbers more roughly to save memory
  • open weights: learned numbers anyone can download
  • Hugging Face hub: free website for sharing AI models
  • RAG: look up documents, paste them into the prompt
  • tools: outside programs the model can call
  • agents: models that plan and carry out steps themselves

Quick self-test

  1. “LLMs are estimated using unsupervised learning.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Estimated” here means trained: how the model learns its numbers. “Unsupervised learning” means learning with no right answers at all, only hunting for patterns. So: does an LLM learn with no right answers to check against?

    Answer: False. Why: There is a right answer at every step: the next token in the text. The model covers it up, guesses, then checks. Because the text supplies its own answers, this is called self-supervised, not unsupervised. Think of a puzzle book with the answers printed at the back: no teacher is needed, but there are still answers to check. This was 2025 true/false item (f).

  2. “HuggingFace is an open-source hub for NLP.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Open-source” means free for anyone to use and share. A “hub” is a central meeting place, here a website. “NLP” (Natural Language Processing) means getting computers to work with human language. So: is Hugging Face a free, shared website for language AI?

    Answer: True. Why: Hugging Face works like an app store for AI models where most things are free. People upload models, and others download them. The course’s Notebook 4 downloads a small model from there. This was 2025 true/false item (b).

  3. “Giving an LLM a company handbook through RAG changes its weights.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: RAG means the system searches documents, such as a handbook, and pastes the useful bits into what the model reads. “Weights” are the numbers the model learned in training, its long-term memory. So: does handing it a handbook change its long-term memory?

    Answer: False. Why: RAG is like an open-book exam. The student looks things up in the handbook during the exam, but their brain is not changed by it. Take the book away and that knowledge is gone. Changing the weights needs extra training, called fine-tuning. The lecture puts it as “Retrieval changes context; fine-tuning changes weights”.

  4. “In a mixture-of-experts model only part of the parameters is used for each token.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A mixture-of-experts (MoE) model is built from many smaller “expert” parts. Parameters are the learned numbers. A token is a small piece of text. So: for each piece of text, does only some of the model do the work?

    Answer: True. Why: Think of a hospital with many specialists. A patient with a broken arm sees the bone doctor, not every doctor in the building. In the same way, each token is sent to only a few experts. DeepSeek-V4-Flash uses about 13 billion of its 284 billion numbers for each token.

  5. “Explain in 2–5 sentences: Why is LLM pre-training called self-supervised, and which training step is supervised?”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Why do we say the model “marks its own homework” when it first learns? And which later step uses answers written by people?

    Answer: in pre-training the model guesses the next token, and the real next token in the text is the right answer, so no one labels anything by hand: that is self-supervised. The supervised step is supervised fine-tuning (SFT), where the model learns from instructions paired with answers written by people. Why: the difference is who supplies the right answers: the text itself, or a person. The full model answer to write is in “What the exam asks, and how to answer” above.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • LLM (Large Language Model): a very big computer program that predicts the next piece of text, over and over, to write answers. ChatGPT is a product built on one [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Model: a set of numbers plus rules that turns an input into an output. Like a recipe that turns ingredients into a dish.
  • Parameter / weight: one adjustable number inside the model, like one volume knob. Big LLMs have billions of them. “Parameters” and “weights” mean the same thing here.
  • Training: adjusting the weights by showing the model lots of examples, the way practising scales slowly trains your fingers.
  • Pre-training: the first and biggest training stage: guessing the next token across a huge pile of text.
  • Self-supervised learning: learning where the right answers come for free from the data itself. Covering the next word in a book and checking it is self-supervised.
  • Supervised learning: learning from examples where a person has written the right answer, like emails already marked “spam” or “not spam”.
  • Unsupervised learning: finding patterns with no right answers at all, like sorting customers into groups nobody named in advance.
  • Continued pre-training / mid-training: extra rounds of next-token practice on chosen text, such as long documents or legal texts, to strengthen one skill.
  • Post-training: all the training steps after pre-training that turn a text-guesser into a helpful assistant.
  • Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) / fine-tuning: extra training on examples of a question plus a good answer written by people. Like a new employee studying model answers. Fine-tuning changes the weights.
  • Preference optimization: training the model to give answers people like better, by showing it pairs of answers and which one was preferred.
  • Reinforcement learning (RL): learning from rewards, like a dog getting a treat for sitting. The model gets a “reward” for good answers.
  • Reward / verifiable result: a score for an answer. A verifiable result is one a computer can check, like “did the code pass its tests?”.
  • Token: a small piece of text the model reads: a word, part of a word, a space or a punctuation mark. “strawberry” is three tokens: st | raw | berry.
  • Token ID: the number a token gets in the model’s list. “This” might be number 17.
  • Tokenizer: the tool that cuts text into tokens and swaps each one for its ID number.
  • Vocabulary: the fixed list of all tokens the model knows, like the full box of LEGO pieces.
  • Probability: a chance between 0% and 100%. “50% useful” means the model rates “useful” as a coin-flip likely next token.
  • Transformer: the design (blueprint) that almost all modern LLMs are built on. Chapter 16 explains how it works.
  • Generative: able to write new text, not only sort or label existing text.
  • Inference / answer time: using a finished model to produce answers, with its weights frozen. Like a chef cooking from a recipe they already know.
  • Inference software: the program that runs the model on a computer and produces the answer.
  • Context: all the text the model can see while answering right now: your question, earlier messages, uploaded files.
  • Context window: the maximum amount of text (counted in tokens) the model can see at once, like the size of a desk where papers must fit.
  • System instructions: hidden instructions the app gives the model before your question, like “You are a polite helper”.
  • Deep neural network: a model built from many layers of simple number-crunching units stacked on top of each other. “Deep” means many layers.
  • Layer / hidden layer: one stage of number-crunching. A hidden layer is any layer between the input and the output, which you do not see directly.
  • Representation: the model’s internal list of numbers that summarises what a piece of text means, like a fingerprint of the meaning.
  • Transformer block: one repeated unit of the Transformer. LLMs stack many of them (Chapter 16).
  • Mixture-of-experts (MoE): a model split into many “expert” parts, where only a few experts work on each token. Like a hospital where each patient sees two specialists, not all 200 doctors.
  • Quantization: storing each weight with fewer digits so the model takes less memory. Like rounding 3.14159 to 3.1.
  • Precision: how many digits a number is stored with. Lower precision = shorter numbers = less memory.
  • Memory (computer memory): the space a computer has to hold numbers while it works.
  • Reasoning at answer time: the model “thinks out loud” with extra hidden text before its final answer. It can help on hard tasks but takes longer.
  • Latency: waiting time before the answer arrives.
  • Open weights: a model whose weights you can download and run yourself. You do not necessarily get its training data or recipe.
  • License: the legal terms saying what you may do with something, like the rules on a rental contract.
  • Hugging Face: a website where people share models and datasets for free, often called the AI community’s open-source hub.
  • Hub: a central meeting place; here, a website where models are shared.
  • Open-source: free for anyone to use, share and change.
  • Machine Learning: computers learning patterns from data instead of following hand-written rules, like a spam filter learning from marked emails.
  • Domain material: texts from one field, like law or medicine.
  • NLP (Natural Language Processing): getting computers to work with human language, like translating or summarising.
  • Ollama: a free program for downloading and running LLMs on your own computer; the slide shows its model library [Not in course files — general knowledge: what the program does].
  • Retrieval: searching a collection (say, company reports) and fetching the relevant pieces.
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): first search for relevant text, then paste it into the context so the model can use it. Like handing a student the right page before the question. It changes the context, not the weights.
  • Tools: outside programs the model can ask to run, like a calculator, a web search or a database.
  • Agent: a setup where the model repeats a loop of deciding, using tools and checking, until a task is done, within set permissions.
  • Chat application: using the model through a website or app, like the ChatGPT site.
  • API (application programming interface) / API integration: a doorway that lets your own program send text to the model and get answers back, with no chat window.
  • Local deployment: running the model on your own computer or company servers instead of someone else’s.
  • Memorization: the model storing exact bits of its training text (including mistakes) and repeating them later.
  • Hallucination: the model inventing facts or references that sound right but are false, like a made-up book title.
  • Notebook: a file that mixes short pieces of code with their saved results, used in the course’s exercises.

Sources: Lecture 7 “Introducing Large Language Models” (Vegard H. Larsen, Lecture_llm_intro.pdf), slides 4–20, 25, 29–30 (definition slide 4; next-token loop and self-supervision slide 7; deep networks slide 8; training pipeline slide 9; training vs answering slide 10; reasoning slide 11; MoE and size slide 12; DeepSeek-V4-Flash slide 13; quantization slide 14; four usage modes slide 16; good use case slide 18; risk grid slide 19; RAG, tools, agents slide 20; open weights and Hugging Face slide 25; context window slide 30); course outline GRA4164_2026.pdf; Notebook 4 GRA4164_Interactive_4_A_real_LLM_on_your_laptop.ipynb; 2025 exam with evaluation guidelines (GRA4164_2025-11-27_kl_14_EG.pdf).

15. Tokens and tokenization

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q4(c) (5 points) and T/F (c) asked exactly this. (Q4(c) = question 4, part (c), in the exam’s written section on Transformers and LLMs. T/F = the exam’s true/false statements, worth 2 points each.)

Why this exists

A Large Language Model (LLM) is the kind of program behind chatbots like ChatGPT [Not in course files — general knowledge]. It writes by guessing the next small bit of text, adding it, and guessing again.

But a computer cannot read letters. It can only work with numbers. So before an LLM can do anything, your text has to be turned into numbers.

The first idea is to give every word its own number: “cat” = 1, “dog” = 2, and so on. But what number do you give a word the computer has never seen? Think of a brand-new product name, a typo like “teh”, or a long Norwegian compound word. You would need millions of numbers and still miss words.

The other extreme is one number per letter. That works for any word, but every sentence becomes very long and slow to process.

This chapter is about the clever middle way between the two. It also matters for money: the way text is cut up decides what you pay to use an LLM, as Step 4 shows.

The idea in everyday words

Step 1: cut text into handy pieces.

Instead of whole words or single letters, the text is cut into pieces of in-between size. A piece can be a whole word, part of a word, a space, a punctuation mark or a chunk of digits. Each piece is called a token. A piece smaller than a whole word, like “berry” in “strawberry”, is called a subword.

The tool that does the cutting is a tokenizer. The act of cutting is tokenization.

Common words stay whole, as one token. Rare words are built from a few familiar pieces. For example, “strawberry” is one word but three tokens: st | raw | berry.

Analogy Think of LEGO. If you only had one brick per possible object (a “castle brick”, a “car brick”), you would need millions of bricks and could not build anything new. If you only had the tiniest 1×1 bricks, every model would take forever to build. LEGO sells a fixed set of common pieces in between, and you can build almost anything from them. A tokenizer’s list of pieces is that fixed box of useful pieces.

Step 2: every piece has a number.

The tokenizer has a fixed list of all the pieces it knows. That list is its vocabulary. How many pieces are in the list is the vocabulary size. Each piece has its own number in the list, like a barcode on a product. That number is its token ID.

The model only ever receives these ID numbers. Inside the model, each ID is then turned into a vector: a list of numbers, like [0.2, -1.3, 0.7], that the model can calculate with.

The lecture puts it like this: “A tokenizer splits text into pieces and maps them to vocabulary IDs. Tokens can include spaces, punctuation, or word fragments.” A later lecture says: “We do not input words per se, but tokens.” (“Per se” means “as such”.)

Step 3: tokens are not words.

One word can be one token or several. The lecture says: “Token counts depend on language and formatting; one word need not equal one token.” It also says: “tokens are not the same as words”. The same sentence can need more tokens in Norwegian than in English (you will see real numbers in the walk-through).

Step 4: why the count of tokens matters.

The lecture: “Token counts matter in practice: prices, context limits, and speed are all measured in tokens.”

  • Prices: LLM providers charge by the number of tokens you send and receive. This is the price per token. More tokens means a higher bill.
  • Context limits: an LLM can only look at a certain number of tokens at once. That limit is its context window. More tokens per sentence fills it faster.
  • Speed: more tokens means more computer work. The amount of computer work needed is called compute. It costs time, money and electricity.

Step 5: how the list of pieces is learned.

Nobody writes the vocabulary by hand. It is learned from example text. The most common method is called byte-pair encoding, or BPE. (A byte is the basic unit a computer stores text in; one simple letter like “a” is one byte. BPE got its name from gluing pairs of these [Not in course files — general knowledge].)

Here is how BPE works, in five steps. The course notebook names them like this:

  1. Initialization. Take a pile of example text. This collection of text is called the corpus. Cut every word into single letters. Stick a small tag on the end of each word, the end-of-word marker, written </w>. It lets the method tell “est” at the end of a word apart from “est” in the middle. Each piece in the text at any moment, a letter or an already-glued chunk, is called a symbol.
  2. Counting pair frequencies. Count how often each pair of side-by-side symbols appears. For example, how often “l” is followed by “o”. That count is the pair frequency.
  3. Merging pairs. Take the pair that appears most often and glue it into one new piece. Gluing two neighbours into one is called a merge. Like snapping two LEGO bricks together for good.
  4. Updating the vocabulary. Replace that pair with the new piece everywhere in the text, and add the new piece to the vocabulary.
  5. Iteration. Go back to step 2. Repeat until the vocabulary has the size you want.

Real tokenizers do this on a huge scale. The notebook says “real models train millions of merges on terabytes of text”. (A terabyte is a very large amount of stored data.) The tokenizer of GPT-4o, one of OpenAI’s LLMs [Not in course files — general knowledge], has a vocabulary size of 200,019.

Step 6: using the list on new text.

To cut up a new sentence, start from its letters. Then repeat the same merges, in the same order as they were learned. Common words end up as one piece. Rare words end up as a few familiar pieces.

A rare or unknown word is one that hardly ever, or never, appeared in the example text. BPE can still cut it into known pieces, instead of giving up. Doing well on new things you have not seen before is called generalization.

Step 7: the trade-off BPE balances.

When text is cut into tokens, the result is a row of tokens. That row is called a sequence. How many tokens are in the row is the sequence length.

There is a tug-of-war:

  • A bigger vocabulary means bigger pieces, so fewer tokens per sentence. But the list is bigger to store.
  • A smaller vocabulary means smaller pieces, so more tokens per sentence.

The lecture: “Subword methods such as byte-pair encoding (BPE) balance vocabulary size against sequence length.” In plain words: BPE keeps the list of pieces a manageable size, while keeping sentences from becoming too many pieces long.

Step 8: careful, “token” means something else in older methods.

Earlier in the course, the word “token” had a simpler meaning. An older method called bag-of-words counts how often each word appears in a text and ignores word order. There, tokenization meant “Split text into individual words (tokens) using text.split()”. (text.split() is a Python command that cuts text at the spaces. Python is a programming language.) So “hello world” → {“hello”, “world”}. A token there is a whole word cut out at the spaces.

In LLMs, a token is a learned subword piece. Same word “token”, two different meanings. In the exam, say which one you mean.

Step 9: tokenization is not stemming.

Another older trick is stemming: chopping words down to a rough core by fixed rules. The core of a word, like “run” in “running”, is its root. The bits added to the start or end of a word, like “-ing”, “-ed” or “-s”, are called affixes. The notebook describes stemming as “stripping affixes (e.g., -ing, -ed, -s)”, and says the result “may not necessarily be a valid word”.

One well-known set of stemming rules is the Porter stemmer. Its saved output in the course notebook:

  • running → run
  • runs → run
  • runner → runner
  • ran → ran
  • easily → easili
  • fairly → fairli

The big difference: stemming throws information away, to shrink the word list for bag-of-words. You cannot get “easily” back from “easili”. BPE tokenization keeps all the text. Glue the tokens back together and you get the exact original.

Turning text into token IDs is called encoding. Turning token IDs back into text is called decoding.

What it is good at, and where it breaks.

  • Good at: handling new or rare words, because they can always be built from smaller known pieces.
  • Good at: keeping all the text. You can glue the tokens back together and get the exact original.
  • Good at: working in many languages with one scheme. Working in many languages is called multilingual.
  • Breaks: the model never sees single letters or digits, so it is weak at spelling, counting letters (“how many r’s in strawberry?”) and arithmetic.
  • Breaks: some languages need more tokens for the same meaning. That costs more money and fills the context window faster.

Walk-through example

Part A: BPE by hand, on four words.

Our corpus is four words: low, lower, newest, widest.

Cut into letters. Each word becomes its letters plus the end-of-word marker </w>:

l o w </w> | l o w e r </w> | n e w e s t </w> | w i d e s t </w>

Count the symbols. low has 3 letters plus the marker: 4 symbols. lower has 5 letters plus the marker: 6. newest and widest have 6 letters plus the marker: 7 each. Total: 4 + 6 + 7 + 7 = 24 symbols.

The starting vocabulary. Which different letters are used? d, e, i, l, n, o, r, s, t, w. That is 10. Add the end-marker, and the vocabulary has 11 symbols.

Count the pairs. In the table below, each row is one pair of side-by-side symbols. “Count” is how many times that pair appears across all four words. “Where” names the words it appears in.

Pair Count Where
l o 2 low, lower
o w 2 low, lower
w e 2 lower, newest
e s 2 newest, widest
s t 2 newest, widest
t </w> 2 newest, widest
every other pair (w </w>, e r, r </w>, n e, e w, w i, i d, d e) 1 each —

Work one out in words: “l then o” appears at the start of low and at the start of lower. Nowhere else. So its count is 2.

Break the tie. Six pairs tie at 2. The code takes the first one it met, l o. (This tie rule is our reading of Counter.most_common, the Python command that ranks items by count. The notebook does not say this.)

Merge, again and again. The notebook runs six merges. In the table below, each row is one merge. “Pair merged” is what got glued. “Corpus after the merge” shows all four words after that glue step (the | separates the words). “Total symbols” is how many pieces are left in the whole text. We counted those ourselves.

Merge Pair merged Corpus after the merge Total symbols
1 l + o lo w </w> | lo w e r </w> | n e w e s t </w> | w i d e s t </w> 22
2 lo + w low </w> | low e r </w> | n e w e s t </w> | w i d e s t </w> 20
3 e + s low </w> | low e r </w> | n e w es t </w> | w i d es t </w> 18
4 es + t low </w> | low e r </w> | n e w est </w> | w i d est </w> 16
5 est + </w> low </w> | low e r </w> | n e w est</w> | w i d est</w> 14
6 low + </w> low</w> | low e r </w> | n e w est</w> | w i d est</w> 13

Where do the totals come from? Each merge turns 2 pieces into 1, so it removes one piece each time it happens. Merge 1 happens in 2 words (low and lower), so the text drops from 24 to 22. Merges 2 to 5 also each hit 2 words, so the text drops by 2 each time: 20, 18, 16, 14. Merge 6 hits only 1 word (low), so it drops by 1, to 13.

At the same time, each merge adds one new piece to the vocabulary. Six merges take it from 11 to 17.

What happened. The frequent piece low and the common ending est became single tokens. (est</w> means “est at the end of a word”.) The text got shorter (24 → 13 symbols), and the vocabulary grew (11 → 17). That is the “vocabulary size versus sequence length” trade-off in action: a bigger list, a shorter text.

Try a word it has never seen. This is our own illustration, using the same six merges. The word lowest was never in the corpus. It starts as 7 pieces: l, o, w, e, s, t, </w>. Run the six merges, in order:

  • Merges 1 and 2 (l+o, then lo+w) make “low”.
  • Merges 3 to 5 (e+s, es+t, est+</w>) make “est” with the end-marker.
  • Merge 6 (low+</w>) does not apply, because “low” is not at the end of this word.

Result: low | est</w>. Two meaningful, known pieces, instead of “unknown word”.

(The notebook’s text also describes a possible end result ['low', 'er', 'new', 'est', 'wide']. That is an illustration of where more merges would lead, not the output of the six coded merges.)

Part B: a real tokenizer.

The notebook also runs a real tokenizer. It uses tiktoken, a free Python tool for using OpenAI’s tokenizers [Not in course files — general knowledge]. The vocabulary it loads is called o200k_base. Such a named vocabulary, plus its merge rules, is called an encoding. This one belongs to the GPT-4o family and has a vocabulary size of 200,019.

In the table below, each row is one piece of text the notebook fed in. “Number of tokens” is how many pieces the tokenizer cut it into. “Tokens” shows the pieces, separated by |. These are the notebook’s saved results.

Input text Number of tokens Tokens
The market fell sharply yesterday. 6 The | market | fell | sharply | yesterday | .
Markedet falt kraftig i går. 8 Marked | et | falt | kraft | ig | i | går | .
12345.67 + 89.01 9 123 | 45 | . | 67 | + | (space) | 89 | . | 01
strawberry 3 st | raw | berry

What to see:

  • English vs Norwegian. The first two rows say the same thing: 5 words plus a full stop. English needs 6 tokens. Norwegian needs 8. How much more is that? Divide 8 by 6: you get 1.33. So Norwegian needs 33% more tokens for the same meaning. More tokens means a higher price, more of the context window used, and a harder job for the model. The notebook says: “Tokenization is language-dependent”.
  • strawberry = st | raw | berry. The model never sees the separate letters. That is why LLMs “struggle to spell a word”, as the notebook says, and miscount the r’s.
  • Numbers are chopped into arbitrary chunks (123 | 45). That is why LLMs are “bad at simple arithmetic”, in the notebook’s words.
  • Spaces. The space in front of a word is part of its token (” market”), and a space can be its own token.

Reading the course code

These lines come from the course notebook. A notebook cell is one small block of code with its saved output. You do not need to write code: the exam has not asked students to write code. What matters is knowing what each line does.

pairs[(a, b)] += 1                         # count every neighbouring pair
(a, b), _ = pairs.most_common(1)[0]        # pick the most frequent pair
enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("o200k_base")  # load GPT-4o's real tokenizer
toks = enc.encode(s)                       # text -> list of token IDs
" | ".join(enc.decode([t]) for t in toks)  # show each token as text
  • Line 1: goes through every word and adds 1 to the count for each pair of neighbouring symbols. This is BPE step 2, “Counting Pair Frequencies”.
  • Line 2: takes the single most common pair. most_common is the Python command that lists items from most to least frequent. This is the pair that gets merged (BPE step 3).
  • Line 3: loads the vocabulary of a real model, about 200,000 learned pieces.
  • Line 4: encodes the sentence: turns it into a list of ID numbers. This is what the model actually receives.
  • Line 5: decodes each ID back into its text piece and puts | between them, so we can see the split. Counting the IDs (len(toks) in Python) gives the token counts in the Part B table.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025, question 4(c), 5 points: “Describe in general terms what a token is, how it differs from words, and why we might want to use them”

Model answer A token is the unit of text an LLM actually reads: the tokenizer splits text into pieces such as whole words, word fragments, spaces or punctuation, and maps each to an ID that is turned into a vector (Lecture 7, slide 29). A token is not the same as a word: a common word may be one token, but “strawberry” becomes st|raw|berry, and a Norwegian sentence needs 8 tokens where its English translation needs 6 (tokenizer notebook). We use subword tokens, for example from byte-pair encoding, because they balance vocabulary size against sequence length: rare or new words can be built from known pieces, the vocabulary stays fixed and manageable, compute is more efficient, and the same scheme works across many languages.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: A token is a piece of text that the model turns into a number, and then into a list of numbers. Some words are one token, others get split into several, and different languages need different numbers of tokens. Using pieces lets the model handle any word, even a brand-new one, with one fixed list of pieces. It also keeps texts short enough to process quickly.

The official 2025 grading guide looked for these ideas. Tokenization is “the process of breaking down raw text … into smaller, more manageable pieces called tokens”. It “defines what type of units of text that is turned into (computable) vectors”. And tokens give “better handling [of] rare words, makes compute more efficient and improves generalization, makes multilingual modelling easier.”

2025, true/false (c): “The input to a Large Language Model is actually not words, but tokens”

Model answer True.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: before the model sees your text, the tokenizer cuts it into pieces and swaps each for an ID number. The model reads those pieces, not whole words.

Likely new true/false items:

“one token always equals one word”

Model answer False.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: a common word can be one token, but “strawberry” is three.

“BPE merges the least frequent pair”

Model answer False.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: BPE (byte-pair encoding, the method that builds the list of tokens) merges the most frequent pair.

“the same sentence costs the same number of tokens in every language”

Model answer False.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: in the notebook, the Norwegian sentence needed 8 tokens and the English one needed 6.

Likely short question: “Explain how BPE works.”

Model answer (built from the notebook’s five steps) Start from single characters, with an end-of-word marker. Count every pair of neighbouring symbols. Merge the most frequent pair into one new token and replace it everywhere. Repeat until the vocabulary reaches the target size. The vocabulary is learned from data, and it balances vocabulary size against sequence length.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: begin with letters, keep gluing the two neighbours you see together most often, and stop when your list of pieces is big enough.

What a top-grade answer must include

  1. What a token is: a small unit of text (a word, a word piece, a punctuation mark, or a space). Each token gets an ID number, and that ID is turned into a vector (a list of numbers the model can calculate with).
  2. How it differs from a word: one word can be several tokens (strawberry = st|raw|berry; Markedet = Marked|et). So token counts and word counts differ, and the gap changes from language to language.
  3. Why we use tokens: rare and new words can be built from known pieces. The vocabulary (the fixed list of all tokens) stays a manageable size, and texts do not turn into very long chains of pieces. BPE “balance[s] vocabulary size against sequence length” (sequence length = how many tokens a text becomes). So computing is efficient, it generalises (copes with words it never saw), and it handles many languages.

Bonus: one sentence on BPE: find the pair of neighbouring pieces that appears most often, glue it into one new piece, and repeat.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Defining a token as “a word”. That is the bag-of-words meaning from earlier in the course (text treated as counts of whole words), not the LLM meaning.
  • Giving only the “what” and forgetting the “why”.
  • Confusing tokenization with stemming. Stemming chops words down to a root (so “easily” becomes “easili”) and loses information. Tokenization keeps the full text; it only cuts it into pieces.
  • Saying BPE uses a dictionary written by hand. It is learned from data, by counting which pairs of pieces sit together most often.
  • Saying tokens are always smaller than words. Common words are one token.

Key terms to use

  • token: a small piece of text
  • tokenizer: the tool that cuts text into tokens
  • vocabulary / token IDs: the fixed token list and their numbers
  • subword: a piece smaller than a whole word
  • byte-pair encoding (BPE): builds tokens by merging frequent pairs
  • most frequent pair: the two neighbours seen together most
  • merge: glue two pieces into one new token
  • vocabulary size vs sequence length: bigger token list, shorter token chains
  • rare/unknown words: built from smaller pieces it already knows
  • multilingual: works across many languages
  • context window and price measured in tokens: limits and costs count tokens, not words
  • tiktoken / o200k_base: OpenAI’s tokenizer tool and one of its vocabularies

Quick self-test

  1. “The input to a Large Language Model is actually not words, but tokens.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A Large Language Model (LLM) is the “brain” behind a chatbot like ChatGPT. The “input” is what you feed in. A token is a small piece of text: a word, part of a word, a space or a punctuation mark. So: does the model read pieces rather than whole words?

    Answer: True. Why: Before the model sees your text, a tokenizer cuts it into pieces and gives each piece an ID number. The model only ever sees those pieces. It is like LEGO: the model never gets a finished castle, only a box of standard bricks. This was 2025 true/false item (c).

  2. “In BPE, each step merges the most frequent pair of adjacent symbols.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: BPE (byte-pair encoding) is the method that builds a tokenizer’s list of pieces. “Adjacent symbols” means two pieces sitting next to each other, like “t” and “h”. “Merge” means glue them into one new piece, “th”. So: at each step, does BPE glue together the pair that shows up most often?

    Answer: True. Why: BPE starts with single letters. It counts which neighbouring pair appears most often in the training text, glues that pair into one piece, and repeats. It is like noticing you type “th” all the time and making one key for it. Watch the wording: most often, not least often.

  3. “A Norwegian sentence and its English translation use the same number of tokens.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Take one sentence with the same meaning in two languages. Are both cut into the same number of pieces?

    Answer: False. Why: A tokenizer’s pieces fit some languages better than others. In the course notebook, the Norwegian sentence needed 8 tokens and its English translation needed 6. Since limits and prices are counted in tokens, the same message can cost more in one language than another. The lecture says: “Token counts depend on language”.

  4. “Stemming and BPE tokenization both keep all the information in the original text.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Stemming is an older trick that chops words down to a rough root, so “easily” becomes “easili”. BPE tokenization cuts text into pieces. “Keep all the information” means you could rebuild the exact original text afterwards. So: can you get the exact text back from both?

    Answer: False. Why: Stemming throws parts away, so you cannot get the original word back. BPE only cuts: glue the pieces back together and you have the exact text again. Think of cutting a photo into puzzle pieces (BPE) versus trimming its edges off (stemming). Only one of the two keeps everything, so the statement is false.

  5. “Explain in 2–5 sentences (2025 Q4c): What is a token, how does it differ from a word, and why use tokens?”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: What is the small piece of text an LLM reads? Why is it not always a whole word? And why do LLMs use these pieces at all?

    Answer: a token is a piece of text (a word, part of a word, a space or punctuation) that gets an ID and then a vector. It is not always a word: “strawberry” is st|raw|berry, and Norwegian needs 8 tokens where English needs 6. We use subword tokens, for example from BPE, because they balance vocabulary size against sequence length: new words can be built from known pieces, the list stays fixed, compute is efficient, and it works across languages. Why: the question has three parts (what, how it differs, why), and each needs its own sentence. The full model answer to write is in “What the exam asks, and how to answer” above.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • LLM (Large Language Model): a big program that writes text by guessing the next token, over and over. ChatGPT runs on one [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Token: a small piece of text the model reads: a word, part of a word, a space, a punctuation mark or a chunk of digits. “strawberry” = st | raw | berry, three tokens.
  • Tokenizer: the tool that cuts text into tokens and gives each one its ID number.
  • Tokenization: the act of cutting text into tokens.
  • Vocabulary: the fixed list of all tokens a tokenizer knows, like the full box of LEGO pieces you are allowed to build with.
  • Token ID: the number a token has in the vocabulary list, like a product’s barcode.
  • Vocabulary size: how many pieces are in the list. GPT-4o’s tokenizer has 200,019.
  • Subword: a piece smaller than a whole word, like “berry” in “strawberry”.
  • Byte-pair encoding (BPE): the method that builds a vocabulary by gluing the most frequent pair of neighbouring pieces again and again.
  • Byte: the basic unit a computer stores text in; one simple letter like “a” is one byte. BPE got its name from gluing pairs of these [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Pair frequency: how many times two pieces appear side by side in the text.
  • Merge: gluing two neighbouring pieces into one new piece, like snapping two LEGO bricks together for good.
  • End-of-word marker (</w>): a small tag stuck on the last piece of a word, so “est” at the end of a word is kept apart from “est” in the middle.
  • Corpus: the collection of text you learn from. Here: the four words low, lower, newest, widest.
  • Symbol: one piece in the text at a given moment, either a single letter or an already-glued chunk.
  • Sequence / sequence length: a sequence is the text as a row of tokens; its length is how many tokens are in the row.
  • Vocabulary size vs sequence length (the trade-off): a bigger list means fewer, longer pieces per sentence, but a bigger list to store. A smaller list means more pieces per sentence.
  • Rare / unknown word: a word that hardly ever, or never, appeared in the training text.
  • Generalization: doing well on new things you have not seen before, like the new word “lowest”.
  • Multilingual: working in many languages.
  • Compute: the amount of computer work needed, which costs time, money and electricity.
  • Context window: the maximum number of tokens a model can see at once, like the size of a desk where all papers must fit.
  • Price per token: LLM providers charge by the number of tokens you send and receive, so more tokens = higher bill.
  • Vector: a list of numbers, like [0.2, -1.3, 0.7]. Every token ID is turned into one of these before the model works with it.
  • Bag-of-words: an older method that counts how often each word appears in a text and ignores word order. There, a “token” meant a whole word.
  • Stemming: chopping words down to a rough root by fixed rules, like “running” → “run”. It can produce non-words like “easili”.
  • Affix: a bit added to the start or end of a word, like “-ing”, “-ed” or “-s”.
  • Porter stemmer: one well-known set of stemming rules.
  • Root: the core of a word, like “run” in “running”.
  • tiktoken: a free Python tool for using OpenAI’s tokenizers [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Encoding (o200k_base): the name of one specific learned vocabulary plus its glue rules; this one is used by GPT-4o.
  • Encode / decode: encode = turn text into token IDs; decode = turn token IDs back into text.
  • GPT-4o: one of OpenAI’s LLMs [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Python / code / notebook cell: Python is a programming language; a notebook cell is one small block of code with its saved output.
  • Counter.most_common: a Python command that lists items from most to least frequent.

Sources: Lecture 7 Lecture_llm_intro.pdf slides 13 and 29; notebook llm_tokenizers.ipynb cells 0–18 (saved outputs: stemming cells 1–3, BPE steps cell 15, BPE code cell 16, real-model note cell 17, tiktoken cell 18, language/spelling/arithmetic remarks cell 0); Lecture 9 Lecture_llm_inputoutput.pdf slide 4; Lecture 2a Lecture_bow_cosine_tfidf.pdf slide 7; 2025 exam evaluation guidelines Q4(c).

16. Attention and the Transformer

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q4(b) and Q4(d) (10 points) plus T/F (a) and (i) (4 points).

Why this exists

Read two sentences: “We sat on the river bank” and “I put my salary in the bank.” It is the same word, with two very different meanings. You know at once which bank is meant, because you look at the words around it.

A computer has to be taught to do that. Think of a chatbot like ChatGPT, or a phone keyboard that suggests your next word. To do a good job, it must know that “bank” next to “river” is the land beside water, and “bank” next to “salary” is a place for money.

Sometimes the clue is far away. Take “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired.” To understand “it”, you must look back several words and decide: the animal, or the street? (The animal. Streets don’t get tired.)

So a model needs a way for every word to look at the other words in its text and update its own meaning. That way is called self-attention. It is the heart of the Transformer, the design behind every modern LLM (large language model: a program like ChatGPT that writes text by guessing the next word, over and over).

The idea in everyday words

Step 1: words become lists of numbers

A computer can only calculate with numbers. So each word is turned into a list of numbers, for example [2, 1]. A list of numbers like this is called a vector. Each slot in the list is a dimension: in [2, 1], the first dimension holds 2 and the second holds 1. Real models use long lists, typically 512 numbers per word.

The list that stands for a word is its embedding (or word embedding). Words with similar meanings get similar lists. The model finds each word’s list in a big lookup table with one row per word it knows. A table of numbers with rows and columns is called a matrix, so this lookup table is the embedding matrix.

One small detail: the text is first cut into pieces called tokens. A token is usually a word or a part of a word. In this chapter, you can treat “token” and “word” as the same thing.

Here is the problem. The lookup table gives “bank” the same list in every sentence. An older method called word2vec works exactly like that: it learns one fixed list per word, whatever sentence the word is in. What we want instead is a contextual (or context-specific) embedding: a list for “bank” that changes with its neighbours.

The course uses this example. In “I walked along the pond, and noticed that one of the trees along the bank had fallen into the water…”, “bank” should end up close to “water”. In “Hoping on a high return, the bank had issued a lot of credit to the investor”, “bank” should end up close to “credit”. Self-attention is how we get there. In the course’s words: “In Transformers, the word embeddings are context specific”.

Step 2: the library — query, key and value

Picture a library. You walk in with a question, say “What kind of place is a bank?”. Every book has a label on its spine. Inside every book are its contents. You check how well each spine label matches your question. Then you read a lot from the books whose labels match well, a little from the others, and you combine what you read into your answer.

Self-attention does this for every word. Each word gets three new lists of numbers:

  • the query: the word’s question, “what am I looking for?” This is the question you bring to the library.
  • the key: the word’s label, “what do I offer?” This is the label on a book’s spine.
  • the value: the word’s actual content, which gets passed on. This is the text inside the book.

The course calls this the database analogy (or information-retrieval analogy). Searching a database works the same way: you match what you are looking for against the labels of the stored items, then fetch the contents of the items that match. The course’s own definitions are worth knowing:

  • Query: “the current item you are looking to find more information about … the representation of a specific word for which the model is trying to determine its contextual relevance”.
  • Key: “the searchable items in the database … what the query is matched against to find relevant information”.
  • Value: “the actual information you want to retrieve … the content that is retrieved if their corresponding key matches the query”.

Where do the three lists come from? Each word’s embedding is multiplied by three tables of numbers: one table makes queries, one makes keys, one makes values. These tables are called weight matrices. They are learned: set automatically during training (the long process where the model adjusts its numbers on huge amounts of text), not written by hand. All the learned numbers in a model together are called its parameters.

Step 3: score each match with a dot product

How do you check how well a question matches a label, when both are lists of numbers? You multiply the two lists slot by slot, and add up the results. This is called a dot product.

Here it is with the chapter’s own numbers. The word “bank” asks with the query [1, 1]. The word “river” has the key [2, 1].

  • First slots: 1 × 2 = 2.
  • Second slots: 1 × 1 = 1.
  • Add them: 2 + 1 = 3.

So the dot product of “bank”’s query and “river”’s key is 3. Now try “the”, whose key is [0, 1]: 1 × 0 + 1 × 1 = 1. The bigger number wins: “river” (3) matches the question of “bank” better than “the” (1) does.

The course calls this match number the compatibility score. Higher means more relevant.

Step 4: shrink the scores

Next, every score is divided by the square root of the key’s length. The square root of a number is the number that, multiplied by itself, gives it back: the square root of 9 is 3, and the square root of 2 is about 1.414. Our keys have 2 numbers each, so we divide by about 1.414. A score of 3 becomes 3 ÷ 1.414 ≈ 2.121. This scaling keeps the scores from getting too large when the lists are long.

Step 5: hide the future (only in some models)

Some models write text from left to right, one word at a time. While learning, such a model must not peek at the words that come later. Otherwise guessing the next word would be far too easy: the answer would be right there. The course says it like this: “Remember, it is all about prediction. But, if we know the future, it is easy to predict it. Thus, when traning, Transformers use masking.”

Masking means hiding some words from the comparison. Here the hidden words are the later ones. Their scores are set to minus infinity (written \(-\infty\)), a value smaller than any number. In the next step you will see that this turns their share of attention into exactly zero.

This gives two kinds of self-attention:

  • Causal attention: each word may look only at itself and the words before it. Models that write text left to right use this. The course names a “Causal Self-Attention Layer” inside the decoder, the half of the original Transformer that writes output one token at a time [Not in course files — general knowledge: the encoder’s role; Lecture 9 slide 17 names the decoder’s causal self-attention layer]. The other half, the encoder, reads and understands the input.
  • Bidirectional attention: each word may look at all the words, before and after it. This suits a model that only needs to understand a finished text.

GPT-style models (which write text) use causal attention; BERT-style models (which read and understand text) use bidirectional attention [Not in course files — general knowledge].

In both kinds, each word’s new list has the same length as its old list, but different numbers in it. The course says the outputs have “equal size as x_i, but potentially different numerical values”.

The picture below shows three words. The bottom row, x1, x2 and x3, are the three words going in. The top row, a1, a2 and a3, are their new lists coming out. Each line means “this output uses this input”.

Left, causal: a1 uses only x1, a2 uses x1 and x2, a3 uses all three. Right, bidirectional: every output uses every input.

Step 6: turn scores into shares with softmax

Scores like 0.707 or 2.121 are awkward to use directly. We want shares instead: positive numbers that add up to 1, like splitting 100% of your attention across the words. A rule called softmax does this in two moves.

  1. Make every score positive. Softmax takes a fixed number called e (about 2.718) and raises it to the power of each score. This is the exponential. The result is always positive, and a bigger score gives a much bigger result.
  2. Divide each result by the total of all the results. Now they add up to 1.

With the chapter’s numbers: after shrinking, “bank” has the scores 0.707 (for “the”), 2.121 (for “river”) and 0.707 (for itself). Raising e to these powers gives about 2.028, 8.342 and 2.028. (A calculator or computer works these powers out; you never do them by hand, and the exam won’t ask you to.) The total is 2.028 + 8.342 + 2.028 = 12.398. Divide each by 12.398 and you get 0.164, 0.673 and 0.164. So “bank” gives about 16% of its attention to “the”, 67% to “river” and 16% to itself.

And the masked words? The number e raised to the power of minus infinity is 0. So a word whose score was set to minus infinity gets a share of exactly 0 [Not in course files — general knowledge: the \(e^{-\infty} = 0\) step; the slide shows only the −∞ matrix].

These shares are called attention weights.

Step 7: mix the contents

Now each word builds its new list. It multiplies every allowed word’s value by that word’s share, and adds everything up. This is a weighted sum (or weighted average). It works like a course grade where the exam counts 60% and the project 40%: things with a bigger share count more.

The result is the word’s new, context-aware list. In “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired”, the course shows that “it” gives most of its attention to “animal”. So the new list for “it” carries a lot of “animal” inside it.

The course sums up attention in three steps:

  1. Compatibility score: the dot product of the query with each key. Higher means more relevant.
  2. Weight calculation: softmax turns the scores into weights that are non-negative (zero or above) and add up to 1.
  3. Multiply the weights with the value lists and add them up. This gives “a new representation of the word that incorporates contextual information”.

Step 8: several attentions side by side (multi-head)

One full round of steps 2 to 7 is called a head. Multi-head attention runs several heads at the same time. Each head has its own three tables for making queries, keys and values. So each head is free to notice a different kind of link between words. One might track grammar, which is called syntactic (who does what to whom). Another might track meaning, which is called semantic.

Each head produces its own list for every word. These lists are concatenated, meaning glued end to end: gluing [1, 2] and [3, 4] gives [1, 2, 3, 4]. The glued list is then multiplied by one more learned table to bring it back to the original length. This last step is called a projection.

The sizes fit neatly. A word’s embedding typically has 512 numbers, and each head’s value list typically has 64. With 8 heads, 8 × 64 = 512, so the glued list is exactly as long as the embedding (our calculation).

The course gives two reasons for having several heads. It “Increases the model’s representation capacity. E.g., capturing a richer array of relationships within the data, such as different types of syntactic or semantic connections in a sentence”. And it “Improves learning dynamics and ensures robustness to input variations”. Robustness means still working well when the input changes a little.

Important for the exam: the heads work at the same time, in parallel. So multi-head attention does not make the model slower or less efficient.

Step 9: finish the block, then stack many blocks

After multi-head attention, a few more steps tidy things up.

  • Residual connection: add the step’s input back onto its output. It is a shortcut, so useful information is not lost on the way. The course says it “Makes training the Deep Neural Network easier” and helps by “Enabling feature reuse and avoiding that important features are lost”. A deep neural network is a model made of many stacked layers of simple calculations. A feature (or representation) is a piece of information the model has worked out about a word, stored as numbers.
  • Layer normalization (Layer Norm): rescale the numbers in each word’s list to a standard range, so training stays steady [Not in course files — general knowledge: what the rescaling does; the slide says it “makes training … easier”]. The course: it “Makes training the Deep Neural Network easier”.
  • Feed-forward network (FFN): a small extra calculation applied to each word on its own. The course says it “Adds non-linearity to the mix (self-attention is linear operations)” and “Enables richer feature representations”. A linear step only multiplies and adds, so it can only capture straight-line patterns. A non-linearity lets the model capture curved, more complex patterns.
  • Then another residual connection and another layer normalization.
