All of this together (multi-head attention, add back, normalize, feed-forward, add back, normalize) is one Transformer block, also called a layer. Real models stack many blocks. With each block, the word lists get “richer and richer” in meaning.

Step 10: tell the model the word order (positional encoding)

There is one more problem. Attention looks at all words at the same time. Nothing in it says which word came first. The course puts it this way:

  • “The Transformer’s self-attention mechanism processes all words in the input sequence simultaneously, but does not automatically understand the position or order of words in a sentence.”
  • “E.g., ‘The cat chased the dog’ and ‘The dog chased the cat’ have the same words but entirely different meanings due to the order of those words.”

The fix is a second list of numbers for each place in the sentence: one list that means “1st place”, another for “2nd place”, and so on. This is a positional encoding (or positional embedding). It has the same length as a word’s embedding, and it is added to it slot by slot. It is like stamping a seat number on each ticket. Word plus position together is called the composite embedding; the course writes “X = Composite Embeddings (word + position)”, with the example sentence “Janet will back the bill”. The course again: “By adding these positional embeddings to the word embeddings, the Transformer can maintain information about the sequence order of the input data.”

Note: the position list is added, not glued on the end. The combined list keeps its length.

There are two kinds of position information:

  • absolute position: “this is word 5”;
  • relative position: “this word is 2 places after that one”.

The “Original Transformer work used so-called sinusoidal function”. Sine and cosine are smooth wave patterns that go up and down between −1 and 1. A sinusoidal encoding fills the position list with such waves, some fast and some slow. You will see this with numbers below.

What it’s good at, and where it breaks

The course lists why self-attention is powerful:

  • Good at long-range links. It captures grammar (syntactic) and meaning (semantic) relations “without being limited by the sequence’s distance”. A link between far-apart words is a long-range dependency, like “it” pointing back to “animal” many words earlier. Every word can look straight at every other allowed word.
  • Good at speed in training. It “Allows for processing data in parallell, rather than sequentially. Implies significant improvements in training efficiency”. Parallel processing means doing many calculations at once instead of one after another. Training efficiency means how much learning you get for a given amount of computer time. This suits a GPU, a computer chip that does thousands of simple sums at once [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Good at showing its work. The attention weights give some interpretability: you can look at them to see which words a word paid attention to.
  • Breaks: long texts get expensive. Every word compares itself with every other word, so doubling the text gives about four times as many comparisons [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Breaks: on its own, attention ignores word order. Without positional encoding, “The cat chased the dog” and “The dog chased the cat” would look the same to it.

Walk-through example

This is a made-up example (our own illustration, not from the slides), small enough to do by hand. The sentence is “the river bank”: three words. To keep it tiny, every list has only 2 numbers. In a real model, each word’s query, key and value would come from multiplying its embedding by the three learned tables. Here we skip that and pick the lists directly.

Read each value’s first number as “money-ness” and its second number as “nature-ness”.

The three lists for each word. In the table below, each row is one word. The three columns are that word’s query (its question), key (its spine label) and value (its contents). One cell, for example the “bank” row under “Value”, is [2, 1]: the contents “bank” passes on are 2 parts money, 1 part nature.

Token (rows) Query \(q\) Key \(k\) Value \(v\)
the [1, 0] [0, 1] [0.5, 0.5]
river [0, 1] [2, 1] [0, 2]
bank [1, 1] [1, 0] [2, 1]

Notice that “bank”’s own value, [2, 1], leans towards money. Let’s see what happens when it looks at its neighbours.

Step 1: match scores (dot products). In the next table, each row is the word doing the looking (its query). Each column is the word being looked at (its key). Each cell is the dot product of that row’s query and that column’s key: how well they match.

k(the) k(river) k(bank)
q(the) 0 2 1
q(river) 1 1 0
q(bank) 1 3 1

Here is the “bank” row worked out in words:

  • With “river”: query [1, 1], key [2, 1]. 1 × 2 + 1 × 1 = 3.
  • With “the”: query [1, 1], key [0, 1]. 1 × 0 + 1 × 1 = 1.
  • With itself: query [1, 1], key [1, 0]. 1 × 1 + 1 × 0 = 1.

So “river” is the best match for “bank”.

Step 2: shrink, then hide the future. Each list has 2 numbers, so divide every score by the square root of 2, about 1.414. A score of 1 becomes 1 ÷ 1.414 ≈ 0.707. A score of 3 becomes 3 ÷ 1.414 ≈ 2.121. A score of 0 stays 0.

Then the causal mask. The line of cells from top left to bottom right, where each word meets itself, is called the diagonal. Cells above the diagonal are the later words, so they are set to minus infinity. The table now looks like this (rows and columns as before):

k(the) k(river) k(bank)
q(the) 0 \(-\infty\) \(-\infty\)
q(river) 0.707 0.707 \(-\infty\)
q(bank) 0.707 2.121 0.707

“bank” is the last word, so every word is before it or is itself. Nothing is hidden in its row. “the” is the first word, so it can only look at itself.

Step 3: softmax along each row. For the “bank” row, as in Step 6 above: e to the power of 0.707, 2.121 and 0.707 gives 2.028, 8.342 and 2.028. They add to 12.398. Dividing: 2.028 ÷ 12.398 = 0.164, 8.342 ÷ 12.398 = 0.673, and 0.164 again. (They add to 1.001 only because of rounding; exactly, they add to 1.)

The next table holds the attention weights. Each row is the word doing the looking. Each cell is the share of its attention it gives to the word in that column. Every row adds up to 1.

Attention weights \(\alpha_{ij}\) the river bank
the 1 0 0
river 0.5 0.5 0
bank 0.164 0.673 0.164

(The symbol \(\alpha_{ij}\) in the corner is explained in the formula section below; it means “the share word in row \(i\) gives to word in column \(j\)”.)

How to read it: “the” can only see itself, so it gives itself 100% (a weight of 1). “river” has two equal scores (0.707 and 0.707), so it splits 50/50 between “the” and itself. “bank” gives most of its attention, 67%, to “river”.

Step 4: mix the values for “bank”. Take each value list, multiply it by its share, then add:

  • 0.164 of “the”’s value [0.5, 0.5] = [0.082, 0.082].
  • 0.673 of “river”’s value [0, 2] = [0, 1.346].
  • 0.164 of “bank”’s own value [2, 1] = [0.328, 0.164].
  • First numbers added: 0.082 + 0 + 0.328 = 0.410.
  • Second numbers added: 0.082 + 1.346 + 0.164 = 1.592.

In one line: \(0.164 \times [0.5, 0.5] + 0.673 \times [0, 2] + 0.164 \times [2, 1] \approx [0.41, 1.59]\).

What it means. “bank” started with the value [2, 1]: more money than nature. Its new, contextual list is about [0.41, 1.59]: now more nature than money. Looking at “river” pulled its meaning towards the riverside. This is the course’s picture of “bank” moving towards “water”, done with numbers. (All numbers checked in Python.)

A tiny positional-encoding example (our illustration, using the course’s formula, which comes in the next section). Say each list has 4 slots, numbered 0, 1, 2 and 3. Take the word in position 1.

  • Slots 0 and 1 use a “speed” of 1. So slot 0 gets sine(1) = 0.841, and slot 1 gets cosine(1) = 0.540.
  • Slots 2 and 3 use a slower speed, 0.01. So slot 2 gets sine(0.01) = 0.010, and slot 3 gets cosine(0.01) = 1.000.

So position 1’s list is [0.841, 0.540, 0.010, 1.000]. Position 2 gives [0.909, −0.416, 0.020, 1.000]. (A calculator gives the sine and cosine values; you never work them out by hand.) Each position gets its own pattern, and that pattern is added to the word’s list, slot by slot.

The formula, explained

The exam has not asked for calculations (2025 had none). But writing the attention formula and naming its parts can strengthen an answer about self-attention. Aim to understand every line; being able to write the first four is a bonus.

Making query, key and value. Each word’s embedding is multiplied by three learned tables to give its query, key and value.

\[q_i = x_i W^Q \qquad k_i = x_i W^K \qquad v_i = x_i W^V\]

  • \(i\) = which word we mean: word 1, word 2, and so on.
  • \(x_i\) = the embedding of word (token) \(i\), a row of \(d\) numbers.
  • \(d\) (also written \(d_{model}\)) = the length of a word’s embedding, typically 512.
  • \(W^Q, W^K, W^V\) = the three learned weight matrices (tables) that turn \(x_i\) into a query, a key and a value. \(W^Q\) and \(W^K\) have \(d\) rows and \(d_k\) columns; \(W^V\) has \(d\) rows and \(d_v\) columns. The course: “Typical sizes are \(d = 512\) and \(d_k = d_v = 64\).”
  • \(d_k\) = the length of each query and key; \(d_v\) = the length of each value (both typically 64).
  • \(q_i\) = word \(i\)’s query (“what am I looking for?”); \(k_i\) = its key (“what do I offer?”); \(v_i\) = its value (“my content”).

Read aloud: “Word \(i\)’s query, key and value are its embedding times three learned tables.”

The match score. The score between word \(i\) and word \(j\) is the dot product of \(i\)’s query and \(j\)’s key, divided by the square root of the key length.

\[\text{score}(x_i, x_j) = \frac{q_i \cdot k_j}{\sqrt{d_k}}\]

  • \(j\) = the word being looked at (word \(i\) is the one doing the looking).
  • \(q_i \cdot k_j\) = the dot product: multiply matching slots and add. Large means a good match.
  • \(\sqrt{d_k}\) = the square root of the key length; dividing by it scales the scores down (the “Scale” box in the course’s diagram).

The shares. Softmax turns word \(i\)’s row of scores into attention shares that are positive and add up to 1.

\[\alpha_{ij} = \text{softmax}(\text{score}(x_i, x_j))\]

  • \(\alpha_{ij}\) (Greek letter alpha) = the attention weight: how much word \(i\) attends to word \(j\). In the example, “bank” gives “river” 0.673.
  • softmax = the rule that turns a row of scores into positive weights that add up to 1. It is taken over all \(j\), for each \(i\).

The new list. Word \(i\)’s new list is the sum of the values of itself and the earlier words, each multiplied by its share.

\[\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i = \sum_{j \le i} \alpha_{ij}\, v_j\]

  • \(\sum\) (Greek capital sigma) = “add up all of these”.
  • \(j \le i\) = only the word itself and earlier words. This is the causal version. For bidirectional attention the sum runs over all \(j\).
  • \(\boldsymbol{\alpha}_i\) (bold alpha) = the new, context-aware list for word \(i\).

Read the four lines aloud in one sentence: “For each word, compare its query with the key of every allowed word, scale by the square root of \(d_k\), turn the scores into weights with softmax, and take the weighted average of those words’ values.”

The same thing for all words at once (matrix form). The Transformer lecture shows this only as a chart of boxes: MatMul (multiply tables) → Scale → Mask (optional) → SoftMax → MatMul. The next lecture writes it as a formula for cross-attention, which is attention where the words being written look at the words of another text, for example the sentence being translated [Not in course files — general knowledge: the translation example]:

\[\text{softmax}\left(\frac{QK'}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

  • \(Q\), \(K\), \(V\) = tables holding all the queries, all the keys and all the values, one row per word.
  • \(K'\) = the key table turned on its side (rows become columns), so that \(QK'\) gives the whole table of dot products at once: the score matrix, one row per looking word and one column per looked-at word.

Either form is fine in the exam; the one-word-at-a-time form above is the one the Transformer lecture uses.

What goes into the first block. The course builds the input like this. Each token is first written as a one-hot list: all zeros except a single 1 that marks which token it is, like ticking one box on a long form. Stacking these gives a table with \(N\) rows and \(|V|\) columns. Multiplying it by the embedding matrix \(E\) (\(|V|\) rows, \(d\) columns) gives a table with \(N\) rows and \(d\) columns.

  • \(N\) = how many tokens are in the text.
  • \(|V|\) = how many tokens are in the vocabulary (all the tokens the model knows).
  • \(E\) = the embedding matrix, one row per vocabulary token.

In plain words: each of the \(N\) tokens picks out its own row from the lookup table \(E\), so you get one embedding row per token. “But, to this input matrix we also add so-called positional embeddings.”

One Transformer block. First, let each word look at all the words (multi-head attention), then add the original input back, then tidy the numbers with layer normalization.

\[T^1 = \text{MultiHeadAttention}(x_i, [x_1, \ldots, x_N]) \quad T^2 = T_1 + X \quad T^3 = \text{LayerNorm}(T^2)\]

Next, run each word through the small feed-forward network, add its input back again, and tidy once more. The result \(H\) is what this block hands to the next block.

\[T^4 = \text{FFN}(T^3) \quad T^5 = T^4 + T^3 \quad H = \text{LayerNorm}(T^5)\]

  • \(T^1, \ldots, T^5\) = the in-between results, step by step (the small number on top is a step number, not a power). The slide writes \(T_1\) with a small number below in line 2; it is the same \(T^1\).
  • \(X\) = the input embeddings (all the \(x_i\) together).
  • \([x_1, \ldots, x_N]\) = all \(N\) words of the text, which each word may look at.
  • \(+ X\) and \(+ T^3\) = the residual connections (adding the input back).
  • \(H\) = the block’s output.

Read aloud: “Attention, add back, normalize; feed-forward, add back, normalize.”

Multi-head attention in symbols: each head, numbered \(c\), has its own tables \(W^Q_c, W^K_c, W^V_c\). With \(h\) heads, the glued outputs form a table of \(N\) rows and \(h \times d_v\) columns (\(N \times hd_v\)). A final learned table \(W^O\) projects this back to length \(d\).

Sinusoidal positional encoding. The even-numbered slots of a position’s list are filled with a sine wave value that depends on the position and on the slot:

\[PE_{(pos,2i)} = \sin\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right) \quad \text{even positions}\]

The odd-numbered slots are filled the same way, but with a cosine wave instead:

\[PE_{(pos,2i+1)} = \cos\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d_{model}}}\right) \quad \text{odd positions}\]

  • \(PE\) = the positional encoding, the position’s list of numbers.
  • \(pos\) = the token’s position in the sequence (1st, 2nd, …).
  • \(i\) here = which pair of slots we are filling. \(2i\) is an even slot and gets a sine; \(2i+1\) is an odd slot and gets a cosine. (Careful: the slide labels these “even/odd positions”, but they are even/odd dimensions of the embedding. Write “dimensions” in the exam.)
  • \(d_{model}\) = the length of the word embeddings (the same as \(d\)).
  • \(10000^{2i/d_{model}}\) = sets the wave’s speed. In the example, with \(d_{model} = 4\): slots 0 and 1 use \(1/10000^{0} = 1\), and slots 2 and 3 use \(1/10000^{2/4} = 0.01\).

Read aloud: “Fill the position list with sine and cosine waves of different speeds, so every position gets a unique pattern.”

The course lists three advantages:

  • Uniqueness: each position has its own list.
  • Relative positions: “the sum of two sinusoids is another sinusoid”, so the model can tell how far apart words are.
  • Scalability: it works for texts longer than those seen in training.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025 Q4(d): “Describe in intuitive terms the motivation for the self-attention layer within the Transformer block.”

In plain words: why does the model need a step where each word looks at the other words? The marking guide wants three things:

  • Query, Key and Value named (what a word is looking for, the label each word shows, and the information each word hands over).
  • The information-retrieval (database search) analogy.
  • The idea that “one token [attends] to earlier/later tokens with varying weights”: each word pays more attention to some words than to others.

Model answer A word’s meaning depends on its context: “bank” means something different next to “water” than next to “credit”, and the helpful words can be far away in the sentence (Lecture 8, slides 7–9). Self-attention lets each token build a new, context-specific embedding by looking at the other tokens with different weights. It works like retrieving from a database: each token’s Query is compared with every token’s Key by a dot product, softmax turns these scores into weights that sum to one, and the new representation is the weighted sum of the Values. Because all tokens are processed in parallel, this handles long-range dependencies and makes training efficient (slide 15).

What this answer is saying, in plain words: The same word can mean different things, and the clue can be far away in the sentence. Self-attention lets each word check all the other words and mix in information from the useful ones. It works like a search: each word sends out a question, compares it with every word’s label, and takes more from the best matches. All words do this at once, which makes it fast and lets far-apart words connect.

2025 Q4(b): “Why do we typically add positional information to the embeddings entering a Large Language Model?”

Model answer (the 2025 marking guide’s answer): self-attention “does not necessarily identify the ordering of the terms. Yet, the ordering is crucial for the meaning”.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Attention looks at all the words at once, so on its own it cannot tell which word came first. But order changes meaning: “The cat chased the dog” is not “The dog chased the cat”. So a position list is added to each word’s list. A strong answer also says the position list is added to the word embedding, and that the original Transformer built it from sine and cosine waves.

2025 T/F (a): “In the Transformer’s self-attention mechanism, you can have two types of attention; causal- and bidirectional-attention.”

Model answer True.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Both kinds exist. Causal: each word looks only at itself and earlier words. Bidirectional: each word looks both ways.

2025 T/F (i): “Multi-head attention mechanisms makes estimation of Large Language Models slower and less efficient.”

Model answer False.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: “Estimation” means training. The heads run at the same time (in parallel), and parallel processing is a source of training efficiency. Extra heads add more ways to spot patterns; they do not slow the model down.

Likely new True/False items:

  • “Masking hides earlier words” → False. It hides future (later) words.
  • “The feed-forward layer adds non-linearity” → True. It lets the model capture curved, more complex patterns, not only straight-line ones.
  • “Positional vectors are concatenated” (glued on the end) → False. They are added.

What a top-grade answer must include

For self-attention:

  • The problem: a word’s meaning depends on context (for example “bank” by a river vs a bank for money), and the helpful words can be far apart.
  • Query, Key and Value with the database analogy: the Query is your search, the Keys are the labels on the files (or book spines), the Values are what is inside.
  • The steps: dot-product scores (a match score between a Query and each Key) → softmax weights (scores turned into shares that add up to 1) → weighted sum of values (mix the Values using those shares).
  • The result is a context-specific embedding: a new list of numbers for the word that fits this sentence.
  • Bonus: all words are handled at the same time (parallel processing), and far-apart words can still link up (long-range dependencies).

For positional encoding:

  • Attention processes all tokens at once, so it is blind to word order.
  • Order changes meaning: “The cat chased the dog” vs “The dog chased the cat”.
  • A position list (numbers standing for “1st place”, “2nd place” and so on; built from sine waves, called sinusoidal, in the original Transformer) is added to each token’s embedding.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Explaining attention without naming Query, Key and Value. The 2025 marking guide asks for them.
  • Saying causal masking hides past words. It hides future words.
  • Saying multi-head attention is slower, or that self-attention reads one word at a time. It works on all words in parallel.
  • Saying positional encoding is needed “because words have different meanings”. That is attention’s job. Positional encoding is about order.
  • Saying word2vec-style vectors (the older one-list-per-word method) already depend on context. They do not: each word gets one fixed list, whatever the sentence.

Key terms to use

  • contextual (context-specific) embeddings — word numbers that change with the sentence
  • self-attention — each word looks at the other words
  • query, key, value — what I seek, my label, what I share
  • dot product — multiply-and-add score of how well lists match
  • compatibility score — how well a Query matches a Key
  • scaling by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) — dividing scores by square root of key length
  • softmax weights — scores turned into shares adding to 1
  • weighted sum of values — mixing the Values using those shares
  • causal vs bidirectional — look back only vs look both ways
  • masking the future, \(-\infty\) — later words get minus infinity, so zero weight
  • multi-head attention, parallel heads, more representation capacity — several attention steps side by side
  • residual connection — adding a step’s input back onto its output
  • layer normalization — rescaling numbers to a steady range
  • feed-forward, adds non-linearity — small extra network for curved patterns
  • positional encoding/embedding, added to token embeddings — position numbers added to each word’s numbers
  • sinusoidal — built from sine and cosine waves

Quick self-test

  1. “In the Transformer’s self-attention mechanism, you can have two types of attention; causal- and bidirectional-attention.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Self-attention is the step where each word looks at the other words to work out its meaning. Causal attention: each word may only look at the words before it (and itself). Bidirectional attention: each word may look both backwards and forwards. Do both kinds exist?

    Answer: True. Why: Think of reading a mystery novel. A model that writes text word by word must read like a first-time reader: no peeking at later pages, because they are not written yet. That is causal. A model that only needs to understand a finished text can read the whole page in both directions. That is bidirectional.

  2. “Multi-head attention makes estimation of LLMs slower and less efficient.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Multi-head” means doing the attention step several times side by side; each copy is a “head” and can look for a different kind of link between words. “Estimation” means training. Does having several heads make training slow and wasteful?

    Answer: False. Why: The heads work at the same time (in parallel), not one after another. Think of four friends each searching one room for lost keys, all at once: it is not slower than one person, and you cover more ground. The extra heads give the model more ways to spot patterns (more “representation capacity”).

  3. “In causal attention, the scores for future words are set to −∞ before the softmax.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Each word gives every other word a score for how well it matches. Softmax is the step that turns scores into shares that add up to 1 (like 70%, 20%, 10%). −∞ means minus infinity, lower than any number. Before turning scores into shares, are later words given the lowest possible score?

    Answer: True. Why: After softmax, a score of minus infinity becomes a share of exactly zero. So future words get zero attention. It is like blacking out the rest of the sentence with a marker so the word cannot peek ahead.

  4. “Positional embeddings are added to the word embeddings.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A word embedding is a list of numbers that stands for a word. A positional embedding is a list of numbers that stands for a place in the sentence (1st, 2nd, 3rd and so on). “Added” means you add the two lists slot by slot, giving one list. Is the place information added on top of the word information?

    Answer: True. Why: Attention on its own cannot tell word order, but order matters (“the cat chased the dog” vs “the dog chased the cat”). So each word’s numbers get its position’s numbers added on top, like stamping a seat number onto each ticket. The list stays the same length; nothing is stuck on the end. The course calls the result “word + position”.

  5. “Explain in 2–5 sentences (2025 Q4d): What is the motivation for the self-attention layer?”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Motivation” means the reason it exists. Why does an LLM need a step where the words look at each other?

    Answer: Write the 2025 Q4(d) model answer given above: context changes meaning (“bank” near “water” vs near “credit”), so each token builds a context-specific embedding by comparing its Query with every Key (dot product), turning the scores into weights with softmax, and taking the weighted sum of the Values; all tokens are processed in parallel, which handles long-range dependencies and makes training efficient. Why: This hits all three things the marking guide asks for: Query, Key and Value named; the database (search) analogy; and each token attending to other tokens with different weights.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • Token: a piece of text the model works with, usually a word or part of a word. “bank” is one token.
  • LLM (large language model): a program that writes text by guessing the next token, again and again. ChatGPT is one.
  • Vector: a list of numbers, like [2, 1].
  • Dimension: one slot in a vector. In [2, 1], the first dimension is 2 and the second is 1.
  • Embedding / word embedding: a list of numbers that stands for a word, so the computer can calculate with it. Words with similar meanings get similar lists.
  • Matrix: a table of numbers with rows and columns.
  • Embedding matrix (\(E\)): the big lookup table with one row (one embedding) for each token in the vocabulary.
  • word2vec: an older method that learns one fixed vector per word, whatever sentence it is in.
  • Contextual (context-specific) embedding: a word’s vector after it has looked at its neighbours, so “bank” by a river and “bank” with money get different vectors.
  • Transformer: the model design built from attention layers that all modern LLMs use.
  • Layer / block: one stage of processing. A Transformer block is one full round of attention plus the extra steps; models stack many of them.
  • Attention / self-attention: the step where each word looks at the other words in the same text and mixes in information from the relevant ones. “Self” because the words look at their own sentence.
  • Query: the word’s question, “what am I looking for?”. The question you bring to the library.
  • Key: each word’s label, “what do I offer?”. The label on a book’s spine.
  • Value: each word’s actual content that gets passed on. The text inside the book.
  • Database / information retrieval analogy: the course’s picture of attention as looking things up: match a question to labels, then fetch the contents.
  • Weight matrix (\(W^Q, W^K, W^V, W^O\)): a learned table of numbers that turns one list into another, like a recipe that turns a word’s embedding into its query.
  • Learned: set by training, not written by hand.
  • Training: the long process where the model adjusts its numbers on huge amounts of text.
  • Parameters: all the learned numbers in the model, including these weight matrices.
  • Dot product: multiply two lists number by number and add up the results. [1, 1] with [2, 1] gives 1×2 + 1×1 = 3. Bigger means a better match.
  • Compatibility score: the course’s name for the match score from the dot product.
  • Square root: the number that, times itself, gives the original. The square root of 9 is 3; of 2 it is about 1.414.
  • Scaling / \(\sqrt{d_k}\): dividing the scores by the square root of the key length, to keep them from getting too big.
  • \(d\), \(d_k\), \(d_v\): lengths of lists. \(d\) = length of a word’s embedding (typically 512); \(d_k\) = length of each query and key; \(d_v\) = length of each value (both typically 64).
  • \(d_{model}\): another name for \(d\), the length of the word embeddings.
  • Softmax: a rule that turns any row of scores into positive shares that add up to 1. Bigger scores get bigger shares. Scores 0.707, 2.121, 0.707 become 0.164, 0.673, 0.164.
  • e / exponential: e is a fixed number, about 2.718. Softmax raises e to the power of each score, which makes every result positive.
  • Attention weight (\(\alpha_{ij}\)): the share of attention word \(i\) gives to word \(j\). In the example, “bank” gives “river” 0.673.
  • Weighted sum / weighted average: adding things up after multiplying each by its share, like a course grade where the exam counts 60% and the project 40%.
  • Causal attention: each word may look only at itself and earlier words, never later ones. Used by models that write text left to right.
  • Bidirectional attention: each word may look at all words, before and after it.
  • Mask / masking: hiding some words from the comparison, here the future words, by setting their scores to minus infinity.
  • Minus infinity (\(-\infty\)): a “smaller than any number” value. After softmax it becomes a share of exactly 0.
  • Score matrix / diagonal: the table of all match scores, one row per looking word and one column per looked-at word. The diagonal is the line from top left to bottom right where each word meets itself; “above the diagonal” means later words.
  • Multi-head attention / head: running several attention steps side by side; each one is a “head” with its own tables and can notice a different kind of link.
  • Concatenate: glue lists end to end. Gluing [1, 2] and [3, 4] gives [1, 2, 3, 4].
  • Projection: multiplying by one more learned table (\(W^O\)) to bring the glued list back to its original length.
  • Syntactic / semantic: syntactic = about grammar (who does what to whom); semantic = about meaning.
  • Robustness: still working well when the input changes a little.
  • Residual connection: adding a step’s input back onto its output, a shortcut so useful information is not lost on the way through many layers.
  • Layer normalization (Layer Norm): rescaling the numbers in each word’s list to a standard range, so training stays steady [Not in course files — general knowledge: what the rescaling does; the slide says it “makes training … easier”].
  • Feed-forward network (FFN): a small extra calculation applied to each word on its own after attention.
  • Linear / non-linearity: a linear step only multiplies and adds, so it can only bend things in straight-line ways. A non-linearity lets the model capture curved, more complex patterns.
  • Deep neural network: a model made of many stacked layers of simple calculations.
  • Feature / representation: a piece of information the model has worked out about a word, stored as numbers.
  • Positional encoding / positional embedding: a list of numbers that says “this is word number 1, 2, 3…”, added to each word’s embedding so the model knows word order.
  • Composite embedding: word vector plus position vector added together.
  • Absolute vs relative position: absolute = “this is word 5”; relative = “this word is 2 places after that one”.
  • Sinusoidal / sine / cosine: sine and cosine are smooth wave patterns that go up and down between −1 and 1. Sinusoidal encoding fills the position list with such waves of different speeds. Position 1 with 4 slots gives [0.841, 0.540, 0.010, 1.000].
  • One-hot: a list that is all zeros except a single 1 that marks which token it is, like ticking one box on a long form.
  • \(N\) and \(|V|\): \(N\) = how many tokens are in the text; \(|V|\) = how many tokens are in the vocabulary.
  • Encoder / decoder: two halves of the original Transformer. The encoder reads and understands the input; the decoder writes output one token at a time, using causal attention [Not in course files — general knowledge: the encoder’s role; Lecture 9 slide 17 names the decoder’s causal self-attention layer].
  • Cross-attention: attention where the words being written look at the words of another text, for example the sentence being translated [Not in course files — general knowledge: the translation example].
  • GPT-style / BERT-style models: GPT-style models write text and use causal attention; BERT-style models read and understand text and use bidirectional attention [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Long-range dependency: a link between words far apart, like “it” pointing back to “animal” many words earlier.
  • Parallel processing: doing many calculations at the same time instead of one after another.
  • GPU: a computer chip that does thousands of simple sums at once, which suits parallel attention [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Training efficiency: how much learning you get for a given amount of computer time.
  • Interpretability: being able to see why the model did something. Attention weights show which words a word looked at.
  • Prediction: the model’s guess, here the guess of the next token.

Sources: Lecture 8 “Transformers” (Leif Anders Thorsrud, Lecture_llm_transformer.pdf), slides 3, 5–20; Lecture 9 “LLMs: Input and output” (Lecture_llm_inputoutput.pdf), slides 5–8, 17 and 18; 2025 exam evaluation guidelines Q4(b), Q4(d).

17. Critical issues around LLMs (the “ESG” question)

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q4(a) (5 points) asked for two ESG issues.

Why this exists

Picture a Norwegian bank that puts a ChatGPT-style assistant on its website to answer customers. At first everyone is happy. Then awkward questions pop up.

  • The assistant runs in huge halls full of computers that use a lot of electricity.
  • One day it tells a customer about a fee that does not exist.
  • Customers type their account details into it, and those words travel to another company’s computers.
  • Only a handful of companies in the world can build an assistant this good, so the bank depends on one of them.

Each of these is a real worry. The exam asks you to name and explain such worries under three headings that companies use for risks that are not about money: Environmental, Social and Governance, or ESG for short.

The idea in everyday words

What an LLM is, and the two ways it uses computers

An LLM (large language model) is a program like ChatGPT. It writes text by guessing the most likely next word, over and over, based on the huge amounts of text it learned from.

It uses computers in two ways:

  • Training: the long, one-off process of building the model. Thousands of computer chips adjust the model’s numbers on huge amounts of text, for weeks.
  • Inference: using the finished model to answer. This happens again for every question from every user, so the course speaks of repeated inference.

Keep both in mind. Many exam traps hide in the idea that only training costs anything.

Three headings: E, S and G

Think of a new factory in town.

  • E (Environmental): it uses lots of electricity and water. This heading is about nature and resources.
  • S (Social): its products are mostly great but sometimes faulty, and a faulty product can hurt people. This heading is about people and society.
  • G (Governance): one or two owners control it, it holds customers’ personal data, and the government has rules about what it may do. This heading is about rules, control and who is in charge.

An LLM raises the same three kinds of worries.

The course groups the worries into four questions. These are its exact words:

  • “Sustainability: What resources do training and repeated inference consume?”
  • “Ownership and Control: Who controls the models, infrastructure, and access?”
  • “Reliability: Are outputs accurate, supported by evidence, and appropriate for the task?”
  • “Privacy and Security: Where does data go, and what can a connected system do with it?”

The 2025 exam called these “Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) issues”. The 2026 slides never use the word “ESG”. So you sort the course’s topics into E, S and G yourself. The walk-through below shows how. Here is each worry, one at a time.

E: sustainability (how much power, water and material it uses)

Sustainability means using resources in a way the planet can keep up with. Resources here are what gets used up to run the model: electricity, water, chips, money and people’s time.

The course says: “Both training and inference consume electricity; cooling, water use, and chip production also matter.” Computers get hot, and cooling them often uses water. The chips themselves have to be made, which also costs resources. All of this adds to the model’s carbon footprint: the amount of greenhouse gas released because of it, for example from making the electricity it uses.

How big is that footprint? The course says it “varies with model size, hardware, workload, and the electricity supply”. Hardware is the physical computers. Workload is how much work they are given. Electricity supply is where the power comes from: wind and water power, or coal. For the same reason, the course warns: “No universal carbon cost per prompt.” (A prompt is the text you type into the model.)

Some ways of using a model need more computing for each job:

  • “Reasoning, long contexts, and repeated agent steps can increase computation per task.”
  • Reasoning (at answer time) means the model writes hidden “thinking” text before its final answer.
  • A long context means giving the model a lot of text to read at once.
  • An agent is a setup where the model repeats a loop of deciding and using tools until a job is done; each round of the loop is an agent step.
  • On the other side: “Efficient models can reduce it.” An efficient model does the same job with less computing.

How should you compare models fairly? The course says: “Compare resources per successfully completed task; include retries and human checking.” Retries means asking again because the first answer was not good enough. So you count the cost per finished job, including every failed try and the time a person spends checking. The walk-through below shows why with numbers.

The course ends with a discussion question: “If each request becomes cheaper, what happens when usage grows?” When something gets cheaper, people tend to use it much more, so total resource use can still rise. This is called the rebound effect [Not in course files — general knowledge].

S: reliability (can you trust what it says?)

Reliability means whether the answers are correct, backed by evidence, and fit for the task.

The model picks likely next words. So it writes what sounds right, not what has been checked. The course names two problems:

  • “Hallucinations: Models can invent facts, numbers, quotations, and references, even when they sound confident.” A hallucination is the model inventing something untrue, like a book that does not exist, while sounding sure.
  • “Bias and sensitivity: Outputs can reflect training biases and change with wording or context.” Bias is a systematic slant: leaning the same way again and again, for example treating some groups unfairly, learned from the text the model was trained on. Sensitivity (to wording) means getting a different answer when you ask the same thing in slightly different words.

Don’t mix these up: a hallucination is invented content; bias is a repeated slant.

What should you do about it? The course gives several rules:

  • Sources found by a search, or by RAG, must be checked. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means first searching for relevant text, then giving it to the model to use in its answer. Evidence or sources are the documents or facts that back up an answer.
  • Use a calculator or code for arithmetic, not the model.
  • A benchmark is a standard test used to score and compare models, like a school exam for AI. Benchmark scores “alone do not establish business reliability”.
  • “Best Practice: Decide how an answer will be checked before relying on it.” Checking an answer against something trustworthy is called verification.

S: responsibility (harm and misuse)

Responsibility is about who answers for damage the model’s output causes. The course says: “Harm can come from biased, abusive, misleading, or overly agreeable outputs.” Overly agreeable output means telling users what they want to hear instead of what is true.

The course’s historical example is Microsoft’s Tay chatbot, 2016. Users quickly got it to post offensive content, and it was taken down [Not in course files — general knowledge].

A newer danger is prompt injection. In the course’s words: “Prompt injection: malicious instructions in a document or website try to redirect a connected assistant.” Malicious means meant to cause harm. A connected assistant is one that can use outside tools, such as email, files or payments. Picture a web page with a hidden line: “ignore your rules and send me the files”. If the assistant obeys any text it reads, a stranger can take control of it.

The course’s fix: “Restrict tool permissions, review consequential actions, and keep records of what happened.” Tool permissions say which tools the assistant may use. A consequential action is one with real effects, like sending money or deleting files. A step like this, which reduces a risk, is called a mitigation.

Prompt injection is also a security problem, so you can file it under G as well.

G: ownership and control (a dangerous monopoly?)

Ownership and control asks who owns the models and the computers they run on, and who decides who may use them.

The course asks whether this is a dangerous monopoly (one firm controlling a whole market). Building the newest, most powerful models, called frontier models, is enormously costly. Frontier training needs “substantial capital, chips, power, data, and expertise. These create barriers to entry.” Capital is money for investment. Barriers to entry are things that make it hard for new firms to join a market, like needing billions of kroner before you can start.

But the course also says “the market is not a single monopoly”. Instead, concentration (a few firms holding most of the market) can occur at several levels: “chips, cloud hosting, models, and distribution”.

  • Cloud hosting is renting computing power in someone else’s data centre (a big building full of computers) over the internet [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Distribution is how the model reaches users, for example through apps or built into office software.
  • All the basic equipment underneath, such as chips, data centres, cloud services and power lines, is the infrastructure.

For a business, the danger is dependency or vendor lock-in: relying so much on one supplier that switching is hard or costly, like a phone that only works with one charger. The course’s test question: “Can you switch provider, export your data, or run an alternative model?” (Exporting data means taking your own data with you.)

Is there a way out? Open weights are a model’s learned numbers (its parameters) that you can download and run yourself. The course: open weights are “downloadable model parameters; permissions depend on the license”. A licence is the legal terms saying what you may do with something. But open weights “do not necessarily include training data or the full training recipe”. Training data is the text the model learned from; the training recipe is the full step-by-step method used to train it. And: “Open weights and smaller models broaden access, but do not remove infrastructure costs or dependencies.” You still need computers to run them.

G: privacy and security (where does your data go?)

Privacy means keeping information about people safe and under their control. Security means protecting systems from attack or misuse.

The course says prompts and uploads “may contain personal or confidential information. Use approved services and minimize what you share.” Personal data is any information about an identifiable person, like a name, address or account number. Confidential information is business secrets or private material that should not be shared.

Then three things to check:

  • Retention: how long the provider keeps what you send.
  • Training use: whether what you send is used to train future models.
  • Processing location: in which country the provider’s computers handle it.

These “depend on the product and contract; verify them.” Also, search tools and agents “should only access records the user is authorized to see”. Authorized means officially allowed.

The law has a say too. The course: “Regulation: GDPR applies to personal data in prompts and outputs. The EU AI Act’s obligations for general-purpose AI model providers have applied since August 2025; rules for high-risk uses were postponed in 2026 to 2027–2028.”

  • GDPR is the EU’s main law protecting personal data.
  • The EU AI Act is the EU’s law setting rules for AI systems.
  • A general-purpose AI model provider is a firm that offers a model usable for many tasks, like an LLM maker.
  • High-risk uses are uses where mistakes can seriously hurt people, such as hiring or credit decisions; stricter rules apply [Not in course files — general knowledge: the examples].

G (also S): copyright and training data used without permission

Huge amounts of text were collected to train LLMs, often without asking the authors. Copyright is the legal right of authors to control copies of their work, so this raises copyright and consent questions.

The 2025 marking guide for Q4(a) accepted this. Its words: “electricity/energy consumption and carbon footprint, large data needed - often used without permission/copy right issues. Other answers might also be ok, but need to be well grounded.”

Copyright is not on the 2026 slides. It is still a safe answer, because the 2025 marking guide accepts it. Say where it comes from. The closest 2026 slide point is that pre-training (the first, big training stage) “can also memorize examples and errors”; the course also lists “memorization” elsewhere. Memorization means the model stores exact bits of its training text and can repeat them later.

How to write the exam answer

Pick exactly the number of issues asked for. For each one:

  1. name it,
  2. give its letter (E, S or G),
  3. explain why it happens (the mechanism),
  4. give one consequence or one fix.

What the ESG sorting is good at, and where it breaks

  • Good at: giving your answer a clear structure: name the issue, give its letter, explain why it happens, add a fix.
  • Good at: covering the main course topics: sustainability, reliability, ownership and control, privacy and security.
  • Breaks: the 2026 slides never say “ESG”, so the E, S, G sorting is our own reading. Some issues fit two letters (privacy can be S or G), so explain your choice.
  • Breaks: copyright was accepted in the 2025 marking guide but is not on the 2026 slides, so say where it comes from.

Walk-through example

Example 1: sorting the course’s issues into E, S and G. The course gives the issues; the E/S/G sorting is our reading, because the slides do not use “ESG”.

In the table below, each row is one issue. The first column is its ESG letter. The second is the course’s name for the issue. The third says where it comes from. The last is one concrete point you could write in the exam.

ESG letter (rows) Course issue Where it comes from One concrete point to write
E Environmental Sustainability 2026 slides Electricity for training and inference; cooling, water, chip production; more reasoning/agent steps = more compute
S Social Reliability (hallucination, bias) 2026 slides Invented facts and references said with confidence; outputs reflect training biases
S Social Responsibility (abuse, Tay, prompt injection) 2026 slides Tay 2016; biased, abusive or “overly agreeable” outputs
G Governance Ownership and control / dangerous monopoly 2026 slides Barriers to entry; concentration in chips, cloud, models; lock-in; open weights only partly help
G Governance Privacy and security, regulation 2026 slides Personal data in prompts → GDPR; EU AI Act; agents’ access rights; prompt injection as a security risk
G (also S) Copyright / training data without permission 2025 marking guide only Large training sets often used without permission

Privacy and prompt injection can be argued as S (harm to people) or G (rules, control, security). Either works if you explain your choice.

Example 2: why you count “per successfully completed task”. These are made-up numbers (our own illustration). In the table, each row is one model. The columns show how much energy one try uses, how often a try succeeds, and the energy per finished job. “Unit” is any fixed amount of energy.

Model (rows) Energy per try Share of tries that succeed Energy per finished job
A 1 unit 50% (half) 2 units
B 1.5 units 100% (all) 1.5 units

Here is where the last column comes from.

  1. Model A. Say you try 10 times. Half succeed, so you get 5 finished jobs. You used 10 × 1 = 10 units. That is 10 ÷ 5 = 2 units per finished job. (Shorter: on average a job needs 2 tries, so 1 ÷ 0.5 = 2.)
  2. Model B. Try 10 times. All 10 succeed. You used 10 × 1.5 = 15 units. That is 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5 units per finished job. (Shorter: 1.5 ÷ 1 = 1.5.)
  3. Compare. A looks cheaper per try (1 unit against 1.5), but B is cheaper per finished job (1.5 units against 2). Counting only the price of one try gives the wrong winner.

That is exactly why the course says to compare “per successfully completed task; include retries”.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025 Q4(a) (5 points): “We discussed several Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) issues related to Large Language Models in this course. Discuss shortly two of these.”

In plain words: pick two worries about LLMs, say which heading each belongs to (environment, people and society, or control and rules), and explain each. “Discuss” means explain, not list. Here is a full answer with two issues, plus an alternative second issue.

Model answer Issue 1 — Environmental: energy and carbon footprint. Both training and using (inference) an LLM consume a lot of electricity, and cooling, water use and chip production add to the footprint (Lecture 7, slide 22). The footprint depends on model size, hardware, workload and how clean the electricity is, and reasoning, long contexts and repeated agent steps raise the computation per task. A firm should therefore compare resource use per successfully completed task, including retries and human checks, and choose an efficient or smaller model where it is good enough. Also, as requests get cheaper, total use may grow, so the overall footprint can still rise.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Building the model and every single answer both use a lot of power, plus water for cooling and materials for the chips. How much depends on the model, the computers and whether the power is clean. Long “thinking” answers and agents use more. So measure the cost per finished job, pick a smaller model if it does the job, and remember that cheaper use can mean much more use.

Model answer Issue 2 — Social: reliability (hallucination and bias). LLMs can invent facts, numbers, quotations and references while sounding confident, and their outputs can reflect biases in the training data and change with the wording of the prompt (slide 26). This can mislead customers or decision makers and treat groups unfairly; the Tay chatbot in 2016 showed how quickly a system can produce abusive content (slide 23). The mitigation is to decide how an answer will be checked before relying on it: check sources, use code or a calculator for numbers, and keep human review for consequential decisions.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: The model can make things up while sounding sure, and it can repeat unfair slants from the text it learned from. That can mislead people and treat groups unfairly, as the Tay chatbot showed. The fix is to plan how you will check an answer before you trust it.

Model answer Alternative second issue — Governance: copyright and data use (accepted by the 2025 guideline, not on the 2026 slides). LLMs need very large training datasets, and these are often collected without the permission of the authors, which raises copyright and consent questions. Because pre-training can also memorise examples (slide 4), a model may reproduce protected or personal text in its output.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Models learn from huge piles of text that were often taken without asking the writers. Because a model can store exact bits of that text, it may repeat someone’s protected or private words.

A likely variant: “Give one Governance issue of LLMs and explain why it matters for a business.”

Model answer Ownership and control is a governance issue: training frontier models needs huge capital, chips, power, data and expertise, which creates barriers to entry and can concentrate power at the level of chips, cloud hosting, models and apps (Lecture 7, slide 24). A firm that builds its workflows on one provider may become locked in, facing price changes or service changes it cannot control. The course’s test question is whether you “can switch provider, export your data, or run an alternative model”; open-weight and smaller models broaden access, but they do not remove infrastructure costs or dependencies.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Building top models costs huge amounts of money, chips and power, so only a few firms can do it. If your company relies on one of them, you can get stuck: they can raise prices or change the service, and you cannot stop them. The test is whether you could switch provider, take your data with you, or run another model. Smaller, open models help, but you still need computers and still depend on others.

Likely True/False items:

  • “Only training, not inference, consumes energy” → False. Using the model (inference) uses electricity too.
  • “Open weights always include the training data” → False. You get the model’s learned numbers, not necessarily what it learned from.
  • “GDPR applies to personal data in prompts” → True. GDPR, the EU’s privacy law, covers personal data in what you type and what comes back.
  • “the LLM market is a single monopoly” → False. Power is concentrated at several levels (chips, cloud, models, distribution), but there is not one single monopoly.

The business-case question too. The exam’s 2025 Block 5 was a reflection question about a real company problem (analysing customer survey answers). When you propose an LLM there, name a pitfall (a risk) from this chapter, such as hallucination (the model making things up) or privacy.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • Exactly the number of issues asked (two).
  • Each issue named and labelled E, S or G.
  • The mechanism for each, meaning why it happens. Examples: computers need power both for training and for inference (every use); models predict text that sounds right, not facts that were checked; a few firms own the chips and the models; prompts carry personal data.
  • One consequence or mitigation for each: what goes wrong, or how to reduce it.
  • Energy/carbon is the safest first choice, because the 2025 marking guide names it. For the second, pick copyright (also in the 2025 guide) or any well-grounded issue from the course (reliability, ownership and control, privacy).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Listing four issues in one line each with no explanation. “Discuss” means explain.
  • Saying only training costs energy. Using the model costs energy too.
  • Writing vague “ESG” issues (“AI is dangerous”) with no mechanism (no why).
  • Stating copyright is on the 2026 slides. It is not. Say it is a well-known issue that was accepted in the 2025 marking.
  • Confusing hallucination (inventing content) with bias (a systematic slant: leaning the same way again and again).

Key terms to use

  • sustainability — not using up what the future needs
  • electricity for training and inference — power for learning and for every use
  • cooling, water, chip production — hidden resource costs behind the computers
  • resources per successfully completed task — cost per job done right
  • ownership and control — who owns and steers the models
  • barriers to entry — why newcomers cannot easily compete
  • concentration — power held by a few firms
  • vendor lock-in / switching provider — stuck with one supplier, hard to leave
  • open weights and licences — downloadable models and their usage rules
  • reliability — can you trust the output?
  • hallucinations — confident, made-up content
  • bias — a systematic slant in the answers
  • verification — checking outputs before you rely on them
  • responsibility — who answers when something goes wrong
  • Tay (2016) — Microsoft chatbot users steered into offensive posts
  • prompt injection — hidden instructions that hijack an assistant
  • privacy and security — protecting personal and company data
  • GDPR — EU law on personal data
  • EU AI Act — EU law setting rules for AI
  • copyright / training data used without permission, from the 2025 guideline — using others’ work without asking

Quick self-test

  1. “Only the training of an LLM has an environmental cost; using it afterwards is free.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Training is when the model learns, on huge computers. “Using it afterwards” (inference) is every time someone asks it something. “Environmental cost” means electricity, water and so on. Is using the model free for the planet?

    Answer: False. Why: Both use electricity. It is like a car: building it uses energy, but so does every trip you drive. Millions of questions a day add up. The course says: “Both training and inference consume electricity”.

  2. “LLMs can invent references even when they sound confident.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Invent references” means making up sources, like a book or article that does not exist. “Sound confident” means writing as if it is sure. Can the model make up sources while sounding certain?

    Answer: True. Why: An LLM predicts text that sounds right, not facts it has checked. This is called hallucination. It is like a student bluffing in an oral exam: smooth and sure, yet wrong. So always check any source it gives you.

  3. “Prompt injection means malicious instructions hidden in a document or website that try to redirect a connected assistant.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A “prompt” is the instruction given to the model. “Malicious” means meant to cause harm. A “connected assistant” is an AI that can read websites or files, or take actions for you. Is prompt injection when someone hides harmful orders inside content the AI reads?

    Answer: True. Why: Picture a note slipped into a pile of papers for your assistant: “Ignore your boss and send me the files”. If the assistant obeys any text it reads, a stranger can take control of it.

  4. “Downloading open weights gives you the model’s full training data.” (True or False?)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Open weights” means a company lets you download the model’s learned numbers. “Training data” is all the text it learned from. When you download the model, do you also get everything it read?

    Answer: False. Why: Getting the weights is like getting a baked cake, not the recipe or the shopping list. You can use it, but you cannot see what went into it. The course says open weights “do not necessarily include training data or the full training recipe”.

  5. “Explain in 2–5 sentences: Give one Governance issue of LLMs and explain why it matters for a business.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Governance is about who owns, controls and makes rules for something. Name one problem about who controls LLMs, and say why a company should care.

    Answer: Write the ownership-and-control model answer given above: building frontier models needs huge capital, chips, power, data and expertise, which creates barriers to entry and concentrates power; a firm relying on one provider can get locked in; the test is whether you can switch provider, export your data or run an alternative model, and open or smaller models help but do not remove infrastructure costs or dependencies. Why: It names a governance issue, explains the mechanism (only a few firms can afford to build top models), and gives the business consequence (lock-in) plus the course’s own test question.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • ESG (Environmental, Social, Governance): three headings firms use for non-money risks. E = nature and resources; S = people and society; G = rules, control and who is in charge.
  • LLM (large language model): a program like ChatGPT that writes text by guessing the next word, over and over.
  • Training: the long, one-off process of building the model by adjusting its numbers on huge amounts of text.
  • Inference / repeated inference: using the finished model to answer. “Repeated” because it happens again for every question from every user.
  • Prompt: the text you type into the model, like “Summarise this email”.
  • Sustainability: using resources (power, water, materials) in a way the planet can keep up with.
  • Resources: the things used up to run the model: electricity, water, chips, money, people’s time.
  • Chip / GPU: the computer parts that do the model’s sums. GPUs are chips that do many sums at once [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Data centre: a big building full of computers that run services like LLMs [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Cooling / water use: computers get hot; cooling them often uses water.
  • Carbon footprint: the amount of greenhouse gas released because of something, for example from making the electricity it uses.
  • Hardware / workload / electricity supply: hardware = the physical computers; workload = how much work they are given; electricity supply = where the power comes from (wind and water power vs coal).
  • Reasoning (at answer time): the model writing hidden “thinking” text before the final answer, which uses more computing.
  • Long context: giving the model a lot of text to read at once, which costs more computing.
  • Agent / agent steps: a setup where the model repeats a loop of deciding and using tools until a job is done. Each loop round is a step.
  • Efficient model: a model that does the same job with less computing.
  • Per successfully completed task: measuring cost per finished job, counting the failed tries and the human checks too. Model B at 1.5 units per job beats Model A at 2.
  • Retries: asking again because the first answer was not good enough.
  • Rebound effect: when something gets cheaper, people use it much more, so total use can still go up [Not in course files — general knowledge].
  • Ownership and control: who owns the models and the computers they run on, and who decides who may use them.
  • Infrastructure: the basic equipment everything runs on: chips, data centres, cloud services, power lines.
  • Frontier model / frontier training: the newest, most powerful models, and the very costly process of training them.
  • Capital: money for investment.
  • Barriers to entry: things that make it hard for new firms to join a market, like needing billions of kroner before you can start.
  • Monopoly: one firm controlling a whole market.
  • Concentration: a few firms holding most of the market at some level, such as chips or cloud hosting.
  • Cloud hosting: renting computing power in someone else’s data centre over the internet.
  • Distribution: how the model reaches users, for example through apps or built into office software.
  • Dependency / vendor lock-in: relying so much on one supplier that switching is hard or costly, like a phone that only works with one charger.
  • Switching provider / exporting data: moving to another company, and taking your own data with you.
  • Parameters: the learned numbers inside a model.
  • Open weights: a model whose learned numbers you can download and run yourself. You do not necessarily get its training data.
  • Licence: the legal terms saying what you may do with something.
  • Training data / training recipe: the text the model learned from, and the full step-by-step method used to train it.
  • Reliability: whether answers are correct, backed by evidence and fit for the task.
  • Hallucination: the model inventing facts, numbers, quotes or references that are not true, while sounding confident.
  • Bias: a systematic slant in the answers, for example treating some groups unfairly, learned from the training text.
  • Sensitivity (to wording): getting a different answer when you ask the same thing in slightly different words.
  • Evidence / sources: the documents or facts that back up an answer.
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): first search for relevant text, then give it to the model to use in its answer. The found sources still need checking.
  • Benchmark: a standard test used to score and compare models, like a school exam for AI.
  • Verification: checking an answer against something trustworthy before you rely on it.
  • Responsibility / harm: who answers for damage the model’s output causes, such as abuse, misleading claims or unfair treatment.
  • Overly agreeable output: the model telling users what they want to hear instead of what is true.
  • Tay chatbot (2016): a Microsoft chatbot on Twitter that users quickly taught to post offensive messages; it was taken down [Not in course files — general knowledge: the details].
  • Prompt injection: hidden instructions placed in a document or web page that try to take over an assistant that reads it.
  • Malicious: meant to cause harm.
  • Connected assistant / tool permissions: an assistant that can use outside tools (email, files, payments); permissions say which tools it may use.
  • Consequential action: an action with real effects, like sending money or deleting files.
  • Mitigation: a step that reduces a risk, like human checks before payments.
  • Mechanism: the reason why a problem happens, like “the model predicts likely words, not checked facts”.
  • Privacy: keeping personal information about people safe and under their control.
  • Security: protecting systems from attack or misuse.
  • Personal data: any information about an identifiable person, like a name, address or account number.
  • Confidential information: business secrets or private material that should not be shared.
  • Retention / processing location: how long the provider keeps what you send, and in which country its computers handle it.
  • Authorized: officially allowed. An assistant should only see records the user is allowed to see.
  • GDPR: the EU’s main law protecting personal data. It applies to personal data in prompts and answers.
  • EU AI Act: the EU’s law setting rules for AI systems, including duties for firms that provide general-purpose AI models.
  • General-purpose AI model provider: a firm that offers a model usable for many tasks, like an LLM maker.
  • High-risk uses: uses where mistakes can seriously hurt people, such as hiring or credit decisions; stricter rules apply [Not in course files — general knowledge: the examples].
  • Copyright: the legal right of authors to control copies of their work.
  • Pre-training: the first, big training stage, where the model learns from huge amounts of text.
  • Memorization: the model storing exact bits of its training text and repeating them later.

Sources: Lecture 7 Lecture_llm_intro.pdf, slides 4, 12, 16, 21–27; 2025 exam evaluation guidelines Q4(a).

Part V — Using LLMs: input/output, training, fine-tuning and prompting

18. What goes into and comes out of an LLM

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — good source of True/False items (temperature, greedy decoding, 512 tokens, cross-attention) and short “explain” questions.

Why this exists

Think of the keyboard on your phone. You type “See you” and it offers “tomorrow” or “soon”. It guesses the next word for you.

ChatGPT does the same thing, on a giant scale. When you ask it a question, the answer appears word by word, as if someone were typing. Each new word is a guess: “what word most likely comes next?”

A program like this is called a large language model, or LLM. It has learned from huge amounts of text to predict what text comes next. Think of it as phone autocomplete, but far bigger and far better.

Behind the screen, an LLM has a strange problem. A computer cannot read words. It can only work with numbers. So three things must happen:

  1. On the way in, your words must be turned into numbers.
  2. On the way out, numbers must be turned back into a word.
  3. At every step, the program must choose one next word out of tens of thousands of possible words.

This chapter is about those two ends (what goes in, what comes out) and about how one word gets picked.

The idea in everyday words

Step 1: cut the text into pieces

First, the text is cut into small pieces. A piece is often a whole word, like “cat”. Sometimes it is part of a word, or a punctuation mark like a comma. The word “unhappy” might become two pieces: “un” + “happy”.

These pieces have a name: tokens. The lecture stresses this on purpose: “We do not input words per se, but tokens.” So when someone says an LLM “reads words”, the correct version is that it reads tokens.

Why pieces and not whole words? The course’s tokenizer material gives the reason: cutting text into pieces “handles rare or unseen words”. A new or rare word can still be built from pieces the model already knows. This also keeps the list of pieces to a manageable size. One side effect: the course notebook notes that you pay (in money, and in space) per token, and Norwegian words or numbers often get cut into more pieces than common English words.

The model has a fixed list of all the tokens it knows. That list is called the vocabulary. It is written \(|V|\), which you read as “the number of tokens on the list”. Think of the full list of words in a dictionary.

Step 2: look up each piece in a big table

Next, each token is swapped for a list of numbers. Every token has its own fixed list, a bit like a secret code. “cat” might be (1.0, 0.0). “the” might be (0.1, 0.2).

A few names for these things:

  • A list of numbers in a fixed order is called a vector. Think of a row of measurements for one person: height, then weight.
  • The vector that stands for one token is that token’s embedding. Think of a postcode that stands for a street.
  • How many numbers are in each list is the dimension, written \(d\). The list (1.0, 0.0) has 2 numbers, so \(d = 2\).
  • A table of numbers with rows and columns is called a matrix. Think of a spreadsheet full of numbers.
  • The big lookup table, with one row of numbers per token in the vocabulary, is the embedding matrix, written \(\mathbf{E}\). It has \(|V|\) rows and \(d\) columns. Think of a phone book: name in, number out.

How does the computer “look up” a row? It writes each token as a row of zeros with a single 1 in the spot for that token. For example, with a vocabulary of four tokens (the, cat, sat, mat), “cat” becomes (0, 1, 0, 0). This kind of row is called a one-hot row (or one-hot vector). Think of a row of light switches where only one is switched on.

Multiplying a one-hot row by the table \(\mathbf{E}\) picks out exactly one row of the table: the row of that token. Every 0 wipes out its row, and the single 1 keeps one. It is like a wall of lockers where you hold only one key: only one locker opens. The slide says the one-hot rows are “just selecting … the elements in E that correspond to the sequence”. You will see this worked out with numbers below.

The slide puts the key point bluntly: “The input in the first block must be word embeddings, not words!”

Step 3: add “where am I?” numbers

The lookup gives “cat” the same numbers wherever it appears. But word order matters: “dog bites man” is not “man bites dog”.

So a second list of numbers is made for each position in the sentence: one for 1st place, one for 2nd place, and so on. Think of a seat number at a cinema. This list is called a positional embedding. In the original design, these lists are built from smooth wave shapes (sine and cosine waves). That recipe is called sinusoidal.

The important detail: the position list is added to the token’s list, number by number. It is not glued on the end. (Gluing lists end to end is called concatenating. The exam may try to trick you with that word.) After adding, each token’s list carries both “which word am I?” and “where am I?”.

Step 4: let the words talk to each other

Now the lists pass through many processing stages, one after another. Each stage is called a Transformer layer. Think of one round of discussion in a group, repeated many times.

In each layer, every token “looks at” the other tokens and updates its own numbers. For example, when the model reads “it”, it glances back to see what “it” refers to. This looking-around step is called attention (or self-attention, because the text looks at itself).

After each layer, every token holds an updated list of numbers. That list is called a hidden state. Think of it as the model’s current “notes” about that token, in light of the whole text so far.

A size limit on the input

The input cannot be endlessly long. The most tokens a model can read at once is called its maximum length, or context window. Think of the size of a desk: only so many pages fit.

The limit “really depends on the exact model”. Two famous families of models make good examples:

  • BERT is a well-known model family built to understand text, for example to judge if a review is positive. The original BERT takes 512 tokens.
  • GPT is a well-known model family built to write text. ChatGPT belongs to this family. The GPT series takes “some thousand tokens”.

Newer models have a context window from “a few thousand to about one million tokens”. The model used in the course notebook has a window of 32,768 tokens.

Why is there a limit at all? Mainly because of computer memory, the working space a computer uses while it calculates. Attention compares every token with every other token, so it needs a lot of memory for long texts.

What if your text is too long? Two things can happen. It “might be truncated automatically”, meaning the part that doesn’t fit is cut off, which can change your output. Think of a photocopier that silently drops the last page. Or it “might throw an error”.

Step 5: score every possible next word

Now comes the output. The slide says: “The output is typically a prediction: the likelihood of the next word in the sequence.”

To make that prediction, the model uses only the last token’s final notes, the hidden state of the last token after the last layer. These notes are like a summary of “the text so far”.

The model compares this summary with the row of every token in the vocabulary. Each comparison gives a raw score. A high score means “this token fits well here”. These raw scores are called logits. A logit can be any number, even a negative one. Think of a judge’s raw marks before they are turned into percentages.

The final part of the model that does this scoring is called the language modelling head (or LM head). Think of the “results board” at the end of a quiz.

Here is a neat trick. To compare the summary with every token’s row, the model reuses the very same table \(\mathbf{E}\) from step 2. It only turns the table on its side, so its rows become columns. Turning a table on its side is called taking its transpose, written \(E'\) or \(\mathbf{E}^T\). The slides call this turned table the unembedding layer: it goes from numbers back to tokens.

Using one table both to read tokens in and to score tokens out is called weight tying. It is like using one English–French dictionary to translate in both directions, instead of buying two. The slide says: “E is used to form the input and to re-shape the output. And, E can be learned during training!”

That last sentence needs two more words. A weight (or parameter) is one adjustable number inside the model, like a dial. Big models have billions of them. Training is the process that sets all these dials so the model predicts well. So “E can be learned during training” means the numbers in the table are not written by a person; training sets them.

Step 6: turn scores into chances

Raw scores are hard to use. We want chances. A probability is a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely something is. 0.665 means 66.5%, about two times in three.

The step that turns raw scores into probabilities is called softmax. It works in three moves:

  1. Make every score positive, and make bigger scores much bigger. It does this by raising a fixed number called \(e\) (about 2.718) to the power of each score. This is called exponentiating. For example, \(e^2 = 7.389\), and \(e^0 = 1\).
  2. Add up all these new numbers.
  3. Divide each one by the total.

The results are all positive and add up to 1. The full set of probabilities, one per token, is called a probability distribution. Think of a weather forecast: 70% sun, 20% cloud, 10% rain.

Step 7: pick one word

Now the model has a chance for every token. It must pick one. The rule for picking is called decoding. (Careful: “decoding” has a second meaning, explained further down.) The slides list these rules:

  • Greedy decoding: always pick the token with the highest probability. Like always ordering the most popular dish on the menu. The slide’s downside: it “produces text that is generic and often quite repetitive”.
  • Random sampling: pick a token at random, but weighted by its chances. Like drawing a ball from a bag where most balls are red, some blue, a few green. The slide’s downside: it “works bad because low probability words are chosen too often”.
  • Top-k sampling: keep only the \(k\) most likely tokens, where \(k\) is a number you choose. Throw the rest away. Then rescale the kept chances so they add up to 1 again (this rescaling is called re-normalising), and draw at random among them. The slide’s downside: “k is fixed, but the shape of the probability distribution shifts in different contexts.” In plain words: sometimes 2 good options exist, sometimes 50, but \(k\) stays the same.
  • Temperature sampling: before softmax, divide every score by a number called the temperature, written \(\tau\) (the Greek letter “tau”). Then draw at random. The slide says: “τ < 1 sharpens the probability distribution. τ > 1 flattens the probability distribution.” Sharper means the favourite wins even more often. Flatter means the underdogs catch up. Think of a “boldness” dial: low means cautious, high means adventurous.
