  • Top-p sampling (also called nucleus sampling) is listed on the lecture’s agenda, but no slide explains it. [Not in course files — general knowledge] Top-p keeps the smallest group of top tokens whose chances add up to at least \(p\) (a number you choose, such as 0.9). It re-normalises and samples. So the number of kept tokens changes with the situation, which fixes top-k’s downside.

A rule that gives exactly the same result every time for the same input is called deterministic. A calculator is deterministic; a dice is not. Greedy decoding is deterministic. A high temperature makes the output less deterministic, not more.

Step 8: add the word and go again

The chosen token is stuck onto the end of the text. Then the whole machine runs again to pick the next token: “So long and thanks for” → “all” → “all the” … This repeats until the answer is finished. [Not in course files — general knowledge] This loop is called autoregressive generation: each new token becomes part of the input for the next one.

The second meaning of “encoding” and “decoding”

The words “encoder” and “decoder” also name two parts of a model. This meaning is different from “decoding = picking a word”.

  • Encoding means “representing the input sequence … into new word representations that capture the sequence meaning and the contextual relationship between the words”. In plain words: read the whole input and give every input word a list of numbers that reflects its meaning in this sentence. The part that does this is the encoder. It outputs one vector per input word.
  • Decoding means generating “an output sequence, one element at a time, based on the encoded representations of the input sequence as well as what it has generated so far”. In plain words: write the output one token at a time, using the encoder’s notes and what has been written so far. The part that does this is the decoder.

A model with both parts is an encoder–decoder model: one part reads, the other writes. The original Transformer was built like this for translation (turning a sentence in one language into another): “I am a dog” → “Jeg er en hund”. The lecture itself “mostly described a decoder structure”.

A decoder block has two kinds of attention:

  1. Causal self-attention. Each token may look only at itself and earlier tokens, never later ones. Like reading a book with the next pages glued shut. This makes sense for a writer: the next words don’t exist yet.
  2. Cross-attention. The writing part (decoder) looks at the output of the reading part (encoder). Like a translator glancing back at the original sentence while writing the translation.

Attention uses three lists made from each token:

  • the query (Q): “what am I looking for?”
  • the key (K): “what do I offer?”, a label
  • the value (V): “here is my content”

Think of a library search. You bring a question (query). The shelves have labels (keys). The books hold the content (values).

In cross-attention, the queries come from the decoder, and the keys and values come from the encoder. The writer brings the question; the reader’s notes supply the labels and the content. This is a favourite True/False trap.

BERT-type versus GPT-type models

Two more ideas are needed before comparing the two families:

  • Bidirectional attention: each token may look both backwards and forwards. Like reading the whole page before deciding what a word means. It is the opposite of causal attention.
  • Pre-training is the first, huge training stage, where the model learns from masses of ordinary text. GPT-type models practise by guessing the next word. BERT-type models practise by guessing masked words: words hidden inside a sentence, like a fill-in-the-blanks exercise.

BERT also puts a special token at the very start of the text, called [CLS]. Its final numbers are used as a summary of the whole text. To sort texts by feeling (positive or negative), a task called sentiment classification, a small extra head is placed on top of the [CLS] token.

The slides never put the two families side by side, so the table below combines what they do say. Each row is one feature. The two columns are the two model families. Each cell says how that family handles that feature.

Feature BERT-type GPT-type
Which part of the Transformer Encoder: “Bidirectional Transformer Encoder” Decoder: the structure “mostly described” in the lecture
Attention Bidirectional: each word sees all words Causal: each word sees only itself and earlier words
Pre-training task Predict “masked words” Predict “the next word”
Typical use Understanding a text: sentiment classification with a head on the [CLS] token; extracting embeddings Generating text token by token
Max length named in slides Original BERT: 512 tokens “Some thousand tokens”

[Not in course files — general knowledge] The slides list “next word (or masked words)” and “causal vs bidirectional” without saying which model uses which. Matching BERT to masked words plus bidirectional attention, and GPT to next word plus causal attention, is standard knowledge. The notebook’s model is loaded with AutoModelForCausalLM (the code command that loads a next-word model), which makes it a GPT-type (decoder-only, next-token) model.

Walk-through example

The example has three parts: the input lookup, the output scores, and the temperature dial. All numbers are made up and tiny, so you can follow them by hand.

Part 1: the input lookup

Imagine a model that knows only 4 tokens: “the”, “cat”, “sat” and “mat”. So the vocabulary size is \(|V| = 4\). Each token gets a list of only 2 numbers, so \(d = 2\).

Here is the lookup table \(\mathbf{E}\). Each row is one token in the vocabulary. The two columns are that token’s two numbers (“dim 1” and “dim 2” mean “first number” and “second number”). One cell is one number of one token’s code. For example, the cell in row “cat”, column “dim 1” is 1.0.

Token dim 1 dim 2
the 0.1 0.2
cat 1.0 0.0
sat 0.0 1.0
mat 0.9 0.1

Now the input sentence “the cat sat”. It has 3 tokens, so the number of tokens is \(N = 3\). Each token is written as a one-hot row. In the next table, each row is one position in the sentence. Each column is one vocabulary token. A cell is 1 if the token at that position is that column’s token, and 0 otherwise.

Position the cat sat mat
1 (“the”) 1 0 0 0
2 (“cat”) 0 1 0 0
3 (“sat”) 0 0 1 0

Let’s multiply row 2 (the “cat” row) by the table \(\mathbf{E}\), by hand. Each number in the one-hot row multiplies one row of \(\mathbf{E}\), and the results are added:

\(0\times(0.1, 0.2) + 1\times(1.0, 0.0) + 0\times(0.0, 1.0) + 0\times(0.9, 0.1) = (1.0, 0.0)\)

The three zeros wipe out the rows for “the”, “sat” and “mat”. The single 1 keeps the “cat” row. The answer, (1.0, 0.0), is exactly the “cat” row of the table.

Do the same for all three rows and you get the model’s input: one list per token, (0.1, 0.2), (1.0, 0.0) and (0.0, 1.0). In table terms: a 3-by-4 table of one-hot rows, times the 4-by-2 table \(\mathbf{E}\), gives a 3-by-2 table. A one-hot row is only a pointer that says “fetch this row”. The next step would be to add the position lists on top.

Part 2: the output scores, with weight tying

Jump to the end of the model. Suppose the last token’s final notes (its hidden state after the last layer) are the list (1, 0.5). The model got this list from all its layers; here we take it as given.

The head compares this list with each token’s row of \(\mathbf{E}\). “Compare” means: multiply the two lists number by number, then add up. This is called a dot product. It is a quick “how well do these two match?” score.

By hand for “cat”, whose row is (1.0, 0.0): \(1\times1.0 + 0.5\times0.0 = 1.0\).

By hand for “mat”, whose row is (0.9, 0.1): \(1\times0.9 + 0.5\times0.1 = 0.9 + 0.05 = 0.95\).

Doing this for all four tokens gives the four logits (raw scores), in the order the, cat, sat, mat:

\(u = (0.2, 1.0, 0.5, 0.95)\)

Here \(u\) is the name for the list of logits. Now softmax turns them into chances. With a calculator: \(e^{0.2} = 1.221\), \(e^{1.0} = 2.718\), \(e^{0.5} = 1.649\), \(e^{0.95} = 2.586\). The total is 8.174. For “cat”: 2.718 / 8.174 = 0.333. Doing all four gives:

\(y = (0.149, 0.333, 0.202, 0.316)\) for (the, cat, sat, mat).

Here \(y\) is the name for the list of probabilities. They add up to 1. “cat” is the most likely next token, at 33.3%, with “mat” close behind. Notice that the same table \(\mathbf{E}\) was used going in (Part 1) and coming out (Part 2). That is weight tying.

Part 3: the temperature dial

Now a sentence: “So long and thanks for”. Imagine the model has only 3 candidate next words, with made-up logits:

  • “all” = 2
  • “the” = 1
  • “fish” = 0

At temperature 1 (no change). Dividing by 1 changes nothing, so softmax works on (2, 1, 0).

  1. Exponentiate: “all” \(e^2 = 7.389\), “the” \(e^1 = 2.718\), “fish” \(e^0 = 1\).
  2. Add: 7.389 + 2.718 + 1 = 11.107.
  3. Divide each by the total: “all” 7.389 / 11.107 = 0.665. “the” 2.718 / 11.107 = 0.245. “fish” 1 / 11.107 = 0.090.
  4. Check: 0.665 + 0.245 + 0.090 = 1.000. So “all” gets 66.5%, “the” 24.5% and “fish” 9%.

With greedy decoding, the model writes “all” every single time. With random sampling, it rolls a weighted dice. Out of 1,000 rolls you would expect about 665 “all”, 245 “the” and 90 “fish”.

At temperature 0.5 (cautious). Divide the scores by 0.5, which doubles them: (4, 2, 0). Exponentiate: \(e^4 = 54.598\), \(e^2 = 7.389\), \(e^0 = 1\). The total is 62.987. So “all” gets 54.598 / 62.987 = 0.867, or 86.7%. The favourite wins even more often.

At temperature 2 (adventurous). Divide the scores by 2, which halves them: (1, 0.5, 0). Exponentiate: \(e^1 = 2.718\), \(e^{0.5} = 1.649\), \(e^0 = 1\). The total is 5.367. So “all” gets 2.718 / 5.367 = 0.506, about 50.6%. “fish” rises to 1 / 5.367 = 0.186, almost 1 time in 5.

The table below collects all three. Each row is one candidate word (its logit in brackets). Each column is one temperature. Each cell is that word’s probability at that temperature, rounded to 3 decimals (so a column may add to 0.999).

Word (logit) τ = 0.5 (sharper) τ = 1 (unchanged) τ = 2 (flatter)
all (2) 0.867 0.665 0.506
the (1) 0.117 0.245 0.307
fish (0) 0.016 0.090 0.186

What the table shows:

  • Low temperature makes the favourite more dominant. “fish” almost never gets picked (1.6%).
  • High temperature evens things out. “fish” now gets picked almost 1 time in 5.
  • Greedy decoding picks “all” every time. In the course notebook, “temperature 0 = always pick the top token”. The code switches to greedy for temperature 0, because dividing by zero is not possible [Not in course files — general knowledge: the notebook gives no reason].
  • Top-k with k = 2, at temperature 1, drops “fish” and re-normalises the other two. Their chances add to 0.665 + 0.245 = 0.910, so divide each by 0.910: “all” = 0.665/0.910 = 0.731, “the” = 0.269.
  • [Not in course files — general knowledge] Top-p with p = 0.9 would keep “all” and “the” too, because 0.665 + 0.245 = 0.910 ≥ 0.9.

So a low temperature makes the model play safe. A high temperature makes it take risks, and at very high values it can produce nonsense.

The formula, explained

The output formula

You have now seen the whole output step in words: take the last token’s final notes, score them against every token’s row, divide by the temperature, and turn the scores into chances. Here it is as a formula:

\[y = \mathrm{softmax}(u/\tau), \qquad u = h^L_N E'\]

  • \(h^L_N\) = the hidden state (final notes) of the last token, after the last layer. The small \(N\) means “token number \(N\)”, the last one in the text. The small \(L\) means “layer number \(L\)”, the last layer. It is one list of \(d\) numbers.
  • \(E'\) = the embedding table \(\mathbf{E}\) turned on its side (its transpose). It has \(d\) rows and \(|V|\) columns. It is the same table used for the input (weight tying). The slides also write it \(\mathbf{E}^T\).
  • \(u\) = the logits: one raw score per token in the vocabulary, so \(|V|\) numbers. Multiplying \(h^L_N\) by \(E'\) is the same as taking the dot product of \(h^L_N\) with every token’s row, as in Part 2.
  • \(\tau\) = the temperature. Dividing by a small \(\tau\) stretches the gaps between scores. Dividing by a large \(\tau\) shrinks them.
  • softmax = exponentiate each score and divide by the total, so all values are positive and add up to 1.
  • \(y\) = the probability of each vocabulary token being the next one.

Without the temperature (that is, with \(\tau = 1\)), the slides write the same thing as \(u = h^L_N\,E'\) and \(y = \mathrm{softmax}(u)\).

Read aloud: “Take the last token’s final vector, score it against every token’s embedding, divide the scores by the temperature, and turn them into probabilities that add up to one.”

Will the exam expect it? In 2025 the exam had no calculations. But a top answer about “what comes out of an LLM” mentions \(u = h^L_N E'\) and softmax, so it is worth being able to write this one line and explain each symbol.

The cross-attention formulas

In words: the questions (queries) are made from what the decoder has written so far, while the labels (keys) and the content (values) are made from the encoder’s reading of the input sentence.

\[Q = W^Q H^{dec(i-1)} \quad K = W^K H^{enc} \quad V = W^V H^{enc}\]

  • \(Q\), \(K\), \(V\) = the queries, keys and values, as explained above.
  • \(W^Q\), \(W^K\), \(W^V\) = three tables of dials (weights) learned in training. Each one turns notes into queries, keys or values.
  • \(H\) = the lists of numbers (notes) coming out of a layer.
  • \(H^{dec(i-1)}\) = the decoder’s notes from the layer before (layer \(i-1\)). This is “the decoder’s current state”, what it has written so far.
  • \(H^{enc}\) = the encoder’s notes about the input sentence.

In words: compare each question with every label, shrink the scores, turn them into weights with softmax, and use those weights to blend the contents.

\[\mathrm{CrossAttention}(Q,K,V) = \mathrm{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK'}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]

  • \(QK'\) = every query compared with every key by dot products (\(K'\) is \(K\) turned on its side). A big number means “this part of the input is relevant to what I’m writing”.
  • \(d_k\) = how many numbers are in each key. \(\sqrt{d_k}\) is its square root. Dividing by it keeps the numbers from getting too big.
  • softmax turns each row of scores into weights that add up to 1.
  • Multiplying by \(V\) blends the contents, giving more weight to the relevant parts.

Read aloud: “For each word being written, check how well its question matches each input word’s label, turn the matches into weights, and take a weighted mix of the input words’ contents.”

This is the same recipe as ordinary self-attention, called scaled dot-product attention. The only difference is where the lists come from: Q from the decoder, K and V from the encoder. You only need to understand this formula. What the exam tests is which side supplies Q and which supplies K and V.

Reading the course code

The course notebook has a helper called chat() that asks the model a question. Here are its key lines, in simplified form. The exam has not asked students to write code; this is here so you can recognise what the notebook did.

if temperature == 0:
    out = model.generate(**inputs, do_sample=False, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens)
else:
    out = model.generate(**inputs, do_sample=True, temperature=temperature,
                         top_p=1.0, top_k=0, max_new_tokens=max_new_tokens)

Line by line:

  • if temperature == 0: checks whether the temperature was set to 0.
  • model.generate(...) asks the model to write text. **inputs hands it your question, already cut into tokens.
  • do_sample=False means “do not roll the dice, always take the top token”. This is greedy decoding.
  • else: covers every other temperature.
  • do_sample=True with the chosen temperature gives temperature sampling.
  • top_p=1.0, top_k=0 switch top-p and top-k off, so only temperature shapes the dice (“pure temperature sampling”).
  • max_new_tokens caps how many tokens the model may write.

The notebook has no saved output. When run, temperature 0 gives the identical answer every time, and higher temperatures give more varied answers.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

From the 2025 exam. True/False item (c) was about tokens versus words. Question 4(c) asked about “token vs word, why tokens”. Both came from the slide that says “We do not input words per se, but tokens.” Your answer should say: the model reads tokens, which are often whole words but can be pieces of words or punctuation; a word like “unhappy” may be “un” + “happy”; and pieces let the model handle rare or unseen words with a vocabulary of manageable size.

Likely True/False items, with the answer and the reason:

  • “Higher temperature makes the output more deterministic” → FALSE. A temperature above 1 flattens the chances, so the output gets more random. “Deterministic” means “the same answer every time”.
  • “Greedy decoding always picks the most likely word” → TRUE. That is the definition of greedy decoding.
  • “The original BERT can take inputs of 512 tokens” → TRUE. The slide gives 512 tokens as the original BERT’s limit.
  • “In cross-attention, queries come from the encoder” → FALSE. The queries come from the decoder (the writing part). The keys and values come from the encoder (the reading part).
  • “Word and position embeddings are concatenated” → FALSE. They are added together, not glued end to end.

Likely short questions. You may be asked to compare decoding strategies (the rules for picking the next word). Or you may be asked why temperature 0 suits extraction tasks, meaning pulling one exact fact out of a text, such as the amount on an invoice. Here is that question with a model answer.

Why might a company set temperature to 0 when extracting invoice amounts, but not when writing campaign slogans?

Model answer The model’s next-token probabilities are reshaped by \(\mathrm{softmax}(u/\tau)\). A low τ sharpens them, and at 0 the model always takes the top token (greedy), so the same input gives the same output. That predictability is what you want when one correct answer exists and another program reads the result. For slogans you want variety, so a higher τ flattens the distribution and lets less obvious words through. The cost is a higher risk of nonsense (Notebook 4 cells 13 and 28).

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Temperature 0 means the model always picks its top word, so the same invoice always gives the same amount. That is good when there is one right answer and a computer will read it. For slogans you want fresh ideas, so you turn the temperature up. The price is that the model may now and then write nonsense.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • For decoding (how the model picks the next word): name at least two strategies, each with its downside. Random sampling (draw a word according to its chances): too many unlikely words slip in. Greedy (always take the top word): generic and repetitive text. Top-k (keep only the k most likely words, then draw): k stays fixed whatever the situation. Temperature: τ < 1 sharpens the chances (safer picks), τ > 1 flattens them (wilder picks).
  • For the output, write: “a probability distribution over the vocabulary for the next token, from the last token’s final hidden state via \(u = h^L_N E'\) and softmax”. In plain words: the model gives a chance to every token it knows (its vocabulary). It starts from its final notes on the last token (\(h^L_N\)) and multiplies them by the embedding table turned on its side (\(E'\)). That gives raw scores (\(u\)). Softmax (the step that turns scores into chances adding up to 1) then turns the scores into chances.
  • For encoder vs decoder: the encoder (reading part) gives a context-aware list of numbers for every input word. The decoder (writing part) produces one token at a time. In cross-attention, Q (the queries) comes from the decoder, and K and V (the keys and values) come from the encoder.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Saying “high temperature = more focused”. It is the opposite: high temperature means more random.
  • Saying the input is words. It is tokens (words or word pieces, like “play” + “ing”).
  • Forgetting that top-k re-normalises before sampling. After keeping the top k words, it rescales their chances so they add up to 1 again.
  • Claiming the head (the last part, which turns numbers into next-word scores) uses all \(N\) hidden states (the model’s final notes, one per token). It uses only the last one, \(h^L_N\).
  • Mixing up which side supplies Q (the queries) in cross-attention. It is the decoder.
  • Presenting top-p (another rule for picking words) as defined in the slides. It is not explained there.

Key terms to use

  • token: a word or a piece of a word
  • one-hot vector: row of zeros with one 1
  • embedding matrix \(\mathbf{E}\): table with one number-row per token
  • positional embedding, added: place-in-sentence numbers, added on top
  • context window / maximum sequence length: most tokens the model reads at once
  • truncation: cutting off text beyond that limit
  • language modelling head: last part giving each token a score
  • logits: raw scores before they become chances
  • softmax over the vocabulary: turns scores into chances summing to 1
  • weight tying: same table E at input and output
  • greedy decoding: always pick the most likely token
  • random sampling: draw the next token by its chances
  • top-k: draw only from the k likeliest tokens
  • temperature τ: dial, low = predictable, high = adventurous
  • encoder: the part that reads the input
  • decoder: the part that writes, token by token
  • causal self-attention: each token looks only at earlier tokens
  • cross-attention: decoder looks back at the encoder’s notes
  • bidirectional, BERT-type: sees the words on both sides
  • [CLS] token: special first token that summarises the text

Quick self-test

  1. “Setting τ > 1 makes the next-word distribution sharper.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: τ is the temperature, the dial for how adventurous the model is when it picks the next word. The “next-word distribution” is the list of chances the model gives every possible next word. “Sharper” means the top word gets even more of the chance. So: does turning the dial above 1 make the model more predictable?

    False. Why: a temperature above 1 flattens the chances. The top word loses some of its lead and unlikely words catch up, so the output gets more surprising. In the walk-through, “all” fell from 66.5% to 50.6% at temperature 2. A temperature below 1 does the opposite and sharpens.

  2. “Multiplying a one-hot row by the embedding matrix E simply selects one row of E.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A one-hot row is a row of zeros with a single 1 that marks which token it is. The embedding matrix E is the big table with one row of numbers for each token. Does multiplying the two pick out that token’s row of numbers?

    True. Why: every 0 wipes out its row of the table, and the single 1 keeps exactly one row. In the walk-through, the one-hot row for “cat” gave back exactly the “cat” row, (1.0, 0.0). It is like a wall of lockers where you hold only one key.

  3. “Weight tying means the same matrix E is used to build the input and to produce the output scores.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: At the start, the model uses table E to turn tokens into numbers. At the end, it must turn numbers back into a score for every token. Is “weight tying” the name for reusing the same table for both jobs?

    True. Why: that is exactly the definition. It is like using one English–French dictionary to translate both ways, instead of buying two.

  4. “In the decoder’s cross-attention layer, the keys and values come from the encoder.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Some models have an encoder (a part that reads the input) and a decoder (a part that writes the output). Cross-attention is the step where the decoder looks back at the input. It uses queries (“what am I looking for?”), keys (labels on the encoder’s notes) and values (the content of those notes). Do the keys and values come from the encoder?

    True. Why: the decoder brings the question (the queries). The encoder supplies the labels being searched (the keys) and what they say (the values). Picture a writer in a library: the writer brings the question, and the library supplies the shelf labels and the books.

  5. “Why might a company set temperature to 0 when extracting invoice amounts, but not when writing campaign slogans?” (Explain in 2–5 sentences)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Why would you want the cautious setting for reading numbers off invoices, but a bolder setting for inventing slogans?

    Answer: the full model answer is in the exam section above. In short: temperature 0 means greedy decoding, so the same invoice always gives the same amount, which another program can rely on. Slogans need variety, so a higher temperature lets less obvious words through, at the cost of more nonsense. Why: low temperature sharpens the chances (safe and repeatable); high temperature flattens them (varied but riskier).

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • LLM (large language model): a program, like ChatGPT, that has learned from huge amounts of text to predict what text comes next. Like a phone’s autocomplete, but far bigger.
  • token: one small piece of text the model reads, often a word, sometimes part of a word or a comma. “Unhappy” might be two tokens: “un” + “happy”.
  • vocabulary (\(|V|\)): the full list of tokens the model knows. \(|V|\) means “how many tokens are on the list”. Like the full list of words in a dictionary.
  • vector: a list of numbers in a fixed order, such as (0.1, 0.2). Like a row of measurements for one person: height, weight.
  • matrix: a table of numbers with rows and columns. A spreadsheet full of numbers.
  • dimension (\(d\)): how many numbers are in each list. A list of 2 numbers has \(d = 2\).
  • embedding: the list of numbers that stands for one token. Like a postcode that stands for a street.
  • embedding matrix (\(\mathbf{E}\)): the big lookup table with one row of numbers per token in the vocabulary. Like a phone book: name in, number out.
  • one-hot vector (one-hot row): a row of zeros with a single 1 that marks which token it is. “cat” in (the, cat, sat, mat) is (0, 1, 0, 0).
  • positional embedding: a second list of numbers that tells the model where a token sits in the sentence. Like a seat number at a cinema.
  • sinusoidal: built from smooth wave shapes (sine and cosine waves). Here, a recipe for making the seat-number lists.
  • concatenate: glue two lists end to end. (0.1, 0.2) and (0.5, 0.5) give (0.1, 0.2, 0.5, 0.5). Word and position lists are not combined this way; they are added.
  • Transformer layer: one processing stage inside the model where tokens exchange information. Like one round of discussion in a group, repeated many times.
  • attention / self-attention: the step where each token looks at the other tokens and decides which ones matter for it. Like reading “it” and glancing back to see what “it” refers to.
  • causal self-attention: attention where a token may only look at itself and earlier tokens, never later ones. Like reading a book with the next pages glued shut.
  • bidirectional: each token may look both backwards and forwards in the text. Like reading the whole page before deciding what a word means.
  • cross-attention: attention where the part that writes the output looks at the part that read the input. Like a translator glancing back at the original sentence.
  • query, key, value (Q, K, V): three lists made from each token for attention. Query = “what am I looking for?”, key = “what do I offer?”, value = “here is my content”. Like a library search: your question, the shelf labels, the books.
  • scaled dot-product attention (\(d_k\)): the attention formula: compare queries with keys by dot products, divide by the square root of \(d_k\) (the length of each key) so the numbers don’t get too big, then softmax.
  • dot product: multiply two lists number by number and add up. (1, 0.5) and (1.0, 0.0) give 1×1.0 + 0.5×0.0 = 1.0. A quick “how well do these match?” score.
  • hidden state (\(h^L_N\)): the list of numbers the model holds for a token after a layer. \(h^L_N\) is the one for the last token (\(N\)) after the last layer (\(L\)). Like the model’s final “summary note” about the text so far.
  • context window / maximum length: the most tokens the model can read at once. Like the size of a desk: only so many pages fit.
  • truncation: cutting off the part of the text that doesn’t fit. Like a photocopier that drops the last page.
  • computer memory: the working space a computer uses while it calculates. Attention needs a lot of it for long texts.
  • BERT: a well-known model family that reads text in both directions and is used to understand text, for example to judge if a review is positive.
  • GPT: a well-known model family that reads left to right and is used to write text, one token at a time. ChatGPT belongs to this family.
  • [CLS] token: a special token put at the start of the text in BERT. Its final numbers are used as a summary of the whole text.
  • masked words: words hidden in a sentence that the model must guess, like a fill-in-the-blanks exercise.
  • pre-training: the first, huge training stage where the model learns from masses of ordinary text.
  • logit (\(u\)): the raw score a model gives each possible next token, before it becomes a probability. Can be any number, even negative. In the example, “all” = 2.
  • softmax: the step that turns raw scores into probabilities: raise \(e\) to each score, then divide by the total. Scores (2, 1, 0) become (0.665, 0.245, 0.090).
  • \(e\) / exponentiate: \(e\) is a fixed number, about 2.718. “Exponentiate” means raise \(e\) to a power, such as \(e^2 = 7.389\). It turns any score into a positive number, and bigger scores into much bigger numbers.
  • probability: a number from 0 to 1 that says how likely something is. 0.665 means 66.5%, about two times in three.
  • probability distribution (\(y\)): the full set of probabilities for all options, adding up to 1. Like a weather forecast: 70% sun, 20% cloud, 10% rain.
  • language modelling head (LM head): the final part of the model that turns the last token’s numbers into one score per vocabulary token. Like the “results board” at the end of a quiz.
  • transpose (\(E'\) or \(\mathbf{E}^T\)): the same table turned on its side, so rows become columns. A 4-by-2 table becomes 2-by-4.
  • unembedding layer: the slides’ name for using \(\mathbf{E}\) turned on its side at the output, to go from numbers back to token scores.
  • weight / parameter: one adjustable number inside the model, set during training. Think of a dial. Big models have billions of them.
  • weight tying: using the same table \(\mathbf{E}\) both to read tokens in and to score tokens out. One phone book used in both directions.
  • training: the process that sets all the dials so the model predicts well.
  • decoding (choosing a word): the rule for picking one token from the probabilities. (The word also has a second meaning: see decoder.)
  • greedy decoding: always pick the token with the highest probability. Like always ordering the most popular dish on the menu.
  • random sampling: pick a token at random, but weighted by its probability. Like drawing from a bag with 665 red, 245 blue and 90 green balls.
  • top-k sampling: keep only the \(k\) most likely tokens, throw the rest away, re-normalise, then sample among those. With \(k = 2\), only the top two are allowed.
  • re-normalise: rescale the kept probabilities so they add up to 1 again. If 0.665 and 0.245 are kept, divide each by their sum 0.910.
  • top-p (nucleus) sampling: keep the smallest group of top tokens whose probabilities add up to at least \(p\), then sample. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • temperature (\(\tau\)): a number the scores are divided by before softmax. Low = cautious and predictable; high = adventurous and varied. Like a “boldness” dial.
  • deterministic: gives exactly the same result every time for the same input. A calculator is deterministic; a dice is not.
  • autoregressive: each new token is added to the input and used to predict the next one. Like writing a story where each sentence builds on the last. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • encoder: the part of a model that reads the whole input and turns it into meaning-filled number lists, one per word.
  • decoder: the part of a model that writes the output one token at a time, using what it has written so far.
  • encoding (in the encoder–decoder sense): turning the input into those meaning-filled number lists.
  • encoder–decoder model: a model with both parts: one reads, one writes. The original Transformer was built like this for translation.
  • translation: turning a sentence in one language into another, e.g. “I am a dog” → “Jeg er en hund”.
  • sentiment classification: sorting a text by feeling, such as positive or negative.
  • extraction: pulling a specific fact out of a text, such as the amount on an invoice.
  • notebook / cell: a notebook is a document that mixes code and text and runs in a web browser. A cell is one box of code or text in it.
  • model.generate, do_sample, max_new_tokens: code commands from the notebook. generate asks the model to write text; do_sample says whether to roll the dice; max_new_tokens caps how many tokens it may write.
  • AutoModelForCausalLM: the code command that loads a left-to-right, next-token (GPT-type) model.
  • T/F: a True/False exam question.

Sources: Lecture 9a LLMs: Input and output (Lecture_llm_inputoutput.pdf), slides 3–18; Lecture 9b Training and fine tuning, slides 4, 22 and 23; Lecture 8, slide 11; Lecture 7 Introducing LLMs, slide 30; Interactive Notebook 4, cells 2–3, 6, 13, 22 and 28; tokenizers notebook (llm_tokenizers.ipynb), cell 15.

19. How LLMs are trained

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — 2025 T/F (f) “LLMs are estimated using unsupervised learning” (answer: FALSE); training terms make easy True/False items.

Why this exists

A large language model, or LLM, is a program like ChatGPT. It has learned from huge amounts of text to guess what text comes next. Think of the autocomplete on your phone keyboard, but far bigger and far better.

Inside, an LLM is a machine with billions of little dials. Each dial is one number. When the model reads a sentence and guesses the next word, the guess depends on where all these dials are set.

A brand-new model has all its dials set at random. Ask it to finish “So long and thanks for” and it writes gibberish. To get something like ChatGPT, every one of those billions of dials has to be set to a good position. Nobody could ever do that by hand.

So we need an automatic way to set the dials, using enormous piles of ordinary text from books and websites. That automatic process is called training. This chapter explains how it works, and what all its key words mean.

The idea in everyday words

The dials

Each dial inside the model is called a weight or a parameter. Both words mean the same thing here: one adjustable number. Big LLMs have billions of them.

You will see sizes written like “0.34B” or “1.6T”. B means billion (a thousand million). T means trillion (a thousand billion). So “0.34B parameters” means 340 million dials.

The guessing game

Training is a guessing game, played over and over.

  1. Grab a sentence from the pile of text, for example “So long and thanks for all the fish”.
  2. Hide the next word. Show the model only “So long and thanks for”.
  3. Let the model guess. The model knows a fixed list of text pieces, called its vocabulary. (The pieces are called tokens: often whole words, sometimes parts of words.) For every token on that list, the model gives a probability, a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely it thinks that token is to come next. For example, it might give “all” a probability of 0.3, meaning 30%. The model’s full list of probabilities, one per token, is called its probability vector. (A vector is a list of numbers in a fixed order.)
  4. Reveal the true word. Here it is “all”. The true word that the guess is compared with is called the target.
  5. Measure how wrong the guess was. Look at how much probability the model gave the true word. A lot means a good guess; a little means a bad guess. This “how wrong” score is one number called the loss. Smaller is better. Think of the points you lost on a test.
  6. Nudge the dials so that next time the model gives the true word a bit more probability.
  7. Repeat over trillions of words.

Slowly, the guesses get better and better.

The slides describe the target like this: “the next token in the training text is the target; future tokens are hidden from the prediction.”

How the loss is measured

The loss used for LLMs is called cross-entropy loss. The slide defines it as “the negative log probability the model assigns to the next word in the training sequence”.

“Log” here is a button on any calculator, called the natural log and written ln. You only need three facts about it:

  • For a number between 0 and 1, ln gives a negative answer. For example, \(\ln(0.3) = -1.204\).
  • The closer the number is to 0, the more negative the answer.
  • \(\ln(1) = 0\).

“Negative log probability” means: take the log of the probability, then put a minus sign in front, which flips it into a positive penalty. So if the model gave the true word “all” a probability of 0.3, the loss is \(-\ln(0.3) = 1.204\). If it had given “all” 0.9, the loss would be only 0.105. If it gave “all” a probability of 1 (fully sure, and right), the loss would be 0. The slide says the “loss is minimized if we … predict with probability one the next word”.

A sentence has many positions, each with its own next word. The loss for a whole sentence is “the average cross-entropy loss over the entire sequence”: add up the losses at every position, then divide by how many positions there are.

Why this is called “self-supervised”

Before naming this kind of training, you need three older words.

  • A label is a right answer written down by a person, such as “positive” next to a movie review. Labelled data means examples that come with such answers.
  • Supervised learning means learning from examples that come with the right answer. Like a student doing exercises with an answer key.
  • Unsupervised learning means finding patterns in data with no right answers at all. Like sorting a pile of photos into groups without being told what the groups are. A classic example from earlier in the course is a topic model called LDA, which groups documents into themes without any answer key.

Now look at the guessing game again. Is there a right answer? Yes: the true next word, every single time. But no person wrote it down. The text itself holds the answer. It is like reading a book with a sticky note over the next word: you guess, lift the note and check. Nobody wrote an answer key; the book is the answer key.

This in-between case has its own name: self-supervised learning. The key slide says:

“Training LLMs is often called self-supervised training. Why? We use the actual text and train the model to predict the next word (or masked words). I.e., no need for manually creating training data.”

“Masked words” are words hidden inside a sentence that the model must fill in, like a fill-in-the-blanks exercise. Some models (such as the BERT family) practise this way. Others (such as the GPT family, which includes ChatGPT) practise by guessing the next word. That is called next-token prediction.

This is the trap in the 2025 exam statement “LLMs are estimated using unsupervised learning”. It is FALSE:

  • In unsupervised learning there is no target to compare against. Topic models like LDA only find structure in the data.
  • In LLM training there is a target at every position: the true next word. The loss measures how far the prediction is from that target.
  • So it works like supervised learning, except the labels come from the text itself. The course’s word for this is self-supervised.
  • The word “unsupervised” does not appear in any of the four LLM lecture decks (Lectures 7, 8, 9a, 9b).
  • [Not in course files — general knowledge] Some older textbooks loosely call language-model pre-training “unsupervised” because no human labels are needed. That is exactly the trap. In this course, write self-supervised.

Which way to turn each dial

After each guess, we know the loss. Now we must decide, for each dial, “turn it up or down, and by how much?”

Picture yourself on a foggy mountain, trying to reach the bottom of the valley. You can’t see far. But you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. So you take a small step downhill, feel again, take another step, and so on.

Here the “height” is the loss, and your “position” is the setting of the dials. Some words for this picture:

  • A function is a rule that turns an input into an output. “Square the number” is a function: 2 goes in, 4 comes out. The loss is a function of the dial settings.
  • The slope (also called the derivative) says how much the output changes when you change the input a tiny bit. It is how steep the hill is where you stand. A positive slope means “turning this dial up makes the loss worse”, so you turn it down.
  • When there are many dials, you need one slope per dial. The slope for one dial, with all the others held still, is a partial derivative, written with a curly d, \(\partial\). For example, \(\partial e/\partial b\) means “how much \(e\) changes if only \(b\) changes”.
  • The full list of slopes, one for every dial, is the gradient, written \(\nabla L\) (“the gradient of the loss \(L\)”). It points uphill, so you step the opposite way.
  • The lowest point you are looking for is the minimum (or optimum), like the bottom of a valley.

The rule “step downhill, again and again” is called gradient descent. The slides call it “a general method to find the optimum (or minimum) of a function”.

How big is each step? That is set by a number you choose, called the learning rate, written \(\eta\) (the Greek letter “eta”). The slide says it “affects the degree of updating”. Too big a step and you overshoot the bottom and land on the other side of the valley. Too small and it takes forever.

Working out all the slopes at once: backpropagation

An LLM has billions of dials. How do you get the slope for every one of them?

The model’s calculation is a long chain of small steps. You can draw it as a diagram called a computational graph. Each circle in it, called a node, is one value. Each arrow, called an edge, shows which value feeds into which.

To get a slope through a chain of steps, you multiply the slopes of the steps. This is the chain rule. Example: if A doubles B, and B triples C, then a change in A changes C six-fold (2 × 3). If there are several roads from one value to another, you add up the roads.

There are two ways to apply the chain rule:

  • Forward mode starts at one input and works forwards. It gives only that one input’s slope. The slide: “Forward-mode gives derivative of output with respect to a single input.”
  • Reverse mode starts at the output (the loss) and works backwards. One backward sweep gives the slope for every value at once. The slide: “Reverse-mode gives derivative of output with respect to every node!”

With millions of dials and one loss, reverse mode is far faster. Think of a factory line that made a faulty product: one walk back from the end, station by station, tells you how much each station added to the fault.

Reverse mode has a famous name in machine learning: backpropagation. The slide says backpropagation “is a ML term for reverse-mode differentiation, which in turn is just one way of applying the multivariate chain rule”. (“Differentiation” means working out slopes. “Multivariate” means “with many inputs”.)

Small handfuls: mini-batches and epochs

Looking at all the training text before every single nudge would be far too slow. So each nudge uses only a small random handful of examples.

  • That handful is a mini-batch (or batch): a “small subset of the training dataset selected to perform a single update”. Think of tasting a spoonful of soup instead of the whole pot.
  • One full trip through all the training text is an epoch: “a complete pass through the entire training dataset”. Like reading the whole textbook once.
  • If the mini-batch holds the whole data set, you are doing standard gradient descent.
  • If the mini-batch holds only one example, it is “online training (with a lot of noise)”: one nudge after every single example.
  • The mini-batch size is a tuning parameter: a setting you choose yourself, rather than one the model learns.

Gradient descent where each step uses a random mini-batch is called stochastic gradient descent, or SGD. “Stochastic” means “random”. The slides say SGD is the standard method for large networks because it is “more efficient and scalable”, gives “(potentially) faster convergence”, and “introduces noise … that might help in terms of generalization (prevent over-fitting)”. In plain words:

  • Noise is random wobble in the steps, because each mini-batch is a bit different.
  • Convergence means settling down at (or near) the lowest point.
  • Generalisation means doing well on new examples, not only the ones trained on.
  • Over-fitting means memorising the training examples instead of learning the general pattern. Like learning test answers by heart without understanding.
  • Regularisation is anything that discourages over-fitting.

Teacher forcing

A sentence is read one position at a time. Each position is called a time step. During training, what should the model see as “the earlier words” at each step: the true words, or its own earlier guesses?

The answer is the true words. This is called teacher forcing: “give the model the correct history sequence to predict the next word rather than feeding the model its best case from the previous … time step”. Think of a teacher who corrects each word before you write the next one.

Better versions of gradient descent

The slides list two improvements:

  • Learning-rate decay: make the steps smaller as training goes on. The learning rate is then written \(\eta_k\), where \(k\) is the step number. Like slowing down as you get close to a parking spot.
  • Adaptive optimisers: AdaGrad, AdaDelta, RMSProp and Adam. [Not in course files — general knowledge] These are improved versions of gradient descent that adjust the step size automatically for each dial.

Things that make training hard

The slides list these problems:

  • The loss is non-convex: its landscape has many hills and valleys, not one simple bowl. You might end up in a valley that isn’t the deepest one.
  • Parameter initialisation: the starting positions of the dials before training begins matter.
  • Vanishing and exploding gradients. [Not in course files — general knowledge] These are slopes that shrink to almost nothing, or blow up to huge numbers, as they are passed backwards through many layers. Either way, the dials stop learning sensibly.
  • Saturation and dead neurons. [Not in course files — general knowledge] These are parts of the network that get stuck and stop reacting to their input, so they stop learning. The slide says “layer normalization helps”. [Not in course files — general knowledge] Layer normalization means rescaling the numbers inside each layer so they stay in a sensible range.
  • Shuffling the data after each epoch (mixing the order of the examples, like shuffling flashcards) acts as a form of regularisation.

When training is finished: the full pipeline

Real LLMs are trained in stages. The course lists these:

  1. Pre-training: “learn to predict tokens from large collections of text, code, and, for some models, other media”. This is the giant first stage, and it is self-supervised.
  2. Continued pre-training / mid-training, when used: extra rounds of pre-training, often on more specific text.
  3. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): further training that “learn[s] from examples of instructions and desired responses”. This step is supervised, because people wrote those good answers.
  4. Preference optimisation / reinforcement learning: “improve responses using preferences or rewards”. The model is rewarded for answers that people (or a scoring system) prefer. Like a dog getting treats for good behaviour.

“Recipes differ across models.” The result is a set of updated weights. At answer time those weights are fixed. So when you chat with the model, it is not learning from you.

Fine-tuning in general means extra training of an already-trained model on one specific task. For a task like sentiment classification (sorting texts into positive or negative), the slide says fine-tuning “requires supervised training and training data already classified”. In other words: someone must first tag example texts as positive or negative.

Training is “not for all”

Training a model from scratch is hugely expensive. Model size grew about 10 times a year. The slide gives these models as examples. The names only serve to show the growth. Each row below is one model. The columns give the year it appeared and its number of dials (B = billion, T = trillion).

Model Year Parameters (dials)
Transformer 2017 0.05B
BERT 2018 0.34B
GPT-2 2019 1.5B
GPT-3 2020 “170B” (as printed on the slide)
Switch Transformer 2021 1.6T

Training “requires massive amounts of training data [and] large computational resources”. A recent example from the course: DeepSeek-V4-Flash has 284B parameters, uses about 13B of them per token, and was pre-trained on more than 32 trillion tokens. “Training a frontier model from scratch is beyond a typical laptop.” (A frontier model is one of the biggest, most advanced models of its time.) That is why most users prompt or fine-tune an existing model instead.

Walk-through example

Five tiny examples, one for each idea: the loss for one word, the loss for a sentence, gradient descent, backpropagation, and mini-batches.

1. The loss for one word

The input is “So long and thanks for”, and the true next word is “all”. We use the natural log (ln); the slide writes only “log”.

The table below shows what happens to the loss as the model’s guess gets better or worse. Each row is one possible probability the model might give the true word “all”. The second column is the resulting loss, \(-\ln P\), where \(P\) is that probability.

P(model says “all”) Loss \(= -\ln P\)
1.0 0 (perfect, “loss is minimized if we … predict with probability one the next word”)
0.9 0.105
0.3 1.204
0.01 4.605

By hand for the row 0.3: the calculator gives \(\ln(0.3) = -1.204\). The minus sign flips it: \(-(-1.204) = 1.204\). Reading down the table: the less probability the true word gets, the bigger the penalty. A model that gave “all” only 1% gets a penalty of 4.605.

2. The loss for a whole sentence

Suppose that at three positions in a sentence, the true next word got probabilities 0.5, 0.2 and 0.4.

The three losses are \(-\ln(0.5) = 0.693\), \(-\ln(0.2) = 1.609\) and \(-\ln(0.4) = 0.916\).

The sentence loss is their average: (0.693 + 1.609 + 0.916) / 3 = 3.218 / 3 = 1.073.

3. Gradient descent with one dial

Real models have billions of dials. Imagine a toy model with only one dial, called \(v\). Its loss is \(v \times v\), written \(L(v) = v^2\). The best position is \(v = 0\), where the loss is 0.

For this “square it” rule, the slope at any point is 2 times \(v\). (That is a school-maths fact; you don’t need to work it out.) So at \(v = 2\) the slope is 4.

One step of gradient descent: new \(v\) = old \(v\) minus (learning rate × slope).

With a learning rate of 0.1, by hand:

  1. Start at \(v = 2\). The loss is 2 × 2 = 4.
  2. The slope is 2 × 2 = 4. It is positive, so we turn the dial down.
  3. The step is 0.1 × 4 = 0.4.
  4. New position: 2 − 0.4 = 1.6. New loss: 1.6 × 1.6 = 2.56. Smaller than 4, so the step helped.
  5. Next step: the slope is 2 × 1.6 = 3.2, the step is 0.1 × 3.2 = 0.32, and \(v\) becomes 1.28.

Now a learning rate that is too big, 0.9. The step is 0.9 × 4 = 3.6, so \(v\) jumps from 2 to 2 − 3.6 = −1.6. It has leapt right over the best spot (0) to the other side.

The table below follows both runs for four steps. The slide shows dots, not numbers, so the two learning rates are our own choice. Each row is one step number (step 0 is the start). Each column is one learning rate. Each cell is the dial position \(v\) after that step.

Step η = 0.1 (small) η = 0.9 (large)
0 2 2
1 1.6 −1.6
2 1.28 1.28
3 1.024 −1.024
4 0.819 0.819

How to read it: with the small learning rate, \(v\) creeps steadily towards 0 (the slide’s green dots). With the large one, \(v\) bounces from one side of 0 to the other (the slide’s red dots).

4. Backpropagation on a tiny graph

The slide uses this small calculation. Start with two inputs, \(a = 2\) and \(b = 1\). Then:

  • \(c = a + b = 3\)
  • \(d = b + 1 = 2\)
  • \(e = c \times d = 6\)

The diagram below draws this as a computational graph. Each oval is a node (one value). Each arrow shows which value feeds which. The small number on each arrow is the local slope: how much the arrow’s end changes if its start goes up by 1.

Where do the numbers on the arrows come from? Work each one out in words:

  • \(c = a + b\). If \(a\) goes up by 1, \(c\) goes up by 1. So \(\partial c/\partial a = 1\). The same holds for \(b\): \(\partial c/\partial b = 1\).
  • \(d = b + 1\). If \(b\) goes up by 1, \(d\) goes up by 1. So \(\partial d/\partial b = 1\).
  • \(e = c \times d\). If \(c\) goes up by 1, \(e\) goes up by \(d\), which is 2. So \(\partial e/\partial c = d = 2\).
  • Likewise, if \(d\) goes up by 1, \(e\) goes up by \(c\), which is 3. So \(\partial e/\partial d = c = 3\).

Now the question: how much does \(e\) change if \(b\) changes? The slide says it is “the sum over all possible paths” from \(b\) to \(e\), multiplying the arrows along each path. In words: follow each road from \(b\) to \(e\), multiply the numbers along that road, then add the roads together.

\[\frac{\partial e}{\partial b} = 1\times 2 + 1\times 3 = 5\]

The road through \(c\) gives \(1 \times 2\). The road through \(d\) gives \(1 \times 3\). Together, 5. In the same way, \(a\) has only one road (through \(c\)), so \(\partial e/\partial a = 1 \times 2 = 2\).

Reverse mode starts at \(e\) and works backwards, so one pass gives the slope of \(e\) with respect to every node (\(a\), \(b\), \(c\), \(d\)). That is backpropagation. In a real LLM, \(e\) would be the loss and the nodes would include the billions of dials.

5. Epochs and mini-batches

Say you have 10,000 training sentences and mini-batches of 100. Each mini-batch gives one nudge of the dials. So one epoch (one full pass through all 10,000) contains 10,000 / 100 = 100 weight updates.

The formula, explained

The cross-entropy loss

You have seen the idea: the penalty is minus the log of the probability the model gave to the true next word. Here it is as a formula:

\[L_{CE}(\hat y_t, y_t) = -\log \hat y_t[w_{t+1}]\]

  • \(L_{CE}\) = the cross-entropy loss (the “CE” stands for cross-entropy).
  • \(t\) = the position in the text we are at.
  • \(\hat y_t\) = the model’s probability vector over the whole vocabulary at position \(t\). The little hat means “the model’s guess”.
  • \(y_t\) = the “correct” distribution: all the weight on the true next word.
  • \(w_{t+1}\) = the true next word in the training text (the word at position \(t+1\)).
  • \(\hat y_t[w_{t+1}]\) = the probability the model gave to that true word. The square brackets mean “pick this word’s entry from the list”.
  • \(-\log\) = turns a probability near 1 into a loss near 0, and a probability near 0 into a big loss.

Read aloud: “The loss at position t is minus the log of the probability the model gave to the word that really came next.”

The gradient descent update

You have seen the idea: move every dial a small step, of size \(\eta\), in the downhill direction of the loss. As a formula:

\[v \to v' = v - \eta \nabla L\]

  • \(v\) = the parameters (dials) now; \(v'\) = the parameters after one step. The arrow \(\to\) means “is replaced by”.
  • \(\nabla L\) = the gradient: for each parameter, how much the loss rises if that parameter rises a little.
  • \(\eta\) = the learning rate, or step size.
  • The minus sign means “go against the slope”, which is downhill.

Read aloud: “New weights = old weights minus learning rate times the slope of the loss.” In the walk-through: 2 − 0.1 × 4 = 1.6.

A typo on the slides

The mini-batch SGD recipe on slide 16 prints the update as “θ ← θ + η_k ĝ”, with a plus sign. Here θ (“theta”) is the list of all dials, and ĝ is the slope estimated from one mini-batch. For making a loss smaller, it must be a minus, as on slide 9. In the exam write \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta_k \hat g\).

Will the exam expect these formulas? In 2025 the exam had no calculations. You should understand both formulas and be able to explain them in words. Writing the update rule with the correct minus sign is a nice touch in a learning-rate answer.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

From the 2025 exam. True/False item (f): “LLMs are estimated using unsupervised learning” → FALSE. (“Estimated” here means “trained”.) The right word is self-supervised: the text itself supplies the right answers.

Likely True/False items, with the answer and the reason:

  • “Backpropagation is reverse-mode differentiation / the chain rule” → TRUE. Backpropagation (the method that works out every dial’s slope) is the same thing as reverse-mode differentiation, which is one way of applying the chain rule.
  • “A mini-batch of size one is standard gradient descent” → FALSE. A mini-batch of one is called online training. Standard gradient descent uses all the data in each step.
  • “An epoch is one pass through the full training set” → TRUE. An epoch is one full read-through of all the training data.
  • “Teacher forcing feeds the model its own predictions” → FALSE. Teacher forcing feeds the model the true earlier words, not its own guesses.
  • “Fine-tuning a sentiment classifier needs labelled data” → TRUE. A model that tells positive from negative texts needs texts already tagged positive or negative.

Likely short questions. “Why is LLM pre-training called self-supervised?” or “Explain the role of the learning rate”. For the learning rate, use the points in the top-grade box below. For self-supervised, here is a model answer.

Why is LLM pre-training called self-supervised, and how does it differ from fine-tuning a sentiment classifier?

Model answer In pre-training the model reads ordinary text and predicts the next (or a masked) word. The true word is taken from the text itself, so no one has to label data. The prediction is compared with the true word using a cross-entropy loss, and the weights are updated by gradient descent and backpropagation. So there is a target, as in supervised learning, but it is generated from the data, hence “self-supervised”. Fine-tuning a sentiment classifier is ordinary supervised learning: it needs texts already labelled as positive or negative (L9b slides 4, 22).

What this answer is saying, in plain words: In its first training, the model guesses the next word of normal text, and the text itself shows the right word. So nobody has to mark up any data by hand. The model checks how wrong it was and adjusts its dials a little each time. Teaching it to spot positive or negative reviews is different: for that, people must first tag example reviews as positive or negative.

What a top-grade answer must include

  • For “self-supervised”, make three points. (1) The model predicts the next word, or a hidden (“masked”) word. (2) The right answer (the target) comes from the text itself, so nobody has to label data by hand. (3) The loss is cross-entropy (a penalty that is big when the model gave the true word a low chance) against the true next word. It is made smaller by gradient descent (stepping downhill on the loss) with backpropagation (working out each dial’s slope in one backward sweep).
  • Then contrast. Unsupervised methods, such as LDA (a topic model that finds themes), have no target at all. Fine-tuning or SFT (supervised fine-tuning) is supervised: it learns from labelled examples.
  • For the learning rate (how big each downhill step is): too high overshoots or bounces around; too low is slow. Make it smaller over time, or use adaptive optimisers (methods that adjust the step size by themselves), such as Adam.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Writing “unsupervised” for LLM pre-training (the first, big training stage). It is self-supervised.
  • Saying the model is trained on human-labelled data at the pre-training stage. Pre-training uses plain text with no labels.
  • Copying the plus sign from slide 16. The update rule there has a typo: it must be a minus, \(\theta \leftarrow \theta - \eta_k \hat g\) (move the dials against the slope, so you go downhill).
  • Saying the LLM keeps learning while you chat with it. Its weights (the learned dials) are fixed when it answers.
  • Mixing up epoch (one full pass through all the data) and mini-batch (a small handful of examples for one step).

Key terms to use

  • self-supervised pre-training: first training; text supplies its own answers
  • next-token (or masked-word) prediction: guess the next or hidden word
  • cross-entropy loss: penalty for low chance on true word
  • average loss over the sequence: penalty averaged across all positions
  • gradient: list of slopes, one per dial
  • gradient descent: step downhill on the loss, repeatedly
  • learning rate η: size of each downhill step
  • backpropagation = reverse-mode differentiation = chain rule: one backward sweep gives every slope
  • computational graph: map of all the calculation steps
  • stochastic gradient descent: downhill steps using random handfuls of data
  • mini-batch: small handful of examples per step
  • epoch: one full pass through all the data
  • online training: one example per step, very noisy
  • teacher forcing: show the true earlier words in training
  • learning-rate decay: step size shrinks over time
  • Adam/RMSProp/AdaGrad: optimisers that adjust their own step size
  • non-convex: loss landscape with many hills and valleys
  • vanishing/exploding gradients: slopes shrink to nothing or blow up
  • shuffling: mixing the order of examples each epoch
  • supervised fine-tuning (SFT): extra training on example instructions and answers
  • preference optimisation: rewarding the answers people prefer

Quick self-test

  1. “LLMs are estimated using unsupervised learning.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: “Estimated” here means “trained” (how the model’s dials get set). “Unsupervised learning” means learning with no right answers at all, only spotting patterns. Is that how LLMs are trained?

    False. Why: the course calls it self-supervised. There is a right answer every time: the next word in the text. The model guesses it, and the cross-entropy loss measures how wrong the guess was. It is like a book with a sticky note over the next word: nobody wrote an answer key, but the book itself is the answer key.

  2. “If the mini-batch size equals the full sample, we essentially perform standard gradient descent.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Gradient descent is learning by small steps downhill on the loss. A mini-batch is the handful of examples used to decide each step. If that handful is the whole data set, is that ordinary gradient descent?

    True. Why: ordinary gradient descent looks at all the data before each step, so a “handful” that contains everything is the same thing. Tasting a spoonful is a mini-batch; tasting the whole pot is the full sample.

  3. “Reverse-mode differentiation gives the derivative of the output with respect to every node in one pass.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: A derivative (slope) says how much the result changes if you nudge one thing. A node is one value in the model’s chain of calculations. Does one backward sweep through the chain tell you this for every value at once?

    True. Why: that is what reverse-mode differentiation (backpropagation) does. In the walk-through, one backward pass from \(e\) gave the slopes for \(a\), \(b\), \(c\) and \(d\). Forward mode would give only one input’s slope per pass.

  4. “The cross-entropy loss is zero when the model gives the true next word probability one.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The cross-entropy loss is minus the log of the chance the model gave the true word. “Probability one” means the model was 100% sure of the right word. Is the penalty then zero?

    True. Why: the log of 1 is 0, so the penalty is \(-\log 1 = 0\). It is the top row of the loss table in the walk-through. A weather forecaster who said “100% rain” on a day it rained loses no points.

  5. “Why is LLM pre-training called self-supervised, and how does it differ from fine-tuning a sentiment classifier?” (Explain in 2–5 sentences)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Where do the right answers come from in the model’s first training, and why is that different from teaching it to sort reviews into positive and negative?

    Answer: the full model answer is in the exam section above. In short: in pre-training, the true next (or masked) word comes from the text itself, so there is a target but no human labelling, hence “self-supervised”. Fine-tuning a sentiment classifier is ordinary supervised learning, because it needs texts already labelled positive or negative. Why: the difference is who supplies the right answer: the text itself, or a person.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • LLM (large language model): a program, like ChatGPT, that has learned from huge amounts of text to predict what comes next. Like phone autocomplete, but far bigger.
  • training: the process of setting the model’s dials so it predicts well. Like practising piano until your fingers know the piece.
  • weight / parameter: one adjustable number (one dial) inside the model. Big LLMs have billions of them.
  • B / T (as in 0.34B, 1.6T): B = billion (a thousand million), T = trillion (a thousand billion). Counts of parameters or of tokens.
  • token: one small piece of text, often a word or part of a word. “Unhappy” might be “un” + “happy”.
  • vocabulary: the full list of tokens the model knows.
  • vector: a list of numbers in a fixed order, such as (0.3, 0.5, 0.2).
  • target: the right answer the model’s guess is compared with. Here, the true next word, such as “all”.
  • label / labelled data: a right answer written down by a person, such as “positive” next to a review. Labelled data = examples that come with such answers.
  • supervised learning: learning from examples that come with the right answer. Like a student doing exercises with an answer key.
  • unsupervised learning: finding patterns in data with no right answers at all. Like sorting photos into groups without being told what the groups are.
  • self-supervised learning: there is a right answer, but it comes from the data itself, not from a person. Like covering the next word in a book with your thumb and then checking.
  • topic model / LDA: a method from earlier in the course that groups documents into themes without any answer key. A classic unsupervised method.
  • pre-training: the first, giant training stage on ordinary text, before any special task.
  • next-token prediction: guessing which token comes next. The main pre-training task for GPT-type models.
  • masked words: words hidden inside a sentence that the model must fill in. The pre-training task for BERT-type models.
  • BERT, GPT: two famous families of LLMs. BERT practises on masked words; GPT (which includes ChatGPT) practises on next words.
  • probability: a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely something is. 0.3 means 30%.
  • probability vector (\(\hat y_t\)): the model’s full list of probabilities, one per vocabulary token, at position \(t\). The little hat means “the model’s guess”.
  • loss: one number that says how wrong the model was. Smaller is better. Like the points you lost on a test.
  • cross-entropy loss (\(L_{CE}\)): the loss used for LLMs: minus the log of the probability given to the true next word. Probability 0.3 gives loss 1.204.
  • log / natural log (ln): a calculator function. For numbers between 0 and 1 it gives a negative number, and the closer to 0, the more negative. ln(1) = 0.
  • negative log probability: the log of a probability with a minus sign in front, so the result is a positive penalty.
  • average loss over a sequence: add up the losses at every position and divide by how many there are. (0.693 + 1.609 + 0.916) / 3 = 1.073.
  • function: a rule that turns an input into an output. “Square the number” is a function: 2 goes in, 4 comes out.
  • optimum / minimum: the best point. For a loss, the lowest point, like the bottom of a valley.
  • slope / derivative: how much the output changes when you change the input a tiny bit. Like how steep a hill is where you stand.
  • partial derivative (\(\partial\)): the slope with respect to one input while all the others are held still. \(\partial e/\partial b\) = “how much \(e\) changes if only \(b\) changes”.
  • gradient (\(\nabla L\)): the full list of slopes, one for every dial. It points uphill, so you step the opposite way.
  • gradient descent: repeatedly take a small step downhill on the loss. Like walking down a foggy mountain by always stepping where the ground slopes down.
  • learning rate (\(\eta\), “eta”): how big each downhill step is. Too big and you overshoot; too small and it takes forever.
  • learning-rate decay (\(\eta_k\)): making the steps smaller as training goes on (\(k\) = step number). Like slowing down as you get close to a parking spot.
  • backpropagation: the method that works out every dial’s slope in one backward sweep, starting from the loss. Like tracing blame backwards through a chain of people after a mistake.
  • chain rule: to get the slope through a chain of steps, multiply the slopes of the steps. If A doubles B and B triples C, then A changes C six-fold.
  • reverse-mode vs forward-mode differentiation: two ways of applying the chain rule. Reverse mode starts at the output and goes backwards, giving all slopes in one go. Forward mode starts at one input and gives only that one slope.
  • computational graph / node / edge: a diagram of a calculation. Each circle (node) is one value, and each arrow (edge) shows which value feeds which. The numbers on the arrows are the local slopes.
  • epoch: one complete pass through all the training data. Like reading the whole textbook once.
  • batch / mini-batch: a small group of examples used for one nudge. Like tasting a spoonful of soup instead of the whole pot.
  • online training: nudging after every single example (a mini-batch of size one). Very noisy.
  • SGD (stochastic gradient descent): gradient descent where each step uses a random mini-batch. “Stochastic” means “random”.
  • noise: random wobble in the steps, because each mini-batch is a bit different.
  • convergence: settling down at (or near) the lowest point.
  • generalisation: doing well on new examples, not only the ones trained on.
  • over-fitting: memorising the training examples instead of learning the general pattern. Like learning test answers by heart without understanding.
  • regularisation: anything that discourages over-fitting.
  • tuning parameter: a setting you choose yourself (like the mini-batch size), rather than one the model learns.
  • adaptive optimisers (AdaGrad, AdaDelta, RMSProp, Adam): improved versions of gradient descent that adjust the step size automatically for each dial. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • non-convex: a loss landscape with many hills and valleys, not one simple bowl. You might end up in a valley that isn’t the deepest one.
  • parameter initialisation: the starting positions of the dials before training begins.
  • vanishing / exploding gradients: slopes that shrink to almost nothing, or blow up to huge numbers, as they are passed backwards through many layers. Either way, the dials stop learning sensibly. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • saturation / dead neurons: parts of the network that get stuck and stop reacting to their input, so they stop learning. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • layer normalization: rescaling the numbers inside each layer so they stay in a sensible range. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • shuffling: mixing the order of the training examples after each epoch, like shuffling flashcards.
  • teacher forcing: during training, always show the model the true earlier words, not its own earlier guesses. Like a teacher correcting each word before you write the next one.
  • time step: one position in the sequence, one word after another.
  • continued pre-training / mid-training: extra rounds of pre-training, often on more specific text, before the task-training steps.
  • SFT (supervised fine-tuning): further training on examples of instructions paired with good answers.
  • preference optimisation / reinforcement learning: further training where the model is rewarded for answers that people (or a scoring system) prefer. Like a dog getting treats for good behaviour.
  • fine-tuning: extra training of an already-trained model on a specific task, such as sorting reviews into positive and negative.
  • sentiment classification: sorting a text by feeling, such as positive or negative.
  • fixed weights at answer time: once training is done, the dials do not move while you use the model.
  • frontier model: one of the biggest, most advanced models of its time.
  • Transformer, BERT, GPT-2, GPT-3, Switch Transformer, DeepSeek-V4-Flash: names of specific models, used on the slides to show how fast model size grew.
  • \(\theta\) (“theta”) and \(\hat g\): on slide 16, \(\theta\) is the list of all dials and \(\hat g\) is the slope estimated from one mini-batch.

Sources: Lecture 9b LLMs: Training and fine tuning (Lecture_llm_trainingandfinetuning.pdf), slides 4–19 and 22; Lecture 7 Introducing LLMs (Lecture_llm_intro.pdf), slides 7, 9, 10, 13.

20. Fine-tuning vs prompt engineering vs embeddings, RAG, zero-/few-shot and alignment

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 2025 Q4(e) (fine-tuning vs prompt engineering, 5 points) and 2025 T/F (j) (zero-shot); also the natural toolbox for the business-case reflection.

Why this exists

A bank gets thousands of customer complaints every week. Some are about card fees. Some are about the app crashing. Some are about loans. The bank wants each complaint sorted into the right bin, so the right team sees it fast.

The bank could use a chatbot program like ChatGPT for this. Such a program has read huge amounts of text, so it already “knows language”. But it has never seen this bank’s bins. It has never seen how this bank’s customers write. So how do you get a general-purpose language program to do one specific job well?

There are two big options:

  • change what you tell the program, or
  • change the program itself.

There are also two in-between options. This chapter explains all four, and how to choose between them. The exam asked about exactly this in 2025.

The idea in everyday words

Start with the program. A program like ChatGPT is called a large language model, or LLM. It has learned, from huge amounts of text, to guess which word comes next. Inside, it is a giant machine full of adjustable dials. Each dial is one number. The model has hundreds of millions of them, or more. One dial is called a parameter or a weight. These two words mean the same thing in this chapter.

How the dials got set. The dials were set during a long first round of training. The model was shown text, guessed the next word, saw how wrong its guess was, and every dial was nudged a tiny bit to make the guess less wrong. This was repeated billions of times. This first, big, general round is called pre-training. A model that has finished it is a pre-trained LLM. It “knows language”, but not your task.

The standard way to do the nudging has a name: SGD, short for stochastic gradient descent. “Stochastic” means “using a small random handful of examples at each step”. You do not need the maths. Picture it as “guess, measure how wrong, nudge the dials, repeat”.

How you talk to it. You send the model a piece of text. That text is called the prompt. It can hold instructions, examples, documents and your question. Everything the model can see in one request is called its context. The context disappears after the answer. The next request starts fresh. The model reads text in small pieces called tokens. A token is often a word, sometimes part of a word. Companies that run these models charge per token. There is also a limit on how many tokens the model can read at once. That limit is the context window.

Now the key distinction. There are two different things you can change:

  • the context (what the model reads this time), or
  • the weights (the dials inside the model).

A lecture slide puts it in one sentence, and it is the most important sentence in this chapter:

“Uploading a document changes the context. Fine-tuning changes the weights.”

Picture the model as an experienced consultant you have hired. Here are the four ways to get them to do your job.

Way 1: write them a better brief (prompting). You change only what you say. You give clear instructions, the exact shape of answer you want, maybe a solved example. The consultant’s skills stay exactly as they were. Writing prompts that get good, reliable answers is a skill. It is called prompt engineering.

Prompting comes in a few flavours:

  • If you give instructions only, with no solved examples, that is called zero-shot [Not in course files — general knowledge]. The “zero” means zero examples.
  • If you add one or a few solved examples to the prompt, that is called few-shot. The model copies the pattern it sees.
  • If you ask the model to reason step by step before giving its final answer, that is called chain-of-thought [Not in course files — general knowledge].

In none of these does a single dial move.

Way 2: hand them the right folder first (RAG). Before the consultant answers, a search step finds the relevant company documents and pastes them into the prompt. Say, the bank’s fee rules. This has a name: RAG, short for retrieval-augmented generation. “Retrieval” means finding documents. “Generation” means the model writing its answer. The search tool is called the retriever. Again, no dial moves. Only the context changes.

Way 3: ask only for their notes, and judge yourself (embeddings). The model can turn any text into a list of numbers that sums up what the text is about. Such a list is called an embedding, or a vector. You ask the model only for these number lists. Then you train your own small, simple sorting program on them. A program that sorts things into categories is called a classifier. The big model’s dials stay untouched. Only your small model is trained.

Way 4: send them on a training course (fine-tuning). Here you do change the model.
