  1. You collect many complaints that staff have already sorted by hand. Examples that come with the right answer written down by a person are called labelled data. The course also says “training data already classified”.
  2. You bolt a small new output part onto the top of the model. Its only job is to choose between your bins. This part is called a head. The course calls it a problem-specific head (or task head).
  3. You train with the same loop as before: show a complaint, let the model guess the bin, measure how wrong it was, nudge the dials, repeat. Training on labelled examples, with the right answers as the target, is called supervised training.
  4. You choose which dials may move. Either only the new head’s dials move, and all the old ones are locked in place. Locked dials are called frozen, and this version is called head-only fine-tuning. Or all the dials in the model move. That is full fine-tuning.

This whole process is called fine-tuning. Afterwards the model’s insides are different. It has become a specialist in your bins.

Fine-tuning is one example of a wider idea called transfer learning: reusing what a model learned on one task to help with another. Think of a violin player who learns the viola much faster than a beginner would. A field or type of data, such as “bank complaints” or “film reviews”, is called a domain.

Where alignment fits. Chat models like ChatGPT got extra training after pre-training, so that they follow instructions and give helpful, safe answers. This is often called alignment [Not in course files — general knowledge]. The course lists two steps:

  1. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT): training on “examples of instructions and desired responses”.
  2. Preference optimisation / reinforcement learning: “improve responses using preferences or rewards”. In plain words, answers people prefer are rewarded.

(Calling these two steps “alignment” is [Not in course files — general knowledge]; the course slide does not use the word.) The common name for the second step, when the preferences come from people rating answers, is RLHF, short for “reinforcement learning from human feedback” [Not in course files — general knowledge]. Alignment does change the weights. But it is done by the provider (the company that makes and runs the model), not by you.

Which way is best? It depends.

  • Prompting is good for starting fast and cheap, with no labelled data and no training. It breaks when you need the same behaviour every time at huge volume. It can be inconsistent, you pay for every token on every request, and only so much fits in the context window.
  • Fine-tuning is good for a stable, high-volume task: you get a consistent specialist. It breaks when you lack labelled data, computer power or skills, or when the bins keep changing (then you must train again).
  • RAG is good for answers that must rest on your own, up-to-date documents. It breaks when the search step finds the wrong document.
  • None of them guarantees correct answers. The course says: “Retrieval changes context; fine-tuning changes weights. Neither guarantees accuracy.” Always check the results against a sample that people have sorted by hand.

Walk-through example

Part 1: one bank complaint, four ways. The complaint is: “You charged my card fee twice this month.”

Zero-shot prompt. You send: “Sort this complaint into one of: fees, app, loans. Reply with one word.” A capable model should reply “fees”. Dials changed: 0.

Few-shot prompt. You send the same instruction, plus one solved example: “Example: ‘The app crashes when I log in.’ → app”. Dials changed: still 0. The model copies the pattern it sees in the prompt.

Head-only fine-tuning, in miniature. This is where we count dials. To do that, you need to know what the head receives.

When the model reads a complaint, it produces an embedding: a list of numbers that sums up the whole complaint. Imagine that list has only 4 numbers. (Real models use far more. Part 2 uses 1,024.) The new head must turn those 4 numbers into one score for each of the 3 bins. The bin with the highest score wins.

How many new dials does the head need?

  1. Each bin’s score is built from all 4 summary numbers. Each of those 4 numbers gets its own dial (a weight that says how much that number matters for this bin). So each bin needs 4 dials. With 3 bins, that is 4 × 3 = 12 dials.
  2. Each bin also gets one extra “starting level” dial. It is like the zero setting on a kitchen scale. This kind of dial is called a bias. That is 3 more dials, one per bin.
  3. Total: 12 + 3 = 15 new dials.

Only these 15 are trained. Every other dial in the model is frozen.

Part 2: the course’s own example, a film review. The course’s slides use this review: “entirely predictable and lacks energy”. The task is to label its feeling as positive or negative. The feeling in a text is called its sentiment. Imagine a firm with many such reviews to label.

The slides use a particular model family called BERT. Its full name is Bidirectional Transformer Encoder. “Bidirectional” means it reads the whole text in both directions at once. “Transformer” is the name of the inner design that modern LLMs are built on. Models like this are often used for understanding tasks such as sentiment.

BERT puts a special marker at the very start of every text, written [CLS]. So the input looks like “[CLS] entirely predictable and lacks energy”. After BERT has read the text, the list of numbers it holds at the [CLS] position acts as a summary of the whole text. The course says the [CLS] token “denotes the sequence-level embedding”, meaning one number list for the whole text.

Now, what head goes on top? A normal LLM already has a head. It is the language modelling head (or LM head). It gives a raw score to every word the model knows, as a candidate for the next word. Raw scores like these, before any conversion, are called logits.

For sentiment you swap that head for a new one. The new head gives only 2 raw scores: one for positive, one for negative. It then turns them into chances. A chance, or probability, is a number between 0 and 1 saying how likely something is. The chances for all options add up to 1. The step that turns raw scores into probabilities is called softmax. So the new head is called a softmax head. It might say, for example, “negative: 0.9, positive: 0.1”. (Those two numbers are only an illustration.)

The course’s recipe, step by step:

  • use a pre-trained BERT-type model;
  • let the [CLS] token stand for the whole-text summary;
  • add a new softmax head on top of it;
  • “Use SGD to train the new parameters in the model and potentially update the pre-trained parameters as well”.

This “requires supervised training and training data already classified”.

Counting the head’s dials. Let \(d\) stand for the length of the [CLS] number list. The slides show a BERT with 0.34 billion dials. That is 0.34 × 1,000,000,000 = 340 million. A model of that size uses \(d = 1024\) [Not in course files — general knowledge: d = 1024]. So the summary list has 1,024 numbers. The head has 2 outputs (positive, negative).

Same counting as Part 1:

  • weights: 1,024 numbers × 2 outputs = 2,048;
  • biases: one per output = 2;
  • total: 2,048 + 2 = 2,050 new dials.

How small is that? Divide by the size of the whole model and turn it into a percentage: \(2{,}050 / 340{,}000{,}000 \times 100 = 0.0006\%\). So head-only fine-tuning trains about 0.0006% of the model. For the bank’s 3 bins it would be 1,024 × 3 + 3 = 3,075 dials. That is still less than 0.001% of the 340 million.

This is why head-only fine-tuning is cheap. Full fine-tuning moves all ~340 million dials as well. It can adapt the model more deeply, but it costs far more.

Part 3: the five routes side by side, for this review.

  • Zero-shot prompt. The system prompt is a set of standing instructions sent before the user’s text, like the house rules on a staff noticeboard. Here it says: “Classify the review as positive or negative. Reply ONLY with one word.” Weights changed: none. Labelled data: none, though a few labelled reviews are still needed to check how often it is right.
  • Few-shot prompt. Same instruction plus one solved example in the allowed labels, e.g. “Example: ‘A gripping, beautifully acted film.’ → positive”. (The course’s practice notebook uses the same idea with its own example, ‘Great screen, awful speakers.’ → mixed, because its list of allowed labels includes “mixed”.) Weights changed: none.
  • RAG. Not really needed for sentiment. It fits questions like “What does our return policy say?”: the retriever pastes the policy text into the prompt. Weights changed: none.
  • Embeddings + own model. Send each review to the LLM and take its embedding. With BERT, people often take the number lists from its last 4 layers (its last 4 processing stages) and average them: “the average of the last 4 layers”. Then train a simple classifier of your own on, say, a few hundred labelled reviews. The LLM’s weights: unchanged. Your small model is trained.
  • Head-only fine-tuning. Put a softmax head with 2 outputs on the [CLS] list. That is 2,050 new dials, trained on labelled reviews. Everything else is frozen.
  • Full fine-tuning. Same head, but SGD also updates all ~340 million pre-trained weights. This is the most flexible route, and the most expensive in computer power and data.

Part 4: the comparison table. Each row is one approach. The columns say what changes, what data it needs, how costly it is, and when to use it. Read one cell like this: the “Prompting” row, “What changes” column, tells you that prompting changes only the context.

A few words the table uses. Compute means computer power. A GPU is a special chip that does the heavy maths of training fast. Over-fitting means the model memorises its training examples instead of learning the general pattern, so it does badly on new ones. Hallucination means the model stating something false with confidence, such as a made-up quote. Tf-idf is a word-matching way of scoring how relevant a document is to a search. It gives extra weight to words that are rare across the collection. A downstream model is the later model that uses the LLM’s output for the task you care about. Clustering means grouping similar texts together without labels.

Approach What changes Data needed Cost / skill When to use
Prompting (zero-/few-shot, format, chain-of-thought) Only the context (instructions, examples). Weights fixed. None to start; a small labelled set to check quality Cheapest to try; pay per token at run time; no training Quick start, changing tasks, few or no labels, a capable general model
RAG Context: retrieved documents are added to the prompt. Weights fixed. A document collection plus a retriever (a search tool, using tf-idf word matching or embeddings) Build and maintain search; longer prompts cost more tokens Answers must rest on company or up-to-date facts; reduces hallucination (confident made-up answers) but “neither guarantees accuracy”
Embeddings + own model Nothing in the LLM; you train a separate small model on its vectors Labelled data for your small model Moderate; the small model is cheap to run and easy to validate Classification, clustering or search at scale; when you want a transparent, cheap downstream model
Head-only fine-tuning A new task head (e.g. softmax on [CLS]); all other weights frozen Labelled training data (“already classified”) Low–moderate training cost; needs ML skills A stable, high-volume task with labels; limited compute
Full fine-tuning The new head and all pre-trained weights More labelled data Highest: GPUs (special maths chips), expertise, risk of over-fitting (memorising instead of learning) Prompting and head-only are not accurate enough, the domain is special, and the volume justifies the cost

(“ML skills” means machine-learning skills: knowing how to train models. “Validate” means checking how often a model is right.)

Part 5: what the course actually shows about prompting. The lecture on prompt engineering is not in the course files. The course files give three sources instead.

  1. The assignment grading guidelines say: “Core skills include providing appropriate context and tone and chain-of-thought input.” Tone is the style of the answer, such as formal, friendly or short.
  2. The practice notebook lists the techniques you used to get answers in a strict machine-readable format, “one change at a time”. That format is JSON: a strict text layout other programs can read, like {"sentiment": "negative"}. The techniques:
    1. set temperature 0. The model normally picks each next word partly by chance among the likely ones. Temperature is the dial for how adventurous that choice is. At 0 it always picks the single most likely word, so the same input gives the same answer.
    2. a system prompt that spells out the exact output format: Reply ONLY with JSON of the form {"sentiment": "positive|negative|mixed", "aspect": "..."}. No other text.
    3. “add an example to the system prompt (few-shot)”.
    4. tell the model what to do with edge cases. An edge case is an unusual example that doesn’t fit the rules neatly, such as a lukewarm review.
    Later the notebook adds grounding: telling the model to answer only from a text you give it. Its instruction: “Answer using ONLY the provided excerpt. If the excerpt does not contain the answer, say that it does not.” It is like an open-book exam where you may only use the book on the desk. The notebook then adds RAG.
  3. A lecture slide gives the training steps after pre-training: supervised fine-tuning (SFT), then preference optimisation / reinforcement learning, as explained above under alignment.

On chain-of-thought, the course makes a related point. Models can “spend extra computation before returning a final answer”. This “increases latency and resource use”. Latency means the waiting time before the answer arrives. And “a persuasive explanation does not guarantee correctness”.

Part 6: the course’s business case. A firm wants to classify 100,000 reviews a month. This number of items to process is the volume. Prompting a small model running on a laptop takes 5–30 seconds per review. So at that volume, the cost and time per review add up fast. Naive Bayes is a simple, fast word-counting classifier from earlier in the course. It is fast and cheap, but it needs labels.

Fine-tuning becomes worth it when three things hold: you have (or can create) a labelled set, the task is stable, and the volume is high enough that a cheaper, faster specialised model pays back the training effort. Whatever you choose, validate it against a hand-labelled sample and a simple benchmark. A hand-labelled sample is a set of examples people sorted, used for checking. A benchmark is a simple method to compare against, like “always guess the biggest bin”.

The formula, explained

The only formula here counts the new dials in a task head:

\[\text{new dials} = d \times m + m\]

  • \(d\) = the length of the summary number list the head receives (1,024 in the course example).
  • \(m\) = the number of labels the head chooses between (2 for positive/negative, 3 for the bank’s bins).
  • \(d \times m\) = the weights: one dial for every pair of “summary number” and “label”.
  • the final \(+\, m\) = the biases: one starting-level dial per label.

Read aloud: “the head needs one dial for each summary number for each label, plus one extra dial per label.” With \(d = 1024\) and \(m = 2\): \(1024 \times 2 + 2 = 2{,}050\).

You do not need to write this formula in the exam. In 2025 there were no calculations. But being able to say “head-only fine-tuning trains only about 2,050 of 340 million parameters” makes it very clear why it is cheap.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

2025 Q4(e), 5 points: “Describe the difference between fine-tuning and prompt engineering.”

The graders’ guideline said: fine-tuning re-estimates part of the model or extra layers; prompting keeps the weights and improves the context. “Re-estimate” means re-train, so the dials get new values.

Model answer Fine-tuning is transfer learning: we take a pre-trained LLM, add a problem-specific head (for example a softmax layer on the [CLS] embedding for sentiment) and re-train on labelled data. Either only the new head or all parameters are re-estimated, so the model’s weights change. Prompt engineering leaves the weights unchanged and instead improves the context the model sees: clear instructions, the required output format and tone, examples (few-shot), step-by-step reasoning, or retrieved documents. Prompting is quick and needs no labelled data but is less controllable. Fine-tuning needs data, compute and skills but can give a more consistent specialist model for a stable, high-volume task.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Fine-tuning takes a trained model, adds a small layer for your task, and trains it more on examples with the right answers, so the model itself changes. Prompt engineering leaves the model as it is and gives it better instructions, examples or documents to read. Prompting is quick and needs no tagged examples, but the results are harder to control. Fine-tuning takes data, computer power and skill, but for a big, steady task it can give a more consistent specialist.

2025 T/F (j): “Zero-shot involves re-estimating only the final output layer.”

Model answer FALSE. Zero-shot means no re-estimation at all: the weights stay fixed and you only write instructions. Re-estimating only the final layer is head-only fine-tuning (“only the parameters in the new model head”). That is a training method which needs labelled data. The statement swaps a prompting idea for a fine-tuning idea.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Zero-shot is only asking, with no examples, and nothing inside the model changes. Re-training only the top layer is a kind of fine-tuning. The statement mixes up the two.

Likely new True/False items.

“RAG updates the model’s weights.”

Model answer FALSE. RAG only changes what the model reads (the context), not its weights.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: A search step pastes documents into the prompt. The model reads them this time, but its dials stay the same.

“Fine-tuning is a form of transfer learning.”

Model answer TRUE. Fine-tuning is an instance of transfer learning: reusing a model trained on one job for a new job.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Fine-tuning reuses what the model already learned and adapts it to your task. That reuse is exactly what “transfer learning” means.

“Few-shot prompting changes the model’s parameters.”

Model answer FALSE. Few-shot means putting a few examples in the prompt; the parameters stay the same.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Showing the model examples is still only part of what it reads. No dial moves.

Likely business-case question: “Which approach should a firm use to classify 100,000 reviews a month, and why?”

Model answer Prompting a small local model takes 5–30 seconds per review on a laptop, so the per-review cost and time add up fast at that volume. Naive Bayes is fast and cheap but needs labels. Fine-tuning becomes worth it when you have (or can create) a labelled set, the task is stable, and the volume is high enough that a cheaper, faster specialised model pays back the training effort. Whatever you choose, validate it against a hand-labelled sample and a simple benchmark.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Asking an LLM one review at a time is slow and costly when there are 100,000. Training a specialist pays off only if you have tagged examples, the job stays the same, and the volume is big. Either way, check the results against reviews people have sorted, and against a simple method.

What a top-grade answer must include For fine-tuning vs prompting:

    1. Fine-tuning = transfer learning (reusing a trained model for a new job). You add a task-specific head (a small extra layer for your task, e.g. a softmax on the [CLS] token for sentiment). Then you re-train with labelled data (examples already tagged with the right answer). You update only the head or all parameters, so the weights change.
  • (2) Prompting = the weights stay fixed. You improve the context (everything the model reads before it answers): instructions, format, tone, examples (few-shot), chain-of-thought (asking it to reason step by step), retrieved documents.
  • (3) One line of judgement. Prompting is fast and needs no labels, but it is harder to control and limited by the context window (how much text the model can read at once). Fine-tuning needs data, compute (computer power) and skills, but at high volume it can give a consistent, cheaper specialist model.
  • (4) If you have room, mention the third route: extracting embeddings (taking the model’s number lists for your texts and using them in your own model).

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Saying zero-shot or few-shot “trains” the model. It does not change the model at all.
  • Saying RAG or uploading a file teaches the model for good. It only changes the context (what the model reads this time).
  • Forgetting that fine-tuning needs labelled data (examples tagged with the right answer).
  • Describing only one side of the comparison.
  • Claiming fine-tuning always beats prompting.
  • Presenting zero-shot or chain-of-thought definitions as quotes from the slides. They come from the prompt-engineering lecture (not in the course files) or general knowledge.

Key terms to use

  • transfer learning: reusing a trained model for a new job
  • pre-trained LLM: big model already trained on lots of text
  • fine-tuning: extra training that changes the model’s dials
  • problem-specific (task) head: small extra layer added for your task
  • [CLS] token: special first token that summarises the text
  • softmax head: layer turning scores into chances per label
  • update all parameters vs only the head: re-train everything, or only the new layer
  • labelled / “already classified” data: examples tagged with the right answer
  • supervised: learning from examples with right answers
  • prompt engineering: writing better instructions for the model
  • system prompt: standing instructions given before the user’s text
  • context: everything the model reads before answering
  • output format: the exact shape the answer must have
  • tone: the style of voice of the answer
  • zero-shot: instructions only, no examples
  • few-shot: a few worked examples in the prompt
  • chain-of-thought: asking the model to reason step by step
  • grounding: answer only from a text you supply
  • RAG: search step pastes relevant documents into the prompt
  • “context vs weights”: prompting changes the input; fine-tuning changes the model
  • embedding extraction (average of last 4 layers / API): take the model’s number lists for your texts
  • SFT: supervised fine-tuning on example instructions and answers
  • preference optimisation / RL (alignment): rewarding the answers people prefer

Quick self-test

  1. “Zero-shot learning involves re-estimating only the final output layer of the model.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Zero-shot means asking the model to do a task with instructions only, no examples. “Re-estimating only the final output layer” means re-training the model’s last layer. Does zero-shot re-train that last layer?

    False. Why: zero-shot changes no weights (dials) at all; you only write a request. Re-training only the last layer (the head) is a kind of fine-tuning, called head-only fine-tuning. It is the difference between briefing a consultant on a new task and sending them on a training course.

  2. “Retrieval-augmented generation changes the model’s weights.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a set-up where a search step finds relevant documents and pastes them into the prompt. The weights are the model’s learned dials. Does RAG change those dials?

    False. Why: RAG only changes what the model reads this time. The course puts it this way: “Retrieval changes context; fine-tuning changes weights”. It is like handing a consultant the right folder before a meeting: they are better informed today, but they have not been retrained.

  3. “When fine-tuning, one can update all model parameters or only the parameters in the new head.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Fine-tuning is extra training for one task, and the new head is the small layer added on top for that task. The parameters are the model’s dials. Can you choose to re-train either all the dials or only the new layer’s dials?

    True. Why: both options exist. You can re-train every dial in the model, or leave the old dials as they are and train only the new layer on top. It is like either retraining a whole team or only training the new person who joined it.

  4. “Adding an example of the desired answer to the system prompt is called few-shot prompting.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The system prompt is the standing set of instructions given to the model before the user’s text. If you put a worked example of a good answer in there, is that called few-shot prompting?

    True. Why: few-shot means showing the model one or a few examples of what you want. It is like showing a new colleague one finished report before asking them to write the next one.

  5. “Describe the difference between fine-tuning and prompt engineering.” (Explain in 2–5 sentences)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Explain how “training the model more” differs from “writing better instructions for it”.

    Answer: the model answer is the one given above under 2025 Q4(e): “Fine-tuning is transfer learning: we take a pre-trained LLM, add a problem-specific head (for example a softmax layer on the [CLS] embedding for sentiment) and re-train on labelled data. Either only the new head or all parameters are re-estimated, so the model’s weights change. Prompt engineering leaves the weights unchanged and instead improves the context the model sees: clear instructions, the required output format and tone, examples (few-shot), step-by-step reasoning, or retrieved documents. Prompting is quick and needs no labelled data but is less controllable. Fine-tuning needs data, compute and skills but can give a more consistent specialist model for a stable, high-volume task.”

    Why: fine-tuning changes the model’s dials using tagged examples; prompting leaves the dials alone and improves what the model reads. Each has a cost and a benefit, and a good answer names both sides.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • LLM (large language model): a program, like ChatGPT, that has learned from huge amounts of text to predict what comes next.
  • weight / parameter: one adjustable number (a dial) inside the model. Changing weights = changing the model’s insides.
  • pre-training / pre-trained LLM: the big first round of general training; a model that has done it “knows language” but not your task.
  • SGD (stochastic gradient descent): the “guess, measure how wrong, nudge the dials, repeat” method, using a small random batch of examples each step.
  • prompt: the text you send to the model: instructions, examples, documents and the question.
  • context: everything the model can see in this request. It disappears after the answer.
  • token: one small piece of text, often a word or part of a word. Providers charge per token.
  • context window: the most tokens the model can read at once.
  • prompt engineering: the skill of writing prompts that get good, reliable answers. Like writing a clear brief for a new colleague.
  • system prompt: standing instructions sent before the user’s text, such as “Reply ONLY with JSON.” Like house rules on a staff noticeboard.
  • zero-shot: asking the model to do a task from instructions alone, with no examples and no change to its weights. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • few-shot: putting one or a few solved examples in the prompt. Still no change to the weights.
  • chain-of-thought: asking the model to reason step by step before giving its final answer. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): a search step finds relevant documents and pastes them into the prompt, then the model writes the answer. Like a librarian handing the consultant the right folder first.
  • retrieval / retriever: finding relevant documents / the search tool that does it.
  • embedding / vector: a list of numbers that stands for a word or a whole text. A “sequence-level embedding” is one such list for a whole text.
  • embedding extraction / “average of the last 4 layers”: taking the model’s number lists for your texts and using them elsewhere. With BERT, people often average the lists from its last 4 layers.
  • API: a web service your program sends text to and gets results back from, such as number lists. Like a vending machine for model outputs.
  • classifier: a model that puts things into categories, e.g. complaint → “fees”.
  • downstream task: the later task you actually care about, such as sorting complaints, that uses the model’s output.
  • fine-tuning: extra training of a pre-trained model on your own labelled examples, so its weights change. Like sending a trained nurse on a short course to specialise in one ward.
  • transfer learning: reusing what a model learned on one task to help with another. Like a violin player learning viola faster than a beginner.
  • domain: a field or type of data, such as “bank complaints” or “film reviews”.
  • head (model head, task head, problem-specific head): a small output part bolted onto the top of the model for one job. Like a new attachment on a drill.
  • language modelling head (LM head): the usual head that scores every word the model knows as the possible next word.
  • logits: the raw scores a head gives each option before they become probabilities.
  • probability: a number from 0 to 1 saying how likely something is; all options add up to 1.
  • softmax / softmax head: the step that turns raw scores into probabilities; a head that ends with it gives one probability per label.
  • label / labelled data / “already classified”: examples that come with the right answer written down by a person, such as a review marked “negative”.
  • supervised training: training on labelled examples, with the right answers as the target.
  • sentiment: the feeling in a text, such as positive or negative.
  • BERT / Bidirectional Transformer Encoder: a model family that reads the whole text in both directions. Often used for understanding tasks such as sentiment.
  • [CLS] token: a special marker placed at the start of the text in BERT. Its final numbers act as a summary of the whole text.
  • frozen layers / head-only fine-tuning: all the old dials are locked; only the new head’s dials are trained (2,050 in the course example).
  • full fine-tuning: both the new head and all the old dials are trained (all ~340 million).
  • bias (in “2 biases”): one extra dial per output that sets its starting level, like the zero setting on a kitchen scale.
  • temperature 0: the setting where the model always picks its most likely next word, so the same input gives the same answer.
  • tone: the style of the answer, such as formal, friendly or short.
  • output format / JSON: the exact shape the answer must have. JSON is a strict text format other programs can read, like {"sentiment": "negative"}.
  • edge case: an unusual example that doesn’t fit the rules neatly, such as a lukewarm review.
  • grounding: telling the model to answer only from a text you give it. Like an open-book exam with only one book allowed.
  • hallucination: the model stating something false with confidence, such as a made-up quote.
  • latency: waiting time before the answer arrives.
  • tf-idf: a word-matching way of scoring how relevant a document is to a search, giving extra weight to rare words.
  • Naive Bayes: a simple, fast word-counting classifier from earlier in the course.
  • clustering: grouping similar texts together without labels.
  • alignment: teaching a model to follow instructions and give helpful, safe answers. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • SFT (supervised fine-tuning): training on examples of instructions paired with good answers.
  • preference optimisation / reinforcement learning: training where answers people prefer are rewarded.
  • RLHF (reinforcement learning from human feedback): the common name for training a model on human ratings of its answers. [Not in course files — general knowledge]
  • provider: the company that makes and runs the model.
  • compute / GPU: compute = computer power. A GPU is a special chip that does the heavy maths of training fast.
  • ML skills: machine-learning skills, i.e. knowing how to train models.
  • over-fitting: memorising the training examples instead of learning the general pattern.
  • validate / hand-labelled sample / benchmark: validate = check how often the model is right. A hand-labelled sample is a set of examples people sorted, used for checking. A benchmark is a simple method to compare against, like “always guess the biggest bin”.
  • volume: how many items you need to process, such as 100,000 reviews a month.

Sources: Lecture 9b Training and fine tuning, slides 19–23 (fine-tuning definition slide 20, example slides 21–22, alternatives slide 23, 0.34B BERT slide 19); Lecture 7 Introducing LLMs, slides 9 (SFT, preference optimisation), 10 (“Uploading a document changes the context…”), 11 (extra computation, latency), 20 (RAG, “Neither guarantees accuracy”); Interactive Notebook 4, cells 14–25 and 28 (cell 17 prompting steps, cells 19–24 grounding and RAG); Assignments 2026 slides 20, 22, 23 (5–30 seconds per review), Assignment 4.2 c; 2024/2025 assignment evaluation guidelines. Note: the Lecture 11 slides (“Prompt engineering and model alignment”, 16 Nov) are not in the course folder. If you took notes in that lecture, use its exact terms next to this chapter.

21. Lessons from running a real LLM locally (Interactive Notebook 4)

Exam priority: ★★ Medium — rarely asked directly, but excellent, concrete material for the business-case reflection (2025 Block 5, 20 points) and for T/F items on tokens, temperature and RAG.

Why this exists

Reading about chatbots like ChatGPT is one thing. Using one for real work is another.

Imagine a Norwegian company. It wants a chatbot program to label customer reviews, and to answer staff questions from its staff handbook. Before spending money, the managers want to know five things:

  1. What will it cost?
  2. Will it give the same answer twice?
  3. Can its answers be fed straight into other software?
  4. Will it make things up?
  5. Can it find the right page of the handbook when someone asks in their own words?

The course has a hands-on exercise that tests all five, using a small, free chatbot program running on your own laptop. This chapter walks through what that exercise shows, and turns each finding into a business rule you can use in the exam.

The idea in everyday words

The program. A chatbot program like ChatGPT is called a large language model, or LLM. It writes text one small piece at a time, each time guessing a likely next piece. Inside, it is a big machine full of adjustable dials. Each dial is one number, set during training. One dial is called a parameter or a weight.

The exercise. The course exercise is a notebook: a document that mixes computer code and explanations, and runs in a web browser. Code is instructions written for the computer. This notebook uses the programming language Python. The notebook is split into boxes called cells. Each cell holds some code or some text, and you run a code cell by pressing a button. Think of a recipe book where each step can be “cooked” at the press of a button. The course calls it Interactive Notebook 4.

The usual way vs. the notebook’s way. Normally, to use a big model like ChatGPT from a program, you sign up (an account), get a password for programs (an API key), and send your text over the internet to the company’s computers (the cloud). The company that runs the model charges a small price for every piece of text going in and out. That is a per-token fee (tokens are explained below).

The notebook does none of that. It downloads a small free model once, and then runs it on your own laptop: “no account, no API key, no cloud”. The model is called Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct. “0.5B” means 0.5 billion, so half a billion dials. “Instruct” means it was trained to follow instructions and chat. It is downloaded from Hugging Face, a website where people share models, like an app store for AI models.

This is possible because the model’s makers publish its dials for anyone to download. That is called open weights. Running a model on your own computer is called local deployment. One big plus is privacy: your text never leaves your machine.

Why use such a small model? It is weak and slow. But that is the point. It is like test-driving a small car before buying a fleet. The small car is not the best car. But every weakness you notice (fuel use, how it handles in snow) tells you what to check before you put 100 of them on the road. In the same way, the tiny model makes the typical LLM failures easy to see.

The five tests, in plain words.

  1. Cost test. Feed in the same sentence in English and in Norwegian. Count how many pieces the model cuts each one into. More pieces means more cost.
  2. Same-answer test. Ask the same question three times. Count how many different answers come back, at different settings of a “boldness” dial.
  3. Software-ready test. Ask the model to label 4 reviews in a strict format that other programs can read. A small checking program counts how many replies are usable. Then improve the instructions one change at a time.
  4. Making-things-up test. Ask the model to quote a real speech. Try three ways: with no source text, with the right source text, and with the wrong source text.
  5. Find-the-page test. Chop many speeches into short pieces. Let a word-matching search pick the best pieces and paste them into the instructions. Check whether the search still finds the right piece when the question uses different words.

Each test ends in one business rule. The walk-through below goes through them one by one and names each idea as it appears.

Walk-through example

The notebook has no saved outputs. That means the counts and scores it prints only appear when you run it yourself. So this chapter quotes no numbers from those printouts. The numbers below come from the notebook’s own text and settings, or from small examples worked by hand.

Test 1: tokens and cost.

An LLM does not read whole words. It reads small pieces of text called tokens. A token is often a whole word, sometimes part of a word, or a chunk of a number. A token that is only part of a word is called a subword token. The tool that cuts text into tokens is the tokenizer. Think of a butcher with a fixed set of cuts.

The notebook feeds in three test sentences:

  • English: “The central bank raised the interest rate to fight inflation.”
  • Norwegian: “Sentralbanken hevet renten for å bekjempe inflasjonen.”
  • Numbers: “Invoice 2024-11-07: NOK 1,234,567.89 due within 30 days.”

First it counts words. It does this with a line of code, len(text.split()). It cuts the text wherever there is a space and counts the parts. Count the English sentence yourself: The, central, bank, raised, the, interest, rate, to, fight, inflation. That is 10 words. The Norwegian sentence has 7 words. The numbers sentence has 8.

Then it counts tokens. The notebook says this tokenizer “was built mostly from English text”. So common English words are often one token each. A long Norwegian word like “Sentralbanken” gets chopped into several pieces. So do number strings like “1,234,567.89”. When you run it, the Norwegian sentence shows more tokens per word than the English one. Tokens per word means how many tokens, on average, one word turns into.

Why this matters for money: you pay per token. So the same price per token, but more tokens per word, means a bigger bill for a Norwegian document. The real cost once you count tokens is called the effective price. The notebook asks you to think about comparing two providers on price; this is the answer.

A small detail: the space in front of a word is part of its token. So ” bank” (with a space in front, called a leading space) and “bank” are different tokens.

Tokens also measure how much the model can read. The most tokens it can read at once is its context window. For this model it is 32,768 tokens. Think of it as the size of the desk the model works on.

Business rule 1: “Tokens are the unit of cost and of context. Languages and formats the tokenizer saw less of (Norwegian, numbers, codes) cost more tokens per word.”

Test 2: temperature and the same answer twice.

When the model picks its next word, it does not always take the single most likely one. It rolls a kind of weighted dice among the likely candidates. A setting called temperature controls how bold that roll is. Low temperature means predictable. High temperature means varied.

At temperature 0, the model always picks the single most likely next word. This is called greedy picking. The same question then gives the same answer every time.

The computer’s dice need a starting number, called a seed. A different seed gives different rolls. The notebook has a setting called N_SAMPLES, which is how many times to ask the same question. Here it is 3. It asks the same question 3 times, each with a different seed. Then it prints “k distinct answers out of N”, where N is the number of tries and k is how many different answers came back.

What happens:

  • At temperature 0, all answers are identical.
  • As the temperature rises, the answers become more varied.
  • At high temperature (the notebook suggests trying 2.0), they stop making sense.

Business rule 2: “Temperature trades predictability for variety. Use 0 for extraction and classification; higher values only when you want variety.” For example: use 0 for pulling invoice amounts or labelling reviews. Use a higher value for creative work, such as writing ten campaign slogans.

Test 3: answers that software can read.

If an LLM’s answers go straight into other software, they must have an exact shape. The notebook uses JSON: a strict text format such as {"sentiment": "positive"}. Here “sentiment” means the feeling of a review. Text that other software can read without a human is called machine-readable.

A small checking program, the format checker, scores how many of 4 reviews give usable output. It uses a command called json.loads. That command tries to read a reply as JSON and fails if the reply is broken. The checker also checks that the right keys (field names like “sentiment”) and allowed labels are there.

You then improve the score one change at a time:

  1. set temperature 0;
  2. write a system prompt (standing instructions sent before the user’s text, like house rules) with an explicit output format (spelling out exactly what shape the answer must have);
  3. add a few-shot example (one solved example in the instructions, to show the pattern);
  4. add rules for edge cases (examples that don’t fit the labels neatly).

The hard case is: “The app is fine, I guess. Nothing special.” The allowed labels are positive, negative and mixed. This review is lukewarm, so it fits none of them neatly. The list of allowed answers is called the label set. The notebook says choosing it is “a business decision, not a coding one”.

Business rule 3: “A system prompt with an explicit format makes output far more reliable — but not perfectly so. ‘Reliable’ has to be checked by code around the model, and the label set is a business decision.”

Test 4: making things up.

When a model states something false with confidence, such as an invented quote, that is called a hallucination.

The notebook asks the model to quote Gerald Ford’s 1975 State of the Union speech. (The State of the Union is a yearly speech by the US president.) A simple check, which the notebook calls the scoreboard, looks for Ford’s real words “not good” in the reply.

Three tries:

  • No source text. The model “predicts plausible text; it does not look things up”. So it dodges the question or invents a quote.
  • The right source text, at temperature 0. You paste in the right passage of the speech (an excerpt) and tell the model to answer only from it. This is called grounding. It is like an open-book exam where you may only use the book on the desk. Now the model can quote correctly.
  • The wrong source text. You paste in a passage from Washington’s 1791 speech instead. The small model may present that text as the answer. It does this even with the notebook’s firm extra instruction, the STRICT instruction: if the answer is not in the excerpt, say so.

Business rule 4: “Without context the model dodges or hallucinates. The right context (at temperature 0) fixes it. The wrong context can be worse than none.”

Test 5: finding the right page.

Why a search step is needed at all. The notebook uses a corpus: a collection of texts. Here it is all the US State of the Union speeches, called SOTU for short. Together they are about 2 million tokens long. The model can read at most 32,768 tokens at once. Divide: 2,000,000 / 32,768 = about 61. So the speeches are about 61 times too long to fit on the model’s desk. The model can only be shown a few chosen pieces, and a search step has to choose them.

This set-up has a name: RAG, short for retrieval-augmented generation. “Retrieval” means finding text. “Generation” means the model writing its answer. Step one, search for relevant pieces. Step two, paste them into the instructions. Step three, let the model answer. The search tool is called the retriever.

The speeches are cut into short slices called chunks. A setting called CHUNK_SIZE sets how many words each chunk has. Each chunk is labelled with the president and the year. The best-matching k chunks (k is a small number you choose) are the top-k chunks, set by TOP_K.

How the search scores chunks. It uses word matching. Before matching, it throws away very common words like “the”, “for” and “we”. These are called stop words. They appear everywhere, so they say nothing about the topic.

Then it scores words with tf-idf. A word counts more if it appears often in this chunk but is rare across all chunks. So “elderly” counts a lot; a word in every chunk would count little.

Each chunk becomes a vector: a list of numbers in a fixed order, one number per word in the vocabulary. The question becomes a vector too. Then the search compares the question’s list with each chunk’s list. The comparison score is cosine similarity: a score from 0 to 1 of how alike two word lists are. 0 means nothing in common.

Cosine similarity is built on a dot product: multiply the two lists number by number, and add the results up. If a word is missing from either text, its number is 0 there, so that word adds nothing. If two texts share no words at all, the dot product is 0, and so the cosine is 0.

A toy example, worked by hand. This small example was made for this guide, using the same tools the notebook uses. There are three short chunks:

  • Chunk A: “We will protect Social Security for the elderly.”
  • Chunk B: “We must build more roads and bridges.”
  • Chunk C: “Our schools need better teachers.”

After removing stop words such as “we”, “will”, “for”, “the”, “our”, “must” and “more”, this is what is left:

  • Chunk A: protect, social, security, elderly.
  • Chunk B: build, roads, bridges.
  • Chunk C: schools, need, better, teachers.

Now count how many words each question shares with each chunk.

  • Question 1 asks about “Social Security for the elderly”. It shares 3 words with chunk A (social, security, elderly), 0 with B and 0 with C. So chunk A wins. Correct.
  • Question 2 asks the same thing in other words: “pensions for old people”. The words “pensions”, “old” and “people” appear in no chunk. It shares 0 words with A, 0 with B and 0 with C. Every chunk scores 0, so the search has nothing to go on. The model then gets the wrong text, or none.

Saying the same thing in other words is called a paraphrase.

The computer turns these counts into cosine scores. Here is what it printed. Each row is one question. The columns A, B and C show the cosine similarity between that question and each chunk. The last column lists the words of the question that also appear somewhere in the chunks (the words “the index knows”).

Query A B C Query words the index knows
“…promise about Social Security for the elderly?” 0.866 0 0 social, security, elderly
“…promise about pensions for old people?” 0 0 0 (none)

How to read it: 0.866 is high (the maximum is 1), so chunk A is a strong match for question 1. Every 0 means “no shared words at all”. You can even check the 0.866 by hand. In chunk A, all 4 remaining words appear in no other chunk, so they all get the same weight. In the question, the 3 known words also get equal weight. Cosine then works out as the 3 shared words divided by \(\sqrt{4} \times \sqrt{3}\), which is \(3 / 3.46 = 0.866\). The exam will not ask you to do this; the point is what the zeros mean.

The second row is all zeros because no question word is shared with any chunk. So the dot product is 0, and the cosine is 0. The retriever finds nothing, and the LLM is fed irrelevant text.

The notebook’s own words: “tf-idf only matches literal words. Modern RAG systems use dense embeddings (Interactive Notebook 3) to match meaning.” Dense embeddings are number lists that capture what a text means, not which words it uses. They can often tell that “pensions” and “Social Security” are related. Matching exact words is called literal-word matching.

How often the retriever finds the right chunk is called its hit rate.

Business rule 5: “RAG is only as good as its retriever. Literal-word retrieval misses paraphrases.”

Turning the five results into business advice. These points link the notebook to the course’s slides on business use. They are ready-made material for the exam’s business-case question.

  • Cost is counted in tokens, and depends on language and format. Budget extra for Norwegian text, and for numbers and codes.
  • Pick the temperature to suit the task. Use 0 for extraction or classification (invoice amounts, review labels). Use a higher value for creative work (ten campaign slogans).
  • Build checks around the model. 4 out of 4 valid JSON does not prove 100,000 out of 100,000. Add a format checker, a validation sample (a set of examples people have labelled by hand, to check how often the model is right), and a benchmark. A benchmark is a simple method the LLM must beat. One example is Naive Bayes, a simple, fast word-counting sorter from earlier in the course. Another is the majority class: always guessing the most common label. This matches the course’s call for “Verifiable Results” and “Manageable Errors”.
  • Ground the model, and test the retriever. Hallucinations “sound confident”. The wrong context can be worse than none. So measure the retrieval hit rate for both literal and reworded questions. Consider embedding-based retrieval for paraphrases.
  • Weigh the risk against how easy errors are to check. Summarising survey feedback is low-consequence but hard to check, so inspect examples. Anything that triggers payments needs human approval.
  • Running locally keeps data on your own machine (privacy) and has no per-token fee. But a small model is weaker and slow: 5–30 seconds per review on a laptop.

The whole chain of steps around the model (input, model, checks, output) is called a pipeline.

Reading the course code

The exam has not asked students to write code. You only need to recognise what these lines do. Here are the key lines of the notebook’s mini-RAG step, simplified:

tfidf = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english")
X = tfidf.fit_transform(chunk_text)
sims = cosine_similarity(tfidf.transform([QUESTION]), X)[0]
top = sims.argsort()[::-1][:TOP_K]
  • Line 1 sets up a tf-idf scorer that throws away English stop words. TfidfVectorizer is the ready-made code tool that does tf-idf.
  • Line 2 builds a table of all the speech chunks and fills it with tf-idf scores. The table has one row per chunk and one column per word, and each cell shows how much that word counts in that chunk. This table is called a document-term matrix. Treating each text as a bag of word counts, ignoring word order, is called bag-of-words. Here chunk_text holds all the chunks, each CHUNK_SIZE words long and labelled “president, year”.
  • Line 3 turns the question into a tf-idf list using the same vocabulary. Then it computes the cosine similarity between the question and every chunk. sims holds one score per chunk.
  • Line 4 puts the scores in order with argsort, a command that sorts them from smallest to largest. [::-1] flips the order so the biggest comes first. [:TOP_K] keeps the first TOP_K. So top holds the best-matching chunks.

There is a switch in the code called GENERATE. If GENERATE = True, the chosen chunks are pasted into the prompt with the system instruction “Answer using ONLY the provided excerpts, and mention which president and year”, at temperature=0. When run, the cell prints the number of chunks, each retrieved chunk with its similarity score, and “Query words the index knows”.

What the exam asks, and how to answer

Directly, as True/False items. These are likely ones.

“A Norwegian sentence typically costs fewer tokens than its English translation.”

Model answer FALSE. Tokens are the word pieces the model reads and charges for. Norwegian words get chopped into more pieces, so Norwegian costs more.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: The tokenizer was built mostly from English, so Norwegian gets cut into more pieces, and you pay per piece.

“At temperature 0 the model gives the same answer every time.”

Model answer TRUE. Temperature 0 means greedy decoding (always taking the top word), so there is no randomness.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: With the boldness dial at zero, there is no dice roll. Same question, same answer.

“A tf-idf retriever will find a passage about ‘Social Security for the elderly’ when asked about ‘pensions for old people’.”

Model answer FALSE. A tf-idf retriever (a search tool that matches the exact words used) finds literal word matches only, and these two phrases share no words.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Word-matching search needs the same words. No shared words means a score of 0, so it finds nothing.

Indirectly, in the reflection question. The 2025 Block 5 question (20 points) asked you to analyse 1,000+ free-text survey answers about how customers see a firm. You had to propose at least two methods, with your reasons (motivation) and what could go wrong (pitfalls).

Model answer (outline) Notebook 4 gives you concrete pitfalls straight from the course: hallucination (the model inventing facts), format failures (answers in the wrong shape), label-set choices (which answer options to allow), token cost in Norwegian, retrieval missing paraphrases (the search tool missing questions asked in other words), and validating against a benchmark (checking the LLM beats a simple method).

What this answer is saying, in plain words: If you propose an LLM for the survey answers, name the things that can go wrong from this notebook, and say how you would check the LLM against a simpler method.

A likely short question: “A Norwegian company wants an LLM to answer staff questions from its internal handbook. Name two risks shown in Notebook 4 and how to handle them.”

Model answer First, the model hallucinates when it lacks the facts, so it should be grounded with RAG: retrieve the relevant handbook passages and tell it to answer only from them, at temperature 0. Second, the retriever can miss questions asked in other words. A tf-idf retriever only matches literal words, so “pension” will not find “retirement benefits”. Embedding-based retrieval and a test of the hit rate on reworded questions reduce this. Norwegian text also costs more tokens per word, which raises cost and fills the context window faster.

What this answer is saying, in plain words: Risk one: when the model does not know the facts, it makes them up. So you find the right handbook pages, paste them in, and tell the model to use only those pages, with no randomness. Risk two: a word-matching search misses questions asked in different words, so use a search that understands meaning and test how often it finds the right page. Also, Norwegian text costs more and fills the model’s reading space faster.

What a top-grade answer must include When you propose an LLM in a business case, give three things.

  • How you will use it. Either a prompted classifier (the LLM sorts each text into a label because you asked it to) at temperature 0 (no randomness), with an explicit output format and a few-shot example (one solved example in the instructions). Or RAG (a search step pastes the right documents into the prompt), grounded in company documents (told to answer only from them).
  • How you will validate it (check that it works): a hand-labelled sample (texts a person has tagged with the right answer), accuracy against a benchmark such as Naive Bayes (a simple word-counting classifier) or the majority class (always guessing the most common label), and a code check of the format.
  • At least one specific pitfall: hallucination (made-up facts), wrong context (the wrong document pasted in), Norwegian token cost, lukewarm or sarcastic answers that fit no label, retrieval missing reworded questions.

Tie it to the course’s grading criteria for the assignment: evidence, understanding, honest evaluation, judgement.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Treating the LLM’s output as automatically correct.
  • Saying “use an LLM” without saying the temperature, the output format or how you will check it.
  • Forgetting that tokens (word pieces), not words, set the cost.
  • Assuming RAG (search-then-answer) solves hallucination. It only helps if the search step finds the right text.
  • Quoting notebook numbers that were never printed. The notebook has no saved outputs.

Key terms to use

  • subword tokens: word pieces the model reads
  • tokens per word: how many pieces each word becomes
  • effective price: real cost once you count the tokens
  • context window (32,768 tokens): most text the model reads at once
  • temperature 0 / greedy: always pick the top word; no randomness
  • system prompt: standing instructions given before the user’s text
  • explicit output format: the exact answer shape, e.g. JSON
  • few-shot example: a worked example shown in the prompt
  • label set: the list of allowed answers
  • format checker: small program that tests each reply is valid
  • validation sample: texts a person tagged, to check the model
  • benchmark: a simple method the LLM must beat
  • hallucination: confident-sounding but made-up answer
  • grounding: answer only from a text you supply
  • STRICT instruction: if the answer isn’t there, say so
  • retrieval-augmented generation (RAG): search step pastes relevant text into prompt
  • chunk size: how long each cut-up piece of text is
  • top-k chunks: the k best-matching pieces passed on
  • tf-idf + cosine similarity: match texts by shared, rarer words
  • literal-word matching vs dense embeddings: same words vs same meaning
  • hit rate: how often the right chunk is found
  • local deployment / open weights (Hugging Face): free model run on your own computer

Quick self-test

  1. “In Notebook 4, the retriever uses dense embeddings to find relevant passages.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The retriever is the search step that finds the bits of text to hand the model. Dense embeddings are lists of numbers that capture a text’s meaning, so they can match texts that use different words. Does the notebook’s search work by meaning?

    False. Why: it uses tf-idf + cosine similarity, which matches texts by the words they share (a bag-of-words method that ignores meaning and word order). Dense embeddings are suggested as the better choice. It is like a librarian who only finds books whose titles contain your exact words, instead of one who understands what you mean.

  2. “Giving the model the wrong source text can be worse than giving it no source at all.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The source text is the passage you paste in for the model to answer from. Can a wrong passage do more harm than giving no passage?

    True. Why: with a wrong passage, the small model may present that passage as the answer, even when told to say so if the answer is not there. With no passage, it dodges or makes things up, but at least it is not handed false facts to repeat. It is like being handed the wrong map: you may end up further away than if you had no map.

  3. “Because the SOTU corpus is larger than the model’s context window, the notebook retrieves a few chunks instead of feeding all speeches.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: The SOTU corpus is the collection of US State of the Union speeches. The context window is the most text the model can read at once. Since all the speeches are too long to fit, does the notebook pick out a few short pieces (chunks) instead?

    True. Why: the speeches add up to about 2 million tokens (word pieces), but the model can read only 32,768 at once. It is like a suitcase: you cannot pack the whole wardrobe, so you pick the few clothes you need for this trip.

  4. “Once a prompt gives 4 out of 4 valid JSON replies, the pipeline can safely run on 100,000 reviews without checks.” (True/False)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: JSON is a strict text format that other programs can read. A valid JSON reply is one in the right shape. The pipeline is the whole automatic process. If 4 test replies come out right, can you run it on 100,000 reviews and stop checking?

    False. Why: 4 good replies do not prove 100,000 good replies. The notebook says reliability “has to be checked by code around the model”. It is like a new driver who parked well 4 times: that does not mean you never need to look again.

  5. “A Norwegian company wants an LLM to answer staff questions from its internal handbook. Name two risks shown in Notebook 4 and how to handle them.” (Explain in 2–5 sentences)

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Name two things from the notebook that could go wrong with a handbook chatbot, and say how you would fix each.

    Answer: the model answer given above: “First, the model hallucinates when it lacks the facts, so it should be grounded with RAG: retrieve the relevant handbook passages and tell it to answer only from them, at temperature 0. Second, the retriever can miss questions asked in other words. A tf-idf retriever only matches literal words, so”pension” will not find “retirement benefits”. Embedding-based retrieval and a test of the hit rate on reworded questions reduce this. Norwegian text also costs more tokens per word, which raises cost and fills the context window faster.”

    Why: the notebook showed both failures directly: the model invents quotes without the right source, and word-matching search scores 0 for reworded questions.

Words used in this chapter

What the words mean (from zero).

  • LLM (large language model): a program, like ChatGPT, that predicts text one token at a time.
  • notebook / cell: a notebook is a document that mixes code and explanations and runs in a web browser. A cell is one box of code or text in it. Like a recipe book where each step can be “cooked” by pressing a button.
  • code / Python: instructions written for the computer. Python is the programming language the notebook uses.
  • Qwen2.5-0.5B-Instruct: the name of the small model used. “0.5B” means half a billion dials (parameters). “Instruct” means it was trained to follow instructions and chat.
  • parameter / weight: one adjustable number (dial) inside the model, set during training.
  • Hugging Face: a website where people share models, like an app store for AI models.
  • account / API key / cloud: the usual way to use a big model: sign up (account), get a password for programs (API key), and send your text to the provider’s computers over the internet (cloud). The notebook needs none of these.
  • local deployment / open weights: running the model on your own computer, which is possible because its dials (weights) are published for anyone to download.
  • per-token fee: what online providers charge: a small price for every token in and out.
  • privacy: keeping data away from outsiders. Running locally means your text never leaves your machine.
  • token: one small piece of text, often a word, sometimes part of a word or a number.
  • tokenizer: the tool that cuts text into tokens. Like a butcher with a fixed set of cuts.
  • subword token: a token that is only part of a word. A long Norwegian word like “Sentralbanken” may be cut into several.
  • tokens per word: how many tokens, on average, one word turns into. Higher means more cost.
  • effective price: what a document really costs once you count its tokens. Same price per token, but more tokens per word, means a higher bill.
  • leading space: the space in front of a word. ” bank” (with a space) and “bank” count as different tokens.
  • len(text.split()): a line of code that counts words by cutting the text at the spaces. The English test sentence gives 10.
  • context window: the most tokens the model can read at once (here 32,768). Like the size of a desk.
  • corpus / SOTU: a corpus is a collection of texts. SOTU is the State of the Union speeches by US presidents, the corpus used here (about 2 million tokens).
  • temperature (T): the “boldness” dial for picking words. Low = predictable, high = varied.
  • greedy (T = 0): always pick the single most likely next word, so the same question gives the same answer every time.
  • seed: a starting number for the computer’s random dice. A different seed gives different rolls.
  • N_SAMPLES: a setting in the code: how many times to ask the same question (here 3).
  • JSON / machine-readable: JSON is a strict text format such as {"sentiment": "positive"}. Machine-readable means other software can read it without a human.
  • sentiment: the feeling in a text, such as positive or negative.
  • system prompt: standing instructions sent before the user’s text, like house rules.
  • explicit output format: spelling out exactly what shape the answer must have.
  • few-shot example: a solved example placed in the prompt to show the pattern.
  • label set: the list of allowed answers, such as positive / negative / mixed. Choosing it is a business decision.
  • edge case / lukewarm: an example that doesn’t fit the labels neatly, like “It’s fine, I guess.”
  • format checker / json.loads: a small program that tests whether each reply is valid. json.loads tries to read a reply as JSON and fails if it is broken.
  • validation sample: a set of examples people have labelled by hand, used to check how often the model is right.
  • benchmark / majority class: a simple method to compare against. “Majority class” means always guessing the most common label.
  • Naive Bayes: a simple, fast word-counting classifier from earlier in the course, often used as a benchmark.
  • classifier: a program that sorts texts into labels.
  • hallucination: the model stating something false with confidence, such as an invented quote.
  • grounding / excerpt: giving the model a source text (an excerpt) and telling it to answer only from that. Like an open-book exam.
  • STRICT instruction: the notebook’s firm extra instruction: if the answer is not in the excerpt, say so.
  • scoreboard: the notebook’s simple check of whether the reply contains the real words of the speech (“not good” for Ford 1975).
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): first search for relevant chunks, then paste them into the prompt, then let the model answer.
  • retriever: the search tool inside RAG.
  • chunk / CHUNK_SIZE: a short slice of a long text. CHUNK_SIZE sets how many words each slice has.
  • top-k chunks / TOP_K: the k best-matching chunks that get pasted into the prompt.
  • stop words: very common words like “the”, “for”, “we” that a search tool ignores.
  • tf-idf / TfidfVectorizer: a way of scoring words: a word counts more if it is frequent in this chunk but rare across all chunks. TfidfVectorizer is the code tool that does it.
  • vector: a list of numbers in a fixed order. Here, one number per vocabulary word for each chunk.
  • document-term matrix: a table with one row per chunk and one column per word, each cell showing how much that word counts in that chunk.
  • bag-of-words: treating a text as a bag of word counts, ignoring word order.
  • dot product: multiply two lists number by number and add up. If two texts share no words, it is 0.
  • cosine similarity: a 0-to-1 score of how alike two word-lists are, built on the dot product. 0 = nothing in common; 0.866 = a strong match.
  • argsort: a code command that puts scores in order, used to pick the top chunks.
  • GENERATE = True: a switch in the code. When on, the retrieved chunks are sent to the model to write an answer.
  • literal-word matching vs dense embeddings: matching the exact same words, versus matching number lists that capture meaning. Dense embeddings can often tell that “pensions” and “Social Security” are related.
  • paraphrase: saying the same thing in other words.
  • hit rate: how often the retriever finds the right chunk.
  • pipeline: the whole chain of steps around the model: input, model, checks, output.
  • T/F: a True/False exam question.
  • reflection (business case): the exam’s longer question where you propose methods for a firm and discuss their pitfalls.

Sources: Interactive Notebook 4 A Real LLM on Your Laptop (GRA4164_Interactive_4_A_real_LLM_on_your_laptop.ipynb), cells 0–28 (tokens cells 6–9; temperature cells 10–13; JSON cells 14–17; hallucination cells 18–21; corpus size and retrieval cell 22; mini-RAG cell 24; dense embeddings cell 25; takeaways cell 28); Assignments 2026 slides 20–24 (Assignment 4.2 a hit rate; slide 23, 5–30 seconds per review; slide 24 grading criteria); Lecture 7 slides 18 (“Verifiable Results”, “Manageable Errors”), 19 (risk vs ease of checking), 20, 26 (hallucinations “sound confident”). The notebook has no saved outputs, so no token counts or scores from it appear here; the tf-idf toy example is the guide’s own, run with the cell 24 tools.

Part VI — Putting it together

22. Choosing the right method for a business case (the reflection question)

Exam priority: ★★★ High — 20 of 100 points in 2025, and the question that most separates a C from an A.

Start from zero

The problem. A company has a pile of text it can’t read by hand: 1,000 survey answers, 50,000 product reviews, or years of news articles. Management asks a simple question, like “do customers like us?” or “what are people complaining about?”. The exam’s last question (20 of 100 points) gives you a situation like this. It asks which tools from the course you’d use, why, and what could go wrong. You don’t need maths for it. You need to know what each tool does, in one sentence, and when it fits.

The toolbox, one plain sentence per tool. Every tool turns a pile of text into something a manager can read: a score, a label, or a list of themes.

  1. Dictionary (word list): you write a list of words yourself, e.g. positive = {good, great, love} and negative = {bad, slow, rude}, then count how often they appear in each text. More positive than negative words means a happier text. (Ch. 7)
  2. Boolean search: a search rule with AND / OR / NOT, like in a library catalogue: an article counts only if it contains “economy” AND “policy” AND “uncertain”. You count how many texts match each month. (Ch. 7)
  3. tf-idf + cosine similarity: a way to score how similar two texts are by the distinctive words they share. Common words like “the” count for almost nothing; rare, telling words count a lot. Use it to find texts that look like a reference text. (Ch. 4–5)
  4. Naive Bayes: a spam-filter-style sorter. You first label some texts by hand (e.g. 300 answers marked “happy” or “unhappy”). It learns which words show up in each group, then sorts all the new texts. (Ch. 9)
  5. Regularised (text) regression, e.g. Lasso: predicts a number (like a 1–10 satisfaction score) from the words in a text. It is built to ignore most words and keep only the few that really matter, so it doesn’t fool itself when there are more words than texts. (Ch. 8)
  6. Topic model (e.g. LDA): the computer sorts all the texts into themes by itself, like sorting mail into piles without being told the piles. You then read each pile’s top words and name it (“delivery”, “price”, “staff”). (Ch. 10)
  7. Word embeddings (e.g. word2vec): gives every word a spot on a “meaning map”, so that similar words sit close together (“cheap” near “inexpensive”). Useful for finding synonyms you forgot to put in a word list. (Ch. 13)
  8. Fine-tuned language model (e.g. BERT): take a ready-made model that already “reads” well, and train it a bit more on your hand-labelled examples. It understands context (“not good” is negative), but needs labels and computing power. (Ch. 20)
  9. Prompted LLM (like ChatGPT): don’t train anything; write clear instructions (“Label this answer as positive, negative or neutral”) and maybe give a few examples. Fast, but it can make things up, so you must check it against texts you labelled yourself. (Ch. 20–21)

How to choose, in three questions.

  1. Do you already know what you’re looking for? If yes (e.g. “mentions of climate”), use a word list or Boolean search. If no (“what are people talking about?”), use a topic model.
  2. Do you have texts with answers attached? Examples: star ratings next to reviews, or a few hundred answers you labelled by hand. If yes, you can train a sorter (Naive Bayes, fine-tuned model) and check any method’s accuracy.
  3. Does context matter? Negation (“not good”), sarcasm, or words with two meanings call for a language model (fine-tuned or prompted) rather than word counting.

A great answer picks two tools that do different jobs. For example, one measures how people feel and the other finds what they talk about. It says why each fits this firm and is honest about where each can go wrong.

What the words mean (from zero).

  • Supervised: the method is told the answer in advance. Usually that means you give it examples with the right answer attached (texts already labelled “happy” or “unhappy”), like a student learning with an answer key. In this course, word lists also count as “supervised”, because you fix the rule yourself (“count these words”) and the computer learns nothing on its own. The course’s phrase for this is “we know the functional form”: you know exactly what output you’ll get for any input.
  • Unsupervised: no answers and no rule. The computer finds the structure itself (e.g. topic models finding themes).
  • Self-supervised: the answers come free from the text itself (hide the next word, guess it). This is how word embeddings and LLMs learn.
  • Label: the right answer attached to a text, e.g. “positive”, or a star rating.
  • Classify / classifier: sort texts into boxes (positive / negative, spam / not spam).
  • Baseline: the simplest possible method, used as a yardstick. If the fancy method can’t beat “always guess the most common answer”, it’s useless.
  • Validation / out of sample: checking a method on texts it hasn’t seen, compared with answers you trust. Like testing a student on new exam questions, not on the ones they memorised.
  • Overfitting: a method that memorises its examples instead of learning the pattern, so it looks perfect on old data and fails on new data.
  • Pitfall: a way the method can go wrong in this particular case.
  • Normalise: make texts comparable, e.g. count hits per 1,000 words, so long texts don’t win automatically.
  • K (number of topics): how many piles you ask the topic model to make. You choose it, and the results change with it.
  • Seed instability: run a topic model twice and you may get slightly different piles, because it starts from a random point.
  • Polysemy: one word, several meanings (“green” = a colour, or eco-friendly).
  • Negation / sarcasm: “not good” means bad; “great, another delay” means bad. Word counting gets both wrong.
  • Hallucination: an LLM confidently making something up.
  • GDPR: the EU’s data-protection law. Sending customers’ answers to an outside AI company may break it. [Not in course files — general knowledge, apart from the course’s mention of GDPR among LLM issues.]
  • RAG (retrieval-augmented generation): first look up the relevant documents, then give them to the LLM with the question, so it answers from real sources.
  • Index (= 100 in a base period): a number scaled so that a chosen starting month equals 100. Then 120 means “20% more than at the start”.

The idea in plain words

The reflection question gives you a business situation with text in it and asks: which tools from this course would you use, why, and what could go wrong? Think of yourself as a carpenter with a toolbox. Each tool from the course is good at one job:

  • dictionary
  • Boolean search
  • tf-idf + cosine
  • Naive Bayes
  • regularised regression
  • topic model
  • word embeddings
  • a fine-tuned LLM
  • a prompted LLM

The examiner checks three things:

  1. Did you pick tools that fit this job?
  2. Can you say what number each tool will produce for the client?
  3. Do you know where each tool breaks?

Analogy

A doctor does not prescribe every medicine in the pharmacy. They pick two or three that fit the diagnosis, explain why, and warn about side-effects. Your answer should read the same way: diagnosis (what the firm wants to know), prescription (two or three methods), side-effects (pitfalls in this case).

The exam definition (what the graders say they want)

  • 2025 evaluation guideline: “A good answer should mention methods that are well motivation[sic] and relevant for the problem, and also identify one or more pitfalls with the proposed method in the current context. Would then be great if the methods complement each other in that regard.”
  • Assignment evaluation guidelines (2024/2025): students should “know when the different tools might be appropriate to apply”, understand “how different pre-processing steps, and other modelling choices, might affect the answers”, and “critically reflect on in which situations this might be more relevant than using … the other tools learned about in this course”. For a business case: “Provide a well explained motivation for why and how to use text data in this case” and “Identify and critically discuss how the methods learned about in this course can be used.”
  • BI grade A: “excellent judgement and a high degree of independent thinking.”

The method chooser (one table to memorise)

If the firm wants… Use Supervised? Gives you (the number) Main pitfalls
