To track a concept it can name in advance (uncertainty, ESG, a product) Boolean search / dictionary (Ch. 7) “Supervised” in the course’s sense: you set the rule yourself, nothing is learned (see “What the words mean” above; slide 7) Hits or tone per document, normalised (e.g. per 1,000 words; index = 100 in a base period) Subjective word lists; must know what to search for; polysemy, synonyms, negation, sarcasm; language
To find documents similar to a reference text, or to each other tf-idf + cosine similarity (Ch. 4–5); Engle et al. climate index Unsupervised measure Similarity score 0–1 per document Literal word overlap only (misses paraphrases); depends on preprocessing
To discover what people talk about (unknown themes) Topic model: LDA, LSA/SVD (Ch. 10) Unsupervised Topic shares per document; top words per topic Choice of K; seed instability; labels are your interpretation; needs enough text
To predict a category (positive/negative, spam, party) from text, with labelled examples Naive Bayes (Ch. 9); regularised logistic regression (Ch. 8) Supervised Predicted class / probability; accuracy vs baseline Needs labels; overfitting when p ≫ n; leakage in the train/test split
To predict a number (GDP growth, a rating) from text Regularised text regression, Lasso/Ridge (Ch. 8) Supervised Fitted value; out-of-sample R² p ≫ n: in-sample fit is meaningless; use cross-validation
To measure meaning and similarity between words; track how meaning changes Word embeddings: PMI + SVD, word2vec (Ch. 13) Self-supervised Word vectors, cosine similarity, analogies Needs a big corpus (or a pre-trained model); static vectors ignore context; noise over time
Context-aware classification at high accuracy, with labelled data Fine-tune a BERT-type model with a new head (Ch. 20) Supervised Class probabilities per document Needs labelled data and compute; less transparent
Fast classification/extraction with no or few labels Prompt an LLM, zero-/few-shot, with format + temperature 0; RAG for documents (Ch. 20–21) No training Labels/fields per document Hallucination, inconsistency, cost per token, privacy/GDPR if sent to an external provider; must validate on a labelled sample

A 6-step template for the reflection answer

  1. Restate the goal as measurable outputs. Example: “a tone score per respondent; the share of answers about ESG”. One or two sentences.
  2. Describe the data and preprocessing, with one judgement call. For example, keep “not”, since stop-word lists remove it and flip meaning (“not good” → “good”; Interactive 1).
  3. Method 1: the simple, transparent baseline (dictionary/Boolean, or tf-idf + cosine). Cover what it does, why it fits here, the number it delivers, and its pitfalls in this case.
  4. Method 2: a method that fixes method 1’s main weakness. Unsupervised discovery (LDA) if method 1 needs known words; contextual models (fine-tuned BERT or a prompted LLM) if method 1 cannot handle context. Cover the same four points.
  5. Validation: use any labels you have to check every method. Survey ratings, star ratings and a hand-labelled sample all work. Compare against a simple baseline, and evaluate out of sample.
  6. Wider pitfalls: representativeness of the texts, language, privacy/GDPR, cost, explainability to management.

A tiny worked example — a second case, outlined

Case (our own illustration): a Norwegian bank wants a monthly indicator of how much climate risk is discussed in Norwegian news about its borrowers.

  • Goal → numbers: a monthly index (base = 100) and a per-firm score.
  • Method 1 — tf-idf + cosine similarity to a climate reference text, as in Engle et al. (2020): the WSJ Climate Change News Index (Lecture 2, slide 23; the course data even includes climate_reference.txt). It is transparent and needs no labels. Pitfall: it works on literal word overlap, so Norwegian-language news needs a Norwegian reference text, and paraphrases are missed.
  • Method 2 — Boolean “transition risk” search in the spirit of EPU (Lecture 3, slide 8). For example: (climate OR emissions OR carbon) AND (regulation OR tax OR policy), normalised by the number of articles per month. Pitfall: the word lists are subjective, and polysemy is a problem (“green” as a colour).
  • Method 3 (complement) — word embeddings to expand the word list with near-synonyms (cosine-nearest neighbours of “emissions”; our suggestion). The course shows that embeddings can measure exactly this: Kapfhammer, Larsen & Thorsrud (2020), “Climate risk and commodity currencies”, which measures transition risk for Norway with word embeddings (Lecture 6, slide 31). Pitfall: embeddings need a large corpus, and meanings drift over time.
  • Validation: read a random sample of high-scoring and low-scoring articles; check the index spikes at known events (e.g. the Paris Agreement).

How this shows up on the exam

In 2025 this was Block 5 (20 points, ½–1 page). Expect a new business setting, such as customer reviews, news, reports, emails or survey answers. The question gives an explicit list of what to cover: motivation (why this method fits), problem solved, and pitfalls (what could go wrong). Earlier blocks of the exam also test “when is method X appropriate” (when is it the right tool).

What a top-grade answer must include

  • At least the number of methods asked for (two), each one from the course and named precisely.
  • For each method: why it fits this firm, the concrete output (what number management actually gets), and at least one pitfall that is specific to this case.
  • Methods that complement each other (cover each other’s weak spots). For example: one supervised (learns from tagged examples) and one unsupervised (finds patterns with no tags); one transparent (easy to see why it decided) and one context-aware (understands word order and meaning); or one that checks the other.
  • A validation step (how you will check the results are right) and one preprocessing judgement (a choice about cleaning the text first, e.g. whether to remove stop words).
  • About one page, organised with short headings or bold method names.

Common mistakes that lose marks

  • Listing methods without linking them to the firm’s questions.
  • Generic pitfalls (“the model may be wrong”) instead of pitfalls tied to the case. Examples: answers in several languages, a small corpus (too few texts), negation (“not good”), survey selection bias (the people who answer are not typical customers), GDPR (the EU data-privacy law).
  • Proposing an LLM as magic: no check of its results, no mention of hallucination (made-up answers) or cost.
  • Ignoring labels that are already there (survey scores, star ratings). They make supervised learning and checking possible.
  • Going far beyond the length limit.

Key terms to use

  • supervised / unsupervised / self-supervised (learns from tags / no tags / text supplies answers)
  • dictionary-based (count words from a hand-made word list)
  • Boolean search (find texts with AND / OR / NOT rules)
  • normalisation (clean text: lower case, remove punctuation, etc.)
  • tf-idf (word counts re-weighted so rare words count more)
  • cosine similarity (how alike two texts’ word profiles are)
  • topic model (LDA) (finds hidden themes in many texts)
  • number of topics K (how many themes you tell LDA to find)
  • Naive Bayes (simple word-counting classifier that learns from labels)
  • regularisation (penalty that stops a model over-fitting)
  • out-of-sample validation (test on texts the model never saw)
  • baseline (simple method your model must beat)
  • fine-tuning with a classification head (extra training with a new labelling layer)
  • prompt engineering (zero-/few-shot, chain-of-thought) (writing instructions; no examples / some examples / step-by-step)
  • RAG (search step pastes relevant documents into the prompt)
  • hallucination (confident-sounding but made-up answer)
  • GDPR (EU law on handling personal data)

Quick self-test

  1. True or false: “An unsupervised topic model is the best choice when the firm already knows exactly which concept it wants to track.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: An unsupervised topic model (such as LDA) reads many texts and finds the themes in them by itself, with no hints. “Already knows which concept it wants to track” means the firm knows what it is looking for, for example “complaints about delivery”. Is a theme-finding tool the best pick in that case?

    False. Why: when you know the concept and its words, a dictionary approach (counting words from your own list) or a Boolean search (rules like “delivery AND late”) does the job directly. Topic models are for discovering themes you did not know about. If you know you are looking for your keys, you search your pockets; you do not sort the whole house to see what turns up. (Source: Assignment 2, Q2.2c framing; Lecture 3)

  2. True or false: “If a survey contains star ratings next to the free text, these can be used to train or validate a text classifier.”

    What it’s asking, in plain words: Free text is what people wrote in their own words. A text classifier is a model that sorts texts into groups, such as happy or unhappy. “Train or validate” means teach it or check it. Can the star ratings be used for that?

    True. Why: the stars are labels (ready-made right answers next to each text). So supervised learning, such as Naive Bayes or fine-tuning, becomes possible, and you can check the model against them. It is like a set of practice questions that comes with the answer sheet. (Source: Lecture 3 slides 22–27; training slide 22)

  3. Short answer (2–5 sentences): A retailer receives 50,000 product reviews per month with star ratings and wants to know why customers are unhappy. Name two complementary methods.

    • Model answer: First, use the star ratings as labels to train a supervised sentiment classifier. Naive Bayes on word counts is a transparent baseline; a fine-tuned BERT-type model with a classification head handles negation and context better. Evaluate both out of sample against the majority-class baseline. Second, run LDA on the low-rated reviews to discover the themes behind dissatisfaction (delivery, size, quality), giving topic shares that can be tracked monthly. The classifier measures how unhappy customers are, and the topic model explains why. Pitfalls: topics depend on K and the random seed, and ratings are noisy labels.

    What this answer is saying, in plain words: Method one: use the stars as answers to teach a model to tell happy from unhappy reviews. Start with a simple word-counting model, try a stronger one that understands phrases like “not good”, and test both on reviews they have not seen. Method two: take only the bad reviews and let a theme-finder show what people complain about, such as delivery or size. The first says how unhappy people are, the second says why, but the themes can shift with your settings and star ratings are not always accurate.

Sources: 2025 exam Block 5 and its evaluation guideline; assignment evaluation guidelines 2024/2025; Lecture_bow_based_methods.pdf (method map slides 4–6; dictionaries 7–12; regressions 15–19; Naive Bayes 22–27; topic models 31–59); Lecture_neuralnets_wordembeddings.pdf; Lecture_llm_intro.pdf slides 18–27; Lecture_llm_trainingandfinetuning.pdf slides 20–23; Interactive notebooks 1–4.

23. One-page exam-day cheat sheet

In plain words. This is a recap for the night before the exam. Each line gives first what the thing is, in everyday words, then what to remember for the exam: the course’s phrase, the formula, or the trap. If a line doesn’t ring a bell, go back to its chapter (the number is in brackets).

Turning text into numbers

  • The workflow (Ch. 1): collect the texts → clean them (lowercase, remove punctuation, cut into words, drop very common words like “the”, strip word endings) → turn them into numbers → run a method → interpret the result. Four challenges: huge amounts of text, messy text, words with several meanings (“bank”), and ethics (bias, privacy, “black box” models nobody can explain).
  • Bag-of-words (Ch. 3): throw a text’s words in a bag and count them; word order is lost. Exam phrase: “word occurrences are treated as independent; the context is not modelled.”
  • Document-term matrix (Ch. 3): a table with one row per document, one column per word, and counts in the cells. Size: \(n \times p\) (\(n\) documents by \(p\) different words). Mostly zeros (“sparse”). Word pairs (“low unemployment”), called 2-grams, keep a little word order.
  • Three ways to adjust the counts (Ch. 4):
    • Row shares: divide each count by the document’s total number of words, so long documents don’t win just by being long. \(x_i = c_i / m_i\).
    • Yes/no (binary): record only whether a word appears (1) or not (0), so repeating a word ten times doesn’t count ten times. \(x_{ij} = 1\) if \(c_{ij} > 0\).
    • tf-idf: multiply each count by a “rarity bonus”, so rare, telling words count more and words found everywhere count for nothing. \(\text{tf-idf}_{ij} = c_{ij}\log(n/d_j)\), where \(d_j\) is the number of documents that contain word \(j\). A word that is in every document gets 0.
  • Similarity (Ch. 5): treat each document’s row as an arrow.
    • Cosine similarity looks only at the angle between two arrows: 1 = same direction (same mix of words), 0 = nothing in common. Document length doesn’t matter.
    • Euclidean distance is the straight-line gap between the arrow tips, so it is thrown off by length. Slide example: Euclidean 1.46 vs 1.35, cosine 0.99 vs 0.84.
    • Drawing question: two arrows from the origin with a small angle = high cosine; one arrow pointing a very different way = low cosine.

Methods built on word counts

  • Supervised vs unsupervised (Ch. 6):
    • Supervised = the method is told the answers, through labelled examples or a rule you fix yourself.
    • Unsupervised = it finds structure on its own.
    • Word lists count as “supervised” in this course because you set the rule (“we know the function”).
    • Text regression predicts the outcome from the words; Naive Bayes learns which words each class produces. LSA and LDA are unsupervised.
  • Boolean search and EPU (Ch. 7): an AND/OR search rule, and you count the matching articles. EPU = an article counts if it has (uncertain OR uncertainty) AND (economic OR economy) AND at least one policy word (regulation, federal reserve, deficit, congress, legislation, white house). Monthly counts across 10 US newspapers are scaled to average 100 over 1985–2009.
  • Dictionary (word-list) tone (Ch. 7): tone = number of positive words − number of negative words, adjusted for length. Finance uses its own list (Loughran–McDonald). Weaknesses: subjective; you must know what to search for; can’t tell meanings apart (polysemy); misses synonyms.
  • Text regression (Ch. 8):
    • Predicts a number from word counts.
    • The trap: far more words than documents (\(n \ll p\), the “curse of dimensionality”), so ordinary regression memorises instead of learning.
    • The fix is a penalty that shrinks most word weights to zero: Lasso, \(\min\{l(\alpha,\beta) + n\lambda\sum_j \omega_j|\beta_j|\}\). \(\lambda\) = the strength of the penalty; \(\lambda = 0\) gives ordinary regression (OLS), and a bigger \(\lambda\) shrinks more weights to 0.
    • Choose \(\lambda\) by cross-validation (test on held-out data).
    • Judge the model only on new data (out-of-sample R²), never on the data it learned from.
  • Naive Bayes (Ch. 9):
    • A spam-filter-style sorter into categories, never for predicting a number.
    • Score per class = how common the class is × how typical each word is for that class: \(v_{nb} = \arg\max_k P(v_k)\prod_j P(c_{ij}\mid v_k)\).
    • Add +1 to every word count so a single unseen word doesn’t zero out a class (Laplace smoothing).
    • “Naive” = treats words as independent; “Bayes” = uses Bayes’ rule.
    • Slide example: 27% vs 73% → class b.
  • Topic models (Ch. 10): find themes by themselves. A topic is a group of words that appear together, and each document is a mix of topics.
    • LSA runs SVD (a computer procedure that squeezes the table into its main patterns) on the word-count table. You keep \(K\) themes. Its scores can be negative, so they are not probabilities.
    • LDA tells a story of how documents are written: pick the document’s topic mix, then for each word pick a topic and then a word from that topic. Everything is a probability: each document’s topic shares add up to 100%, and each topic’s word shares add up to 100%.
    • For both: you choose \(K\), and should check the results are stable across runs.

Predicting words, and word meanings

  • n-gram models (Ch. 11):
    • Predict the next word from the word before it. Chance of word B after word A = (times “A B” appears) ÷ (times A appears).
    • Add-one smoothing gives unseen pairs a small chance.
    • Loss = how surprised the model is on average.
    • Perplexity = \(e^{\text{Loss}}\), roughly “how many options the model is torn between”. If it guesses uniformly among 27 letters, the perplexity is 27.
    • Temperature: low = more confident and repetitive; high = more random.
  • Word embeddings (Ch. 13):
    • Give each word a list of numbers, a spot on a meaning map, so that similar words sit close together.
    • The key idea is Firth’s “You shall know a word by the company it keeps”.
    • PMI table: word × word, showing how much more often two words appear together than chance would predict. \(M_{ij} = \log_2\frac{p_{ij}}{p_i p_j}\). PPMI = negative values set to 0.
    • Run SVD on the PMI table and the rows become word embeddings.
    • word2vec is a small 2-layer neural network. CBOW guesses a word from its neighbours; Skipgram guesses the neighbours from a word.
    • One-hot vector: a list of zeros with a single 1 that marks the word. In the first layer it picks out that word’s column, which is its embedding (about 300 numbers).
    • word2vec gives each word one fixed meaning; BERT changes the meaning with context.
    • King − Man + Woman ≈ Queen.

Large Language Models (LLMs)

  • What an LLM is (Ch. 14):
    • A next-token predictor.
    • Built in three stages: pre-training on huge text by guessing the next word (self-supervised), then supervised fine-tuning on example answers, then preference training.
    • “Uploading a document changes the context. Fine-tuning changes the weights.”
    • The context window = how much text it can see at once.
    • Hugging Face = the open-source hub for models.
  • Tokens (Ch. 15): the pieces an LLM reads, often whole words but sometimes parts of words (un + believ + able). Tokens ≠ words. BPE builds the token list by repeatedly gluing together the most frequent pair of pieces.
  • Self-attention (Ch. 16): each word looks at the other words and decides which matter for its meaning.
    • Query = what I’m looking for; key = what I offer; value = my content.
    • Match score = query · key ÷ \(\sqrt{d_k}\), then softmax turns the scores into shares that add up to 1. Output = the values mixed by those shares.
    • Causal = may look only at earlier words, used for writing text; future words are blocked. Bidirectional = looks both ways, used for understanding (BERT).
    • Multi-head = several attention “readers” side by side, each catching a different kind of link. This makes the model richer, not slower.
    • Positional encoding is added to each word’s numbers, because attention on its own can’t see word order (“cat chased dog” vs “dog chased cat”).
  • Critical issues (Ch. 17):
    • Sustainability: energy for training and for every use, plus water and chips.
    • Ownership and control: a few big firms; open weights as the alternative.
    • Reliability: made-up answers (“hallucination”), bias.
    • Responsibility: bias, abuse, prompt injection, the Tay chatbot.
    • Privacy and security: GDPR, the EU AI Act.
    • The 2025 grading guide also accepted copyright, meaning training data used without permission.

Using LLMs

  • Input and output (Ch. 18):
    • Each token’s one-hot vector picks out its embedding, and position information is added.
    • The final step (the “LM head”) gives a probability for every token in the vocabulary.
    • Choosing the next token: always the top one (greedy), a random draw, a draw from the top \(k\), or a draw after a temperature adjustment, softmax\((u/\tau)\).
    • BERT reads at most 512 tokens.
    • An encoder understands, a decoder writes; in cross-attention the decoder’s queries look at the encoder’s keys and values.
  • Training (Ch. 19):
    • Hide the next word, let the model guess, and measure how wrong it was with cross-entropy, \(-\log\hat y[w_{t+1}]\): a small value if it gave the true word a high probability.
    • Nudge the weights a little in the direction that reduces the error (gradient descent, \(v \to v - \eta\nabla L\)).
    • Backpropagation works out how to nudge each weight.
    • SGD / mini-batch = use a few examples at a time; epoch = one full pass through the data.
    • It is self-supervised: the text itself is the answer key.
  • Fine-tuning vs prompting (Ch. 20):
    • Fine-tuning = send the model back to school on your labelled examples. You add a new final layer (“head”) and update all the weights or only the head. It needs labels.
    • Prompting = write better instructions; the weights stay untouched.
    • Zero-shot = an instruction with no examples and no weight change [Not in course files — general knowledge]. Few-shot = a few examples in the prompt (Interactive 4).

24. Answer-writing strategy for each question type

In plain words. The 2025 exam used a handful of question types again and again. Each type has a recipe that earns full marks. The “command words” are the phrases in the question that tell you which recipe to use.

True/False (Block 1; 2 points each)

  • Command words: “Answer only whether they are true or false.”
  • Recipe: find the one claim in the sentence. Look for the twist that makes it false:
    • a method used for the wrong job, e.g. Naive Bayes for numbers;
    • a weakness sold as a strength, e.g. word lists “capture polysemy well”;
    • a benefit flipped into a cost, e.g. multi-head attention “makes it slower”;
    • a wrong definition;
    • a near-miss word, e.g. “unsupervised” when the course says “self-supervised”.
  • Length: write one word, True or False. Don’t explain, and don’t hedge.

“What is…?” / “What is the underlying assumption?” (2a, 3a, 3c)

  • Recipe:
    1. The core idea, in the course’s words.
    2. What it looks like: the table or formula, with its size. For example, “documents in rows, words in columns, counts in the cells; \(n \times p\)”.
    3. A one-line example.
    4. One consequence, e.g. “so word order is lost”.
  • If the question has two parts (“…and what is the document-term matrix?”), answer each part in its own sentences.
  • Length: 3–5 sentences.

“Describe… include the motivation” / “Why…?” (2b, 4b, 4c)

  • Recipe: for each item, say what it is AND why you’d use it, meaning the problem it solves. Give exactly the number of items asked for, or at most one more.
  • Length: 4–6 sentences.

“Use a concrete example discussed in this course” (2c)

  • Recipe: first describe the method in general. Then name the course’s example and give its details. For Boolean search that’s the EPU index: its three word groups, the normalisation, the 10 newspapers. A made-up example loses marks here.
  • Length: 4–6 sentences.

“Describe in intuitive terms” (4d)

  • Recipe:
    1. An example sentence (“bank”; “it” referring to “the animal”).
    2. The analogy: query, key and value, like searching a library or a database.
    3. The steps in words.
    4. Why it helps: it links far-apart words, works in parallel, and you can inspect it.
  • Length: 5–7 sentences.

Compare two things: “difference/similarity”, “biggest conceptual difference” (2d, 3b, 4e)

  • Recipe:
    1. One line on each method.
    2. One sentence that states the contrast directly, e.g. “Fine-tuning changes the weights; prompting changes only the context.”
    3. What they have in common.
    4. When to use which.
  • If it says “max two sentences”, write two sentences, no more.
  • Length: 2–6 sentences.

Draw (3d: “Make an graph…” [sic])

  • Recipe:
    • Draw and label two axes.
    • Draw the arrows starting from the corner where the axes meet.
    • Mark the angles. Write “cos ≈ 1” next to the small angle and “cos ≈ 0” next to the large one.
    • Add one sentence saying that arrow length doesn’t matter, only direction.
  • Length: the drawing plus 2 lines.

“Discuss shortly two…” issues (4a)

  • Recipe: for each issue:
    1. Name it, and say whether it is environmental, social or governance.
    2. Why it happens.
    3. One consequence or fix.
  • Two well-explained issues beat five listed ones.
  • Length: 2 short paragraphs.

Reflection: “Propose at least two methods… motivation, problem, pitfalls” (Block 5, 20 points)

  • Recipe: follow the 6-step template in Chapter 22, using bold method names as mini-headings.
  • Length: ½–1 page.

Always

  • Use the course’s own words (see “Key terms to use” in each chapter).
  • Answer every part of every question.
  • Give one concrete course example whenever you can.
  • Keep 10–15 minutes at the end to re-check your True/False answers and make sure no sub-question was skipped.
  • Write legibly. The exam is hand-written, so short, clear sentences beat long ones.
